text:
BECANCOUR, QUE.- Much of the heavy machinery at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing affected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause.

This marks the latest sign for the town of Bécancour, located in a region known as “Battery Valley,” that plans for the area to become a hub of an EV manufacturing boom may not come to fruition.

“Decisions on further investment and project timing at Bécancour will depend on the outcome of the evaluation, project economics, market conditions, and customer needs,” Rio Tinto said in a statement.

The global metal and mining giant said it remains confident in the long-term outlook for lithium processing in Quebec and Canada, despite a decline in lithium prices as global demand for battery materials and electric vehicles has slowed.

The fallout could hit the town of Bécancour, which is nestled along the shores of the St. Lawrence River halfway between Montreal and Quebec City.

The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province. In the same plan, the province promised to develop Bécancour into a hub.

Slow EV sales halt economic boost

As EV batteries and plants started to set up shop in the town’s industrial park in 202, Bécancour estimated it would see a boost of 1,500 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, including in the restaurant industry and service sector.

The population grew slightly with the arrival of workers at construction sites. To accommodate them the city planned to expand schools, build housing and even purchase new ladder trucks for the local fire station.

However, when sales of EVs slowed, some projects were paused, while others were completely scrapped. In March, Nemaska announced it would scale down the pace of building its processing plant.

Though Quebec owns 46.1 per cent of Nemaska, the province’s new government said this week it would not spend a penny more on the project for the time being.

“Our sincere hope is that this is going to work, because I don’t want to be the guy to write off the $1.1 billion we invested,” said Quebec Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy Stéphane Paquet.

But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification.

“The battery file is here to stay,” said the prefect of the region Mario Lyonnais. “I am confident that the Nemaska plant will open. When it does, we will be ready and we will continue to prepare.”

Lyonnais says the battery boom was happening very quickly and that it was hard for the municipalities in the region to keep up with the pace of scaling up services.

He says the slowdown may allow the area more time to be fully ready for the grand opening of Nemaska and for a time when EV battery manufacturing delivers the region a boost.

title: Government bans export of lithium-ion battery black mass - Renewable Watch
description:
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Department of Commerce, has issued a notice prohibiting the export of lithium-ion battery black mass under ITC(HS) Code 85491400 with immediate effect.
The measure aims to ensure that black mass generated from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste is processed and recycled domestically.
Moreover, black mass contains recoverable critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are essential for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
The export ban is expected to improve feedstock availability and capacity utilisation for domestic recycling and refining units, while encouraging further investments and employment in the sector.
The measure complements the National Critical Mineral Mission and its Rs 15 billion incentive scheme for developing critical mineral recycling capacity from secondary sources.
text:
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Department of Commerce, has issued a notice prohibiting the export of lithium-ion battery black mass under ITC(HS) Code 85491400 with immediate effect. The measure aims to ensure that black mass generated from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste is processed and recycled domestically.

Moreover, black mass contains recoverable critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are essential for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles and energy storage systems. The export ban is expected to improve feedstock availability and capacity utilisation for domestic recycling and refining units, while encouraging further investments and employment in the sector. The measure complements the National Critical Mineral Mission and its Rs 15 billion incentive scheme for developing critical mineral recycling capacity from secondary sources.

description:

ROCKVILLE, Md., Nov. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- X-Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: XE) (“X-energy” or the “Company”), a leading developer of advanced nuclear reactors and fuel technology, today announced third quarter 2026 financial results and operational highlights.

“Our third quarter results and recent project developments reflect meaningful progress in executing our strategy and advancing our technology toward commercial deployment. We are building momentum as we deepen relationships with leading energy and industrial companies and advance opportunities across our pipeline,” said J. Clay Sell, CEO of X-energy. “The NRC recently issued the construction permit for Dow’s Long Mott project in Texas and it was received over a month ahead of schedule. This marks the first construction permit issued by the NRC in the United States for an advanced nuclear project site designed to provide industrial process heat.”

“Furthermore, we are excited to collaborate with AEP, a major investor-owned utility with extensive experience and expertise developing and operating critical energy infrastructure. This project in Indiana represents our second announced commercial deployment opportunity supported by Amazon and gives us greater visibility into our path toward deployment. During the quarter, we also completed the vertical construction of our TX-1 fuel fabrication facility, and the next phase includes interior buildout and equipment installation. In addition, the acceptance of our Xe-100 reactor into the United Kingdom’s Generic Design Assessment process represents an important step toward advancing our opportunity in the U.K. with Centrica.”

“We are in a differentiated position of strength, supported by our strong balance sheet and significant funding. Our regulatory progress marks a major milestone for our technology, while our growing commercial momentum bolsters our pipeline of reactors and demand for TRISO-X fuel,” concluded Sell.

Operational Highlights

NRC Issues Construction Permit for Dow’s Long Mott Project: Dow and X-energy announced that the NRC has approved the Construction Permit Application (“CPA”) for the proposed Long Mott Generating Station in Seadrift, Texas ahead of schedule. The permit marks an important milestone in the regulatory review process for the proposed advanced nuclear project, which is being developed under the U.S. Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (“ARDP”). The project is intended to provide zero-carbon emissions electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow's Seadrift Operations site, replacing existing energy and steam assets near their end-of-life. The NRC's approval follows a comprehensive review of the proposed facility, site characteristics, construction plans, environmental considerations and safety-related information submitted as part of the CPA process. Issuance marks the first NRC CPA approval of a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (“HTGR”) in nearly 60 years, the first-ever pebble-bed HTGR approval and the first-ever for an advanced nuclear industrial deployment.

Selects Fluor for Design and Engineering Services: For Energy Northwest’s Cascade Advanced Energy Facility near Richland, Washington, Fluor will provide engineering, design development, supply chain, estimating and project controls services for the areas of the plant containing the Xe-100 reactors and the systems that support them (the "nuclear island"). The agreement between X-energy and Fluor represents their second commercial contract for nuclear island engineering and design, building on Fluor's ongoing work for the Company’s first proposed Xe-100 project in Texas under the ARDP. This enables X-energy and Fluor to incorporate learnings from one project into the next, with the aim of targeting long-term cost and schedule reductions through standardization and highly repeatable project execution.

Executes First Order for Steam Generator Components: Announced the first procurement order of steam generator tubing from Alleima and Doosan Enerbility for the Company’s Xe-100 advanced SMR. This follows the signing of a strategic framework by the three companies earlier this year as the Company scales its supply chain to meet its growing commercial pipeline. Execution advances a safety-significant, long-lead component for the first deployment of the Xe-100. Alleima will leverage its expertise in high-temperature alloys to manufacture specialized steel tubing, which Doosan will bend into helical coils using its proprietary fabrication processes. These coils are a central component of the Xe-100 steam generator, safely removing heat to produce high-temperature steam at up to 565°C, and allowing a single Xe-100 to deliver both electricity and high-temperature process heat for industrial applications.

Partners with AEP and Amazon : Announced a JDA with AEP to advance feasibility work for a proposed 960 MW Xe-100 SMR project in Indiana. Amazon will provide certain project development funding for the effort, marking the second commercial deployment opportunity under X-energy and Amazon’s collaboration aimed to bring more than 5 GW of new nuclear capacity to the U.S. grid by 2039. X-energy and AEP will evaluate the development of a 12-unit Xe-100 plant in Sullivan County, Indiana. The proposed project would redevelop the AEP-owned brownfield site for advanced nuclear power, adding clean baseload capacity to help meet growing demand for safe, reliable energy.

U.K. Regulators Begin Design Review for Xe-100: The U.K. Government has directed regulators to accept the Xe-100 reactor for design review and advance X-energy’s and Centrica’s efforts to deploy up to 6 GW of new nuclear in the U.K. GDA acceptance formally triggers the process of assessing the design's acceptability for deployment and operation ahead of the technical and environmental evaluations required for site-specific licensing and permitting. The assessment is expected to take approximately three years and will be administered by the U.K. Office for Nuclear Regulation, the Environment Agency, and Natural Resources Wales. The submission builds on the Xe-100's U.S. licensing progress and is expected to benefit from expanded collaboration between the U.K. regulators and the U.S. NRC, enabling transfer of NRC-reviewed design documentation and safety analyses into U.K. design reviews.

TX-1 Vertical Construction Complete, Advances to Next Phase : Vertical construction for the shell of the Company's TX-1 fuel facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee was completed on schedule in the third quarter. The project has advanced into its next phase of construction, which will include interior buildout, installation of fuel fabrication equipment and continued construction of supporting facilities. Once operational, TX-1 is expected to produce approximately 700,000 TRISO-X fuel pebbles annually, equivalent to 5 metric tons of uranium (“MTU”), with capacity to provide fuel for up to 11 Xe-100 reactors. The U.S. NRC granted TRISO-X a 40-year Special Nuclear Material License covering the facility earlier this year, the first-ever NRC Category 2 fuel fabrication license issued for the processing of high-assay low-enriched uranium. TX-1 is expected to be the first new commercial-scale advanced U.S. nuclear fuel fabrication facility built in more than 50 years.

This was primarily due to increases of $54.7 million and $141.9 million in Direct costs and increases of $43.9 million and $120.4 million in Selling, general, and administrative expenses for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to the comparable prior-year periods.

The increase in Direct costs was primarily driven by expanded activity under the ARDP Agreement. Subcontracting costs increased by $23.5 million and $52.8 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively. Direct materials costs increased $15.6 million and $33.3 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively. Additionally, compensation costs increased by $15.3 million and $53.0 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, including $10.9 million and $42.0 million from higher employee headcount to support the expanded activity under the ARDP Agreement, and $4.4 million and $11.0 million from increased non-cash equity-based and unit-based compensation expense for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 due to equity grants to certain former holders of Profits Interest Units (“PIUs”) in connection with the Company’s IPO in April.

The increase in Selling, general, and administrative expenses was driven by an increase in non-cash equity-based and unit-based compensation expense of $18.4 million and $49.2 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, due to the equity grant to certain PIU holders discussed above. Compensation costs increased a further $9.0 million and $29.4 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, primarily due to higher employee headcount. Additionally, infrastructure and professional service costs increased by $8.0 million and $23.8 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased a further $8.5 million and $12.0 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, from contractor costs related to corporate projects, including design costs for TX-2.

Net cash used in operating activities in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 was $215.8 million of net cash compared to $92.7 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. The increase in cash used in operating activities is primarily driven by increases in activity on the ARDP Agreement, deposits to vendors for long-lead materials, and corporate headcount and corporate contractors during the nine months ended September 30, 2026 compared to the nine months ended September 30, 2025.

Net cash used in investing activities in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 was $289.5 million of net cash compared to $41.8 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. The increase in net cash used in investing activities was attributable to investments in held-to-maturity securities and capital expenditures. During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we purchased investments of $425.3 million, which were offset by proceeds from investment maturities of $233.9 million. There was no investment activity during the nine months ended September 30, 2025. During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared to the corresponding prior year period, we had a $98.8 million increase in capital expenditures related to the construction of facilities, which was offset by a $42.5 million increase in reimbursements received for the capital expenditures qualifying under government grant programs.

Net cash provided by financing activities in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 was $1.1 billion of net cash compared to $50.2 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. The net cash provided by financing activities during the nine months ended September 30, 2026 was primarily due to $1.1 billion of net proceeds from X-energy’s initial public offering. The net cash provided by financing activities during the nine months ended September 30, 2025 was primarily due to the January 2025 issuance of Series C-1 preferred units of $53.4 million, offset by $2.5 million of cash paid for associated issuance costs.

title: Weathering the storm: Tracking federal actions against offshore wind - Clean Air Task Force
description:
Cataloging the multi-pronged efforts to obstruct offshore wind development and implementation both emphasizes the uncertainty currently facing offshore wind and highlights the impact of federal actions on the industry.
Fifty percent tariffs on steel and aluminum, two key materials in offshore wind components, have substantially increased costs for offshore wind developers.
DOI then paused the leases of five offshore wind projects (including Empire Wind and Revolution Wind again) on December 22nd, 2025, citing undisclosed national security concerns.
The developers of all five projects—Empire Wind, Revolution Wind, Vineyard Wind 1, Sunrise Wind, and Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind—brought lawsuits in response, and courts granted either preliminary injunctions or stays in each case.
DOI made requests with similar rationales for Revolution Wind, for Maryland Offshore Wind, and for New England Wind.
text:
Offshore wind is a vital technology that can generate clean electricity and bolster grid resilience. At a time when volatile fossil fuel prices and projected increases for energy demand threaten energy security and inflate costs for ratepayers, offshore wind offers a high-capacity clean generation source for states looking to decarbonize and improve energy affordability. Since the start of 2025, however, the federal government has attempted to systematically dismantle the American offshore wind industry through actions such as presidential memoranda and executive orders, offshore wind lease buybacks, permitting freezes, stop work orders, and, to a lesser extent, legislation such as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). In response to challenges brought by affected states, project developers, and trade organizations, courts have enjoined or struck down many of the administration’s actions. But the administration has appealed some of these decisions, and the status of many offshore wind projects remains threatened.

Information on the status of the industry today is not well documented or centralized. And yet, understanding the status of offshore wind is critical, given the importance of the industry to the United States’ long-term energy prospects and the often-limited decarbonization and generation options for coastal population centers. Cataloging the multi-pronged efforts to obstruct offshore wind development and implementation both emphasizes the uncertainty currently facing offshore wind and highlights the impact of federal actions on the industry.

Broader context for clean energy

Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, many actions by the Department of Energy (DOE) have created uncertainty for developers and investors across several clean energy industries. Cuts in federal funding for clean energy projects have had substantial impacts on many states, eliminating jobs and economic opportunities and threatening states’ abilities to meet clean energy goals. Government-wide staffing cuts, including an approximately 20% decline in staffing at DOE since January 2025, have slowed the permitting process for energy projects significantly.

Offshore wind has been implicated in this broader context of funding cuts for clean energy and changes to government staffing. For example, staffing cuts at the DOE Wind Energy Technologies Office and the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), which sits within the U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) and is the lead agency on offshore wind permitting, have damaged agency capacity to permit and develop offshore wind. The administration also eliminated wind research and development and financial assistance programs at DOE, further obstructing offshore wind deployment.

Other administration actions, such as instituting tariffs, have increased project costs for several clean energy industries, including offshore wind. Fifty percent tariffs on steel and aluminum, two key materials in offshore wind components, have substantially increased costs for offshore wind developers. For example, in July 2026, the developer Dominion Energy increased its estimated total costs for the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project by approximately $300 million dollars from its April 2026 cost estimate, citing tariffs to justify the increase.

In addition to the industry-wide challenges listed above, the administration has carried out a series of targeted actions to disrupt wind development, and in particular development of offshore wind. This blog documents the actions taken against the offshore wind industry since 2025 and identifies the implications these actions may have on efforts to build a reliable, decarbonized grid.

What has happened in the offshore wind industry?

Withdrawal of all areas of the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) from offshore wind leasing

On the day of President Trump’s inauguration in 2025, the administration froze offshore wind permitting, withdrew all areas of the OCS from offshore wind leasing, and started a review of leasing and permitting practices through a presidential memorandum. In response to a lawsuit filed by states and a clean energy trade association (in which CATF and partners filed an amicus brief), the Federal District Court for Massachusetts vacated the lease freeze section of this memorandum in December 2025. However, federal agencies are still not permitting projects on the OCS.

Stop work orders and lease pauses

Next, BOEM began issuing stop work orders against fully permitted offshore wind projects. The first order, issued in April 2025, paused construction of the New York-based project Empire Wind and was ultimately lifted in May 2025. Even though BOEM eventually retracted the order, it reportedly cost Empire Wind’s developer approximately $200 million, or about $50 million per week while in effect. In August 2025, another stop work order targeted the Revolution Wind project off the coast of Rhode Island and Connecticut. Revolution Wind sued, and in September 2025, the Federal District Court for D.C. granted a preliminary injunction, allowing the project to proceed.

DOI then paused the leases of five offshore wind projects (including Empire Wind and Revolution Wind again) on December 22nd, 2025, citing undisclosed national security concerns. These projects were fully permitted and had already begun construction, with one project (Vineyard Wind 1 in Massachusetts) near completion and actively delivering power to the grid. The developers of all five projects—Empire Wind, Revolution Wind, Vineyard Wind 1, Sunrise Wind, and Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind—brought lawsuits in response, and courts granted either preliminary injunctions or stays in each case.

Shortly after the DOI lease suspensions, regional clean energy associations filed a lawsuit alleging that some federal agencies were arbitrarily “disfavoring” development of wind and solar compared to other energy sources through actions such as delaying or vacating permitting approvals. They received a preliminary injunction on April 21st, 2026, and the federal government is currently appealing.

Lease buybacks

Since March 2026, the administration has used lease buybacks and settlements to remove several offshore wind lease areas from future development, potentially constraining the industry’s long-term growth if the settlements withstand judicial scrutiny. In these settlements, DOI agreed to pay developers an amount equal to their initial wind lease purchase price in exchange for the return of the wind leases to the federal government, with the stipulation that the developer reinvests this money into fossil fuel or other infrastructure. There have been five buybacks of twelve different leases as of November 2026, with a total cost of approximately $4 billion.

However, these settlements are not a refund to developers. They are new expenditures of taxpayer dollars from the Judgment Fund, which exists to pay court judgments and settlements for lawsuits against the federal government. They are therefore the subject of five lawsuits from nine states to date, including complaints filed by coalitions of northeastern states and two others filed by California.

National security claims

As part of the previously routine permitting process for both onshore and offshore wind, DOD is required to issue determinations that verify that the turbines do not interfere with national security. In April 2026, however, DOD stopped processing these determinations entirely, freezing permitting for proposed wind projects on both private and federal land. A coalition of clean energy trade associations subsequently filed a lawsuit against DOD, and CATF and seven other environmental groups filed an amicus brief in support of that lawsuit in June. In August, the Federal District Court in Oregon granted a preliminary injunction requiring that DOD begin issuing routine determinations once more.

President Trump also issued a proclamation on October 22, 2026 that declared wind turbine product imports to be a threat to national security. The proclamation cites a report from the Secretary of Commerce that reportedly identified cybersecurity, grid, and radar interference concerns from relying on foreign imported products. The proclamation directs the Secretary of Commerce to pursue trade negotiations and agreements with foreign trade partners and monitor the imports of wind products, but it refrained from imposing new or additional tariffs.

Creation of the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA)

In July 2026, the Trump administration initiated a process to combine BOEM and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) into the MMA. The Obama administration had originally separated these two offices after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010 to create an organizational firewall between safety/environmental oversight functions and revenue collection functions, which had inherent conflicts of interest. The administration is recombining BOEM and BSEE, despite the conflicts of interest, in part to implement several executive orders that advance objectives related to fossil fuels and critical minerals. This includes Executive Order 14285, which focuses on developing additional capacity to assess and extract offshore critical mineral resources. Alongside staffing cuts at agencies like BOEM, the establishment of the MMA reduces and siloes BOEM’s role in permitting offshore wind, which requires substantial staffing and expertise. The organizational restructuring that would create the MMA is consistent with the administration’s other moves prioritizing offshore critical mineral extraction and fossil fuel development while deprioritizing offshore wind development. These actions constrain BOEM’s ability to exercise its authority to issue leases for renewable energy, despite Congress’s clear grant of authority to issue leases for that purpose under Section 8(p) of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA).

Reexamining existing permits

In October 2026, the administration filed a series of motions in multiple legal challenges to offshore wind projects, agreeing with claims about BOEM’s construction and operations plans under OCSLA and seeking to have those approvals remanded to the agency. These motions are intended to allow DOI to reexamine permits for several projects that already cleared rigorous permitting processes, and, in the case of Revolution Wind, that are already fully built and in operation. DOI made requests with similar rationales for Revolution Wind, for Maryland Offshore Wind, and for New England Wind. This follows a court order from August 10, 2026 that granted a request from BOEM to reconsider its own approval of the Atlantic Shores Project, which was issued over the objection of the project developer.

Reduced tax incentives in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)

In addition to the administration’s actions, Congress has reduced the tax incentives available for offshore wind development through the July 2025 passage of the OBBBA. The law accelerated the termination of the 45X (Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit) for manufacturing wind components, and limited eligibility for 45Y (Clean Electricity Production Tax Credit) and 48E (Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit) for wind projects that begin construction after July 4, 2026. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, 45Y and 48E would have remained available until 2032 or the year the U.S. power sector achieved an emissions reduction target, while 45X was set to phase down in 2030 and expire in 2032. Following enactment of the OBBBA, wind projects “beginning construction” before July 4, 2026 remained eligible for 45Y and 48E. Developers could establish that construction had begun for the purpose of these credits by satisfying a 5% safe harbor provision, meaning they would need to demonstrate that they had spent 5% or more of the total cost of the project prior to July 4, 2026.

However, that same week in 2025, the administration issued an executive order that directed the Secretary of the Treasury to implement and enforce the OBBBA termination of clean energy tax credits. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) subsequently released a notice that eliminated the 5% safe harbor methodology for wind tax credit eligibility. Several environmental groups challenged the IRS’s implementation of President Trump’s executive order, and on June 6th, 2026, the Federal District Court for D.C. vacated and remanded the notice.

What are the implications?

From the beginning of the second Trump administration, actions by the federal government have obstructed offshore wind development. Despite the administration’s nearly unbroken record of court losses related to wind energy, the lag between federal actions, lawsuits, and legal verdicts costs American ratepayers: any delay in offshore wind construction and permitting prevents necessary energy generation from getting online to meet continuing load growth projections. And, because of the specialized equipment needed to build offshore wind, delays often compound if the developer misses a construction window, racking up substantial additional costs. Upstream, the communities investing in developing a U.S. supply chain and manufacturing sector, such as specialized shipbuilders in Louisiana, are seeing their investments sit idle.

The uncertainty created by interfering with lawfully issued permits, halting permit processing for specific technologies, and interrupting construction of projects already in development also has long-term consequences for the energy sector and the American economy. Energy projects often require years of planning, development, and construction prior to initiating operations. Energy industry investors, faced with uncertainty due to arbitrary federal actions, may assess a riskier environment for all energy sector investment, and they will likely respond by reducing their exposure across all technologies. Investors need some degree of certainty that their long-term energy projects will be built even as power changes hands between political parties. The administration’s efforts to reexamine approvals of projects already permitted, under construction, and even in operation also emphasize the importance of ensuring that permits, once issued, remain durable through a project’s lifetime.

Offshore wind offers immense potential for domestic economic growth if given the opportunity for investment, as projections indicate that it could generate more than 186,000 jobs across its national supply chain and could demand $42 billion in US steel over the next two decades. The administration’s actions against offshore wind therefore threaten to cede a profitable and high potential U.S. industry to international competitors in China and the European Union, who are already leaders in offshore wind; as of 2025, China had deployed approximately 52 gigawatts (GW) of offshore wind, while the EU had deployed 21 GW, with both planning to install significantly more over the next few years. The offshore wind lease buybacks add to these geopolitical concerns, effectively removing a domestic and clean source of electricity in offshore wind and largely replacing it with infrastructure for export of liquified natural gas (LNG). Pursuing this course of action when the United States needs more domestic electricity generation to meet increasing energy demand weakens U.S. energy security and increases costs for ratepayers.

In addition, efforts to dismantle offshore wind impair many U.S. states’ abilities to meet projected load growth and decarbonization goals. The federal blockade forces many states to increase use of oil and gas peaker plants to meet high energy demand, generating more emissions and decreasing local air quality. Federal barriers to offshore wind also generate immense uncertainty for states working to proactively develop long-term energy and transmission plans.

Several of these states have also invested heavily in offshore wind workforce development (and continue to do so), with specialized training programs that are now in jeopardy. In addition to the training programs themselves, individuals who are already working in the offshore wind industry face severely constrained job prospects and risk their highly specialized training becoming a sunk cost.

In a separate post, CATF examines whether project certainty provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would prevent near-term actions stopping clean energy projects and recommends changes to that bill to improve its efficacy.

The case for offshore wind remains strong despite continued uncertainty

The series of actions taken by the second Trump administration against offshore wind has been wide-ranging and disruptive, but offshore wind remains an important and viable technology that can assist states in addressing projected load growth, improving reliability, and meeting decarbonization goals. Projects that have been completed, such as Vineyard Wind 1 in Massachusetts, are offering critical value to the grid. Offshore wind has also significantly outperformed other energy resources and reduced electricity costs during severe weather events. Vineyard Wind 1, for example, had a much higher capacity factor—a measurement of how much electricity the project actually generated in a given time period compared to the maximum amount of electricity it could have generated— than natural gas plants during Winter Storm Fern. The capacity factor for South Fork Wind, an offshore wind project off the coast of Long Island, was essentially equivalent to the most efficient natural gas plants during the same winter storm, while also reducing power prices. Offshore wind makes a difference during heat waves as well, adding needed capacity to the grid when there is high electricity demand for cooling and lowering costs for ratepayers by reducing the need to turn on expensive peaker plants.

title: Power Shift: State Election Wins Open Path for Climate Progress - Yale E360
description:
In Texas, which is facing a massive buildout of gas power, the incoming governor pledged a moratorium on new data centers.
While climate change was barely mentioned in these elections, many races were dominated by two closely related issues: data centers and utility regulation.
In the midterm elections, ballot measures to restrict data centers passed in 44 cities across the country and failed in only one.
In practice, that could mean laying more costs on data centers and utility shareholders and less on consumers.
Beyond hemming in data centers and utilities, several other election outcomes hold promise for the environment.
text:
After their sweeping victories in the midterm elections, Democrats will control both houses of Congress, meaning they will be able to shape the budget, conduct vigorous oversight and investigations, and refuse to confirm nominees for judgeships and other high positions — but their power will be constrained. Any ambitious new bill to tackle climate change, for example, will face President Trump’s veto pen.

But there are other ways for Democrats to make progress on climate, energy, and the environment — by wielding their newfound power in the states.

In the November 3 elections, Democrats flipped control of governors’ offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and Texas, and are on track to win in Alaska, where votes are still being counted. They also attained trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both houses of the state legislature — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin.

This brings to 29 or 30 the number of states that will have Democratic governors in January, and to 22 the states in which Democrats have unified control of government. Meanwhile, Republican trifectas were broken in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

In Texas, which is facing a massive buildout of gas power, the incoming governor pledged a moratorium on new data centers.

While climate change was barely mentioned in these elections, many races were dominated by two closely related issues: data centers and utility regulation. Public outcry over the growth of data centers, which are driving ever more burning of natural gas, and the rising cost of electricity mean that Democrats have a mandate to advance energy reforms in the states they control.

By one estimate, tech companies are intent on spending more than $647 billion over the coming years to develop natural gas infrastructure in the U.S. to serve the voracious power demands of data centers. The planned expansions would grow the existing fleet of gas generators by roughly two-thirds. Natural gas is already the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. (behind petroleum, but far greater than coal), and this investment would lock in its use for decades.

Against this backdrop, public opposition to data centers has rocketed. In the midterm elections, ballot measures to restrict data centers passed in 44 cities across the country and failed in only one. In her successful campaign for governor of Texas, which is facing the largest natural gas buildout in the nation, Gina Hinojosa pledged an immediate moratorium on new data centers. Many other winning candidates also promised more controls on data center construction.

Looking ahead, governors have the opportunity to appoint regulators who will further rein in data centers and the power utilities profiting from rising energy prices. Retail electricity rates are set by state public utility commissions, and in 38 states the commissioners are named by the governors. The newly elected Democratic governors of Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Maine all campaigned on promises to appoint commissioners who would work to favor the interests of ratepayers over those of monopoly utilities.

In practice, that could mean laying more costs on data centers and utility shareholders and less on consumers. It could also mean encouraging more rooftop and community solar to help lower electric bills. Utilities have long campaigned against such projects, which cut into their profits.

In Georgia, where commissioners are elected, Democrats just won a majority of seats on the five-member commission, promising greater scrutiny of the utilities. In Pennsylvania, legislation to lower power bills by reducing utility profits recently stalled in the Republican-controlled state senate, but under the new Democratic trifecta, this legislation is expected to be signed into law. In Michigan, about 80 percent of voters approved a ballot measure that will block utilities from campaign spending (which the utilities are already challenging in court). And in Colorado, voters rejected a ballot measure, championed by gas utilities, that would have established a “right to natural gas” and blocked local moves to phase out gas appliances.

Most federal environmental laws set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Beyond hemming in data centers and utilities, several other election outcomes hold promise for the environment. The Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry, has long consisted of three Republican members. A Democrat won election to the body with a platform that included capping orphan wells and banning gas flaring — two important means of stemming emissions from drilling. He can now put these issues on the agenda. His election also makes it possible for Democrats to win control of the commission in 2028.

Democratic candidates for state attorney general triumphed over Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas. Republican attorneys general have been at the forefront of litigation aimed at weakening environmental regulations, and they have moved in concert to protect oil and gas companies from being held accountable for climate damages. These states are expected to reverse their positions in many cases, which might tilt the scales in some.

What else might Democrats do with all their new power?

Given the focus of almost all campaigns on affordability, not many states are likely to adopt measures that would transparently increase consumer costs, such as a tax on carbon. However, states have many other tools. Most federal environmental statutes, such as the Clean Air Act, set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Of the 10 states that burn the most coal for power, Democrats will now control the governor’s office in seven: Texas, Kentucky, Illinois, Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia, and Iowa. Governors in those states have considerable ability to shut coal plants down, for example, by setting air pollution standards that are too expensive for plants to meet.

If coal plants are to be shuttered and the use of natural gas slashed, the nation will need much more renewable energy, particularly wind and solar, to meet its growing electricity demand. One way to ramp up wind and solar is through renewable portfolio standards, which require utilities to acquire a certain percentage of their power from renewable sources. Today, 27 states have such standards, but many are so low that they have already been met. Democratic wins mean that more states can adopt renewable portfolio standards or strengthen and enforce those already on the books.

State leaders can also clear roadblocks for new renewable energy development. Over the last 30 years, more than 850 cities and counties have adopted restrictions on wind and solar, often spurred on by residents’ objections to large renewable installations proposed in their communities. In response, several states have adopted laws that centralize authority over such facilities, allowing them to override local bans. New York’s law has been especially successful at boosting wind and solar installations. Other states that now have Democratic trifectas could adopt similar laws.

States can encourage the uptake of electric vehicles by building more charging stations and providing rebates to EV buyers.

States may also encourage household solar by making it easier for homeowners to obtain approvals for rooftop arrays; enabling net metering; legalizing balcony solar; easing the siting of battery storage systems; and facilitating virtual power plants, which allow energy companies to link together and control home batteries, solar panels, thermostats, and other assets to balance the grid.

While states cannot require citizens to buy electric vehicles, they may encourage their uptake by building more charging stations, requiring new parking lots and garages to install fast chargers, and providing rebates to EV buyers to offset the recent loss of federal subsidies.

States can reduce emissions from the residential sector by incentivizing the installation of heat pumps, strengthening energy efficiency standards for buildings, and — though federal courts are split on whether this is permissible — barring new natural gas hookups.

These measures are only a fraction of what states can do. The Model Climate Laws Initiative, a joint project of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law and Environmental Advocates NY, has posted more than 2,000 model and actual state and local laws, and it stands ready to draft many more. Thoughtful policies aimed at cutting power bills, curbing pollution, and advancing clean energy have been circulating for a long time. It is time to put those policies into action.

text:
This Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) announces the availability of funds under the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act (DERA) Program and solicits applications from eligible entities to incentivize and accelerate the upgrade or retirement of the nation’s legacy diesel engine fleet. Eligible activities include the retrofit or replacement of existing diesel engines, vehicles, and equipment with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and California Air Resources Board (CARB) certified or verified technologies.

There are several ways DERA recipients may implement projects and fund project partners, depending on the roles and responsibilities of each. If the applicant is the owner of the target vehicles, the applicant may directly implement the project. If the applicant is partnering with diesel fleet owners, the applicant may award subawards or participant support costs (e.g., rebates). Please refer to Section 9.B. for detailed guidance on funding partnerships.

After an extensive review of the program, the EPA revamped DERA requirements to ensure alignment with the Administration’s priorities, improve the quality of projects funded, expand the availability of technology choices, and respond to stakeholder requests for a simplified program structure. Consistent with agency grants direction, updates to 2 CFR §200.204 and DERA statutory requirements, this NOFO reflects these changes and inputs when compared to previous funding notice opportunities.

title: Climate progressives won the midterms without saying 'climate' - Grist.org
description:

In part, this diversity of messaging tactics reflects the fractured nature of the climate movement since Trump retook office with a checklist of Biden-era environmental regulations to roll back.

But that doesn’t mean that the public has become disengaged from the climate crisis.
“I think we will actually see a lot of momentum around stopping the climate crisis.
text:
On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name for himself years ago by connecting public health to the climate crisis. He published a fierce defense of the Green New Deal at the time, touting its economic, health, and planetary benefits. But last month at the Detroit Economic Club, El-Sayed didn’t mention the Green New Deal at all.

Instead, the only mentions of such a plan came from his opponent, who used it as an attack on El-Sayed and the Democratic party as a whole. “We need to make sure we don’t have the largest tax increase in the history of the country,” Rogers said, “which is, that’s what the other team is talking about doing.”

A vote for El-Sayed would ring in an era of “big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal,” Rogers continued. It’s become a common refrain since President Donald Trump’s effort to rebrand the climate movement’s push for widescale public investment in renewable energy as a “Green New Scam.”

Two weeks later, El-Sayed handily won the race.

Even though many of the newly elected Democrats did not talk about the Green New Deal by name, the think tank Climate and Community Institute describes El-Sayed as belonging to a new class of green economic populists who are running for public office (and winning) by connecting the need for climate action to soaring utility bills and the hoarding of wealth by a handful of individuals and companies.

El-Sayed “clearly gets it,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at Climate and Community Institute, or CCI. The senator-elect’s platform, which proposes stricter regulations on data centers and energy companies, is “really exciting,” he said. These are promising climate agenda items — even if Democrats don’t explicitly call them that. For example, voters may oppose data centers in their backyard for any number of reasons, but some number of them are required for our digitalized reality and progressives now have an opportunity to take the companies behind them to task and get them to commit to reducing their strain on the local environment. Likewise, where voters came out in support of lowering utility bills, electeds now can talk further about investing in cheaper renewable energy systems like solar and wind power.

Bigger led a recent analysis that scored candidates in this year’s primary and midterm elections based on three questions: Is the candidate pushing for renewable energy or other climate actions? Do they name the rising cost of living as a voter issue, and have a plan to lower those costs? Do they articulate a populist vision by blaming wealthy corporations and powerful individuals for both the climate and affordability crises? CCI argues that candidates like El-Sayed who check all three boxes are the climate champions of the moment.

Other progressives named in the report include Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, the climate group that first sounded the alarm for a Green New Deal in 2018. Lawrence, who will represent Michigan’s 7th District in the next Congress, points to his history of climate organizing on his website: “I will be among the most knowledgeable and dedicated members of Congress on water, climate and energy policy,” he writes. “I will fight for investment to secure the climate we depend on, adapt to the changes we can’t prevent, and finally drive our electric bills down.”

These “new folks headed to the House and the Senate who are really on board with a robust transformative approach to climate,” said Bigger, represent “a major shift.”

But not all climate progressives heading to Washington next year are so allergic to calling it the Green New Deal: Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York City name it specifically on their campaign websites and in the press. Still, this new wave of climate leaders may feel it’s time for the decarbonization agenda to get a refresh; Valdez and Avila Chevalier’s websites also include mentions of “a livable planet for all” and “a livable world for everyone,” respectively. In part, this diversity of messaging tactics reflects the fractured nature of the climate movement since Trump retook office with a checklist of Biden-era environmental regulations to roll back.

If progressive Democrats’ messaging on climate has shifted, said Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, it’s because the terrain they’re fighting in has changed, too. “I think, as the climate crisis gets worse and worse, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the strategy, policy-wise, needs to be incorporating climate change into every single aspect of what we’re doing,” she said. In other words, climate policy should not be framed as a separate issue from the economy, infrastructure improvements, or foreign policy. “It should be the defining framework within which we have to think about how we run our society,” said Shiney-Ajay.

In 2018, the Sunrise Movement burst onto the national stage by protesting outside House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi’s office — with the Green New Deal as their top priority. Just seven years later, members of the Sunrise Movement voted to reorganize around the priority of fighting authoritarianism and, in particular, the second Trump administration. Shiney-Ajay acknowledged that the climate movement has suffered in recent years.

But that doesn’t mean that the public has become disengaged from the climate crisis. In fact, voters across the political spectrum are more attuned to it than ever. “People are actually really hungry for something to do about climate change,” said Shiney-Ajay. “I think we will actually see a lot of momentum around stopping the climate crisis. And I certainly hope to build a movement that makes that possible.”

text:
The 12th World Green Infrastructure Congress , organised by the University of Lleida, saw 10 LIFE projects from 9 Member States and Ukraine shared practical, scalable solutions for greener cities, many of which feature in the new Greening cities with the LIFE Programme publication .

From European policy discussions to scientific research and real-world projects, the congress created a space where different perspectives could meet and move the conversation forward on how to make green infrastructure and nature-based solutions a core part of urban planning.

Opening the Congress, CINEA Director Paloma Aba Garrote said LIFE projects ‘turn policy ambition into practical action in their cities’. She emphasised that green infrastructure is vital to tackling heatwaves, flooding, biodiversity loss, air pollution, and resource pressure. She highlighted that that green infrastructure must be planned, financed and implemented as an essential part of our cities, noting that investing in urban green infrastructure means investing in healthier, more resilient, and more liveable cities.

How Barcelona and Lleida are putting green infrastructure in action

Star of the show was BIG4LIFE, which uses Building Integrated Greenery (BIG) systems including green roofs, living façades, rooftop gardens and vertical greenery to transform urban spaces and cooling down temperatures in our cities by using water and energy-saving techniques applied in architecture, building design and landscaping such as xeriscaping. Through monitoring 8 site buildings, the project’s innovative energy and irrigation management system has demonstrated that can reduce water consumption by up to 80% a major benefit for Mediterranean cities facing increasing water stress. The monitoring and participatory maintenance model involving residents and building owners is being replicated in Genoa and Athens, with further roll-out planned in Warsaw. Ms Aba Garrote toured two pilot buildings sites such as the Pérez-Iborra School in Barcelona. Its green roof garden combines, biodiversity features, a vegetable garden, rainwater harvesting, solar panels and monitoring equipment. The roof also functions as an outdoor classroom where students learn about sustainability and urban nature, while smart sensors feed continuous environmental impact data back to the University of Lleida.

Ms Aba Garrote had a discussion with the students who proudly explained how important the garden is in their environmental education, and how they contribute to providing science data. The University of Lleida is collecting data through a smart monitoring system installed on the green roof. These sensors continuously gather information about how the green garden is performing in cooling down temperatures and how it affects positively the local environment.

Nature-based solutions along the river Ebro

The LIFE Programme also builds climate resilience beyond urban centres. In Zaragoza, Ms. Aba Garrote visited LIFE Ebro Resilience , which uses nature-based solutions to restore the Ebro river basin while helping local communities adapt to flood risks. The project will benefit over 22 000 local residents, with plans for similar measures across 307 km of riverbed spanning 3 Spanish regions and 56 municipalities, reaching up to 1 million citizens. As project coordinator David Gargantilla noted, long-term success requires conservation along with ‘clear communication and cooperation with citizens, regions and municipalities, and economic actors, such as farmers throughout the basin’.

In addition to the LIFE Programme stand, LIFE also hosted a workshop — Greening European cities with LIFE: inspiring urban transformation in Europe — with the core message that LIFE projects serve as practical, actionable models for future urban development.

title: Kazakhstan to develop national satellite methane regulatory program for oil and gas ...
description:
“Kazakhstan’s methane satellite program sends a meaningful signal that leadership starts with action supported by transparency,” said James Turitto, Oil and Gas Methane Director at Clean Air Task Force.
“Kazakhstan is demonstrating what becomes possible when governments turn satellite methane data into action.
Working with UNEP, the country has already mitigated 10 major methane emissions events identified through the Methane Alert and Response System, addressing more than 31,000 tonnes of methane emissions.
Combined with locally owned capabilities, this approach could set a precedent for other methane-emitting countries and help accelerate methane emissions reductions globally.” said Vasily Yablokov, Product Director, AIRMO.
“Our work with government and industry partners in Kazakhstan over several years has shown the value of combining methane satellite data with practical action on the ground.
text:
ANTALYA – At COP31, during the Global Methane Pledge Ministerial meeting, the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Kazakhstan announced plans to develop a national satellite-based program to support regulations of methane emissions from the country’s oil and gas sector.

The program builds on the Memorandum of Understanding signed in September 2025 by the Ministry of Ecology, the Global Methane Hub, Carbon Mapper, and Clean Air Task Force (CATF). It will be developed with support from the Fossil Fuel Regulatory Programme (FFRP), a partnership of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) and CATF, with additional technical support from the International Energy Agency (IEA), the UN Environment Program’s (UNEP) International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO), Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, AIRMO, and Carbon Limits. It also draws on Kazakhstan’s established space industry and its experience in Earth observation.

“This initiative is part of implementing Kazakhstan’s Carbon Neutrality Strategy to 2060. As we strengthen our approach to methane in the oil and gas sector, independent satellite data will help make it evidence-based and effective,” said Alibek Kuantyrov, Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of the Republic of Kazakhstan. “Reducing methane brings practical benefits for the climate, the economy and our international partnerships, and it helps keep us in step with evolving global expectations. As the world gathers in Antalya, we are taking a first concrete step that will evolve over time, and we hope it will strengthen cooperation on methane across Central Asia. At the national level, Kazakhstan is also developing its own space-based methane monitoring capabilities, with the aim of creating a domestic satellite solution.”

The program will be run by the regulatory agency and enable the use of satellite and aerial data to identify large methane releases at oil and gas facilities and connect that information directly to operators so that detection leads to verified repairs. It will complement Kazakhstan’s requirements on leak detection and repair, flaring, and venting.

“Kazakhstan’s methane satellite program sends a meaningful signal that leadership starts with action supported by transparency,” said James Turitto, Oil and Gas Methane Director at Clean Air Task Force. “While many methane reductions can and should be implemented immediately, high-quality emissions data is crucial to achieving deeper and more sustained reductions over time. The last few years have proven that advanced technologies play a vital role in comprehensive methane regulation and emissions reductions. At a time when some governments are seeking to delay methane accountability, this program shows how other producing countries can take proactive steps to build credibility, strengthen accountability, and accelerate methane reductions.”

Quotes from International Partners

“Methane super-emitters from the oil and gas sector offer the biggest near-term opportunities to mitigate this potent greenhouse gas. We applaud Kazakhstan’s leadership to address these events and look forward to working with the government and other partners to leverage data to empower targeted action, grow local capacity, and establish a successful model for others to follow,” said Riley Duren, CEO of Carbon Mapper.

Kazakhstan is showing how national leadership, strong regulations and international partnerships can turn methane commitments into concrete action. This initiative is an important step towards delivering measurable emissions reductions and offers a model for other oil and gas producing countries,” said Martina Otto, Head of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition Secretariat

“By connecting satellite detections to regulators and operators, Kazakhstan is demonstrating a commitment to action on mitigating methane emissions, one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to slow warming. Kazakhstan is building a system where finding a leak leads to fixing it. We have better technology than ever to find and fix methane leaks in the oil and gas sector, and this is a model other producing countries can follow,” said Chris Konek, Lead Scientist, Global Methane Hub.

“Kazakhstan is demonstrating what becomes possible when governments turn satellite methane data into action. Working with UNEP, the country has already mitigated 10 major methane emissions events identified through the Methane Alert and Response System, addressing more than 31,000 tonnes of methane emissions. Its efforts to systematically integrate satellite monitoring into national regulation represent an important step forward, showing how cutting-edge data can drive tangible methane reductions.” said Giulia Ferrini, Head of UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory.

“Kazakhstan has built a strong space industry and is now applying this expertise to methane monitoring through its own satellite programme and national monitoring platform. AIRMO is proud to support these efforts through our partnerships with Ghalam and Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary, contributing our satellite technology, sensors and data processing algorithms. As a technology provider, we see the inclusion of satellite monitoring in national regulations as an important step towards faster detection and mitigation of major methane emissions. Combined with locally owned capabilities, this approach could set a precedent for other methane-emitting countries and help accelerate methane emissions reductions globally.” said Vasily Yablokov, Product Director, AIRMO.

“The IEA welcomes Kazakhstan’s leadership and concrete action on methane and is pleased to support the development of its satellite monitoring and response program. Effective use of satellite data can help address large emissions events, driving emissions reductions while supporting Kazakhstan’s energy security and climate goals. We look forward to continuing our collaboration on developing a robust methane regulatory framework informed by international best practices,” said Christophe McGlade, Head of the Energy Supply Unit, International Energy Agency.

“Our work with government and industry partners in Kazakhstan over several years has shown the value of combining methane satellite data with practical action on the ground. A national satellite-based program can strengthen this link, helping turn the detection of major emissions events into timely mitigation,” said Anastasia Isaenko, Principal Consultant, Carbon Limits.

“We look forward to supporting Kazakhstan’s satellite monitoring program. Having spent more than a decade detecting methane from individual facilities, we’ve seen firsthand how much progress is possible when government and industry align on a clear vision for action,” said Stéphane Germain, CEO, GHGSat.

Press Contact

Natalie Volk, Senior Communications Manager, Clean Air Task Force, nvolk@catf.us, +1-703-785-9580

About Clean Air Task Force

Clean Air Task Force (CATF) is a global climate organization working to advance the full range of solutions needed for a healthy climate and a thriving planet. Founded in 1996, CATF conducts research and analysis to identify promising solutions, then works across governments, industry, and partners in more than 40 countries to deliver them at scale. It takes no funding from governments or the industries it works to influence, so its analysis and advocacy follows the facts. Over 30 years, its work has helped shape major climate and energy policy around the world. CATF is consistently recognized as one of the most effective climate organizations in the world by independent evaluators including Giving Green and Founders Pledge. Learn more at cleanairtaskforce.org.

text:
Delivered by Innovate UK on behalf of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the competition is designed to support UK businesses and researchers to develop new battery technologies.

The competition focused on sourcing and processing battery materials, recycling valuable materials, strengthening UK manufacturing and reducing reliance on overseas supply chains.

Recycling batteries

Lithium Battery Recyclers Ltd has been awarded more than £1.2 million to lead project Reclaim, to develop a new UK process for recycling end-of-life electric vehicle batteries.

The process, developed by the University of Leicester, uses a tiny quantity of vegetable oil in water to separate valuable battery materials, including graphite, without acid leaching or hazardous chemicals.

The project will scale up the technology at a pilot facility in Widnes, Cheshire, and test the recovered materials for reuse in new batteries.

It aims to reduce the energy needed for recycling and keep valuable battery materials in the UK to support domestic manufacturing.

Reducing waste

Hyperbat, now part of Unipart Manufacturing Group, has received more than £2.4 million to lead a project.

This aims to reduce the number of electric vehicles written off because their batteries are damaged or no longer working as expected.

At present, it can be difficult to assess whether these batteries are safe to repair or reuse.

This can lead to unnecessary vehicle write-offs, higher insurance costs and valuable materials being lost.

The project will develop a clear process for checking each battery and deciding whether it can be repaired, reused , given a second life for energy storage or safely recycled.

The work could keep batteries in use for longer, reduce waste and create skilled jobs in the UK.

Feasibility studies

The competition has also awarded just over £6.2 million to 15 shorter feasibility studies exploring new ideas across the battery supply chain.

Running for between six and 12 months, these projects will test whether early-stage technologies could improve how batteries are made, used, reused and recycled.

This will help the most promising ideas move towards further development and commercial use.

Superdielectrics Group and Sytronix have been awarded almost £500,000 to test a new type of battery that could help data centres manage the rapid changes in electricity demand.

The water-based battery is designed to store and release power quickly, helping data centres run more AI servers without placing additional strain on local electricity networks.

The project will build on an existing battery pack and test how it responds to the changing power needs of AI systems.

If successful, the technology could help data centres make better use of their existing grid connections and expand without requiring immediate upgrades to local power supplies.

It could also provide a safer alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries and reduce reliance on imported battery materials.

Investment in skills

The Battery Innovation Programme has also awarded £3.6 million to three regional skills initiatives.

These will accelerate the development of the UK’s battery manufacturing workforce and strengthen national capability across the battery value chain.

The investment will support the delivery of industry-focused nationally accredited training programmes across England.

These will equip learners with the skills needed to secure careers in one of the UK’s fastest-growing advanced manufacturing sectors, and help businesses access talent to meet increasing demand.

University Centre Somerset will deliver Level 2 and 3 battery manufacturing training for the South West battery cluster.

University College Birmingham, and Newcastle University with New College Durham in the North East, will expand their training to Levels 4 and 5.

Dr Valentina Gentili, Director of the Battery Innovation Programme, said:

As global demand for batteries continues to grow, it is increasingly important that the UK focuses on the areas where it can deliver the greatest impact and strategic value. The projects supported through this competition demonstrate the breadth of innovation taking place across the UK battery sector.

By investing in new technologies, strengthening supply chains and supporting business growth, we are helping to build the capabilities, expertise and partnerships that will further strengthen UK sovereign capability and position the UK as a leader in battery innovation.

Minister for Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall, said:

This funding will give Britain’s battery manufacturing industry the support they need to power the industries of the future and keep our country at the cutting edge of innovation.

Through our Modern Industrial Strategy we’re doubling down on Britain’s high-growth sectors like advanced manufacturing, and I want to congratulate all the winners on their success and their role in reinforcing Britain’s leadership in this fast-growing industry.

text:
real motors brings project: ARES closer to production

South Carolina-based Real Motors has brought its futuristic electric café racer, Project: ARES, onto the road, with new working prototypes and a limited production run planned for 2027. First introduced in 2024, the motorcycle attracted attention for its sculptural bodywork and sci-fi influences. Two years later, the company has opened preorders for its first 250 units, while a recent independent test ride offers a closer look at how the machine actually performs.

The latest prototypes retain the distinctive proportions of the original design, with broad body panels wrapping around the electric drivetrain and a sharply tapered seat extending over the rear wheel. In bright red, the 03 prototype takes on the appearance of a futuristic racing machine, complete with oversized white graphics and a rectangular headlight. Its front forks are concealed beneath prominent aerodynamic covers, giving the motorcycle a particularly solid presence from the front.

translucent bodywork reveals the machine beneath

Another prototype by Real Motors, numbered 04 and nicknamed ‘Ghost,’ explores the same design in black. Its dark, translucent bodywork allows glimpses of the mechanical components beneath the surface, including the electrical wiring running through the motorcycle. Without the familiar arrangement of a combustion engine and fuel tank, the design team has been able to reconsider the proportions of a traditional café racer, creating a continuous surface across much of the bike’s body.

Beneath this exterior, the electric powertrain has already demonstrated approximately 100 horsepower, with Real Motors reporting 1,000 Nm of torque at the rear wheel after gearing. The prototype carries an estimated weight of 485 pounds, giving it considerably more mass than its streamlined appearance might suggest. The low handlebars place the rider in the familiar forward-leaning café racer position, with the broad central body occupying much of the space between the knees.

an electric motorcycle with an analog feel

The riding experience is central to the project for Real Motors. The company describes its approach as ‘Electric Analogue,’ an attempt to preserve the physical connection between rider and machine even as the traditional engine gives way to an electric drivetrain. The controls remain familiar, while a small digital display provides essential riding information. The emphasis is on the sensation of operating the motorcycle and the immediate response of its electric motor.

During a recent test ride published by The Verge, journalist Tim Stevens found the Ghost prototype’s acceleration surprisingly smooth, with power delivered progressively across three riding modes. Its handling told a slightly different story. The motorcycle required more deliberate steering through corners than its racing-inspired silhouette might suggest, with the substantial battery weight contributing to its character on the road. The experience offers an early look at how Real Motors’ unconventional design translates into an actual riding machine.

the first 250 motorcycles are planned for 2027

Real Motors is now preparing Lot 01, a limited production run of 250 motorcycles worldwide. The currently listed production configuration uses a 65-kW electric motor paired with a 13.4-kWh battery, with an estimated top speed of 110 mph. These specifications differ from those of the higher-powered prototypes and Founder’s Edition. Prices for Lot 01 begin at $20,000, with North American deliveries currently anticipated in early 2027.

The company is also offering a selection of exterior liveries, allowing customers to choose how the sculptural bodywork will be finished. Its earlier Founder’s Edition is already sold out, while final specifications for Lot 01 are expected to be disclosed before manufacturing begins.
