description: As the market for Chinese electric vehicles intensifies in South Korea, efforts to enhance...
text:
As the market for Chinese electric vehicles intensifies in South Korea, efforts to enhance the competitiveness of domestically produced electric vehicles through tax incentives are lagging. A bill proposing tax benefits for domestic production has been introduced in the National Assembly, but the scope of support remains undecided, and there is a possibility that export volumes could be excluded. Concerns are rising within the automotive industry that the tax incentives may end up being ineffective.
On November 11, the National Assembly's Finance and Economy Committee held a meeting to review the proposed tax law amendments. The automotive industry is particularly focused on whether tax credits for domestically produced electric vehicles will be implemented and what the extent of those benefits will be. With major countries like the United States and China actively promoting their electric vehicle industries, tax support for domestic production facilities remains a legislative challenge.
The proposed bills in the National Assembly differ in terms of eligibility and calculation methods for tax credits. The government’s proposal includes the establishment of a domestic production tax credit based on the income tax or corporate tax proportional to the sales of eligible items produced and sold domestically. In contrast, a revised bill introduced by Democratic Party lawmaker Lee Un-ju includes provisions to extend tax credits to vehicles produced domestically and exported.
If tax benefits are only provided for vehicles sold domestically, electric vehicles intended for export would be excluded from support. Hyundai Motor Group has set a goal to increase its annual domestic electric vehicle production to 1.51 million units by 2030, with 61% of that total, or 920,000 units, earmarked for export. Analysts warn that if tax credits are limited to domestic sales, the support's effectiveness for export-oriented production facilities could be significantly restricted.
Additionally, industry representatives are calling for the introduction of direct refund systems that would allow companies to benefit even if they do not generate sufficient taxable income, alongside tax support linked to production performance. They argue that given the ongoing large-scale investments in facilities for electric vehicle transition, relying solely on corporate tax reductions may limit the effectiveness of the support.
An industry official stated, "Since domestically produced electric vehicles are supplied not only to the domestic market but also to overseas markets, excluding export volumes will inevitably limit the effectiveness of tax support. To enhance the competitiveness of domestic factories, support that considers overall production performance is necessary."

title: UK and Japan agree offshore wind industrial cooperation framework
description:
The UK and Japan have agreed on a framework to strengthen cooperation in offshore wind development, with a focus on floating and deepwater technologies, supply chain development and investment in both markets.
The agreement aims to combine the UK's experience in offshore wind policy, market frameworks and project delivery with Japan's industrial and manufacturing capabilities.
The countries will also build on existing collaboration between the UK's Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult and Japan's Floating Offshore Wind Technology Research Association.

text:
The UK and Japan have agreed on a framework to strengthen cooperation in offshore wind development, with a focus on floating and deepwater technologies, supply chain development and investment in both markets. The UK-Japan Offshore Wind Industrial Compact was signed on 10 November 2026 by Michael Shanks, UK Minister of State for Energy, and Kei Takagi, Japan’s State Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry.

The agreement aims to combine the UK's experience in offshore wind policy, market frameworks and project delivery with Japan's industrial and manufacturing capabilities. Its objectives include supporting the commercial deployment of fixed-bottom, floating and deepwater offshore wind, strengthening supply chains, reducing costs and developing a common technical roadmap. The two countries also intend to encourage investment and exports and strengthen energy security through domestic renewable electricity generation.

The compact identifies four areas for cooperation.

The first concerns co-investment in offshore wind projects in both countries. The UK welcomes further Japanese investment in its offshore wind sector, while the two governments will support the development of Japan's early-stage fixed-bottom projects through cooperation and the exchange of expertise. They will also explore joint initiatives involving UK developers, Great British Energy, Japanese developers and financial institutions, particularly for floating and deepwater offshore wind.

The second area covers testing and demonstration of floating and deepwater technologies, including foundations and other enabling systems. This includes cooperation on foundation substructure development, technical standards and research. The countries will also build on existing collaboration between the UK's Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult and Japan's Floating Offshore Wind Technology Research Association. Other areas include subsea engineering, robotics and digitalisation.

The third area focuses on developing a sustainable and competitive offshore wind supply chain, particularly for turbines. The governments intend to strengthen cooperation between industry and government, support the adaptation of fixed-bottom offshore wind technologies for floating applications and encourage companies from both countries to participate in supply chain projects.

The fourth area involves sharing UK expertise and policy frameworks to support the development of Japan's offshore wind market. Topics include project financing, market and regulatory frameworks, technical standards, environmental impact assessments, grid operation, system integration, skills and certification.

Implementation will be coordinated by government agencies in both countries. Great British Energy and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero will lead on the UK side, while Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry will coordinate the Japanese contribution.

text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Carlos Giménez of Florida has invited Elon Musk to relocate Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Texas to Florida, citing the state’s business environment and the recent Democratic victories in Texas during the November 2026 midterm elections.

In a letter to Musk, Giménez urged the billionaire to consider moving Tesla’s headquarters and expanding its operations to Florida, arguing that the state offers lower taxes, business-friendly regulations and greater economic freedom.

The invitation comes after Democrats secured major victories in Texas, ending decades of Republican dominance in several key statewide contests. Florida Republicans, meanwhile, retained control of all statewide offices, prompting Giménez to present the state as an alternative destination for Musk’s businesses.

Giménez cites Texas political shift

“With the recent election of self-described Democratic Socialists to positions of power in Texas, I share your concerns about excessive government interference, politically motivated investigations, and policies that punish success,” Giménez wrote in his letter.

READ: SpaceX, Tesla to spend $16.8 billion on Terafab plant in Texas (August 6, 2026)

“No company should face political retaliation for creating jobs, investing in American innovation, and contributing to our nation’s prosperity,” he added.

Giménez argued that Florida offers a different regulatory and political environment, with lower taxes and policies designed to attract businesses and investment.

“Florida offers a fundamentally different approach. Our state has championed lower taxes, responsible regulation, and the freedom to innovate without unnecessary government intrusion,” he wrote.

Tesla’s Texas presence remains substantial

Tesla moved its corporate headquarters from California to Austin, Texas, in 2021. The company operates its Gigafactory in Austin, where it manufactures the Model Y and Cybertruck. Musk’s wider Texas business footprint also includes SpaceX facilities, battery operations and other technology projects.

The political shift has raised questions about the future regulatory environment for Musk’s companies. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson have indicated plans for greater scrutiny of certain business arrangements involving Musk’s companies, including state incentives, environmental concerns and public land use.

However, Hinojosa has said she remains open to working with Musk and his companies under conditions that protect Texans’ interests.

Florida renews efforts to attract Musk

Giménez, a former Miami-Dade County mayor, highlighted South Florida’s infrastructure, technology sector and workforce as advantages for Tesla.

title: Editorial: Honda withdraws from withering US market for EVs | Opinion | herald-dispatch.com
description: Former President Joe Biden wanted to lead America into a new age where battery-powered vehicles had replaced those using fossil fuels and internal combustion engines. His problem was that not enough people were willing to follow him and he didn’t get a second term to finish his plan.
text:
Are Americans supposed to be pleased that President Donald Trump is blaming Ukra…

For several months I’ve asked the question: What would happen in November, the f…



A Honda logo is shown at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit on Jan. 14, 2019.

Former President Joe Biden wanted to lead America into a new age where battery-powered vehicles had replaced those using fossil fuels and internal combustion engines. His problem was that not enough people were willing to follow him and he didn’t get a second term to finish his plan.

Auto makers invested heavily in electric vehicle production but eventually learned that consumers were more interested in gasoline-electric hybrids.

On Monday, Nov. 9, American Honda Motor Co. announced it will build a new assembly plant near its existing facility at Marysville, Ohio, northwest of Columbus. The total investment in the plant and in retooling other Honda manufacturing facilities in George and Alabama to support hybrid production in Ohio will be about $3 billion, Honda said. The expansion will create more than 2,000 new American jobs and increase Honda’s auto production capacity to about 1.3 million vehicles a year, Honda said.

“The new Ohio Honda plant will be one of the most advanced in the world when it comes online in 2029 with leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems to improve efficiency, quality and competitiveness,” Honda said in its official announcement. “While supporting growing demand for hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles, the plant will provide Honda with the flexibility to adapt production as customer demand, market conditions and electrification trends evolve.”

That’s quite a turnaround from Honda’s former strategy of focusing on EVs. In March, Honda Motor Co. Ltd. said it had canceled the development and market launch of three EV models that had been planned for production in North America. The decision was made as part of the reassessment of the company’s automobile electrification strategy due to various factors including recent changes in the business environment, the company said. American tariff policy and changing consumer tastes in both the United States and China played a role in the decision, Honda said.

Honda had overestimated demand for EVs and suffered an operating loss in the fiscal year that ended March 31.

Last month, the federal Energy Information Administration said 23% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States in the third quarter of this year were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, down slightly from 24% the third quarter of last year. Sales growth of hybrids has slowed as the average sale price for a new vehicle passed $50,000, according to the EIA. Meanwhile, battery vehicle sales were only 6% of new light-duty vehicle sales, down from 10% in the third quarter of last year.

Honda is not the first major automaker to backtrack on a commitment to build electric vehicles. GM did the same thing about a year ago, and that strategic decision cost the company an estimated $1.6 billion. Ford jumped off the EV train in 2024.

EVs are great for short trips in good weather, but they have their drawbacks. Range can be limited, especially if the vehicle has a heavy load or is towing a trailer. Charging takes more time than filling a gas tank. As EV owners in Chicago discovered in 2024, EVs can be slow or impossible to charge in arctic cold weather. Also, federal tax credits for buying EVs expired in September 2025.

EVs have their place, but with existing technology they are not always the best option for most buyers. Hybrids fill the gap between batteries and internal combustion.

People who supported conversion to electric vehicles often pointed to their environmental benefits in slowing climate change. Since President Donald Trump won his second term, climate change — that formerly existential threat to human existence — has fallen far down on the list of priorities for public discussion. Likewise, companies seldom talk about their ESG — environment, social, governance — efforts now compared to a few years ago.

Why climate change and ESG are almost forgotten now can be debated, but it shows how large companies are just as likely to jump on trends as everyday folks are and how quickly priorities can change before anyone notices.

DENVER, CO – November 11, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE –

Climate Alignment is scheduling pre-winter site assessments of rooftop units, furnaces, boilers and split systems for restaurants, breweries, medical facilities and other commercial operators ahead of the heating season, according to the company. Assessments are requested through the company’s website or by phone.

Each assessment follows the scope of the company’s commercial heating repair work, according to its service page. On rooftop units, technicians check heat exchangers, economizers, reversing valves and refrigerant circuits, and on boilers the work includes gas pressure calibration, heat exchanger inspection and a carbon monoxide risk assessment. For food service and cold storage sites, the visit can also cover the heating circuits on walk-in coolers and freezers, including anti-sweat heaters and defrost systems, along with pump and loop diagnostics on glycol chiller systems. The page describes heating failures in medical facilities, breweries and food service as compliance and safety issues, and it frames walk-in heating and defrost failures as a risk to the cold chain.

Elevation is a recurring factor in the work. The company’s service page states that air at 5,280 feet is about 18% less dense than at sea level and that factory settings are engineered for sea level. Repairs include high-altitude orifice kit adjustments and calibration of superheat, subcooling, gas pressure and pressure controls, and the page cites rapid freeze and thaw cycles as a source of stress on condenser coils. The company says it calibrates every repair to high-altitude operating parameters.

“Heating problems often surface on the first cold night of the season. An inspection before winter gives an operator time to plan a repair instead of reacting to a failure,” said Nathan Boeke, owner of Climate Alignment.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that heating systems, water heaters and other gas-, oil- or coal-burning appliances be serviced by a qualified technician every year. The agency reports that more than 400 Americans die each year from unintentional carbon monoxide poisoning not linked to fires and that more than 14,000 are hospitalized.

The company handles commercial systems only and does not service residential split systems, according to its heating page. Scheduled appointments are typically confirmed within one business day, and emergency calls are dispatched 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Office hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Climate Alignment has worked on commercial heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration systems for more than 12 years, according to the company, which describes itself as a family-owned, licensed and insured contractor. Its technicians hold EPA Section 608 certification, and the company states that its work follows City of Denver mechanical codes and EPA refrigerant handling regulations. Under Section 608 of the Clean Air Act, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires technicians who maintain, service, repair or dispose of equipment that could release refrigerants into the atmosphere to be certified.

Beyond heating, the company installs, maintains and repairs walk-in coolers and freezers, reach-in units, display cases, ice machines, remote systems, glycol chillers for breweries and rack systems. Its maintenance programs include calibration, scale prevention and economizer tuning, and the company assists customers with Xcel Energy rebate documentation for qualifying motor and control upgrades, including anti-sweat heater controls, according to its website.

“Many of the same sites run refrigeration and heating side by side. Checking both on one visit lets a kitchen or brewery go into winter with a clear picture of its equipment,” Boeke said.

Operators can request an assessment through the site assessment form on the company’s website. Service details are listed on the Google Business Profile for Climate Alignment.

News Digest - November 11, 2026

The good news continues as TWDB's latest drought report shares that drought conditions have contracted statewide for the fifth straight week. It was also reported that statewide water supply storage ended October at 71.9%, which is 7.8 percentage points lower than normal for this time of year.

State Revolving Funds (SRF), totalling $43 billion over five years, ended in September without a clear plan from Congress to be extended. The SRF's two programs, the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) and the Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF), have assisted projects like lead pipe replacement and sewer repairs, but Congress must now plan how to budget it going forward.

The council will consider the above at its December 1, 2026 meeting.

NGL Water Solutions Permian, LLC has accepted a draft permit from the TCEQ for a produced water treatment project in Reeves County, Texas. The project aims to treat produced water from oil and gas operations for potential discharge into Salt Creek and the Upper Pecos River downstream of Red Bluff Reservoir. The treated water has potential to be utilized in irrigation, farming, and cooling water for data centers, power plants, and other industrial users.

Bill filing for the 90th session of the Texas Legislature opened on Monday, November 9, with a rush of 1,260 bills being filed by 5 pm on opening day. A central focus was, and will continue to be, scrutiny of data centers, including a bill from Senator Judith Zaffirini in collaboration with the state Water Development Board to require data centers to share information on water usage.

text:
The California Democrat and current ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee is suspicious of all the “now or never.”

The most important voice in Congress criticizing the Senate’s bipartisan energy permitting deal is Representative Jared Huffman.

A California Democrat who previously worked in environmental legal advocacy, Huffman has long been among the most impassioned lawmakers on climate issues. Under the first Trump administration, his voice was often the loudest calling for oversight and accountability on energy and climate policy. Under the second Trump administration, he has been a spirited defender of offshore wind.

Should Democrats take control of the U.S. House of Representatives in the coming midterm elections, as expected, then Huffman is first in line to become chair of the lower chamber’s Natural Resources Committee. This makes him one of the few people able to armchair quarterback permitting talks in Congress right now.

The proposed legislation currently on the table, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would fundamentally reshape how federal project permitting happens. It would constrain National Environmental Policy Act reviews. It would radically alter transmission approvals. It would let companies sue the government for damages if they can show that an agency was unduly discriminating against them based on fuel type. It would limit state and tribal authority to object against projects under the Clean Water Act. And it would make this whole process more transparent by instituting digital reporting requirements.

Huffman thinks it also gives too much benefit to oil and gas interests, and is an unnecessary capitulation to fossil-friendly Republicans who will likely lose power in this November’s midterm elections, anyway. He wants Democratic lawmakers to wait until after election day to consider what they do with the bill.

I reported on Congress for years and often spoke with Huffman in the Capitol hallways; he knew me on a first-name basis. So last week, when a friend pointed me to a tweet of his criticizing the Senate bill by quoting my writing, I took note. His issue concerned the discrimination provision in the bill, which sets a rolling five-year average for approvals as a baseline for what constitutes normal regulatory behavior. Successful lawsuits under this provision would be paid out of the Judgment Fund, a Justice Department account Trump has used for his offshore wind developer buyouts.

This part of the bill, Huffman wrote, “might pay some clean energy developers money from the judgment fund when they are screwed, but nothing to actually approve their projects. This is potentially a replay of the fake settlements that have bought out offshore wind projects,” he added.

I reached out to Huffman’s team and asked to talk about what he meant by that. What followed was a 20-plus-minute back-and-forth about the future of permitting reform in the U.S. and what may happen after a midterm election defined by public anger over a rush to build another type of large-scale infrastructure: data centers.

The following transcript has been lightly edited for clarity.

So let’s start with your tweet. You quoted a portion of our story about BAAJA that I had written about the “permitting certainty” provisions in the bill, and specifically the fact that developers could be awarded damages under the bill for discriminatory treatment. Could you elaborate on your point?

I don’t want to get too deep into the weeds, but this is the big thing being offered as an end to the war on clean energy, which was always the threshold matter before you get to a bipartisan permitting deal.

It is built on this framework, basically, of cutting checks from the judgment fund. And I believe that requires some close scrutiny and consideration because we have seen this gamed already to the tune of $4 billion to buy out offshore wind developers.

Well I know this can get quite technical, but the underlying point you were making was, this may not be as helpful as people think. I guess I was just wondering if you can you walk me through —

It depends what you want.

If you’re a clean energy developer and you’re worried about your shareholders and your balance sheet, this gives you at least some money when you get screwed. And it may come with some strings attached, like you have to turn around and invest it in [liquified natural gas]. That’s been the playbook from the Trump administration.

If you’re a clean energy CEO — some of them, at least — that helps you mitigate risk. That’s probably better than nothing and will be attractive to some people. But if you care about climate policy [and] whether this is a meaningful assurance of permitting certainty to renewables, I think there’s a lot more to question here.

You also said in your tweet that there’s nothing in the bill to get projects approved. Can you speak to that? Because those who negotiated it clearly say otherwise.

Well, there are shot clocks and all sorts of other things that are designed to speed things up. There’s also broad categories of exemptions — categorical exemptions and other things like that, most of which will benefit fossil fuel projects.

I have no doubt there’s going to be permitting acceleration and certainty for fossil fuel projects. You also have this five-year baseline mechanism being codified here that will further cement a high level of fossil fuel projects for many years to come, and will really operate as a ceiling.

title: China's clean energy products win global praise for driving green transition at COP31
description:
China has worked with the United Nations to advance international cooperation on addressing climate change, firmly upholding and fully implementing the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, vigorously promoting South-South cooperation on climate change, and actively supporting the UN-led Early Warnings for All initiative, he said.
Similarly, Chris Bowen, COP31 President of Negotiations and Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, praised China's contribution to making clean energy more affordable worldwide on Tuesday.
The growing international recognition of China's role in tackling climate change reflects the country's rising economic and technological strength, according to a Chinese expert.
By prioritizing domestic industrial interests over the urgent need to accelerate the energy transition, Western governments risk turning trade protectionism into another barrier to global climate action.
Yet when China offers a more affordable path to decarbonization through its clean energy technologies, those same governments respond by slapping tariffs on Chinese products.
text:
The China Pavilion at COP31 Photo: IC

As world leaders gather in Türkiye for COP31 amid renewed disputes over climate finance and a retreat from global climate cooperation by the US, China is emerging as an increasingly influential force in the fight against climate change. Its booming clean energy industry has made green technologies more affordable for developing countries, drawing praise from Western climate leaders even as Washington and Brussels impose trade barriers on Chinese products - exposing a growing contradiction between climate ambitions and economic protectionism.

Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, as President Xi Jinping's special representative, met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Antalya Leaders' Summit at the 31st meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, per the Xinhua News Agency.

China is committed to setting clear targets and ensuring their implementation, and stresses the need to be true in word and resolute in deed, which will continue to provide valuable stability and certainty for global climate governance, Han said.

China has worked with the United Nations to advance international cooperation on addressing climate change, firmly upholding and fully implementing the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, vigorously promoting South-South cooperation on climate change, and actively supporting the UN-led Early Warnings for All initiative, he said.

The global response to climate change currently faces numerous challenges, Han said, noting that developing countries, in particular, are confronted with difficulties including funding shortages, technological shortcomings and inadequate capacity in implementing their nationally determined contributions, challenges that the international community must address together.

At this year's COP31, former US secretary of state John Kerry, who also served as special presidential envoy for climate, told the Guardian that China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe - including the US - must now follow.

"The only country that has hugely accelerated [in embracing low-carbon power and rapid electrification] is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day," said Kerry.

Similarly, Chris Bowen, COP31 President of Negotiations and Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, praised China's contribution to making clean energy more affordable worldwide on Tuesday. Bowen made the remarks at a side event titled "Ecological Civilization and Beautiful China Practice" at the China Pavilion, according to a China News report.

Speaking at a COP31 side event, Huang Runqiu, China's minister of ecology and environment, highlighted China's progress in green transformation, pollution control and environmental conservation, citing a series of figures: the country has completed ultra-low-emission upgrades for 1.17 billion kilowatts of coal-fired power capacity and 1 billion tons of crude steel production capacity, according to a readout published by the ministry on Wednesday.

China has also led the world in electric vehicle production and sales for 11 consecutive years. Over the past five years, average concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) have fallen by 20 percent, while the number of days with severe air pollution has dropped by 25 percent, said Huang.

This year's COP comes after a year of devastating extreme weather, marked by soaring temperatures and deadly heat waves across Europe and beyond, while the absence of the United States has further complicated global efforts to tackle climate change. COP observers and international media have turned the spotlight back on China, wondering if "China will finally step into the leadership role" in global climate action, as the Guardian asked.

The growing international recognition of China's role in tackling climate change reflects the country's rising economic and technological strength, according to a Chinese expert. Once viewed largely as a costly undertaking, the fight against climate change has increasingly become an economic opportunity, driven in part by China's rapid advances in clean energy technology and manufacturing, Bao Cunkuan, a professor in the Department of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Fudan University, told the Global Times.

For developing countries, particularly those in the Global South, where energy costs can place a heavy burden on economic development, the expansion of China's renewable energy industry has helped make clean power more affordable and accessible, allowing countries to pursue economic growth while reducing emissions, said Bao.

As for growing calls for China to assume a greater leadership role in global climate governance, the expert said the country's influence should be measured not by whether it formally takes the lead, but by its capabilities and concrete achievements in advancing the green transition.

China actions

At a press conference last month, Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, said that China was calling for the COP31 climate summit to focus on implementing existing commitments and addressing both longstanding gaps in emissions cuts and climate finance, as well as new challenges from unilateralism and protectionism.

China is by far the world's largest producer of the solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric cars needed to cut emissions. However, ​that technology is increasingly seen as a threat by countries concerned about the competitive impact on their local industries, per Reuters.

The US has imposed steep tariffs ‌on Chinese solar products and electric cars while the European Union has done the same for autos, imposed restrictions on some solar components and is investigating a major Chinese wind company.

Steep tariffs imposed by the United States and European countries on Chinese clean energy products risk undermining the very climate goals they have pledged to pursue, said Ma Jun, director of the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs.

With much of the world already lagging in the transition to renewable energy, such protectionist measures threaten to drive up costs, slow the adoption of affordable green technologies and hinder global efforts to combat climate change, Ma said. By prioritizing domestic industrial interests over the urgent need to accelerate the energy transition, Western governments risk turning trade protectionism into another barrier to global climate action.

According to a Reuters analysis, China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country. That figure nearly matched the total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change.

Ma said he had spoken with climate experts from Pakistan who described how falling prices had made Chinese solar panels increasingly affordable for ordinary households, prompting more families to embrace the technology.

By installing rooftop solar panels, these households have been able to reduce their dependence on an unreliable power grid and gain greater control over their electricity supply. Beyond making daily life easier, access to affordable, reliable electricity has also created opportunities for families to start small businesses, earn a living and improve their economic prospects, Ma said.

Therein lies the irony of global climate politics: Wealthy nations have yet to fulfill their climate finance commitments to developing countries, even as they lecture China over its emissions and environmental record.

Yet when China offers a more affordable path to decarbonization through its clean energy technologies, those same governments respond by slapping tariffs on Chinese products. For all their "lofty" rhetoric about saving the planet, it is becoming increasingly clear who is driving the green transition forward — and who is standing in its way, said experts.

text:
AURORA, CO – November 11, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE –

A+ Hybrid Batteries, a mobile hybrid battery replacement company serving Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, is advising owners of older hybrids to consider replacing a failing battery before replacing the vehicle, one year after the federal electric vehicle tax credit ended. The company said more of its customers are choosing to keep and repair the hybrid they already own rather than trade it in.

NPR reported on September 30, 2026, that the federal tax credit of up to $7,500 for new electric vehicles ended on September 30, 2025, after Congress repealed it as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. According to Edmunds data cited in the report, electric vehicles fell from 11.4 percent of new car sales in September 2025 to 5.8 percent a month later and have held between 5 and 6 percent of sales through 2026. Over the same period, hybrid sales rose almost 27 percent, according to Edmunds.

The NPR report also noted that the average electric vehicle transaction price was over $54,000 in August 2026, compared with an average of just under $50,000 for gas-powered vehicles, according to Cox Automotive. Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds, told NPR that many consumers set aside their electric vehicle plans or bought a hybrid instead, most likely because of the lower price point.

For drivers who already own a hybrid, the question is often what to do when the original battery wears out. Kelley Blue Book estimates that replacing a failed hybrid battery can cost between $2,000 and $8,000 depending on make and model, and says today’s hybrid batteries typically last at least 10 years, or between 100,000 and 150,000 miles. Many early Toyota Prius and Camry Hybrid models may now be past that range while the rest of the vehicle remains in regular use.

A+ Hybrid Batteries said that for owners weighing a new vehicle purchase, a battery replacement on a hybrid that is otherwise in good condition can be a lower-cost way to keep a dependable car on the road. The company services Toyota Prius models from 2001 through 2019, both generations of the Camry Hybrid built from 2007 through 2016, and hybrids from Honda, Ford, Hyundai, Kia, Lexus, Nissan, and Subaru. Technicians travel to a customer’s home, office, or another location, run a module-by-module diagnostic, and replace the battery on-site when it is needed, typically within 30 to 45 minutes.

The company publishes its pricing for Toyota battery replacement on its website. Listed prices start at $950 for a reconditioned battery with a six-month warranty, $1,180 for a reconditioned battery with a three-year warranty, and $2,450 for a new OEM-grade battery with a five-year warranty, with mobile service and installation included. Final cost depends on the model year and the battery selected, and customers pay after the work is complete.

A+ Hybrid Batteries said a diagnostic before any replacement is an important step for owners deciding whether to keep a vehicle. Some drops in fuel economy or power may come from other parts of the hybrid system rather than the battery itself, and the company said it tells customers when the battery is not the cause before any work is done.

“A year ago, a lot of the people who called us assumed a failing hybrid battery meant it was time for a new car. Now we are hearing from more drivers who want to keep the car they already know, especially once they look at what a new vehicle costs. An older Prius or Camry Hybrid with a healthy battery can stay on the road for years, and our job is to give owners an honest diagnosis so they can make that decision with clear numbers in front of them,” said Nahome Yifru, owner of A+ Hybrid Batteries.

A+ Hybrid Batteries was founded on June 24, 2020, and is based in Aurora, Colorado. The company provides mobile hybrid battery diagnostics and replacement for vehicle owners across Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, with locations in Atlanta, Aurora, Baltimore, Dallastown, and Fairfax, and has announced plans to bring its service to even more states soon. Its replacement batteries carry warranties of up to five years depending on the battery selected.

“The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built is ‘how can we have our voices heard?’”

Today, during a Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee hearing, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly pressed Justin Schwab, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Air and Radiation, on the agency’s proposal to eliminate longstanding public comment requirements for certain air pollution permits, including for data centers building their own power plants. Kelly also secured a commitment from Schwab to prioritize final approval of a Maricopa County air quality rule aimed at reducing air pollution from off-road equipment.

Kelly raised concerns that EPA’s proposal to eliminate the 30-day public comment period for certain air pollution permits could leave communities without a say in new data center projects: “As you know, there’s a massive boom in data center development across the country. The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built is, ‘how can we have our voices heard?’ That’s especially true if a data center is proposing to build what’s called behind-the-meter generation. Or in other words, they’re going to build their own power plant. For decades, EPA has required at least 30 days for the public to review and comment on proposed permits. Seems rather reasonable.”

Kelly questioned who pushed for the rollback after seven major data center developers responded to an October inquiry from Kelly, and none indicated they had requested the change: “Earlier this year, EPA proposed a new rule that would allow states to eliminate the public comment opportunity for any minor source facility that emits less than 100 tons of pollution per year. I think that’s unacceptable, and what I can’t understand is who asked for this.”

Last month, Kelly and Whitehouse urged EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to withdraw the proposal, arguing that faster permitting should not come at the expense of transparency or communities’ ability to shape decisions that affect them. During the hearing, Schwab committed to looking into the senators’ letter after Kelly pressed him to ensure EPA provides a response.

Kelly also secured a commitment from Schwab to advance Maricopa County’s efforts to improve air quality: “Just last week, EPA formally approved the county’s Rule 205, which allows businesses to generate emissions credits by replacing older, higher-polluting vehicles with cleaner ones. I appreciate that progress, but Rule 204, which would establish a similar program for off-road equipment, still needs final approval.”

When Kelly asked whether Schwab would prioritize EPA’s ongoing work with Maricopa County to move Rule 204 toward final approval as quickly as possible, Schwab responded, “Yes. If confirmed, I do commit to prioritize in that regard.”

Click here to download a video of Kelly’s remarks. See the transcript below:

Sen. Mark Kelly: Thank you, Madam Chair and thank you, Mr. Schwab, for being here today. I’d like to first ask you about Maricopa County’s efforts to improve air quality, which has spanned multiple administrations. Just last week, EPA formally approved the county’s rule 205, which allows businesses to generate emissions credits by replacing older, higher polluting vehicles with cleaner ones.

I appreciate that progress, but rule 204, which would establish a similar program for off road equipment, still needs final approval. Mr. Schwab, if confirmed, will you commit to prioritizing EPA’s ongoing work with Maricopa County to move rule 204 toward final approval as quickly as possible?

Justin Schwab, Nominee, Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation: Thank you for the question, Senator. Yes. If confirmed, I do commit to prioritize in that regard.

Kelly: Well, thank you. Mr. Schwab, next, I want to talk about data centers. As you know, there’s a massive boom in data center development across the country. The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built, is how can we have our voices heard? Kelly: Well, that’s what I’m asking but from your personal life, would you be comfortable with a data center that admitted just less than, the cutoff is 100 tons, just less than the 100 tons of NOx or PPM 2.5 near your home without a guaranteed opportunity to give your own input. That’s the question.

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. It would depend on the particular circumstances of the facility.

Kelly: The circumstance is a data center is being built, and it’s going to admit, let’s say, a just under 100 tons of night nitrous oxide of NOx. Would you be comfortable with that without having an opportunity to give your own input on the issue?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. As I said, matters of permitting are appropriately where consistent with federal law, the prerogative of state and local governments. And those are the ones that know their communities best.

Kelly: Yes, so you don’t think homeowners, people in the region of where the data center is being built should get a say if it’s just less than the 100 tons or you don’t think it’s up to them at all.

Schwab: Senator, the Congress Enacting the Clean Air Act, has provided those areas in which federal law does require all state permitting process to engage, to include a public participation phase. And there are other areas in which federal law does not have that express requirement. And there is a pending proposal in that regard from.

Kelly: Well, it sounds like your answer is no. I’m trying to understand where are you on this? If it’s less than 100 tons, you don’t think people should get an input. You keep coming back to the law, but I’m just asking you your opinion.

Schwab: My opinion is that, as a general principle, state and local governments and agencies understand their communities and their concerns best.

Kelly: Well, earlier this year, EPA proposed a new rule that would allow states to eliminate the public comment opportunity for any minor source facility that emits less than 100 tons of pollution per year.

I think that’s unacceptable and what I can’t understand is who asked for this. So, I worked with Ranking Member Whitehouse to ask nine of the leading data center developers said seven of them responded, and none of them said they asked EPA to make this rule. So, Mr. Schwab, you’ve been at EPA since these rules were proposed and you’ve been in the Trump administration since the president took office.

So maybe, you know, like who asked the EPA to roll back these common-sense protections?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. The proposal is not specific to data centers. The proposal addresses generally requirements for minor —

Kelly: Who asked to roll them back? Because it wasn’t the data centers. So must have been somebody, unless it was just decided internally that you don’t think the community should have an input.

Schwab: Senator, the policies of the United States is articulated by the president’s executive orders are where consistent with law, to reform permitting processes to ensure that they do not include non-statutory non legally required provisions that may hinder development.

Having said that, it is the prerogative of state and local governments in the first instance where federal law is silent on a question to determine what level of public participation may be appropriate under their own —

Kelly: It sounds like you’re saying it came from the White House. Well, what I’m going to ask you here is, will you commit to speaking with Administrator Zeldin and his team about the letter we sent to make sure we get an answer to our letter.

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. I’m not familiar with this letter, but, yes, I do confirm the looking into the letter.

text:
In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.

The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities.

The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power.

But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.

Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future.

'Meteoric Growth'

Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles.

At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants.

“The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.”

Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances.

With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand.

Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably.

Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects.

“As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said.

State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates.

In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage.

“It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.”

Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit.

Community Concerns

For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke.

Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands.

Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities.

“They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.”

The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials.

Industry leaders say the Moss Landing facility was built using an older design, prior to the issuance of safety standards from the National Fire Protection Association that cover most systems on the grid today. Newer projects use an updated battery chemistry that burns at lower temperatures, and store the batteries in isolated, modular containers so that fires don’t spread to nearby units.

As a result, battery fires have become much more rare and far less devastating. Earlier this month, the Electric Power Research Institute, an independent nonprofit, published an analysis of battery system failures dating back to 2011.

The report found that failures (defined as large thermal events such as arc flashes, fires or explosions) have declined 97% in the U.S. since 2018, when adjusted for the amount of battery power on the grid. The incidents that have happened in new systems have largely remained small and contained, said Lakshmi Srinivasan, who authored the analysis.

“Specific design choices have really reduced not only the likelihood of a failure, but the impact of a failure if it happens,” she told Stateline.

Srinivasan said the risk profile of battery farms is similar to that of electrical transformers, components of the electrical grid that already exist in many communities.

But some communities feel a slim chance of disaster is still too high. Residents in Snoqualmie, Washington, have voiced opposition to a proposed battery project just outside city limits, prompting the city and several neighboring communities to enact moratoriums on such facilities.

“We need to think more carefully about what the worst-case scenario is, not just what’s typical,” said Dan Murphy, a council member in the city of Snoqualmie. “The science says (battery farms) are getting safer, but we’re still early.”

Amid the local backlash, the developer, Jupiter Power, has indicated that it will pursue approval from state-level energy siting regulators, removing the project from King County jurisdiction.

Murphy said his community supports clean energy, but objected to the site location near homes, a playground, a waterway and a critical evacuation route. He said Jupiter Power kept locals in the dark until they thought the project was a done deal.

“We are a very reserved and polite community,” he said. “To see the outcry and the animation and the mobilization, it’s really struck a nerve with our residents.”

In a document responding to community concerns, Jupiter Power noted that battery farms must be built near substations, which are located in close proximity to the communities they serve. That reality, the company said, makes it unrealistic for local officials to demand that battery systems keep their distance from populated areas. In King County, the company found, all 157 substations that are suitable for a battery project are located within a quarter-mile of schools, daycares, hospitals, natural areas or other sensitive sites.

Jupiter Power did not grant an interview request, but referred questions to Clean and Prosperous, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on reducing emissions.

“For any battery storage project there will inherently already be energy infrastructure nearby,” said Kelsey Nyland, communications director with Clean and Prosperous. “It often feels like we expect clean energy projects to be perfect in a way that we don’t expect from fossil fuel projects.”

Nyland noted that Washington state ranks dead last in the nation for clean energy growth, despite its ambitious climate goals. Battery storage, she said, can help population centers in western Washington harness surplus wind and solar power from rural eastern Washington.

She added that Washington has only one operational battery storage facility, making it difficult to alleviate local’s concerns by touring a nearby site.

Similar disputes have played out in dozens of communities across the country, and many have passed temporary measures banning the construction of battery storage facilities.

Earlier this month, a pair of former economic officials from the Biden administration wrote in The Washington Post that battery farms had been caught in a case of “mistaken identity” amid the nationwide backlash to data centers, which have stirred up similar feelings about industrial siting and environmental risks. But while data centers increase pressure on the grid, battery farms reduce it, they wrote, making the “conflation” an expensive mistake.

Some local activists have asked for battery farms to be sited in remote areas, where they would pose fewer risks. But industry leaders say they’re simply following the incentives set forth by utilities, which prioritize projects that can connect to the grid near population centers.

“If you have a source of power right where the power’s being consumed, the more efficient your system’s going to be,” Malaquias Encarnacion, managing director with Carina Energy, a development services firm that works on battery storage projects.

Carina Energy has tracked 175 battery farm moratoriums enacted or proposed by communities across the country. In some cases, Encarnacion said, those actions have been temporary measures enacted by local governments to give themselves time to learn about the issue.

“If I didn’t know anything about it, I would be nervous as well,” he said, encouraging developers to engage with communities early to alleviate those concerns.

text:
Hunter renewable projects could add more than 600 megawatts (MW) of new generation plus 800+ megawatt hours (MWh) of storage.

Projects will support AirTrunk’s NSW energy needs, including its proposed Kurri Kurri site.

Partnership builds on the newly opened Mulwala Solar Farm in New South Wales.

AirTrunk on track to match all electricity use with renewables by 2030.

Hyperscale data centre specialist AirTrunk and renewable energy developer, builder, owner and operator European Energy Australia have signed an exclusivity agreement to progress two renewable energy projects in the Hunter region in New South Wales, Australia.

The proposed projects include a 260 MW solar project, an 800+ MWh battery project and up to 350 MW wind project in the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. Together, they could add more than a gigawatt of new renewables generation and storage to NSW’s electricity system.

The companies are progressing project development and discussing a potential long-term power purchase agreement to support AirTrunk’s NSW energy requirements, including its proposed Kurri Kurri data centre campus.

The projects are expected to begin operating between 2030 (solar and battery) and 2032 (wind), with European Energy planning to connect them to Ausgrid’s upgraded 132 kilovolt network in the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. The connections will be subject to final connection arrangements, approvals and further technical assessments.

AirTrunk meeting government expectations for new energy supply

The Australian Government expects new data centres to secure new and additional clean energy generation and/or storage to offset their demand, while managing energy use and contributing to a secure and stable electricity grid. The NSW Data Centre Guidelines similarly expect operators to fund the additional energy supply and infrastructure their projects require, without shifting net costs to households, businesses or communities.

AirTrunk is working with energy partners and networks to bring new supply forward alongside its growth. The proposed Hunter projects and discussions about a long-term power purchase agreement form part of that work. The projects and potential agreement remain subject to further development, approvals and final arrangements.

Robin Khuda, Founder and CEO of AirTrunk, said: “Digital growth must bring new energy with it. The Australian Government’s expectations and NSW’s guidelines set a high bar for the industry. This partnership is an important step towards delivering on that commitment.”

Sabooh Whitelaw, AVP Energy at AirTrunk, said: “We understand the community wants to know how Kurri Kurri’s electricity needs will be supported. Our focus is on bringing new renewable generation forward and securing renewable electricity through long-term supply arrangements.”

Catriona McLeod, Managing Director, European Energy Australia said: “It’s great to see AirTrunk and the tech sector embracing renewable energy – partnerships like this allow us to bring more renewables online and add more energy to the grid.”

The partnership builds on AirTrunk and European Energy Australia’s work at the 31 MW Mulwala Solar Farm, which officially opened this week and is now supplying renewable electricity to NSW’s grid. The companies will continue to explore further renewable energy opportunities.

New Hunter renewables to support AirTrunk’s Kurri Kurri proposal

AirTrunk is proposing a data centre on the former Kurri Kurri smelter site at Loxford, reusing land with an established industrial history. The project would support jobs and economic opportunities in the Hunter and make use of existing infrastructure.

Over the past four months, AirTrunk has engaged with the local community through information sessions, project updates and a drop-in hub. AirTrunk will continue listening and sharing information as the proposal progresses through the planning process.

Whitelaw added, “The Hunter projects are an important step, but more renewable generation and firming will be needed to support Kurri Kurri and AirTrunk’s wider NSW needs. We’ll continue working with developers and energy partners to progress further projects across Australia”.

AirTrunk is on track to match all electricity use with renewables by 2030

AirTrunk is committed to matching 100% of its electricity use with renewable energy by 2030 as part of its Net Zero 2030 target. In FY26, around 73% of its electricity use was matched with renewable energy across the portfolio. The company is working to increase that share by supporting new renewable generation and securing long-term supply as its operations grow.

text:
Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

text:
Austin, Texas—Nov 11, 2026

Utilities using Oracle Opower have achieved record year-to-date peak energy demand reduction in North America. Oracle Opower programs activated across more than 70 winter and summer events, delivering 1 gigawatt (GW) of demand reduction, helped utilities maintain grid reliability and manage peak electricity demand more affordably for millions of residents across the United States. Through behavioral demand response (BDR) and peak time rebates (PTR) programs, Opower enabled utilities to expand participation in their virtual power plant (VPP) and demand response efforts to a broader range of customers, including those without connected devices.

By encouraging customers to reduce or shift electricity use during peak demand periods, Oracle’s AI- and behavioral science-powered programs help utilities tap into flexible capacity across their customer base and promote distributed energy resource (DER) adoption while helping customers lower their energy bills. For example, showing a customer that shifting air conditioning use by 15 minutes could save them money during a peak event, and then following up with how their household performed, is far more compelling than a generic request to use less power. With Opower PTR programs, utility customers can also earn monetary incentives when they reduce their energy use during peak events.

Top highlights achieved in 2026 include:

Oracle delivered 1 GW of demand reduction, the equivalent to more than 3 Fredonia Generation Stations in Washington state—“peaker” power plants that provide backup electricity during demand surges

Oracle helped utilities reduce peak demand by delivering a record 73 events across winter and summer seasons, an increase of nearly 50% compared to 49 total events in 2025

Utilities achieved an average peak savings of 16,592 kilowatts (kW) per event—equivalent to meeting the peak demand from 4,150 homes*

4.3 million customers were engaged, an increase of 30% compared to 3.3 million in 2025, demonstrating the rapidly growing reach and accessibility of these programs

Utilities’ record-breaking results

Puget Sound Energy (PSE), a Washington state investor-owned utility serving 6,000 square miles primarily in Western Washington, has successfully incorporated BDR into its VPP approach. Today, the utility’s Flex Events BDR program with Oracle has grown to represent a significant customer-facing facet of its set of load flexibility solutions as part of a broader VPP strategy. Utilizing customer communication channels, including text messaging, interactive voice calls, and email, the Flex Event program has driven statistically significant peak load reduction of up to 16.6 MW per event during three successive seasons of deployment.

Earlier this year, PSE adjusted its Flex Events program to include a bill credit of $0.50/kWh in addition to behavioral messaging, giving customers a further incentive to reduce usage during peak events. “This summer we introduced performance-based incentives to our behavioral opt-out program, Peak Time Savings, to broaden access to the benefits of demand response and provide customers with a more direct reward for taking action during demand response events,” said Tom Smith, Supervisor for Demand Response for Puget Sound Energy. “We're excited to continue partnering with Oracle to design customer-focused solutions that are easy to participate in, reduce barriers to engagement, and deliver meaningful value to the people we serve.”

CPS Energy, the nation’s largest public power, natural gas, and electric company serving San Antonio and portions of seven adjoining counties, also achieved record-breaking results this summer, with more than one-third of nearly a million customers participating in BDR events. CPS Energy added, “We want everyone in our community to benefit from reducing peak demand. Oracle’s Behavioral Demand Response brings more than 350,000 customers of all backgrounds into our Virtual Power Plant. We called 12 events this summer, reaching nearly 19 megawatts during the month of August.”

Year-round program enhancements

Earlier this year, Oracle expanded its BDR and PTR programs to support year-round events, giving utilities the opportunity to replicate summer successes before, during, and after winter storms hit. As many regions of the country move closer to dual peaking or winter peaking grid demand, this functionality will help utilities respond accordingly. Opower’s solutions also now allow utilities to simultaneously target different customer segments with different messaging or product variations, ensuring each customer gets the right communication for them.

“Behavioral demand response and peak time rebates are growing pillars of demand reduction,” said Matt O’Keefe, group vice president and head of Opower, Oracle. “These programs give utilities more ways to deepen savings, reward customers, and contribute to virtual power plants that draw on the participation of entire communities. Expanding these programs means more households can share in the savings while helping keep the grid reliable.”
