text:
The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN report last month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Extreme heat, glacier collapse killed thousands

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives will hash out climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the climate conference — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

A question of implementing promised climate action

Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 20 26.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

'Critical decade' for clean energy tech, electrification

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran seeks compensation for war-related environmental damage

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was updated on November 11 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

description:

It also says these sites account for less than 5% of oil and gas production, but up to half of methane emissions from wells.

text:
The Trump administration is trying to ease regulations around methane emissions from oil wells — and the clock is ticking to make public comments.

Previous 2024 Biden-era rules stated companies needed to get rid of 100% of emissions from wells. Now the Environmental Protection Agency, including Regional Administrator Cyrus Western, is saying methane emissions should be reduced by at least 95%.

“That's a pretty high score … Why should they get dinged?” said Western, the administrator for Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and other mountain and plains states.

Western said the changes will specifically help operators of low-producing, or “marginal,” wells. He said many of these well operators are small, mom-and-pop businesses that have few employees and produce a few barrels of oil a day.

“ Why would we force them to tie a hand behind their back, and maybe some of them even go out of business entirely, when there's an alternative that sets a very high standard?” Western said.

However, some environmental groups, such as the Environmental Defense Fund, say that standard isn’t high enough. Jon Goldstein is the associate vice president for energy transition at the nonprofit.

“Rolling back these safeguards would mean more wasted energy, more methane pollution and greater health risks for communities living near oil and gas operations,” Goldstein said in a press release.

The EDF also says that the majority of low-producing wells are owned by large companies, not small businesses. Companies with fewer than 10 sites control just 3% of low-producing well sites, while large companies dominate ownership, according to an EDF analysis of information from Enverus, an energy analytics company. It also says these sites account for less than 5% of oil and gas production, but up to half of methane emissions from wells.

It’s not yet clear how much more methane emissions there could be under the Trump proposal, compared to the Biden rules, as the EPA didn’t provide a figure. On its website, though, the agency says that methane traps at least 28 times more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, accounting for 11% of global emissions.

Juan B. Mancias, tribal chairman of the Carrizo Comecrudo Nation of Texas (Esto’k Gna), also opposes the changes. In public comments to the EPA, he asked the agency to “retain effective methane safeguards.”

“Our ancestral relationship to land is not a commodity to be balanced away solely against industrial operating costs,” Mancias said. “We are the land; its air and waters sustain our people and future generations. EPA must protect those relationships through a defensible, transparent regulatory record.”

Western said that while his agency is easing regulations around emissions, it will still punish wrongdoers.

“This is not a get-out-of-jail-free card for people to just emit pure methane into the atmosphere for days, weeks, or months or years on end,” he said.

The proposal could also eliminate another Biden-era environmental regulation, the Super Emitter Program, which would have required companies to respond to credible reports of major methane leaks.

Those 2024 regulations never went into full effect nationally with the change of administrations, but Colorado became the first state to adopt them in September, according to Colorado Public Radio. The Environmental Defense Fund says Colorado could now cut around 30,000 metric tons of methane from leaking into the atmosphere through 2038.

The public comment period on the proposed changes nationwide goes through Dec. 16.

name: Clean Energy
title: The Unlikely Allies Behind Congress' New Energy Deal - Atmos Magazine
description:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a permitting reform bill that would speed up approvals for energy infrastructure projects on public land.
As you can imagine, environmental and clean energy groups are divided over whether to support the bill and help get it through ASAP, or send it packing.
Whitehouse says BAAJA will be a boon for clean energy.
Clean energy and climate groups echo Whitehouse’s arguments, including Evergreen Action, a group started by former Washington Gov.
A proposal’s congressional approval doesn’t necessarily translate to federal permit approval—and Trump has shown his hand when it comes to clean energy projects.
text:
We rarely hear the word compromise these days, especially in politics. I often feel like bipartisanship died with the last season of The West Wing, or at least the first Trump term.

But a new bill making its way through Congress right now is framed as a solution to a problem industries on both sides of the energy debate have long grappled with: how to get faster approvals to build infrastructure on public lands.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a permitting reform bill that would speed up approvals for energy infrastructure projects on public land. The Senate voted Monday to move BAAJA to a full vote, teeing it up for a fast-track approval.

The bill would more readily greenlight solar arrays, wind farms, and modernize electric grids and power lines. But it would do the same for data centers and gas pipelines.

BAAJA supporters consider it essential to clear infrastructure backlogs, cut the red tape of complex, slow environmental reviews, and get more energy of all kinds online quickly. Opponents argue the bill would negatively impact protected land, weaken species protections, skip tribal and historical reviews, and increase emissions.

As you can imagine, environmental and clean energy groups are divided over whether to support the bill and help get it through ASAP, or send it packing.

It’s important to note that this bill was created with true bipartisan support.

Senate Republicans Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia introduced BAAJA alongside Democrats Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

And Whitehouse’s support is not something to view lightly. He’s held more than 300 weekly “Time To Wake Up” speeches on the floor since 2012 that press his colleagues to confront the climate crisis, address the financial and environmental impacts of fossil fuels, and reckon with the outsized influence of dark money in politics.

Whitehouse says BAAJA will be a boon for clean energy. “This bill is a BIG step to fight climate change,” he wrote on X this week. “It would lower power sector emissions, accelerate clean energy, and avoid emissions equivalent to those from nearly 35 million gasoline-powered vehicles.”

He also argues that certain provisions in the bill would lower data center costs for ratepayers by forcing companies to pay more for grid expansion. BAAJA could save ratepayers $55 billion over 10 years, according to an independent analysis from Grid Strategies LLC.

Clean energy and climate groups echo Whitehouse’s arguments, including Evergreen Action, a group started by former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee staffers. (Inslee himself has not taken an official stance on the bill).

On the other hand, AI and gas companies also champion the bill for being pro-energy. BAAJA would benefit the gas industry in two ways: by allowing it to build out more of its own energy infrastructure; and by paving the way for more data centers, which are predominantly powered by gas.

The Data Center Coalition, whose members include Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, reportedly spent $480,000 on lobbying between July and September, including on the permitting reform bill. Other groups that divulged their lobbying on the bill include the American Petroleum Institute, the Edison Electric Institute, and the National Mining Association.

API’s aggressive bill advocacy included sending a “BAAJA on the Hill” taco truck around the Capitol building on Tuesday to distribute free tacos.

It read: “Pass permitting reform. Lower energy costs. Brighter Opportunities.”

Many see BAAJA as a rare compromise. But is it worth it?

While considering what compromise might look like in a bill that could pass, I’m reminded of words from political scientist Leah Stokes, whom I spoke with previously about her efforts to pass the largest climate bill in American History: the Inflation Reduction Act.

That bill was trimmed repeatedly: from a $6 trillion reconciliation package, to a $3.5 trillion Build Back Better framework, to a scaled-back $1.75 trillion proposal. In the end, the Inflation Reduction Act passed with nearly $400 billion in climate investments.

It was still a win for the planet, Stokes told me, even in its imperfection.

“I really felt despair sometimes when the bill would shrink,” she said, “but I also felt like, you know, something is better than nothing. And losing out on this huge opportunity to pass a climate bill means that we could wait another decade to make this happen.”

Of course, that doesn’t mean BAAJA is the right compromise. If it passes, it’s important to consider the losers as much as the winners. Gas companies, the AI industry, and solar manufacturers could all make some big gains. But the climate could be left reeling.

The Center for Biological Diversity argues that BAAJA provides “massive long-term structural advantages to the fossil fuel industry and minimal short-term improvements to electricity transmission policy that might marginally benefit renewable energy.” One of its directors likened the bill to a “climate kill shot that condemns our most vulnerable communities to suffer decades more fossil fuel pollution.”

Oil Change International, a nonprofit campaigning for a just transition to clean energy, warns BAAJA would allow for “a massive, unprecedented buildout of gas power plants and pipelines,” arguing that’s why the permitting legislation would “fail to trigger a clean energy revolution.”

But research indicates that long term, the pluses might outweigh the minuses.

Independent research provider Rhodium Group found that yes, the bill will both increase clean energy resources by driving an additional 17-249 GW of clean resources, and increase fossil fuel production by increasing liquefied natural gas exports by 8-15%.

Taken together, though, Rhodium estimates BAAJA could reduce greenhouse gas emissions by between 5 and 148 million metric tons annually by 2040. Allowing clean energy to be deployed more readily—even alongside fossil fuel infrastructure—will arguably allow the industry to grow quickly enough to ultimately eclipse fossil fuels on the market, driving down emissions in the long term.

But that’s if the bill is implemented as promised.

One big concern is federal intervention. A proposal’s congressional approval doesn’t necessarily translate to federal permit approval—and Trump has shown his hand when it comes to clean energy projects.

As climate writer Lissa Harris asked Bill McKibben: “Why do we presume any of these mfers will do anything but wipe their ass with this deal when Boss Baby decides he hates a wind project next year?”

It turns out her concern was well-founded.

Hours after Trump’s Monday BAAJA endorsement, he told reporters at the White House that he wouldn’t approve any wind projects despite the bill. “Wind turbines are a major loser,” he said.

Congressional Democrats, on the brink of power come January, seem keen to slow BAAJA down. Following the midterm election results, analysts at investment banking firm TD Cowen cut their outlook for the bill’s success from roughly 40% to 25%. Timing is on Democrats’ side: A Senate approval would send the bill to the House, and the holidays—when congressional members take time off to go home—are fast approaching.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said last week that the permitting bill falls short, criticizing it for a “failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Over the weekend, a new amendment was added to BAAJA—77 pages of updates—meant to answer objections from tribes, environmentalists and utilities. Not everyone is convinced.

Even if Democrats take up the bill next year, it’s unclear what it would look like on the heels of such such clear messaging from American voters last week against data centers.

I can’t see Democrats starting their tenure leading the new Congress by trumpeting a bill that benefits the very industry whose opposition helped pave their road to victory.

Kahl: Oriana.

Mastro: That's a perfect segue to what I wanted to say about policy impact about how do we talk to the U.S. government? It's not only the U.S. government. As someone who works on China, the amount of which professors and students are engaging with China is less and less over time because all of these things have become politically difficult.

And to me, Stanford is an environment in which you should be able to take those risks. This is a place where you can have dialogues with the Chinese. This is a place where policy, political officials should feel like they can come and talk and engage with these issues.

And so to try to have that kind of interconnectivity in May, I launched this policy lab on the Indo-Pacific. I call it “policy-guided.” What that means is instead of sort of doing all this research and then writing an op-ed and hoping someone reads it and then maybe it has some impact, I identify the decision makers that have influence on that research area early on in the process, and I engage with them throughout the whole process so that they have a stake in making sure that they're getting the information they need when they need it.

And part of that is educating students not only on the substance on Indo-Pacific, but also skill sets. So part of that is we just launched something called the Commander Series, where I bring combatant commanders—so these are four-star generals who are in charge of every region of the world—to campus every quarter. They give a big public talk, which again, given the political environment, given everything, did come with some convincing. We now have three lined up for this year. But it's possible. It's possible to continue to engage. And then in addition to the public talks, ask them to do private master classes with the students.

Like having that exposure to students to do kind of the real world work and to have that direct policy impact, is it harder? Yes. Is it still possible at a place like Stanford? Absolutely.

Kahl: I want to really foot stomp something because at the intersection of what Oriana and Steve just said: yes, there's a degree to which we're not as plugged into Washington as maybe in previous administrations. But the flip side of that is, actually, Stanford is a safer space for conversations among those parts of Washington that want to have conversations outside of Washington because we are further away.

We are seen as less ideological. We're not seen as particularly partisan. We're seen as a font of technical knowledge because Silicon Valley plays its own role in the current ecosystem for better or worse. So that's also an opportunity, not just a constraint.

Endy: I love this question. We heard that we're in a moment of epochal change not seen since the Renaissance. That's stunning. I'm going to carry that for a long time.

I wonder what Mr. and Mrs. Stanford think of us. If they appeared today and saw what we are now, how would they react? One of the things I go back and read is the purpose they wrote in the charter of the university. And there's a sentence, this really interesting sentence. It says: “to have an influence in behalf of humanity.”

And the first time I read it, I thought it was a typo. I thought it was supposed to be “on” behalf of humanity. But it says “in behalf of,” which really means out there doing stuff. And I think we could do a lot better in that regard.

I think we're pretty good at being Stanford. I think we could do a lot better in behalf of humanity. And FSI and CISAC is very much about that. But what does that look like? And and so I'll check some things out that may seem adjacent, but I think they're important. Number one.

I used to be chair of undergraduate admissions and financial aid for the university. We're not need-blind for international applicants. We are for domestic, but not for international. We could do it, but we always manage to not do it. This would be a good year to do it.

The second thing I think we need to do is we need to bring Stanford out into the United States. I used to teach a version of Introduction to Bioengineering to five hundred high school students in Title I high schools. And they were registered as Stanford students as high school students in low income high schools throughout the country.

I think we could have a service requirement for undergraduates where they're teaching fellows in high schools as upperclassmen helping with this. We could have five thousand extra students a year as high school students. So I think there's some macro moves the university could make that would amplify what FSI and other places are doing, and we need to get on with it.

Kahl: This is such a great place to end because the panel today was global threats and essentially what we can do about them. And I think what you heard, and frankly, where I think FSI is unique, not only at Stanford, but in the world in many respects, is that so many of the things that we read about or that we watch on YouTube are at the cross currents of these huge geopolitical changes, these world changing technological developments, and contentious domestic politics in the future of democracy here and around the world. Like these are the things that all of us care about.

Just as people as Americans, we are deeply invested at FSI. And I think what you've heard is like we can choose to engineer a world of abundance and opportunity, or we can create a lot of dangerous things that make life worse. We can choose to defend freedom in the United States and around the world, or we can choose not to. We can choose to wield American power with wisdom and with a degree of restraint, or unwisely with hubris, like an international wrecking ball.

These are choices. These are not inevitabilities. These are choices. And I think at FSI, we believe we can help empower the right choices, especially by empowering our students. The thing that keeps me most optimistic when we have conversations like this — I think everybody up here would agree — is how awesome our students are, and how much more incredible they are at, you know, as twenty-year-olds than we were as twenty year olds.

And what I often say is smart and incredible as all these people on stage and all the other people you encounter, all the people in this room are, we're not going to solve the world's problems.

The best we can do is keep the problems solvable and empower our students to solve our problems. And the good news is our students are completely capable of doing that.

So thank you very much, and thanks again to our panelists.

text:
After a second round of amendments, Oil Change International reaffirms opposition to the Trump-backed Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) and calls on the Senate to reject the bill.

Elizabeth Bast, Executive Director of Oil Change International says:

“The new amendments do nothing to address major concerns about this bill, particularly how it overwhelmingly benefits the fossil fuel industry and Big Tech.

“Even with amendments, BAAJA still fast-tracks fossil fuel projects and makes it virtually impossible for communities to stop them. This bill still limits future administrations’ ability to meaningfully address the climate crisis and enable a just transition away from fossil fuels. It still strips away State and Tribal governments’ power to protect clean water and cultural resources.

“This bill will not address the cost of living crisis that drove so many Americans to the polls last week. The American Petroleum Institute’s (API) own analysis doesn’t show a reduction in energy costs – it simply suggests that prices may not rise as high as they otherwise would. It still leaves energy costs for U.S. households and businesses significantly rising over time.

“This bill will not meaningfully address climate change. We will never make real progress on climate if we continue to prioritize policies, like BAAJA, that help unleash more fossil fuels. Energy sources need to shift from fossil fuels to clean energy – not lock in fossil fuel dominance entrenched in this bill.

“The Senate must not rush to vote on this bill. The amendments are not adequate to address the serious concerns of Tribal Nations, environmental justice communities, and climate and energy experts. Monday’s vote was a clear demonstration that this bill is not ready for final passage, as every Democratic Senator on the Environment and Public Works Committee voted against ranking member Whitehouse’s bill. As senators voted, Trump himself admitted that even with BAAJA in place, his administration would continue to block wind projects.

“Rushing the vote on BAAJA will have grave consequences. Instead, we need policies that will support renewable energy without giving the fossil fuel industry everything it’s been asking for.”

text:
In the wake of Democrats’ sweeping victories across the nation, post-election polling commissioned by organizations focused on clean energy and environmental issues found that energy affordability was at the top of many voters’ minds as they cast their ballots.

On Tuesday, Climate Power, a strategic communications organization focused on building support for climate action, shared polling data examining how energy costs shaped the midterm results. Climate Power, alongside the League of Conservation Voters, EDF Action and the NRDC Action Fund, commissioned Hart Research for an online survey of 1,778 individuals across 62 competitive U.S. House districts who had either voted, or were certain they would be voting.

Breaking down the findings at a press briefing, Jay Campbell, a partner at Hart Research, said while voters were ready to be done with Republicans and President Donald Trump, that rejection did not mean that battleground district voters were enthusiastic about Democrats.

Survey results showed 61% of respondents had negative feelings about Donald Trump, while 57% expressed negative feelings toward congressional Republicans. Even though Democrats won majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, 46% of voters still held a negative perception of Democrats while 41% said they held positive feelings towards the incoming majority party.

As for the takeaway from these responses, Campbell said the people are giving Democrats a chance in Congress, and that they would need to take on that mantle and prove themselves.

Looking into the issues that were most pressing for voters, the cost of food and groceries “blew everything else out of the water,” Campbell said, with 66% of all voters surveyed listing that as their top issue.

However, two separate energy issues were among the top four concerns for voters. Just below the cost of groceries was the cost of gasoline, which was a deciding factor for 41% of voters. The cost of utilities, such as electricity and heating, was the fourth-most prominent issue for voters, with 32% of survey respondents noting it was a key issue in determining their congressional vote.

“The long and short of it is the cost of food and groceries, the cost of gasoline, the cost of heating, these are what people need to see Democrats working on going forward,” Campbell said. “The affordability crisis is very real, and energy is very much a part of it.”

When asked how the United States produces, delivers and manages energy, 58% of voters said the U.S. should have different policies and approaches from those put forward by Trump, while 28% said that the country should stay the course.

Additionally, respondents were asked who they felt benefited more under the Trump administration’s energy policy, consumers like them, or the oil and gas companies and electrical utilities. Twenty-two percent of voters said they had benefited more from the administration’s energy policy while 78% said the companies had benefited more.

“Even when you look at self-identified Republicans, it’s 61 to 39 saying corporations versus people like me have been benefiting,” Campbell said. “That’s a pretty clear and damning sense of where people stand.”

Moving forward, 62% of respondents said it should be a priority for Congress to bring down electricity prices, while only 7% said it was not what lawmakers should be working on.

Campbell also challenged the notion that clean energy is a liberal-coded idea that only appeals to voters on the far left, noting that a majority of swing district respondents said that clean energy was having a positive impact on energy prices.

“Those who voted for a Republican candidate say that using more clean energy rather than less would make energy more affordable by a margin of 40% to 29%,” Campbell said. “Not overwhelming, but very much on the positive side rather than on the negative side.”

However, there is work left for Democrats to do, Campbell noted, citing polling data that showed only about a third of voters say Democrats are making things better for consumers.

And the voters trust them to do that work, Campbell explained, pointing to a comparison between voters surveyed in January, and the most recent survey, conducted between Oct. 26 and Nov. 6.

In January 30% of voters surveyed said they trust Republicans more than Democrats to lower monthly energy bills compared to 26% who had more faith in the Dems.

However, the more recent survey found 43% of respondents trusted Democrats to lower their energy bills, compared to 24% who had more faith in the Republicans.

In the polling data from October and November, 45% of respondents also said they had more faith that Democrats would prioritize the interests of the consumer over corporate profits compared to 23% who placed their trust on this issue in Republicans. Voters also trusted Democrats more on issues like regulating AI data centers, lowering the cost of gas and diesel and improving the reliability of the electrical grid.

“The narrative around these issues has changed dramatically from what we were hearing in previous elections,” Geoff Garin, the president of Hart Research, told reporters at the top of the press briefing.

“The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin continued. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies, and on Trump’s war on clean energy. Every one of these elements led to a damning indictment of Republicans and gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate.”

name: Clean Energy
title: Mission possible? Turning climate promises into action at COP31 – Economy and ecology
authors: Tina Blohm, Yvonne Blos, Tina Blohm & Yvonne Blos
description:
COP31, the climate conference currently underway in Antalya, is taking place at a difficult time for international climate diplomacy.
And while the funding needed for climate action continues to grow, public spending is being cut.
Demanding more ambitious climate action while failing to honour financial commitments undermines the willingness to cooperate globally.
Climate action can only succeed in the long term if it is socially just.
Its success will be measured by whether it advances the implementation of existing commitments, strengthens new alliances and enables concrete steps towards greater climate action.
text:
COP31, the climate conference currently underway in Antalya, is taking place at a difficult time for international climate diplomacy. Geopolitical conflicts and the US withdrawal are making multilateral cooperation more difficult. At the same time, the climate crisis is intensifying and exceeding the 1.5°C threshold is becoming increasingly inevitable. In the United States, climate protection measures are being rolled back and scientific findings called into question. Elsewhere, too, fossil fuels are experiencing a resurgence. And while the funding needed for climate action continues to grow, public spending is being cut.

Nevertheless, the global expansion of renewable energy offers hope. It is transforming energy systems and creating new economic opportunities. The 2015 Paris Agreement also remains a historic achievement. It established a common framework in which almost all countries committed themselves to tackling climate change.

Those expecting the next historic breakthrough from COP31 in Turkey are overlooking its real purpose. At a time of geopolitical conflict, the conference must above all demonstrate that international climate policy is still capable of delivering results — and that long-agreed goals are finally being translated into concrete action.

Many opportunities aside new agreements

The basic rules of the Paris Agreement have largely been negotiated. The central task, therefore, is not to announce new targets. Rather, COP31 must drive progress towards existing goals, monitor their implementation, generate political pressure and demonstrate that the international community remains committed to a common course on climate action. If consensus-based negotiations fail to move forward quickly enough, coalitions of the willing must take the lead — not as an alternative to UN climate negotiations, but as a meaningful complement to the multilateral process.

COP31 also offers an opportunity to strengthen cooperation with middle powers such as Turkey, which holds the presidency and is hosting the conference, while Australia is leading the negotiations. This unusual division of responsibilities could open up new opportunities to bring different interests together.

At the same time, opposition parties, civil society and critical media in Turkey are under immense political pressure. Contradictions in the country’s domestic climate and energy policies could further undermine Turkey’s credibility. Hosting COP31 in Turkey therefore presents two opportunities: to scrutinise the country’s climate and energy ambitions and to demonstrate international solidarity with the Turkish climate movement and critical civil society.

Climate finance continues to be the sticking point at every COP.

Even when developments in partner countries warrant criticism, it remains right to make full use of every opportunity for cooperation. At the same time, there needs to be open dialogue on contentious issues to embed climate and energy policy more firmly in society and enable broad participation. An important measure of the success of Turkey’s COP presidency will therefore also be whether Turkish civil society can freely express its positions and participate effectively in the discussions surrounding the conference.

Many are meanwhile looking to Australia’s leadership of the negotiations, hoping for progress on phasing out fossil fuels and reducing CO₂ emissions. Moving away from coal, oil and gas is one of the defining tasks of our time. It is not only a climate imperative, but also a matter of economic and geopolitical security. Energy crises have repeatedly demonstrated how vulnerable economies are when they remain dependent on fossil fuel imports.

An international roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels could help deliver tangible progress at COP31. Germany has already sent an important signal with its own roadmap for the phase-out of fossil fuels. The task now is to move forward together with other countries. Where multilateral consensus falls short, coalitions of the willing can demonstrate that the transition is nevertheless moving ahead.

The scale of the challenges is illustrated by the host country itself. Although Turkey is pursuing electrification, more than half of its electricity was still generated from coal and natural gas in 2025. It has yet to present a plan for phasing out fossil fuels. Hosting the COP therefore also gives Ankara an opportunity to translate its own climate ambitions into concrete action.

Climate finance presents another major test. Industrialised countries are calling for greater ambition in reducing emissions. Countries in the Global South, in turn, rightly demand financial support to help them do so. The central conflict in the annual climate negotiations remains unresolved: climate finance continues to be the sticking point at every COP.

At COP29 in Baku, an agreement was reached for industrialised countries to provide at least $300 billion a year in climate finance by 2035. However, the gap between this target and the funding actually being provided remains enormous — and is currently widening.

Demanding more ambitious climate action while failing to honour financial commitments undermines the willingness to cooperate globally. Cuts therefore cannot be the answer. Innovative instruments such as international levies on particularly climate-damaging activities in aviation and shipping, debt relief or an international wealth tax could help mobilise new funds without placing further strain on public budgets. Here, too, alliances of pioneering countries could be established.

Climate action can only succeed in the long term if it is socially just.

Climate action can only succeed in the long term if it is socially just. People need to see that they are not bearing the costs alone, but are also benefiting from new jobs, clean energy, better living conditions and economic opportunities. A ‘just transition’ is therefore a fundamental prerequisite for climate policy to gain public acceptance and deliver lasting results. This applies to industrialised countries just as much as to countries in the Global South, which must reconcile their economic development with the transformation of their energy systems.

At COP30 in Brazil, the decision to develop an international mechanism for a socially just transition to a climate-neutral economy marked an important historic achievement that has received far too little attention. The task now is to turn this into a global instrument for socially just climate action that improves international cooperation, promotes common standards and brings existing initiatives together.

The example of Turkey shows that the concept of a just transition must not simply be enshrined in law, but must also be shaped with the active involvement of trade unions. Although Turkey’s 2025 Climate Law defines just transition as a concept and initial consultation processes involving the social partners are under way, it remains difficult to assess how inclusive these processes actually are and whether they enable the effective participation of trade unions, local authorities and the climate movement.

COP31 does not need groundbreaking new agreements. What matters is that existing promises are finally turned into action. Its success will be measured by whether it advances the implementation of existing commitments, strengthens new alliances and enables concrete steps towards greater climate action. This requires a consistent phase-out of fossil fuels, sustainable international financing and a transformation that puts social justice at its heart.

Court Decisions. On October 8, 2026, an earlier state court decision dismissing New York City’s lawsuit against major fossil fuel companies under New York’s consumer protection laws for alleged greenwashing (i.e., holding out certain products as more environmentally friendly than advertised) was affirmed on appeal. This decision demonstrates the significant hurdles that governments and private plaintiffs will encounter when trying to impose greenwashing liability on fossil fuel companies, as “the general public . . . is now well aware of the fact that the use of fossil fuels results in greenhouse-gas emissions and is the primary driver of climate change.” In other words, the general level of knowledge concerning climate-related issues has now made it more difficult to impose liability on those involved with fossil fuels because it is hard to prove the fossil fuel companies engaged in deceptive practices when the public is already aware of and has taken into account the nature of their business.

State Regulatory Action. On October 23, 2026, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against First Street Technology, Inc. in connection with allegedly faulty climate risk factors published by First Street for real estate properties. (First Street provides climate risk scores for individual homes and other real estate listed for sale, including through popular homebuying websites.) Specifically, the Florida AG asserts claims under Florida’s consumer protection laws, focusing on alleged flaws in First Street’s methodology, the resultant climate risk scores, and First Street’s failure to publicly disclose all aspects of its methodology. This action effectively seeks to apply the legal playbook developed by state attorneys general in greenwashing litigation targeting ostensibly green consumer products to climate and sustainability data providers.

title: LNG at a Legal Crossroads: Export Growth, Regulation and the Gulf Coast
description:
The Gulf Coast LNG (liquid natural gas) industry is entering another period of significant development and evolution.
The Gulf Coast has become central to the U.S. LNG industry, and that position is unlikely to change.
The Gulf Coast LNG Landscape The scale of current LNG development illustrates the stakes and volume of energy development.
The result is a multifaceted Gulf Coast development environment in which a project’s legal exposure can extend well beyond the LNG terminal itself.
What Texas Energy Lawyers Should Be Watching The Gulf Coast LNG industry is entering a period in which growth and legal complexity are advancing simultaneously.
text:
The Gulf Coast LNG (liquid natural gas) industry is entering another period of significant development and evolution. For Texas energy companies and relevant counsel, the future will likely require navigating overlapping federal authorizations, environmental review, pipeline infrastructure, and a changing energy policy landscape.

The Gulf Coast has become central to the U.S. LNG industry, and that position is unlikely to change. Developers are increasingly pursuing new modes of transport (like trains) and expanding existing facilities and related pipeline infrastructure from South Texas to the Texas-Louisiana border. But LNG development is not simply a question of whether a project can be built. The more consequential legal questions arise at the intersections between:

Federal and state jurisdiction

Export authorization and facility permitting

Environmental review and project schedules

Infrastructure and commercial commitments

Regulatory approval and litigation risk

Use of legacy assets in newer projects and successor liability issues

For personal injury attorneys handling energy-related injury and wrongful death claims, these intersections can be critical to understanding the operational circumstances behind an incident. They can be instrumental in identifying potentially responsible parties and evaluating the regulatory framework that may inform litigation.

The Gulf Coast LNG Landscape

The scale of current LNG development illustrates the stakes and volume of energy development. In September 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued a draft environmental impact statement for the proposed Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage 4 and Corpus Christi Pipeline Expansion projects. The proposed expansion would add four liquefaction trains with a maximum capacity of approximately 1,200 billion cubic feet per year, two 220,000-gallon LNG storage tanks, additional marine facilities and related pipeline infrastructure.

At the other end of the Texas Gulf Coast, Rio Grande LNG continues to move through federal regulatory processes in their attempt to secure long-term authorization for exports from a proposed six-train facility in Cameron County. The FERC has separately been conducting environmental review of a proposed Train 6 expansion.

Port Arthur presents another example. Department of Energy (DOE) records reflect ongoing federal authorization activity involving Port Arthur LNG Phase II, including proposed additional liquefaction trains. A September 2026 filing sought authorization for some re-exports from the terminal under that is currently under construction in Jefferson County.

The result is a multifaceted Gulf Coast development environment in which a project’s legal exposure can extend well beyond the LNG terminal itself.

Who Regulates LNG and Why Jurisdiction Matters

One of the first questions counsel should ask is deceptively simple: Which agency has jurisdiction over which part of the project?

For onshore and near-shore LNG export facilities, FERC generally has authority under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act to authorize siting and construction. FERC also has authority under Section 7 over certain interstate natural gas pipeline facilities. FERC conducts the applicable environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act for projects within its jurisdiction.

The DOE has a separate role concerning the export of the LNG commodity itself. Under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act, exports to countries with qualifying free-trade agreements are treated differently from exports to non-FTA countries. The DOE conducts a public-interest review for non-FTA exports, considering factors such as domestic supply, energy security, economic impacts, etc.

Other agencies can enter the picture, depending on the issues at hand. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) establishes and enforces federal safety standards for LNG facilities under 49 C.F.R. Part 193. The U.S. Coast Guard also has responsibilities involving LNG vessels and marine transfer areas.

Closer to home, state agencies, including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the Railroad Commission of Texas, may have authority over particular environmental, pipeline or other legal issues.

Pipeline and Infrastructure Dependencies

An LNG terminal cannot operate without the infrastructure that feeds it. Natural gas must be directed to the liquefaction facility. This process requires interstate pipelines, expansions, compression facilities, and interconnections. Additionally, marine infrastructure must be able to accommodate LNG carriers. There are also issues of storage, power, water, roads, and other supporting infrastructure that require separate permits and contractual considerations.

FERC’s current pipeline docket illustrates the scale of that relationship and how the industry is expanding in the Gulf Coast region. One example is the Sabine Crossing Pipeline Project. The project proposal includes a 55.6-mile pipeline spanning Texas and Louisiana with a capacity of 2.7 billion cubic feet per day. There are many other pending projects, but the Sabine Pass project illustrates the extensive reach these projects have.

Litigation and Regulatory Challenges on the Horizon

The next wave of LNG disputes may not resemble traditional environmental litigation. Potential disputes could involve complex and emerging issues:

Permitting and emissions issues

Challenges to federal environmental reviews or project authorizations

Pipeline routing, land-use and property disputes

Ownership and control changes

Marine and navigation concerns

Construction delays

Contractor disputes

Supply and offtake agreements

Force-majeure and change-in-law provisions

Financing and project-development obligations

Safety and operational incidents after projects enter service

Legal exposure in this industry can also evolve over the life of a project, making a lifecycle perspective potentially important. For example, a developer may initially focus on obtaining authorization and financing. But during construction, their attention shifts toward contractor performance, schedule risk and land issues. Then, focus shifts again once operational and regulatory compliance, safety, environmental obligations and commercial performance become more prominent.

That lifecycle perspective may be particularly important for counsel representing companies with multiple projects or long-term infrastructure portfolios.

What Texas Energy Lawyers Should Be Watching

The Gulf Coast LNG industry is entering a period in which growth and legal complexity are advancing simultaneously. For Texas energy lawyers, several issues deserve particular attention.

First – Jurisdictional mapping should occur early. Understanding which agency controls each aspect of a project helps identify where approvals may overlap.

Second – Regulatory assumptions should be stress-tested. Federal energy policy changes. Long-term projects need to account for the possibility that regulatory priorities or agency interpretations will evolve during the project lifecycle.

Third – Infrastructure dependencies deserve the same scrutiny as the LNG facility itself. Pipeline capacity, interconnections, marine facilities and supporting infrastructure can determine whether a project functions as planned and within appropriate safety guidelines.

Finally – Commercial documents should anticipate regulatory uncertainty. Long-term agreements negotiated years before may not apply today when companies encounter circumstances that were difficult to predict. Change-in-law, force-majeure, delay, termination and dispute-resolution provisions can therefore become critical components of project risk allocation.

Major LNG Expansion Means More Awareness of Changing Laws

The Gulf Coast’s LNG expansion presents substantial opportunities for Texas and the broader U.S. energy market. But as the expansion moves forward, important legal questions may arise not from any single regulation or agency, but from the interaction of regulation, infrastructure, contracts and changing energy policy.

For counsel, developers and investors, that is where the legal crossroads begin.

title: Leading small modular nuclear reactor will be late and over budget - Canary Media
description:
North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.
The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades.
It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond.
The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX-300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September.
Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades.
text:
North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.

Ontario Power Generation said in a Tuesday earnings release that the first BWRX-300 unit at its Darlington site will not come online by its October 2030 target and will blow past its budget of $7.7 billion Canadian ($5.4 billion U.S.). The utility didn’t share new targets — it’s working on a revised assessment of cost and schedule that it expects ​“to be substantially completed by mid-2027.” It is the project’s second slip: When Ontario Power announced the design in late 2021, it said the reactor could be completed as early as 2028.

The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades. It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond. The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX-300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September. Developer Blue Energy has also started the NRC application process to build a BWRX-300 in Texas.

Unlike other next-gen nuclear designs recently greenlit for construction in the U.S., GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX-300 uses the same light-water technology that undergirds most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet today. It’s designed to produce 300 megawatts of carbon-free electricity — a substantial amount, but far less than a conventional large-scale reactor.

Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades. Just look at the latest nuclear power plants to be completed in the U.S.: Georgia Power’s Vogtle units 3 and 4, both large-scale AP-1000 reactors that came online in 2023 and 2024, took an extra seven years and $17 billion to wrap up.

Nevertheless, nuclear energy is seeing resurgent financial and policy support in North America and elsewhere as demand for electricity — especially carbon-free electricity — rises.

The Darlington project is part of that wave. In total, Ontario Power Generation plans to build four units at a cost of $20.9 billion Canadian, and federal and provincial investment funds have since committed up to $3 billion Canadian for minority stakes in the project. In the U.S., the Biden administration backed nuclear power as an anchor for an emissions-free grid, and both Trump administrations have embraced it under the banner of ​“energy dominance.”

Proponents of SMRs argue that smaller, repeatable designs like the BWRX will be cheaper and faster to build than large-scale reactors. The idea is that mass manufacturing and construction of these reactors will create a sort of learning-curve effect, so even if the first unit is expensive to make, the 100th unit will be far cheaper. But right now, this is only a hypothesis. Just two SMR plants are operating commercially worldwide, in Russia and China, and some in the nuclear industry argue that it’s more economical to stick with big reactors.

Given that the Darlington project is the first attempt at building a BWRX-300, some budget and timeline overruns aren’t surprising. Ontario Power Generation itself said that the update ​“reflects GE Vernova Hitachi (GEVH) Nuclear Energy’s ongoing engineering for its first-of-a-kind SMR, which has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

“GE Vernova Hitachi is committed to working closely with Ontario Power Generation (OPG) and our partners to deliver the Western world’s first commercial SMR,” a GE Vernova Hitachi spokesperson told Canary Media in an emailed statement. ​“While engineering and design maturity are important considerations, as OPG’s update recognizes, there are multiple interconnected contributions across engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”

While overruns are expected for a first-of-its-kind project, their scale matters. If costs or timelines balloon by too much, it could have a chilling effect on the other efforts to develop BWRX-300 reactors. Vogtle offers a cautionary precedent. Even though its second new reactor was 30% cheaper to build than its first, what’s remembered is the project’s enormous overall price tag.

title: Whose Voices Shape Pollution Policy? | News - McCormick School of Engineering

The study also provides a powerful example of how emerging AI tools can help researchers better understand the complex processes that shape government policy.

text:
When it comes to regulating pollution from heavy-duty trucks, economic concerns may carry more weight than climate and public health benefits, according to a Northwestern Engineering study.

In new research, researchers used AI and other computational tools to analyze nearly 5 million words from public comments submitted to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) during the development of emissions standards for heavy-duty vehicles.

Their analysis revealed a striking pattern. The EPA was more likely to acknowledge comments about costs and implementation timelines as well as comments from the trucking industry than concerns around public health and climate change.

These findings raise questions about whether the regulatory process itself could slow progress toward cleaner transportation. The study also provides a powerful example of how emerging AI tools can help researchers better understand the complex processes that shape government policy.

The study was published Nov. 1 in the journal Sustainable Cities and Society.

“Heavy-duty trucks make up 5 percent of vehicles on the road, but they produce 28 percent of greenhouse gas emissions,” said Northwestern’s Amanda Stathopoulos, the study’s senior author. “Because heavy-duty vehicles make a disproportionate impact, we’ve been trying to understand why the transition from diesel to electric isn’t happening. We decided to look into how the EPA weighs opinions from many different stakeholders.

“We found the EPA gives more attention to stakeholders from the heavy-duty vehicle industry regardless of how substantive their public comments were. And, ultimately, the EPA finalized requirements that were softer than originally proposed.”

Stathopoulos is the William Patterson Junior Professor and associate professor of civil and environmental engineering at the McCormick School of Engineering, where she leads the Mobility and Behavior Lab. Deirdre Edward, a former PhD student in Stathopoulos’ research group, is the study’s first author.

Competing comments

Before finalizing major environmental regulations, federal agencies solicit public comments from manufacturers, industry leaders, environmental organizations, public health advocates, and other stakeholders.

“The barrier to entry to submit a comment is basically zero,” Stathopoulos said. “The process is open to essentially anyone who wants to weigh in on proposed regulations. The idea is the EPA will look at those comments to see if they made an error or missed anything. Based on that feedback, they might revise their plans and make a final ruling that becomes official.”

Although diverse opinions help the regulatory process, these groups often have competing priorities. Some emphasize the environmental and health benefits of stricter standards, while others raise concerns about costs, technological feasibility, and whether manufacturers have enough time to comply. Understanding how agencies respond to thousands of pages of feedback is a massive challenge.

Analyzing millions of words

To understand the impact of these comments, the Northwestern team examined the EPA’s Phase 3 greenhouse gas emissions standards for heavy-duty vehicles. Proposed in April 2023 and finalized in March 2024, the Biden-era regulations sought to establish increasingly stringent emissions limits for new trucks and other heavy-duty vehicles. Although the EPA repealed the standards in February 2026, under the Trump administration, the public comments and regulatory responses still provided a valuable case study for how competing interests shape environmental policy.

With thousands of pages of public feedback, the researchers had plenty of material to examine. Stathopoulos’ team analyzed 1,171 unique public comments containing approximately 4.74 million words, along with the EPA’s official written responses.

“The EPA acknowledges some of the comments with written responses,” Stathopoulos said. “But responses are only legally required if the comment is substantive. Otherwise, they are not obligated to answer.”

Rather than manually sorting through the enormous collection of comments and responses, the team developed a computational framework that combined AI with traditional text-analysis techniques.

“If you were to read all of these words, it would take you months,” Stathopoulos said. “We really needed a computational approach to make sense of all the text.”

Mapping different themes

First, the researchers used computational methods to identify recurring themes in the comments, such as environmental benefits, economic costs and implementation challenges. Then, they used an AI language model to analyze the sentiment expressed in the comments. They also used generative AI to evaluate the substantiveness of each comment, distinguishing between general statements and more detailed arguments.

The team then categorized commenters by stakeholder type and compared their submissions with the EPA’s official responses. By examining both sides of the exchange—what stakeholders said and how regulators responded—the researchers were able to identify patterns.

“We could map out the breakdown of different themes,” Stathopoulos said. “That allowed us to visually plot out the discourse and pinpoint agreement or disagreement.”

Not all arguments receive equal attention

The Northwestern team’s analysis revealed significant differences in the issues raised by different stakeholder groups as well as how the EPA addressed those issues. Most notably, the EPA acknowledged comments focused on costs and implementation timelines more frequently than those advocating for climate and public health.

“This pattern persisted even after we accounted for the substance of the comments,” Stathopoulos said. “We could see really strong trends there. Basically, it didn’t matter what heavy-duty vehicle stakeholders talked about. They always got a response.”

Stathopoulos emphasized that this doesn’t necessarily mean that the EPA agreed with those arguments or changed its policies in response. Instead, the findings reveal differences in regulatory attention, raising questions about how agencies balance competing priorities. And those differences could have implications for cities working to reduce freight-related pollution.

“One explanation is that regulators are particularly attentive to stakeholders with greater legal resources, who may be more likely to challenge a regulation if their concerns aren’t addressed,” Stathopoulos said. “Smaller nonprofits and individual citizens don’t necessarily have the same expertise to frame legal arguments. Our approach could help agencies recognize meaningful concerns that otherwise might get overlooked simply because they weren’t expressed with the right legal language.”

title: COP31: Electrification Is Necessary - But Not Sufficient - to End Fossil Fuel Dependence
description:
As governments consider a global electrification target at COP31, they must ensure it supports commitments to renewable energy and transitioning away from fossil fuels – and does not open the door to more fossil gas expansion.
In short: Electrification is essential and the proposed COP31 target deserves support.
That’s why the proposed global target to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 at COP31 is a welcome and important step.
But it also reveals an important distinction between electrification that reduces emissions and electrification that delivers the scale of reductions needed to meet the Paris Agreement’s goals.
Source: IEA Electrification special report How do we get the COP31 electrification target right?
text:
As governments consider a global electrification target at COP31, they must ensure it supports commitments to renewable energy and transitioning away from fossil fuels – and does not open the door to more fossil gas expansion.

In short:

Electrification is essential and the proposed COP31 target deserves support. Electrifying 35% of energy consumption by 2035 can help cut emissions, lower energy costs, expand energy access, and reduce dependence on volatile fossil fuels – but these benefits risk being too little, too late unless it’s done right.

Electrification alone is not enough. IEA research shows that achieving the 35% target under current energy policies would deliver some emissions reductions, but risks driving new fossil gas investment and falls far short of what is needed to course correct towards limiting warming to 1.5°C.

Strong fossil fuel guardrails are therefore critical. The target must be explicitly linked to renewable energy expansion and plans to transition away from fossil fuel production and use, so growing electricity demand does not become another justification for fossil gas expansion. It also must be backed by public finance for the target to be met.

Does electrification alone end fossil fuel dependence?

Electrification is an important tool to tackle the climate crisis. Replacing fossil fuel-powered cars, heating systems, and industrial processes with electricity can meaningfully reduce emissions, improve energy efficiency, and help build a cleaner, more affordable energy system.

According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) special report on electrification, accelerated electrification could save fuel-importing countries more than $400 billion annually by 2035 compared with 2025 levels, while significantly reducing global oil consumption.

That’s why the proposed global target to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 at COP31 is a welcome and important step. But electrification is necessary, not sufficient, to deliver the transition away from fossil fuels. To deliver on its climate promise, governments at COP31 must ensure any commitments on electrification go hand in hand with three essential conditions: rapidly expanding renewable energy, accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels, and public finance supporting implementation and fair accessibility.

What does the International Energy Agency’s research say about electrification?

The IEA’s analysis shows that more rapid electrification to 2035 can deliver emissions reductions, even with an electricity mix based on business-as-usual policies. But it also reveals an important distinction between electrification that reduces emissions and electrification that delivers the scale of reductions needed to meet the Paris Agreement’s goals.

Sources: IEA Electrification special report; IEA World Energy Outlook 2025

According to the IEA:

Meeting the 35% electrification target with the electricity mix implied by current or stated government policies will reduce energy sector carbon-dioxide (CO2) emissions by 20-25% by 2035. In this case, the world would fail to meet the emissions reductions objectives of the 2023 Global Stocktake and the Paris Agreement, and significantly breach 1.5ºC or even 2ºC.

In the IEA’s Net Zero Emissions (NZE) scenario that supports a 1.5ºC aligned pathway, energy-related emissions need to fall by almost 55% by 2035 – with renewable and efficiency solutions scaling up much faster to replace fossil fuels, eliminating the need for any new oil, gas, and coal production beyond existing fields and mines.

Electrification only gets the world close to a long-term 1.5ºC pathway if renewable energy ramps up to both: 1) fully meet added electricity demand and 2) rapidly displace existing gas – and coal-fired electricity supply.

Does more electricity mean more fossil gas?

Unless it is explicitly renewables-based, a high electrification target risks leaving the door open to further fossil gas expansion that is incompatible with climate goals. Under a scenario where the world reaches the 35% electrification target but electricity generation follows the mix implied by current policies, fossil gas use in the power sector could increase by approximately 430 billion cubic meters (bcm) by 2035, rising 30% above today’s levels.

That’s a very different trajectory from the steep decline in fossil gas use required to meet global climate goals. Under the NZE scenario, fossil gas use in the power sector must decline significantly – by 60% (900 bcm) – by 2035, with fossil fuels nearly phased out of the power sector in advanced economies.

Source: IEA Electrification special report

How do we get the COP31 electrification target right?

Securing a clear recognition at COP31 that a 35% electrification target must be powered by renewable energy and accompanied by robust and immediate measures to phase out fossil fuel supply is not just a question of diplomatic language: it is about ensuring the target has integrity, and is not weaponized by the fossil fuel industry to justify expanding fossil gas supply and infrastructure. The point of COP decisions is to send global signals to governments and markets about the collective direction of travel. Let this signal be clear: the future is in renewables powering an electrified global economy, not in fossil gas.

Wealthy countries must lead in transitioning away from fossil fuels and deliver public finance on fair terms so countries across the Global South can expand affordable renewable energy access, strengthen their electricity systems, and support workers and communities through a just transition.

Electrification is a critical part of building a cleaner, more affordable, and more secure energy future. The proposed COP31 target can help accelerate that shift, but it must be done in a way that is fair and supports fossil fuel phaseout.

text:
Climate mandates collide with economic reality in Britain.

This week it seems that another Net Zero domino will fall. The Government is reported to be on the point of announcing that the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which lays down targets for the sale of new cars, will be watered down. This follows a consultation launched in August. At present, manufacturers are under an obligation to ensure that a rising percentage of their vehicles are pure electric or else face punitive fines of up to £12,000 for every petrol and diesel vehicle they sell over the limit. The required proportion rises from 33% in 2026 to 80% in 2030 and thereafter to 100% by 2035, at which point even hybrids will be banned. The UK car industry is falling well short of the targets, in spite of offering large incentives on electric vehicles. 26.6% of new cars sold in Britain so far this year have been pure electric. The industry also fell short of the 22% and 28% targets in 2024 and 2025 but largely avoided fines because of get-out clauses which made some allowance for increased hybrid sales.

Actually, the situation for UK manufacturers is more dire than the above figures suggest. A growing share of electric vehicle sales are coming from Chinese manufacturers who are able to undercut European ones, thanks in part to China’s dominance in battery manufacturing. Jaecoo accounted for 1.2% of the UK market in 2025 and 3.4% so far in 2026. BYD increased its market share from 2.3% to 3.9% over the same period. In other words, European manufacturers are falling shorter of the ZEV target than the overall figures suggest. It is becoming painfully clear that a continuation of the ZEV mandate on its current trajectory is going to cause further serious damage, if not deliver a fatal blow to UK car manufacturing. Some ministers, including Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, are said to favour reducing the 2030 target to 50%.

Unsurprisingly, Labour’s Net Zero fundamentalists such as Ed Miliband are reported to be against reducing the target. But the issue is complicated by Andy Burnham’s negotiations for a reset of Britain’s relations with the EU. Electric vehicles represent one area in which UK regulation, post-Brexit, has been more stringent than EU regulation. EU rules already allow for a small proportion of cars manufactured after 2035 to have internal combustion engines. The European Parliament’s Environment Committee last week voted for a further relaxation. If Burnham signs up for a deal which forces Britain into “dynamic alignment” with EU regulations, it will almost certainly mean us having to adopt the same EV targets as the EU. Labour ministers who are both Europhile and Net Zero fundamentalists are going to have to choose what is most important to them.

But there is something even more significant to be drawn from the revision of ZEV targets. Virtually every interim target on the way to the Government’s overall, legally binding 2050 Net Zero target is being abandoned, or relaxed, as it flies headlong into reality. New oil-fired boilers were due to be banned from 2026, gas-fired boilers by 2035. There were going to be 600,000 heat pump installations a year by 2028.

All these targets have gone, once it became clear that they could not be met. Moreover, the electricity grid was going to be fully decarbonised by 2030; that target has already been subtly downgraded to 95% carbon-free and is coming under constant pressure. Another target soon to go will likely be the one requiring 10% of jet fuel used by airlines to be Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) by 2030. The Government confirmed this target last month, but as with ZEV, the use of SAF is running well behind track.

Yet at the same time the Government continues to insist that it remains committed to its overall Net Zero target of 2050. But how does it expect to be able to achieve that when it is on a trajectory well short of what it used to think was necessary to achieve this? The year 2050, perhaps, still lies such a distance into the future that the current generation of ministers and MPs feel they don’t need to worry about it too much. At some point, though, the 2050 Net Zero target is going to reach a crunch point at which it has to be relaxed, if not abandoned altogether. I doubt the current Government will want to make the call, but I will give the 2050 Net Zero target until 2030 at the latest.

description:
