description:
Carbon Resources and South Korea-based Cosmo AM&T will jointly set up a ₹4,000-crore battery raw materials manufacturing facility at Naidupeta in the Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh.
Kolkata-based Carbon Resources Private Ltd, a partner in the joint venture, already operates a calcined petroleum coke manufacturing facility at Bobbili in Vizianagaram district.
The proposed facility is expected to strengthen the domestic availability of critical raw materials required for battery manufacturing and reduce India’s dependence on imports.
“Our objective is to develop Andhra Pradesh into a leading hub for electric vehicle and battery manufacturing in the country.
Carbon Resources Group Managing Director Abhinav Kumar Jalan, Cosmo AM&T Vice-President Duke Kyu Park, General Manager Byungdae Kim, Aman Kapoor and Seung Jong Lee, among others, attended the meeting.
text:
Carbon Resources and South Korea-based Cosmo AM&T will jointly set up a ₹4,000-crore battery raw materials manufacturing facility at Naidupeta in the Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh. The proposed facility, to be established under the name Carbon Cosmo Advanced Materials Private Ltd, is expected to generate direct employment for 700 people and indirect employment opportunities for another 3,500–5,000.

Representatives of Carbon Cosmo met Andhra Pradesh Minister for Education, IT and Electronics Nara Lokesh on Wednesday, ahead of the CII Partnership Summit scheduled to be held here during November 12-13, and discussed the proposed investment, manufacturing capacity and future expansion plans.

The plant will come up on 230 acres at Naidupeta using technology from South Korea’s Cosmo AM&T. It will manufacture Ferric Phosphate (FP) and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) cathode materials, which are key raw materials used in lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles and other applications.

Three phases

The company plans to execute the project in three phases. The first phase, with an annual production capacity of 30,000 tonnes each of Ferric Phosphate and Lithium Iron Phosphate, is expected to be operational by mid-2028. The third and final phase is targeted for completion by 2031, when the facility is expected to reach full-scale production.

Upon completion of all three phases, the plant will have an annual production capacity of 1.8 lakh tonnes each of Ferric Phosphate and Lithium Iron Phosphate. Of the total output, up to 1.3 lakh tonnes a year could be exported. Kolkata-based Carbon Resources Private Ltd, a partner in the joint venture, already operates a calcined petroleum coke manufacturing facility at Bobbili in Vizianagaram district.

Its South Korean partner, Cosmo AM&T, is an internationally recognised manufacturer of battery cathode materials, and supplies its products to leading battery manufacturers, including Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution.

The proposed facility is expected to strengthen the domestic availability of critical raw materials required for battery manufacturing and reduce India’s dependence on imports.

Focusing on research

During the meeting, Lokesh emphasised the need to focus on research and technological development alongside manufacturing. He suggested that the company explore the possibility of setting up a dedicated laboratory in collaboration with IIT Tirupati to undertake research on quality testing of battery cathode materials and recycling technologies to recover valuable materials from used batteries.

“Our objective is to develop Andhra Pradesh into a leading hub for electric vehicle and battery manufacturing in the country. The State Government will extend all necessary support for setting up this industry,” he said.

Carbon Resources Group Managing Director Abhinav Kumar Jalan, Cosmo AM&T Vice-President Duke Kyu Park, General Manager Byungdae Kim, Aman Kapoor and Seung Jong Lee, among others, attended the meeting.

title: Losing money on every EV sold?… 'Kia' chooses market share over profit - 머니투데이
description:
The company's strategy is to secure EV market share first, even at the expense of immediate profits, and then offset losses with its hybrid vehicles.
This resulted from widening discounts after U.S. EV demand softened following the expiration of tax credits.
Based on this, Kia's U.S. EV sales last month reached 3,649 units, a 174.2% increase year-on-year.
This calculation stems from the belief that securing market share early as the EV market grows will allow for lower costs through economies of scale.
An industry official explained, "If you lose market share when the EV market is growing, it is difficult to regain it."
text:
Kia is facing growing profitability pressures in the U.S. and domestic markets as it ramps up electric vehicle (EV) sales. The company's strategy is to secure EV market share first, even at the expense of immediate profits, and then offset losses with its hybrid vehicles.

According to industry sources on the 11th, Kia's per-vehicle incentives in the U.S. are $1,800 for internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles and $2,000 for hybrids. For EVs, the incentive is $12,000, six times that of hybrids. This resulted from widening discounts after U.S. EV demand softened following the expiration of tax credits.

The burden is significant even when compared to the U.S. market average. According to Kelley Blue Book, a U.S. automotive pricing information firm, the average incentive for EVs in the U.S. was approximately $6,100 per vehicle in September last month, equivalent to 11% of the transaction price. Kia is spending nearly twice the industry average. Last month, Kia focused on expanding sales by offering cash discounts of up to $10,000 for the EV9 and $5,000 for the EV6. Based on this, Kia's U.S. EV sales last month reached 3,649 units, a 174.2% increase year-on-year.

Domestically, Kia has also seen profitability decline as it lowered prices to boost sales. After Tesla's market share rose, Kia cut its EV prices in the second quarter. Since then, the domestic market has become the area where Kia's EVs post the largest losses. Sales have surged significantly, allowing Kia to surpass 100,000 annual EV sales for the first time among global automakers this year.

In Europe, unlike in Korea and the U.S., Kia is generating profits from its EVs. Europe is Kia's largest market, accounting for 50% of its EV sales. The shares for Korea and the U.S. are 25% and 8%, respectively. In Europe as well, Kia increased incentives by approximately 1,000 euros in the second quarter to compete with Chinese manufacturers, but it maintained a profitable structure. The price gap with Chinese EVs has narrowed from 30% to around 15%.

For now, Kia is prioritizing sales expansion over profit. This calculation stems from the belief that securing market share early as the EV market grows will allow for lower costs through economies of scale. It appears Kia is filling the gap in EV profits with its hybrid vehicles. Hybrids are highly profitable and are seeing concentrated demand in the U.S. Kia's U.S. hybrid sales last month reached 27,409 units, more than double the figure for the same period last year.

Kia is also working to reduce EV costs. Specifically, it plans to cut the costs of key components such as batteries, motors, and heat pumps by approximately 10% annually over three years. The goal is to improve EV profitability within two to three years by simultaneously expanding sales and reducing costs. Kia believes that once the burden of raw material prices and the impact of Middle East conflicts subside, it can restore its operating profit margin to the high 7% or around 8% level next year.

An industry official explained, "If you lose market share when the EV market is growing, it is difficult to regain it." The official added, "It was judged that maintaining sales volume, even if profitability drops slightly, is better for future growth." They continued, "The key is how quickly we can lower EV costs while holding on with hybrids."

Waiver request seeks partial relief from 2027 renewable fuel blending obligations

Governors say RFS adds costs to every gallon of gasoline and diesel sold

Biofuel advocates say cheaper ethanol expands gasoline supply and reduces pump costs

The Republican governors of Alabama and Louisiana petitioned the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to grant partial waivers from renewable fuel blending obligations in 2027, saying it would help lower gas prices.

In a November 9 letter to EPA administrator Lee Zeldin, Alabama Governor Kay Ivey and Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said the Renewable Fuel Standard, which requires fuels sold in the US to contain a minimum volume of renewable fuels blended in them, causes severe economic harm by raising fuel prices.

The governors said White House actions including deferring the federal excise tax on dyed diesel, pressuring European nations to release 100 million barrels from reserves and rejecting an export ban, along with state-level measures, had helped ease price pressures but that more was needed.

The request follows EPA's most aggressive biofuel blending requirements set for 2026 and 2027.

Ivey and Landry said the program's compliance costs result in higher fuel prices.

Biofuel advocates argue ethanol lowers fuel costs and boosts gasoline supplies.

The EPA "evaluates petitions the agency receives in accordance with applicable laws and regulations," it said.

The American Soybean Association said waiving compliance would hurt farm incomes and rural economies, calling it a "giveaway to refineries that are making record profits while U.S. agriculture would be left holding the bag."

title: EV owners could face a new $130 annual federal fee as soon as December | Nation
description: Electric car owners could be forced to start paying an annual national fee as soon as next month if Congress passes legislation containing the tax.
text:
Electric car owners could be forced to start paying an annual national fee as soon as next month if Congress passes legislation containing the tax.

The EV fee was proposed to help pay for roads and would start at $130 annually. The measure was part of a bipartisan draft of a transportation funding bill that the U.S. House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee is considering. Under the proposed legislation, dubbed the BUILD America 250 Act, the fee can be increased by $5 each year until it hits a max of $150 annually. Plug-in hybrid owners would be hit with a $35 fee starting in October that can be increased to as much as $50 by the end of the legislation in 2031.

The proposed fee is included in a larger bill to reauthorize surface transportation funding that is currently set to expire on Dec. 11. The measure was approved by the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, but it has not been approved by the full House or Senate.

The last transportation funding measure approved by Congress was signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021.

With progress on the larger transportation bill that includes the proposed EV fee stalled thus far, Congress passed a temporary extension of federal government funding that extends spending until Dec. 11, according to the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), a nonpartisan and nonprofit organization that advocates for consistent transportation funding.

AASHTO said the temporary transportation funding bill allowed lawmakers to "prevent a federal government shutdown" and "continue Highway Trust Fund programs and annually appropriated general fund programs" at 2026 fiscal year levels until the new December deadline.

That means EV drivers could be forced to start paying the proposed national fee in December.

The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.

Why is Congress considering adding an EV fee?

The federal government currently collects 18.4 cents per gallon on every U.S. gasoline purchase to help pay for road and transit construction projects, and most states also tack on their own fees. EV drivers don’t pay that tax because their vehicles don’t use gasoline.

The money goes into the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Highway Trust Fund and is then distributed to states to help pay for road and transit construction projects. As cars have become more fuel-efficient and more drivers have opted for EVs and hybrids, less money per mile driven has been collected despite increased use of roads. Lawmakers have looked for ways to close that growing gap in federal gasâtax revenue.

The federal gas tax hasn't increased since 1993, and it brings in about $40 billion a year at its current level, according to the Tax Policy Center. President Donald Trump and some lawmakers in Congress have recently proposed suspending the federal gas tax as the average price of gas hovers around $4 per gallon, according to the AAA Auto Club.

The federal government typically spends about $60 billion on transportation projects, and infrastructure advocates say that amount is just enough to maintain the nation's roads and transit systems. Most states also levy their own gas taxes to fund local road projects.

Supporters of the proposed fee say it's time for EV drivers to contribute to the fund that helps pay for the upkeep of the roads they use. Rep. Sam Graves, a Republican from Missouri who chairs the U.S. House Transportation Committee, said in a statement that the EV fee "ensures that electric vehicle owners begin paying their fair share for the use of our roads."

Rep. Rick Larsen, a Washington state lawmaker who is the top Democrat on the panel, said the bipartisan highway bill agreement represents "a commitment to bipartisan lawmaking means finding compromise."

How would the new EV tax be collected?

Electric vehicle owners would have to pay the new fee when they register their cars. The proposal differs from other ideas that have been floated to replace gas tax money that isn't collected from EV drivers, including mileage-based proposals.

Vehicle-miles-traveled, or VMT, programs tax drivers based on miles they drive on U.S. roads instead of how much gasoline they purchase. Mileage-based road tax proposals have long been controversial in U.S. transportation funding debates because critics question how the government would monitor drivers' traveling habits without infringing on their privacy.

Supporters of the current highway bill draft note that the EV tax proposal would involve no tracking or reporting from drivers about their travels. EV owners would simply pay the $130 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.

What would the new fee mean for EV owners?

Electric vehicle owners save an average of about $8,811 in ownership and maintenance costs over 200,000 miles compared with owners of best-selling gas-powered vehicles in the same class, according to Consumer Reports.

A driver who opts for a new or used EV could save $2,200 annually on gas, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Hybrid drivers can save $1,500 on gas each year, according to the agency.

A new $130 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings. EV supporters have argued that additional annual fees increase the cost of owning an electric vehicle.

When state lawmakers in South Carolina were considering a new user fee for EV owners of 4.5 cents per kilowatt-hour on electricity consumed at publicly accessible charging stations, the Electrification Coalition, which lobbies for EV-friendly policies, said in a February 2026 statement that the state's proposal "imposes significant additional costs on EV drivers without increasing the state gasoline tax."

Keith Laing is an automotive reporter on the National Trending Desk at USA TODAY. Contact Keith at klaing@usatodayco.com .

text:
Duke Energy, the electric utility that controls nearly all of North Carolina’s power generation, is pushing forward with a natural gas buildout intended to support a deluge of new data centers.

The utility checked off a crucial step in that process Monday evening, when the Davidson County Board of Commissioners approved a rezoning request from Duke to build a liquified natural gas storage facility along the Yadkin River near Lexington.

The county board split over the zoning change, which passed on a 4-3 vote. A grassroots group, fueled in part by public skepticism of data centers, led opposition to the project in partnership with several environmental advocacy organizations.

One of those organizations, the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, sent the Davidson commissioners a 17-page letter last week arguing that the proposed project conflicts with the county’s land use policies.

Aiswarya Murali, a staff attorney for SCSJ, explained that state statute requires counties to assess whether a rezoning request is consistent with its adopted land development plan.

“Based on our analysis, it is a clear ‘no,’” Murali told Carolina Public Press.

“The land development plan very clearly commits to preserving agricultural land, protecting natural resources, as well as locating industrial development in appropriate places.”

Murali cited air and water pollution, industrial noise, light pollution and burden to neighboring property owners through easements and land acquisitions as potential consequences of the project.

Ultimately, the commissioners narrowly sided with Duke, which assured them of the safety of liquified natural gas and touted the jobs and taxes the facility would bring. Board chair Karen Watford referenced recent power outages in Thomasville as a reason for her aye vote.

“I think about that little old lady down the street, your grandmother on the other side of the county, them losing power for long periods of time and possibly dying because of it,” Watford said.

“I think we need this.”

Commissioner Tripp Kester disagreed.

“The way I look at it is, ‘Is this in the public interest?’” Kester said.

“From everything I’ve heard in the last week … obviously they ain’t interested, and they don’t want it. And I can’t support it.”

Power plants await scrutiny from NC regulators

The rezoning request was for 1,600 acres of land that previously had been designated as a rural agricultural area. Duke Energy has owned the land for decades but hasn’t done much with it other than lease it out to a hunting club.

Now, Duke sees that parcel as a crucial part of a project it’s calling the Davie-Davidson Energy Complex. The company is currently seeking approval for two gas-fired power plants in Davie County. In neighboring Davidson County, it wants to build a liquified natural gas storage facility to support those power plants.

Davie and Davidson are bisected by the Yadkin River. Duke plans to connect the power plants and the storage facility with a pipeline which will run under the river. But before any of those proposed facilities can be built, they need to be approved by state regulators.

If recent history is any tell, approval is far from guaranteed.

The North Carolina Utilities Commission, which consists of five appointed members, must give the go-ahead when it votes later this year to finalize Duke’s integrated resource plan. That’s the biennial document that lays out how much new power generation Duke is permitted to build based on projected demand.

In September, the Utilities Commission blocked Duke’s attempt to build a separate gas-powered power plant in Richmond County, calling its permit application “premature” given that the commission was still reviewing the utility’s integrated resource plan.

Duke had tried to circumvent the traditional timeline and get approval for the power plant before its resource plan had been finalized. The company said it did so because any delay in getting new power plants approved could result in higher construction costs and difficulty meeting increased demand from “large-load” users such as data centers.

The Utilities Commission didn’t buy the argument, writing in its order that potentially higher construction costs didn’t necessitate expedited approval of a project that was certain to raise customers’ rates.

The commission also questioned the accuracy of Duke’s projections, which suggested that electricity demand would spike in the coming years. Approval of the Richmond plant would “impose a significant risk that new generation is approved before the need for that generation is determined,” the commission wrote.

Clean energy advocates criticize pivot to natural gas

The Davie-Davidson and Richmond projects are part of a larger push by Duke to increase its power generation through natural gas. It is currently building gas-fired facilities in Catawba County and Person County, which are expected to come online by 2029 and 2030, respectively.

Natural gas is primarily methane, a greenhouse gas. It is generally considered a cleaner energy source compared to other fossil fuels, such as coal, but it isn’t “zero emission.”

According to Shelley Robbins of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, the reason for Duke’s shift to natural gas is simple.

“Money, money, money,” Robbins said.

Of course, that is not Duke’s position. The company has told regulators that electricity demand is rising in the era of artificial intelligence, and it is merely trying to keep up.

Duke is statutorily obligated to go carbon-neutral by 2050, but renewable energy sources like wind and solar aren’t far along enough to meet the short-term needs. In the interim, it has ramped up development of natural gas facilities and delayed the sunsetting of its coal-fired plants.

New data centers make up most of the increased demand for electricity, but Duke has also been upfront about its efforts to recruit these projects to North Carolina. That makes for a sort of chicken-and-the-egg problem, Robbins said.

Organizations like the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy have criticized Duke for prioritizing its business interests over its customers. Ratepayers are facing a 9.5% increase in their electric bills next year, and that price hike didn’t even account for the potential cost of proposed projects like the ones in Davie and Davidson.

Earlier this year, Duke proposed a “large-load tariff,” which would lock in data centers and other large-load consumers into long-term contracts and require them to pay for any upgrades needed to connect them to the electric grid. The tariff, Duke said, was intended to shield ordinary consumers from having to pay for the energy costs associated with data centers.

However, Robbins pointed out that the proposed tariff doesn’t cover the cost of new power generation, only upgrades to the electric grid.

“These two plants (in Davie County) would not be built but for data centers,” Robbins said.

“The rest of us, we will be paying for data center generation in the form of these large combined cycles.”

text:
As tech companies and President Donald Trump’s administration continue pushing to build out more data centers to drive artificial intelligence development, some proposals are looking to move these facilities underwater.

Scientific American reported Oct. 27 that the Trump Administration is considering proposals for underwater data centers in Cook Inlet, Alaska, and the Gulf of Maine.

While the preliminary permits requested by DeepGreen Holdings LLC would not give the company permission to begin construction, tribal nations and environmental groups have come out in opposition to the proposals, raising concerns about the impacts they could have on ocean temperatures and marine life, including two separate species of endangered whales that live and hunt at the project sites.

There are very few underwater data centers in operation across the globe. While Microsoft previously deployed an underwater data center near Scotland’s Orkney Islands to study the feasibility of underwater data centers, the company shuttered the project, with Noelle Walsh, the president of Microsoft cloud operations and innovation, telling Data Center Dynamics in 2024, “I’m not building subsea data centers anywhere in the world.”

There are also two underwater data centers operating along the coast of China.

While mainland data centers have drawn concerns over their heavy electricity and water usage needed to cool to servers they contain, offshore data centers can use the water they’re immersed in to help cool the equipment.

Although the Great Lakes have yet to draw any proposals for underwater data centers, the region has proven attractive for the facilities due to its plentiful freshwater resources.

In response, environmental groups and policy experts have put together several recommendations and frameworks for addressing the influx of data center proposals, with the Alliance for the Great Lakes, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region’s waters, stressing that Great Lakes states are in need of a plan when it comes to managing increasing water use.

However, if a company were to propose a data center within the Great Lakes, there are guardrails in place, Helena Volzer, the alliance’s director of water resources, told Michigan Advance. While each state does things differently there generally needs to be some kind of permit approval for anything placed on the bottomlands of the Great Lakes, Volzer explained.

In addition to state-level permits, there would also need to be permits from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the federal government, Volzer explained.

While speaking with the Advance, Miyoko Sakashita, the oceans program director at the Center for Biological Diversity, noted that any federal permits also need to comply with the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act.

Volzer also pointed to public opposition to data centers within the region as another barrier a hypothetical Great Lakes data center would need to overcome.

“I think if there’s resistance to building them on land for all of the resource reasons, I can only imagine the resistance there might be to building within the lakes themselves,” Volzer said.

As far as the environmental impacts, Volzer pointed to the warming of nearby waters as one key concern.

“Even in an ocean, you still have that concern. But in a sensitive freshwater ecosystem like the lakes, I would think that would be of even more concern,” Volzer said, noting how warming waters have exacerbated issues with harmful algal blooms in Lake Erie.

Temperature changes can also harm fish populations, Volzer noted, explaining that when fish get accustomed to warmer waters, drops in temperature can kill them.

Sakashita pointed to habitat impacts and noise pollution as major concerns in the center’s opposition to the proposed data centers in Maine and Alaska.

“Many animals are very sensitive to noise for their communication or migration or hunting for food and things like that,” Sakashita said.

Construction of an underwater data center would also carry its own risks for pollution and disrupting the ecosystem, Sakashita explained.

Both Volzer and Sakashita noted that depending on the design of the data center, these developments could contain harmful chemicals that could pollute the waters.

Additionally, the energy source used by the data center could contribute to other environmental impacts, Sakashita explained, noting that the large amounts of power demanded by data centers could result in massive amounts of greenhouse gas pollution if they are powered by fossil fuels.

The data centers in Maine and Alaska would be powered by tidal turbines if constructed. Sakashita noted that turbines can trap animal species and kill small organisms like zooplankton, which could hurt the amount of prey available for other species.

While Volzer was skeptical of the possibility and the feasibility of a data center making its way into the Great Lakes due to the costs, the public perceptions, and the regulations in place, Sakashita warned that those guardrails are under threat.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, proposed in the U.S. Senate, contains rollbacks to the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act, Sakashita explained, noting that tribal nations and states like Michigan could lose their authority over projects like an underwater data center if the bill becomes law.

“It’s really important for us to safeguard our bedrock environmental laws because they do give us some tools to make sure that projects like this are not doing a lot of damage to endangered species or to our habitats that are really important for wildlife,” Sakashita said.

The green light for two major offshore wind projects has been welcomed by Prospect, as they will support thousands of jobs, as well as enhance our energy security, while bringing down emissions and bills for consumers.

Renewable giant company, RWE, together with global investment firm KKR, have announced a total investment of £12 billion, believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history.

This gives the green light to the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms in the North Sea, which aim to be operational by 2030.

The projects will support more than 2,400 jobs during construction and operation, and once operational they will be able to power around three million UK homes with clean energy.

In addition, SSE has announced that the latest phase of its major offshore wind farm, Berwick Bank B, will support 2,600 skilled jobs in manufacturing, engineering and project delivery across the north of England and Scotland, after they contracted Siemens Energy for the manufacturing of wind turbines and substation platforms.

When fully operation, Berwick Bank B could become one of the largest wind farms in the world and could generate 6% of the UK’s current electricity demands.

The flurry of renewable energy announcements comes as the Prime Minister Andy Burnham prepares to attend the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Turkey.

Prospect Senior Deputy General Secretary, Sue Ferns OBE, said:

“The future of our energy mix needs to be both cleaner and cheaper, and these projects have real potential to enhance our energy security while bearing down on bills and emissions.

“This government has supported trade union efforts to ensure that new jobs created in renewables are good quality, unionised jobs, and we are pleased that the government’s Fair Work Charter is in place across offshore wind.

“We must not allow our energy transition to stall, and government needs to use every lever possible to tackle the bottlenecks in our energy system, such as lack of grid capacity.”

title: At COP31, Turkey pushes zero-waste plan to curb climate change - ClickOnDetroit
authors: Suzan Fraser, Sibi Arasu, Victoria Milko And Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press, Suzan Fraser, Sibi Arasu
description:
Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference.
While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge.
Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.
Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.
“Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation.
text:
ANTALYA – As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025.

"Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste."

Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference.

Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled.

“Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion.

If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat.

Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record.

“The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.”

Methane cuts might slow global warming

As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action.

The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds.

While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.

Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.

“Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation.

Circular economy may dent emissions, but challenges remain

A circular economy — an economic model that generally prioritizes recycling and other regenerative approaches that create less waste— would help reduce emissions, but not every country has the resources to take such steps.

Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions."

But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack.

“Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press.

The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies.

The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050.

Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. The technology and infrastructure needed to recycle these materials are also concentrated in a handful of nations, like China. The European Union and the U.S. will likely only have the capacity to recycle 30% of their raw materials by 2040, according to the IEA.

“We must do a better job with our materials retrieval, reuse and recycling,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. She stressed the need to create incentives for “retrieving the materials, taking things apart, being able to reuse them again in a circular way.”

___

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India, Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan and Delgado from Bangkok.

Dive Brief:

Honda on Monday announced a $3 billion plant for Central Ohio, near its original Marysville plant and positioned “to meet growing customer demand for hybrid vehicles in North America,” per a press release.

Intended to accelerate the production of hybrid vehicles and the engines and hybrid systems that power them, the new plant is part of a broader set of investments at Honda operations in Ohio, Alabama and Georgia.

The new Ohio plant will offer an annual capacity of 240,000 vehicles, creating more than 2,000 jobs. It’s set to start production in 2029 pending final government approvals.

Dive Insight:

With other projects underway, Honda says it helps create “an integrated manufacturing network for future hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles,” boosting Honda’s annual U.S. production capacity to about 1.3 million vehicles and its total North American capacity to about 1.9 million units.

After the expansion, Honda’s U.S. production capacity will span plants in Ohio, Alabama, and Georgia, and the new plant and investments will effectively boost Honda’s hybrid production capacity in Ohio by 250%, according to the automaker.

Alongside the U.S. investments, Honda also made a corresponding 166 million Canadian dollar ($118 million) capital investment in Honda’s Canadian manufacturing facilities. It’s part of a broader 867 million Canadian dollar commitment to maintaining the automaker’s workforce of more than 4,000 in Canada and emphasizing “an integrated North American production network.”

Honda confirmed that it plans future investments in its Alliston, Ontario plant to support next-generation hybrid and gasoline models, including the reintroduction of engine manufacturing.

The new Ohio plant will be located between the existing East Liberty and Marysville plants, and Honda said that it “will be one of the most advanced in the world when it comes online in 2029 with leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies, and flexible production systems to improve efficiency, quality and competitiveness.”

The automaker explained in its release that Ohio was selected for this plant due to a multitude of factors, including proximity to its U.S. supplier base, nearby development operations, existing manufacturing plants, and its L-H Battery Company, which started as a joint venture with LG and is now set to supply batteries for hybrids and EVs.

Honda was the first Japanese automaker to build products in the U.S. It started making motorcycles at Marysville in 1979 and started car production there in 1982.

Honda underscored that the new plant is just part of a broader set of investments in U.S. manufacturing that will help expand and strengthen an integrated local production network.

The company pointed to corresponding investments in its Alabama Auto Plant to increase capacity, allowing more flexibility in making the Passport SUV and expanding production of a new V-6 hybrid engine at an adjacent plant.

Honda is also retooling its transmission plant in Ohio to make two hybrid systems for compact and midsize vehicles in North America. That facility will serve as the lead plant for the larger of the two hybrid systems, per the release.

For the new plant in Ohio, Honda pointed to close collaboration with its R&D and manufacturing teams as aspects that will help strengthen Honda’s long-term competitiveness in North America. In February, after reporting a $1.7 billion operating loss over nine months amid shifts in U.S. electric vehicle policy, the company confirmed plans to shift automobile and software-defined vehicle development to Honda R&D so that it could respond “flexibly and swiftly” to market changes.

Honda at that time cited “decelerating market growth” for EVs, following on a shift that started in May 2025 when it pivoted toward expanding its hybrid lineup and reducing EV investments by $21 billion.

Georgia residents are angry at the state’s unchecked data center boom and rising electric bills — and they voted accordingly in last week’s election.
In December 2025, the Republican-led PSC approved Georgia Power’s plan to build nearly 10 gigawatts of new gas-fired power plants and batteries to serve proposed data centers.
Those concerns were heightened earlier this year when OpenAI revealed its plans for a 3.2-GW data center in southeast Georgia.

But to date, Georgia Power has made little progress on enacting this plan, even as it has pushed ahead to expand the scope of its fossil-gas power plant buildout.
text:
Georgia residents are angry at the state’s unchecked data center boom and rising electric bills — and they voted accordingly in last week’s election.

Democrats won every statewide race in Georgia, including two seats on the Public Service Commission. Republicans had held a majority at the powerful utility regulator for 30 years.

The winning candidates, Commissioner-elect Shelia Edwards and reelected Commissioner Peter Hubbard, have made clear that their top priority is to rein in rising electricity bills from Georgia Power, the state’s biggest utility. That likely means the new Democratic majority will challenge Georgia Power’s plans to enact one of the largest fossil-fuel expansions in the nation.

In December 2025, the Republican-led PSC approved Georgia Power’s plan to build nearly 10 gigawatts of new gas-fired power plants and batteries to serve proposed data centers. It did so despite recommendations from commission staff to approve only about one-third of that capacity right away, given the speculative nature of the data center growth projections that the utility used to justify its buildout.

All three Democrats on the five-member commission have signaled opposition to those plans. The two Democrats already on the commission, Hubbard and Alicia Johnson, tried earlier this year to get the PSC to reconsider the planned gas buildout but were thwarted by the GOP majority.

The five new gas-burning plants planned as part of that buildout could cost customers an estimated $50 billion to $60 billion over their multi-decade lifespan and lock in significant amounts of new greenhouse gas emissions, according to estimates from the Southern Environmental Law Center. Hubbard, who worked for 16 years in utility planning and renewable energy project development, has conducted his own analysis that found a ​“cost-optimized portfolio” prioritizing solar, batteries, and energy efficiency could meet expected demand and save billions of dollars compared to the utility’s gas-heavy approach.

Georgia Power’s expensive gas buildout would exacerbate the affordability challenges its customers already face.

The PSC has approved six rate hikes from Georgia Power in the past few years, increasing typical residential utility bills by 33%, or more than $500 a year on average. The utility, which earns a set rate of return on what regulators allow it to spend on power plants, has seen profits swell over that same time.

“Georgia Power is making billions while Georgia families are struggling,” Edwards, who owns a communications consulting firm, said during an Oct. 28 press event hosted by the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, a nonprofit advocacy group. ​“Something is fundamentally wrong with that picture.”

Controlling data center costs — and making them pay their own way

In February, the PSC voted 3–2 against a motion brought by environmental advocates to reconsider the 10-GW gas buildout, with Hubbard and Johnson voting to block the expansion. The Democratic commissioners argued that the utility had failed to prove that data center growth justified the cost.

Nor was their opposition enough to discourage Georgia Power. Just months later, in April, the utility submitted a new request to the PSC seeking permission to add somewhere between 2 GW and 6 GW of additional ​“dispatchable capacity resources.” Utility critics fear this new round will also tilt toward a preponderance of gas power plants instead of solar, batteries, or other cleaner options.

Georgia Power says that its broader customer base will be insulated from cost increases related to its gas buildout, and that growing electricity sales will put ​“downward pressure” on customer rates.

Last year, the all-Republican commission approved a rule that would allow Georgia Power to force data centers and other large customers to cover the costs of the new power plants and grid infrastructure built to serve them. Other utilities and state regulators have made similar pledges via ​“large load tariffs” meant to force data center developers to commit to paying a significant portion of their costs if they don’t get built or shut down early.

“We know our customers depend on us to keep energy reliable and affordable for their homes and businesses,” Rick Anderson, the utility’s senior vice president and senior production officer, said in an April announcement. ​“As we continue to invest in diverse, flexible generation resources, we also continue to work with new large-load customers who are driving much of this growth on appropriate contracts that are designed to cover the cost to serve them.”

But the utility’s critics say it has failed to prove that its contracts with data centers really do protect customers. They also contend that the Republican majority on the commission has rebuffed repeated demands for more transparency into how the requirements might be enforced.

Those concerns were heightened earlier this year when OpenAI revealed its plans for a 3.2-GW data center in southeast Georgia.

The PSC’s three Republican commissioners outvoted Hubbard and Johnson to approve that contract in August, despite concerns that Georgia Power had failed to publicly reveal the terms under which OpenAI would be held responsible for paying the cost of the utility’s investment in grid and power plant infrastructure to serve it.

The few details that Georgia Power has since disclosed haven’t allayed those concerns, said Maggie Shober, research director at the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. ​“They have a statement saying, ​‘The customer pays its full cost over the life of the contract,’ but no information on minimum bills, termination service, exit fees. It’s just, ​‘Trust us, guys,’” she said.

But trust is hard to come by these days. Last week’s election made clear just how large a swath of the public has turned against data centers. In the past few weeks, investors have started doing so as well. Shares of AI-related companies have lost trillions of dollars of value over the past four weeks.

Energy experts have proposed that utilities should seek out alternative resources — solar-charged batteries and virtual power plants, among them — that offer more flexibility and less risk than power plants, which take 30 to 40 years to pay off.

During the Oct. 28 press event, Hubbard said he intended to use his analysis along these lines ​“to push back on these power plants that Georgia Power is putting in front of us.”

The PSC’s new Democratic majority has options. It can launch proceedings demanding the utility ​“take into account the climate change impacts and the costs” of the December procurement plan, Hubbard said. It can also interrogate Georgia Power’s April proposal for up to 6 GW of additional capacity. ​“That’s an opportunity right there to engage and say, ​‘This is the outcome that we want. We don’t want more fossil-fuel power plants. We want clean energy,’” Hubbard said.

Data center companies themselves could help bring these cleaner alternatives online under a plan negotiated between large corporate energy buyers and the utility that was approved by the PSC earlier this year, Shober noted.

But to date, Georgia Power has made little progress on enacting this plan, even as it has pushed ahead to expand the scope of its fossil-gas power plant buildout.

The utility also hasn’t made progress on the distributed solar and battery and virtual power plant programs it agreed to pursue in 2025, said Bob Sherrier, a staff attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center

“Since then, how many gas units have they developed? The priorities have been clear,” he said. With the Democratic majority on the PSC, he added, ​“hopefully they will shift.”

Under its new majority, the commission could also order the utility to provide more transparency into its data center forecasts and apply more stringent requirements for those firms to cover their own costs, he said. ​“We’re going to factor all of this into our analysis.”

Along with its Democratic majority, the commission will also have a supportive partner in Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms. The former Atlanta mayor has promised to issue a temporary moratorium on new data center approvals pending a review of their energy cost and environmental impacts.

“We have to step back and gather that information and come back with a better plan so that people can be at least more willing to look at data centers in not such a negative fashion,” Commissioner-elect Edwards said. ​“The first thing is that they have to pay their own way.”

title: EV owners could face a new $130 annual federal fee as soon as December - Yahoo
description:
The EV fee was proposed to help pay for roads and would start at $130 annually.
The proposed fee is included in a larger bill to reauthorize surface transportation funding that is currently set to expire on Dec. 11.
The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.
EV owners would simply pay the $130 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.
A new $130 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings.
text:
Electric car owners could be forced to start paying an annual national fee as soon as next month if Congress passes legislation containing the tax.

The EV fee was proposed to help pay for roads and would start at $130 annually. The measure was part of a bipartisan draft of a transportation funding bill that the U.S. House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee is considering. Under the proposed legislation, dubbed the BUILD America 250 Act, the fee can be increased by $5 each year until it hits a max of $150 annually. Plug-in hybrid owners would be hit with a $35 fee starting in October that can be increased to as much as $50 by the end of the legislation in 2031.

The proposed fee is included in a larger bill to reauthorize surface transportation funding that is currently set to expire on Dec. 11. The measure was approved by the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, but it has not been approved by the full House or Senate.

The last transportation funding measure approved by Congress was signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021.

With progress on the larger transportation bill that includes the proposed EV fee stalled thus far, Congress passed a temporary extension of federal government funding that extends spending until Dec. 11, according to the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), a nonpartisan and nonprofit organization that advocates for consistent transportation funding.

AASHTO said the temporary transportation funding bill allowed lawmakers to "prevent a federal government shutdown" and "continue Highway Trust Fund programs and annually appropriated general fund programs" at 2026 fiscal year levels until the new December deadline.

That means EV drivers could be forced to start paying the proposed national fee in December.

The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.

Why is Congress considering adding an EV fee?

The federal government currently collects 18.4 cents per gallon on every U.S. gasoline purchase to help pay for road and transit construction projects, and most states also tack on their own fees. EV drivers don't pay that tax because their vehicles don't use gasoline.

The money goes into the U.S. Department of Transportation's Highway Trust Fund and is then distributed to states to help pay for road and transit construction projects. As cars have become more fuel-efficient and more drivers have opted for EVs and hybrids, less money per mile driven has been collected despite increased use of roads. Lawmakers have looked for ways to close that growing gap in federal gas‑tax revenue.

The federal gas tax hasn't increased since 1993, and it brings in about $40 billion a year at its current level, according to the Tax Policy Center. President Donald Trump and some lawmakers in Congress have recently proposed suspending the federal gas tax as the average price of gas hovers around $4 per gallon, according to the AAA Auto Club.

The federal government typically spends about $60 billion on transportation projects, and infrastructure advocates say that amount is just enough to maintain the nation's roads and transit systems. Most states also levy their own gas taxes to fund local road projects.

Supporters of the proposed fee say it's time for EV drivers to contribute to the fund that helps pay for the upkeep of the roads they use. Rep. Sam Graves, a Republican from Missouri who chairs the U.S. House Transportation Committee, said in a statement that the EV fee "ensures that electric vehicle owners begin paying their fair share for the use of our roads."

Rep. Rick Larsen, a Washington state lawmaker who is the top Democrat on the panel, said the bipartisan highway bill agreement represents "a commitment to bipartisan lawmaking means finding compromise."

How would the new EV tax be collected?

Electric vehicle owners would have to pay the new fee when they register their cars. The proposal differs from other ideas that have been floated to replace gas tax money that isn't collected from EV drivers, including mileage-based proposals.

Vehicle-miles-traveled, or VMT, programs tax drivers based on miles they drive on U.S. roads instead of how much gasoline they purchase. Mileage-based road tax proposals have long been controversial in U.S. transportation funding debates because critics question how the government would monitor drivers' traveling habits without infringing on their privacy.

Supporters of the current highway bill draft note that the EV tax proposal would involve no tracking or reporting from drivers about their travels. EV owners would simply pay the $130 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.

What would the new fee mean for EV owners?

Electric vehicle owners save an average of about $8,811 in ownership and maintenance costs over 200,000 miles compared with owners of best-selling gas-powered vehicles in the same class, according to Consumer Reports.

A driver who opts for a new or used EV could save $2,200 annually on gas, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Hybrid drivers can save $1,500 on gas each year, according to the agency.

A new $130 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings. EV supporters have argued that additional annual fees increase the cost of owning an electric vehicle.

When state lawmakers in South Carolina were considering a new user fee for EV owners of 4.5 cents per kilowatt-hour on electricity consumed at publicly accessible charging stations, the Electrification Coalition, which lobbies for EV-friendly policies, said in a February 2026 statement that the state's proposal "imposes significant additional costs on EV drivers without increasing the state gasoline tax."

Keith Laing is an automotive reporter on the National Trending Desk at USA TODAY. Contact Keith at klaing@usatodayco.com.

title: Indonesia Accelerates Energy Transition with Landmark Carbon Market Agreement at COP31
description:
orway and Indonesia sign Indonesia’s first Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, marking a significant milestone in the country’s carbon market implementation.
It represents an important step in translating international carbon market cooperation into practical implementation and mobilizing climate finance for Indonesia’s energy transition.
Through this cooperation, we seek to mobilize carbon finance to support Indonesia’s energy transition and contribute to the achievement of our national climate targets.
By connecting international carbon market cooperation with national energy priorities, the MOPA establishes an important foundation for mobilizing climate finance, scaling up renewable energy investment, strengthening energy security, and accelerating Indonesia’s transition to a low-carbon power system.
The program prioritizes renewable energy generation paired with battery energy storage systems and initially focuses on floating solar photovoltaic technology in Indonesia.
text:
orway and Indonesia sign Indonesia’s first Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, marking a significant milestone in the country’s carbon market implementation.

ANTALYA, TÜRKIYE, November 11, 2026 – Norway and Indonesia have signed a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The agreement is facilitated by GGGI and marks Indonesia’s first MOPA to operationalize Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, representing a significant milestone in the country’s participation in the international carbon markets.

Supported through the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund – a carbon fund hosted under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) – the agreement is expected to be among the largest transactions under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement to date. It represents an important step in translating international carbon market cooperation into practical implementation and mobilizing climate finance for Indonesia’s energy transition.

The signing took place at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31. The agreement signing was witnessed by Moh Jumhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment/Head of Environmental Protection Agency of Indonesia, and Sigrun Aasland, Minister of Climate and Environment of Norway, serving as witnesses. Following the signing, GGGI will work closely with the Government of Indonesia, PT PLN (Persero) – Indonesia’s state-owned electricity company, and the Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment to finalize implementation and operational arrangements.

“This agreement marks a concrete step in implementing the Article 6.2 bilateral agreement between Indonesia’s Ministry of Environment/Environmental Protection Agency and Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment. Through this cooperation, we seek to mobilize carbon finance to support Indonesia’s energy transition and contribute to the achievement of our national climate targets. This cooperation will also support efforts to strengthen Indonesia’s SRUK (Carbon Unit Registry System) and ensure transparent recording and tracking of international transfers. Our priority is to ensure that this cooperation delivers credible mitigation outcomes, upholds environmental integrity, and is implemented in line with Indonesia’s national climate commitments,” said Moh Jumhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment/Head of Environmental Protection Agency of Indonesia.

The MOPA supports the implementation of Indonesia’s Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program, a results-based crediting mechanism designed to accelerate investment in new and additional clean, grid-connected electricity generation. As a sectoral financing mechanism, the GBI can be applied across renewable energy technologies. Its initial technological window in Indonesia focuses on floating solar photovoltaic (PV), in line with national priorities and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

The program addresses financial, regulatory, and grid-related constraints that have slowed renewable energy investment in Indonesia. It provides additional incentive payments when the standard power purchase price is insufficient to make an eligible project financially viable.

By prioritizing new and additional renewable energy generation paired with battery energy storage systems (BESS), the program enables renewable electricity delivery during peak and evening hours, when grid emissions are highest. This approach aims to reduce intermittency, enhance grid stability, and support the transition to a low-carbon power system.

Under the GBI Program, participation is voluntary. Independent Power Producers (IPPs) may apply for inclusion if they meet established financial, technical, and geographic criteria and demonstrate genuine additionality, measurable emission reductions, and positive sustainable development impacts.

The program uses a digital Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system to capture electricity generated and supplied to the grid. The data is reviewed through an independent audit process to ensure accuracy, transparency, and environmental integrity. Following verification, carbon payments are issued to project operators based on actual performance.

The resulting emission reductions are aggregated, authorized, and traded as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) under a cooperative approach between Indonesia and the Norwegian Ministry of Environment, as part of the Norwegian Global Emissions Reduction (NOGER) Initiative. The program applies dynamic baselines anchored in Indonesia’s unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), helping safeguard environmental integrity while supporting national climate objectives.

“Article 6 is moving from readiness to implementation, and this agreement is a clear example of what that transition requires: strong national drive and dedicated partners. GGGI is proud to have facilitated this agreement between Norway and Indonesia, building on our support to countries as they prepare for and take part in carbon markets. Results-based mechanisms like this can give governments and investors the clarity they need to mobilize finance for climate action at scale.” – Sang-hyup Kim, Executive Director of GGGI.

This signing demonstrates Indonesia’s continued efforts to translate climate commitments into bankable projects, commercial agreements, and sustained implementation. By connecting international carbon market cooperation with national energy priorities, the MOPA establishes an important foundation for mobilizing climate finance, scaling up renewable energy investment, strengthening energy security, and accelerating Indonesia’s transition to a low-carbon power system.

About the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI)

The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) was founded as a treaty-based international, intergovernmental organization in 2012 at the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development. GGGI supports its Member States in transitioning their economies toward a green growth model that simultaneously achieves poverty reduction, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and economic growth. With 54 Member States and 30 Partner countries and regional integration organizations in the process of accession, GGGI delivers programs and projects in over 57 countries. These initiatives encompass developing innovative green growth solutions, technical support, capacity building, policy planning & implementation, and assistance in building a pipeline of bankable green investment projects, project financing, investments, and knowledge sharing. GGGI’s work contributes to its Member States’ efforts to fulfill the Sustainable Development Goals and the Nationally Determined Contributions to the Paris Agreement.

For more information, visit www.gggi.org.

About the Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program

The Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program is Indonesia’s policy-based, results-based crediting mechanism under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. It supports the deployment of new and additional renewable electricity generation through incentive payments linked to verified greenhouse gas emission reductions. The program prioritizes renewable energy generation paired with battery energy storage systems and initially focuses on floating solar photovoltaic technology in Indonesia. It is designed to strengthen investment certainty, support national climate objectives, and accelerate the decarbonization of Indonesia’s electricity sector.

About the Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF)

The Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) is a country-driven mechanism that enables governments and private sector – particularly in developing countries and emerging economies – to engage meaningfully in Article 6 carbon markets. By uniquely combining strong preparedness support with structured transaction facilitation, the CTF offers a full-cycle pathway – evolving readiness into results – to access and benefit from international carbon market mechanisms. The CTF facilitates partnerships, supporting host countries in implementing climate action while also helping buyers advance their climate commitments. As a technical enabler and trusted partner, the CTF helps drive forward transparent, high-integrity, and inclusive carbon transactions aligned with the Paris Agreement. The CTF is comprised of the Article 6 Readiness Facility, a multi-donor fund to provide readiness support, as well as three Carbon Funds: the Article 6 Climate Cooperation Fund (ACCTIF) opened by Sweden, the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund opened by Norway, and the Singapore Article 6 Carbon Facility (SACF) opened by Singapore.

title: Congress considers $130 annual federal EV fee: What drivers should know - USA Today
description:
The proposed fee would start at $130 for EVs and $35 for plug-in hybrids, potentially increasing over time.
The EV fee was proposed to help pay for roads and would start at $130 annually.
The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.
EV owners would simply pay the $130 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.
A new $130 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings.
text:
Congress is considering a new annual fee for electric vehicle owners to help fund road maintenance.

The proposed fee would start at $130 for EVs and $35 for plug-in hybrids, potentially increasing over time.

This fee aims to have EV drivers contribute to the Highway Trust Fund, which is primarily funded by gasoline taxes.

Electric car owners could be forced to start paying an annual national fee as soon as next month if Congress passes legislation containing the tax.

The EV fee was proposed to help pay for roads and would start at $130 annually. The measure was part of a bipartisan draft of a transportation funding bill that the U.S. House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee is considering. Under the proposed legislation, dubbed the BUILD America 250 Act, the fee can be increased by $5 each year until it hits a max of $150 annually. Plug-in hybrid owners would be hit with a $35 fee starting in October that can be increased to as much as $50 by the end of the legislation in 2031.

The proposed fee is included in a larger bill to reauthorize surface transportation funding that is currently set to expire on Dec. 11. The measure was approved by the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, but it has not been approved by the full House or Senate.

The last transportation funding measure approved by Congress was signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021.

With progress on the larger transportation bill that includes the proposed EV fee stalled thus far, Congress passed a temporary extension of federal government funding that extends spending until Dec. 11, according to the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), a nonpartisan and nonprofit organization that advocates for consistent transportation funding.

AASHTO said the temporary transportation funding bill allowed lawmakers to "prevent a federal government shutdown" and "continue Highway Trust Fund programs and annually appropriated general fund programs" at 2026 fiscal year levels until the new December deadline.

That means EV drivers could be forced to start paying the proposed national fee in December.

The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.

Why is Congress considering adding an EV fee?

The federal government currently collects 18.4 cents per gallon on every U.S. gasoline purchase to help pay for road and transit construction projects, and most states also tack on their own fees. EV drivers don’t pay that tax because their vehicles don’t use gasoline.

The money goes into the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Highway Trust Fund and is then distributed to states to help pay for road and transit construction projects. As cars have become more fuel-efficient and more drivers have opted for EVs and hybrids, less money per mile driven has been collected despite increased use of roads. Lawmakers have looked for ways to close that growing gap in federal gas‑tax revenue.

The federal gas tax hasn't increased since 1993, and it brings in about $40 billion a year at its current level, according to the Tax Policy Center. President Donald Trump and some lawmakers in Congress have recently proposed suspending the federal gas tax as the average price of gas hovers around $4 per gallon, according to the AAA Auto Club.

The federal government typically spends about $60 billion on transportation projects, and infrastructure advocates say that amount is just enough to maintain the nation's roads and transit systems. Most states also levy their own gas taxes to fund local road projects.

Supporters of the proposed fee say it's time for EV drivers to contribute to the fund that helps pay for the upkeep of the roads they use. Rep. Sam Graves, a Republican from Missouri who chairs the U.S. House Transportation Committee, said in a statement that the EV fee "ensures that electric vehicle owners begin paying their fair share for the use of our roads."

Rep. Rick Larsen, a Washington state lawmaker who is the top Democrat on the panel, said the bipartisan highway bill agreement represents "a commitment to bipartisan lawmaking means finding compromise."

How would the new EV tax be collected?

Electric vehicle owners would have to pay the new fee when they register their cars. The proposal differs from other ideas that have been floated to replace gas tax money that isn't collected from EV drivers, including mileage-based proposals.

Vehicle-miles-traveled, or VMT, programs tax drivers based on miles they drive on U.S. roads instead of how much gasoline they purchase. Mileage-based road tax proposals have long been controversial in U.S. transportation funding debates because critics question how the government would monitor drivers' traveling habits without infringing on their privacy.

Supporters of the current highway bill draft note that the EV tax proposal would involve no tracking or reporting from drivers about their travels. EV owners would simply pay the $130 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.

What would the new fee mean for EV owners?

Electric vehicle owners save an average of about $8,811 in ownership and maintenance costs over 200,000 miles compared with owners of best-selling gas-powered vehicles in the same class, according to Consumer Reports.

A driver who opts for a new or used EV could save $2,200 annually on gas, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Hybrid drivers can save $1,500 on gas each year, according to the agency.

A new $130 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings. EV supporters have argued that additional annual fees increase the cost of owning an electric vehicle.

When state lawmakers in South Carolina were considering a new user fee for EV owners of 4.5 cents per kilowatt-hour on electricity consumed at publicly accessible charging stations, the Electrification Coalition, which lobbies for EV-friendly policies, said in a February 2026 statement that the state's proposal "imposes significant additional costs on EV drivers without increasing the state gasoline tax."

text:
Ford Motor Co. has tapped General Motors Co.'s former president of North America to lead vehicle programs and their operations.

Marissa West joins the Dearborn automaker effective Monday, Nov. 16. The more than 20-year veteran of the industry will support vehicle development, integration, program execution and global product programs across Ford's portfolio just as the company is looking to refresh 70% of its global vehicle portfolio by volume by 2029. The company said West will strengthen its leadership in overseeing the development and delivery of its next-generation vehicles.

“Marissa brings deep experience leading vehicle programs, integrating complex products and delivering successful launches,” said Sam Basile, Ford vice president of advanced product development, cycle planning and programs. “Her leadership and product-development background will be valuable as we work across teams to bring great vehicles and experiences to customers.”

Most recently, West was at French automotive supplier OPmobility, where she was executive vice president and chairperson for its North America business. At GM, she held leadership positions until 2024 amid restructuring in vehicle sales, service and marketing, as well as product development with focuses on vehicle programs, integration and launches.

West earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from Michigan State University and a master of science in engineering from the University of Michigan. She is a board member of UM's Mechanical Engineering Advisory Board, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The debut of new product is often among the biggest manufacturing challenges for automakers, and Ford is betting on its next-generation vehicles like the all-electric Fathom midsize pickup for solidifying its future competitiveness. It has five new vehicles coming by the end of the decade, including four being built in the United States, and it has reformed its industrial systems to emphasize quality after warranty and recall costs piled up.

“I’m honored to join Ford, a company with a proud legacy and an exciting future,” West said in a statement. “I’m eager to get close to the product, collaborate with talented teams around the world and help deliver vehicles and experiences that matter to customers.”

The caucus acknowledged that the legislation, BAAJA, includes important policies the group has advocated, such as stronger federal authority to approve transmission lines, which would accelerate the deployment of clean energy resources.

However, that does not outweigh provisions the members said would “undermine Tribal sovereignty” and overhaul the environmental laws.

The progressive Democrats also pointed out that support for the legislation relies on “an informal agreement” with President Donald Trump to fairly implement the permitting reforms and not block wind power projects, essentially ending the administration’s “illegal blockade on clean energy.”

They pointed to the fact that just this week, Trump said he would not permit any new wind turbines, calling the renewable energy resource “losers.”

“The CPC’s official position is consistent with Democratic Leader Jeffries’ recent statement that the legislation ‘falls short in several areas’ and that he ‘will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our Caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people,’” the caucus said.

Their opposition is further evidence that legislation faces an uphill battle to pass in the House, as many members are calling for negotiations to be delayed until the next Congress, when Democrats have a majority in both chambers.

While the legislation is broadly supported by most Republicans in both chambers, there is a clear divide within the Democratic Party.

BAAJA has the backing of climate and tribal advocates Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), both of whom were directly involved in the negotiations for the original text and subsequent amendment released last weekend.

Twenty other Democrats also voted in favor of invoking cloture for the legislation on Monday evening, advancing the bill toward a final vote. However, several of those who cast an “aye” vote have clarified that they are not yet committing to supporting the bill for final passage.

About 19 Democratic senators have since introduced a new amendment to the bill, aligning closely with the concerns outlined by the Progressive Caucus. The amendment, led by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA), would strike BAAJA’s changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, according to Politico.

text:
(Nov 11): Volkswagen AG said its namesake brand’s sales of electric vehicles (EVs) and hybrids in China climbed to a record last month, and forecast that growth will continue this year as its turnaround efforts in the world’s largest auto market start bearing fruit.

October deliveries of EVs and plug-in hybrids — a category known as new energy vehicles (NEVs) — surged nearly 350% from a year ago to more than 28,000 units, Volkswagen said on Wednesday. New models — including the ID. Aura T6 sport utility vehicle and the ID. Era 5S sedan — drove the increase.

The company said it expects to sustain growth in the coming months, with a goal to rank among the 10 bestselling NEV brands in the country next year.

The results represent a rare green shoot in China for Volkswagen, which recently reported that its ventures in the country had turned unprofitable as it fell further behind local brands in China’s overcrowded auto market. As part of its efforts to catch up, the manufacturer plans to introduce more than 20 new electrified models in the country this year.

The company has increasingly turned to Chinese partners to accelerate its transformation and offer cars catering to local tastes. Its collaboration with Xpeng Inc has produced a new EV architecture, while a software partnership with Horizon Robotics has added new self-driving capabilities.

Still, the automaker will have to show it can generate sustained volume growth in China’s ultra-competitive EV segment after a period of bruising declines in the country’s shrinking auto market.

Volkswagen’s group deliveries in China fell 30% during the first nine months of the year. Fully electric vehicles represented just 3.5% of the group’s sales there in the period, underscoring the gap between Volkswagen’s electrification ambitions and current market position.
