title: GM's LMR battery explained: how it works, why it took 20 years and when it will arrives
description:
A 33% increase on a typical LFP cell would place GM's LMR battery in the 210–220 Wh/kg range.
LMR batteries could also ease pressure on nickel supply chains, as they require considerably less than NMC batteries.
LMR vs NMC vs LFP: how the battery chemistries compare LMR batteries occupy a middle ground between LFP and NMC chemistries.
Ford is also developing its own LMR battery at Ion Park, its Battery Center of Excellence, though limited detail is currently available.
GM's fourth-generation EV platform: what LMR actually changes GM's fourth-generation EV platform combines LMR battery chemistry with a range of optimised technology systems into a more efficient, lighter architecture than GM's existing EV platforms.
text:
There are several classes of lithium-ion battery, each defined by the cathode materials used. One that has attracted significant industry interest is the lithium manganese rich (LMR) battery, following General Motors' (GM) announcement that the technology is finally set to be commercialised, with availability in GM electric vehicles (EVs) expected from 2028 onwards.

LMR battery technology has drawn interest since the late 1990s because it fills the gap between lower energy density but more stable lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, and the less stable but higher-performance nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) chemistry. LMR also aims to reduce reliance on cobalt and nickel by substituting manganese, a material that is considerably more abundant and lower cost.

While the technology holds considerable promise, it has faced substantial challenges, particularly around long-term stability caused by voltage fade. However, these challenges appear to be diminishing as GM and other manufacturers continue to advance the technology.

The 20-year problem: why voltage fade kept LMR off the road

GM's research into LMR technology extends back further than this recent announcement suggests. LMR cathode technology was first developed in the late 1990s by Argonne National Laboratory, with funding from the US Department of Energy.

Despite early promise, LMR batteries have taken considerable time to reach commercial viability due to a number of technical obstacles. In 2012, the Department of Energy's Vehicle Technologies Office (VTO) launched a project led by Argonne National Laboratory to tackle voltage fade in LMR cathodes. More recently, Argonne has led the Earth-abundant Cathode Active Materials (EaCAM) consortium, which is driven by environmental objectives, aiming to reduce dependence on cobalt and nickel.

GM's involvement in LMR battery technology, however, predates this milestone considerably, with the automaker having researched lithium manganese rich cells since 2015. Development accelerated from 2020, and by 2024, approximately one ton of LMR cathodes had been produced at the Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center. At the centre, hundreds of prismatic cells spanning 18 prototype varieties and three cell dimensions were tested, equivalent to 1.4 million miles of EV driving.

In October 2026, GM announced its fourth-generation EV platform, which will incorporate LMR cells alongside improved propulsion technology, simplified electronics, and more advanced driver assistance software. GM has stated it uses simulation and modelling to evaluate over 300,000 battery designs before committing to a physical prototype. Pre-production is planned at an LG Energy Solution facility in late 2027, with full commercial deployment targeted for 2028, though there remains healthy scepticism within the industry as to whether these production targets will be met.

What is an LMR battery? How LMR cathodes work

LMR cathodes are lithium-rich metal oxide cathodes capable of achieving higher energy density than LFP, at a similar cost, with practically zero cobalt content (unlike NMC) and reduced nickel content. A typical high-nickel NMC cathode comprises roughly 85% nickel, 10% manganese and 5% cobalt, whereas LMR cathodes are roughly 35% nickel and 65% manganese. These cathodes can incorporate significant lithium content within the cathode structure, pushing energy density well beyond LFP and into NMC territory.

While the technology remains relatively new, and performance will vary between manufacturers, GM has stated its LMR battery offers a 33% energy density improvement over LFP. LFP chemistry varies: most cells sit around 160 Wh/kg, while the latest high-end LFP batteries, such as CATL's Shenxing Plus, reach 205 Wh/kg. A 33% increase on a typical LFP cell would place GM's LMR battery in the 210–220 Wh/kg range. This reaches the lower end of NMC energy density, though some research suggests LMR batteries could exceed 250 Wh/kg. A Mitsui & Co. Global Strategic Studies Institute report has noted that LMR cathodes could enable energy densities in excess of 500 Wh/kg, though this remains theoretical at this stage.

The key advantage lies in manganese: a considerably more abundant and lower-cost material that could help reduce EV battery costs while improving environmental credentials, given that cobalt mining is known to cause environmental damage and is susceptible to supply chain volatility. Global manganese reserves are estimated at around 1.8 billion tonnes, according to the US Geological Survey. LMR batteries could also ease pressure on nickel supply chains, as they require considerably less than NMC batteries.

In NMC batteries, nickel performs the majority of redox reactions, while cobalt and smaller amounts of manganese act as structural filler. In LMR batteries, this role shifts significantly: manganese becomes the dominant transition metal and becomes actively involved in redox reactions, in a similar manner to lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) batteries.

Manganese has a high oxidation potential, meaning it can lose and gain electrons more readily than other transition metals. This creates a greater potential difference between cathode and anode, enabling the battery to operate at higher voltage and therefore achieve higher energy density than LFP, since energy density is directly related to both capacity and voltage. LMR cathodes also offer high capacities of 250 mAh/g or more. GM has not published the exact composition of its LMR cathode, though academic literature typically describes such cathodes as composite electrodes comprising a Li2MnO3 phase and a conventional layered LiMO2 phase. Automakers are targeting driving ranges of at least 400 miles to offset reliance on high-nickel and cobalt-containing EV battery packs.

Why has commercialisation taken so long?

High manganese loading is known to destabilise the cathode, an issue also observed in LMFP batteries and one of the key reasons LMR has taken so long to reach commercial readiness. High manganese loading can trigger a number of degradation mechanisms, particularly at elevated temperatures or voltages, including manganese dissolution from the cathode, irreversible oxygen release, interfacial structural phase transitions, and interfacial side reactions. These effects can lead to low coulombic efficiency and limited rate performance, but the most significant challenge for LMR batteries remains voltage fade, also known as voltage decay.

Voltage fade occurs over repeated charge and discharge cycles, as metal oxide complexes within the cathode undergo a phase transition from a layered structure to a spinel structure. This phase shift causes a continued decline in operating voltage, shortening battery cycle life relative to other lithium-ion chemistries.

The decay mechanism begins during the first cycle, when a high voltage is required to activate the manganese-rich phase, involving activation of oxygen atoms within the lattice as well as the metals. Oxygen-based reactions are considered among the primary drivers of voltage decay, including attacks on singlet oxygen, formation of Li2O molecules via electrode interfacial reactions, and migration of transition metal ions.

Degradation begins when oxygen is released under high voltage conditions, destabilising oxygen pairs within the cathode and altering the redox couples. This process creates defects within the cathode lattice, which transition metal ions (nickel and manganese) subsequently occupy, along with vacant lithium sites. This rearrangement drives the phase change to a spinel structure, lowering the discharge voltage profile over time. Interfacial reactions also reduce the amount of active lithium, contributing to capacity fade alongside voltage fade, meaning delivered energy declines over time even where ampere-hour capacity appears stable.

Voltage fade is an irreversible thermodynamic process that worsens at higher temperatures. Given that EVs routinely operate at high voltages and elevated internal temperatures, voltage decay can accelerate considerably, a key reason LMR batteries have yet to appear in production EVs. For battery management systems (BMS), estimating true state-of-charge becomes more difficult, as these systems typically rely on a stable open-circuit-voltage curve that becomes less accurate as LMR cells age.

Mitigation approaches explored over the years include coating electrode surfaces with metal oxide particles, metal doping within the cathode, and improved manufacturing processes to reduce defects. GM and LG Energy Solution, its development partner for LMR cells, have not published details of how they have addressed this issue, and independent test centres have indicated they have not yet seen published abuse-test data confirming the GM/LG cells match the safety profile of current LFP and NMC cells. No independent test data is currently available, and this will require scrutiny once cells become commercially available or further data is released.

Nevertheless, GM and LG appear confident the cells are ready for commercial production. GM has publicly stated it has resolved the voltage fade issue, with pre-production of the cells due to begin at an LG Energy Solution facility in late 2027, following development and testing at GM's Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center in Warren, Michigan.

LMR vs NMC vs LFP: how the battery chemistries compare

LMR batteries occupy a middle ground between LFP and NMC chemistries. As noted, LMR composition removes cobalt entirely and significantly reduces nickel content relative to NMC, positioning LMR batteries to be cheaper than NMC and broadly comparable in cost to LFP, which relies on cheap, abundant iron, while offering improved energy density over LFP. GM's claimed 33% energy density improvement over LFP has yet to be independently verified.

NMC remains the energy density leader for the foreseeable future, though it relies heavily on cobalt, a material associated with ethically contentious mining practices, environmental harm, and volatile supply chains.

In terms of cost, LFP has gained significant traction in EVs due to its safety profile and pricing, with LFP packs averaging $81/kWh in 2025, according to BloombergNEF, compared with $128/kWh for NMC. NMC remains the more expensive, higher-performance option, but the use of manganese is expected to bring LMR costs closer to LFP over time, with cost parity likely to be achieved first in China, with US production taking longer to reach comparable pack costs.

One advantage of LMR over NMC is its simpler cathode design, which is also compatible with larger cell formats, potentially offering greater cost improvements at scale. GM has confirmed plans to manufacture large-format prismatic cells.

GM has stated that its fourth-generation platform will deliver around 20% more range per kWh than its current EVs, with LMR cells costing a similar amount to LFP, factoring in benefits from the wider platform, including a 15% reduction in vehicle mass. This stems partly from reduced battery mass, as LMR is expected to deliver equivalent range to LFP using 20% less capacity, and partly from 40% fewer parts per drive unit due to smaller, lighter motors, alongside 30% less wiring enabled by centralised computing architecture.

Safety and climate performance represent further important comparison points. LFP remains the safest chemistry in terms of thermal runaway resistance, while higher-performance NMC compositions, such as NMC 811, are more susceptible to thermal runaway. LFP also offers considerably longer cycle life than NMC. LMR is expected to offer better thermal stability than NMC, though not matching LFP, with cycle life performance dependent on how effectively commercial cells resist voltage fade.

In cold weather, LMR is expected to outperform LFP if real-world results match expectations. LFP is known to lose considerable capacity at low temperatures, reducing range, while NMC performs better in cold conditions. LMR could offer a lower-cost alternative to LFP with improved reliability in sub-zero conditions.

Kurt Kelty, VP of Battery, Propulsion and Sustainability at GM, has used the Chevrolet Silverado EV to illustrate relative driving range: with a high-nickel NMC pack the truck achieves around 490 miles, an LFP pack would cut that to about 350 miles, and an LMR pack is expected to deliver over 400 miles. LFP, LMR and NMC are expected to co-exist in the market for a number of years, much as LFP and NMC do today. Full validation of real-world performance will not be available until at least 2028, assuming mass production proceeds on schedule.

Ford, Tesla, and the race to LMR: who's competing?

GM, alongside commercial partner LG Energy Solution, currently leads the commercial development timeline for LMR technology. Ford is also developing its own LMR battery at Ion Park, its Battery Center of Excellence, though limited detail is currently available. Ford has indicated it is targeting LMR-powered EVs by the end of 2029, placing GM as the current frontrunner, with Ford not far behind.

Tesla has not announced explicit LMR development plans but holds a number of high-manganese cathode patents. LG Energy Solution has reportedly coordinated with Tesla regarding next-generation EV batteries, though Tesla's current focus remains on LFP and its own 4680 cylindrical cells. CATL and BYD, typically at the forefront of battery innovation in China, have so far focused on LFP and LMFP rather than LMR technology, as reflected in BYD's latest Blade 2.0 batteries.

GM's fourth-generation EV platform: what LMR actually changes

GM's fourth-generation EV platform combines LMR battery chemistry with a range of optimised technology systems into a more efficient, lighter architecture than GM's existing EV platforms. The new LMR batteries will use the same Ultium factories that produce GM's existing battery technologies, meaning electrode processes, packaging infrastructure and cathode supplier relationships are already established, with only the chemistry changing. This is central to GM's argument that the batteries will be ready for mass production by 2028 without requiring new manufacturing facilities.

Key components of the fourth-generation platform include:

GM has not yet confirmed which EV models will feature the LMR battery and fourth-generation platform, though crossover SUVs are considered the likely candidates given their market popularity. The Cadillac Escalade IQ has already been confirmed to debut the platform's centralised computing architecture and eyes-off highway driving technology.

Beyond weight-related range improvements, LMR batteries are expected to offer improved safety over NMC. High-nickel chemistries carry greater thermal runaway risk, whereas LMR cathode structures offer improved thermal stability, reducing the likelihood of heat-related incidents. The prismatic cell format further supports this, offering greater thermal stability, improved resistance to impact-related distortion, and fewer potential failure points due to a simplified pack architecture.

When will GM's LMR battery EVs be available?

GM has indicated that the first LMR-powered vehicles will be available in 2028. Pre-production is due to begin at an LG Energy Solution facility in late 2027, with commercial LMR cell production starting at the Ultium Cells plant in Spring Hill, Tennessee, in 2028, once upgrades to the plant are complete. This timeline is contingent on production and operational plans proceeding without disruption.

GM's focus is likely to centre on crossover SUVs, though trucks represent a significant adjacent market. No specific models have been confirmed, though GM has expressed confidence in meeting its production timelines. GM has acknowledged that LMR will not transform the market overnight and is expected to co-exist with NMC and LFP for a number of years, raising questions around the financial viability of large-scale investment given GM's recent EV-related financial challenges.

Following the elimination of certain EV tax credits in the US in September 2025, North American EV sales declined 24% year-on-year across the first nine months of 2026. GM will need to maintain commitment to scaling LMR production against this backdrop of diminishing returns, particularly as Ford is not far behind in its own LMR development, raising the risk of GM losing first-mover advantage should timelines slip.

Having invested in modelling over 300,000 battery designs and validating physical prototypes on LG's pilot production line, GM appears committed to its proposed timelines. However, the more pressing question may not be technical feasibility, but GM's broader financial position with respect to its EV strategy.

At the end of 2025, GM recorded a $6 billion EV-related writedown, converted its Orion plant back to combustion production, and reported $238 million in EV realignment charges in Q3 2026, coinciding with the announcement of the fourth-generation platform. GM has recorded US$11.2 billion in total charges tied to scaling back its EV plans since 2025, raising reasonable questions as to whether its plans will translate into commercially viable EVs. While GM maintains that the largest charges are now behind it, healthy scepticism remains warranted regarding its continued commitment to EV production at scale.

Should GM proceed as planned, the industry will see the first LMR-powered EVs reach the road after two decades of development. It remains to be seen whether these timelines will be met, or whether Ford will close the gap in the race to bring the first LMR EV to market.

title: Samsung and Hyundai announce “One Team” partnership - ArenaEV
description:
Samsung and the Hyundai Motor Group used to operate in parallel universes for generations, competing for talent and national prestige, and carefully avoiding deep entanglement.
That corporate standoff has officially ended at a training center in Seocheon, where the two industrial giants declared themselves a single team.
The heads of Samsung SDI, Samsung Display, Harman, and the semiconductor foundry division were also present.
Behind closed doors at Seocheon, Samsung laid out its entire automotive parts bin for Hyundai's engineering brass.
At the Samsung SDI exhibition booth in Seocheon, solid-state battery cells took center stage alongside prismatic and cylindrical modules.
text:
It's no secret that carmakers are brilliant at bending metal and tuning chassis, but painfully bad at writing computer code. The companies that build our phones and the companies that build our cars have treated each other with cautious suspicion for many years - nowhere was that frostier than in South Korea. Samsung and the Hyundai Motor Group used to operate in parallel universes for generations, competing for talent and national prestige, and carefully avoiding deep entanglement. That corporate standoff has officially ended at a training center in Seocheon, where the two industrial giants declared themselves a single team.

The HMG Appreciation Day looked on paper like a corporate mixer. One hundred and seventy-seven executives and spouses watched a seventy-minute orchestral performance with cellist Han Jae-min and traded compliments about three generations of shared industrial history. But look past all the nostalgic video montages, and the guest list tells you what is actually happening.

Hyundai sent its heavy hitters, including Vice Chairman Jang Jae-hoon and R&D boss Manfred Harrer - the former Porsche and Apple engineer now steering Hyundai and Kia chassis and vehicle development. The heads of Samsung SDI, Samsung Display, Harman, and the semiconductor foundry division were also present. You do not put top battery chemists, silicon architects, and vehicle dynamics engineers in the same room to listen to classical music.

Let's look at the "family history" to understand the importance of this event. Back in November 1985, an ailing Samsung founder, Lee Byung-chul, showed up at the seventieth birthday party of Hyundai founder Chung Ju-yung with a white porcelain vase. It was a rare gesture of warmth between fierce rivals, followed sixteen years later by a quiet meeting between their sons in 2001. Yet Samsung still tried to build its own cars in the late nineties - an expensive adventure that ended with Renault buying the operation - and Hyundai always guarded its supply chain fiercely, preferring to split its battery orders between LG Energy Solution and SK On. When third-generation leaders Lee Jae-yong and Chung Eui-sun met at the Samsung SDI plant in Cheonan and the Namyang R&D center in 2020, the ice finally did break, and the two companies signed their first battery supply contract (first batteries arrived in 2023).

That component deal has now turned into a full marriage of hardware and software. Behind closed doors at Seocheon, Samsung laid out its entire automotive parts bin for Hyundai's engineering brass. There were next-gen automotive semiconductors, Central Control Units, Telecomms Control Units built with Harman, and tiny multilayer ceramic capacitors from Samsung Electro-Mechanics that keep high-voltage radar and camera feeds clean - modern EVs are nothing more than server racks on wheels. By letting Samsung handle the silicon, the OLED screens, and the telecommunications backbone, Hyundai avoids the multi-billion-dollar software pitfalls that Western rivals had to deal with - we only need to look at Volkswagen's Cariad division to understand what's at stake here.

At the Samsung SDI exhibition booth in Seocheon, solid-state battery cells took center stage alongside prismatic and cylindrical modules. We have all heard automakers promise solid-state miracles for the last decade, usually accompanied by timelines that conveniently slide backward every two years, but the physics are worth chasing, and we are finally getting there - apparently. Replacing the liquid electrolyte in an 84 kWh pack with a solid separator cuts fire risk and could easily shave 331 lb to 441 lb off a family crossover. Taking that much mass out of the floor pan does more than extend highway range in winter weather - it means softer springs and improved ride comfort without sloppy body roll in corners.

The executives at the event also spent plenty of time talking about "physical AI" and robotics, and in Hyundai's case, there is real iron behind the talk. Hyundai owns Boston Dynamics, and combining its mechanical actuators with Samsung's foundry chips and vision sensors has an obvious first home: the car factory floor. Before a robot ever folds laundry in your living room, automated systems running on Samsung silicon will be routing wiring harnesses and inspecting battery welds inside Hyundai's assembly plants, driving down manufacturing costs by 15% to 20% over the next product cycle.

For legacy automakers in Detroit, Munich, and Paris, the sight of Korea's two largest conglomerates locking arms should be sobering. European and American brands are scrambling to stitch together patchwork alliances with software startups and foreign cell suppliers, resulting in delayed launches and buggy dashboards. Hyundai and Kia have secured direct access to top-tier foundry chips, displays, and battery chemistry by turning a decades-old domestic rivalry into a single vertically integrated supply chain. Right in their backyard.

text:
Protesters burnt tyres and blocked roads in Syria over fuel prices. French fishers blockaded a fuel depot and clashed with police. Government and household budgets were squeezed around the world as interest rates rose and the sales of electric vehicles roughly doubled year-on-year in several countries, including Australia, Brazil and India.

These were just some of the many knock-on effects of the US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran that began in February. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 25% of the world’s oil trade and 20% of exported liquefied natural gas previously passed, caused what the International Energy Agency (IEA) called “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market”, as fuel prices spiked worldwide.

Nature Spotlight: Energy

The resulting strain has exacerbated the economic pressures already felt from previous shocks, including the Russia–Ukraine war, the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2008 global financial crash, as well as from the continuing effects of climate change. The current global energy-security picture is “really bad on all fronts”, says Dan Marks, an energy-security researcher at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London. “It’s something of a perfect storm.”

Governments seeking to improve national energy security are taking a variety of approaches — from measures to reduce demand and increase electrification to infrastructure updates and incentive programmes to encourage renewable-energy investment. Researchers, meanwhile, are doing their bit, driving scientific and technological advances that have the potential to deliver a stable and sustainable future energy mix.

What is energy security?

Human energy consumption is both growing and changing (see ‘Powering the planet’). Use of global primary energy — naturally occurring energy sources that have not undergone any processing by humans — more than doubled between 1980 and 2025. Over that period, consumption increased from around 85,000 terawatt hours (TWh) annually to 178,000 TWh. That’s approximately 71 times the yearly primary-energy consumption of France.

Electrification — the replacement of technologies that burn fossil fuels with alternatives powered by electricity — is advancing in many countries as various industries look into switching to renewables. Worldwide, electricity demand is predicted to increase by around 40% by 2035, compared with current levels (see ‘The road ahead’). Despite this, many industries are still reliant on fossil fuels. Close to 99% of aviation and more than 90% of shipping relies on fossil fuels, for example. One-quarter of extracted natural gas is used to heat industrial buildings, and around 21% is used for heating and cooking in homes worldwide. Most of the rest (40%) is used to generate electricity. Although the share of primary energy generated by renewables is growing, oil, coal and gas still account for about 80% of energy production.

The IEA defines energy security as reliable, affordable access to all fuels and energy sources. Marks and others highlight that priorities vary internationally, with reliability often seen as of primary importance in high-income countries and affordability taking precedence in low-income nations. The impacts of global shocks to fuel supplies and prices also vary according to how reliant countries are on imported fossil fuels. “There isn’t one global energy-security picture, but many different context-dependent pictures,” says Severin Borenstein, an energy economist at the University of California, Berkeley.

Economies that rely on imported oil products are particularly vulnerable to the current shocks. The World Food Programme, part of the United Nations, estimated in March that the US–Iran war could push an extra 45 million people into acute hunger, taking this year’s total to 363 million, as increasing oil and gas costs push up the prices of fuel, food and other crucial products such as fertilizer. “If, like in a lot of African countries, people are dependent on travelling long distances in vehicles and on other imported oil products, large oil-price increases can be existentially problematic,” says Marks. Some high-income nations have also been hit hard. In Japan — which was importing more than 90% of its crude oil from the Middle East before the conflict — household electricity bills have risen to their highest levels in three years, and government borrowing costs have risen to a 30-year high.

By contrast, nations with domestic fuel supplies have been partially insulated. Although car users in the United States have seen big fuel-price increases, the country’s ample supplies of natural gas have shielded the nation from severe economic hardships. “In most developed free-market economies, there isn’t an energy-security issue in the sense of availability,” says Borenstein. “There are price and macro-economic issues. Some countries, like the United States, are better protected than others.”

Global oil prices have jumped since the US–Iran war broke out. Brent Crude futures contracts, a global oil-price benchmark, hit US$126 a barrel in April — up from around $70 before the conflict. This has affected consumers and businesses, but not as much as some previous energy crises. During the Yom Kippur War, coordinated action by oil-producing countries caused prices to more than triple between October 1973 and January 1974. And oil prices more than doubled after the 1978–79 Iranian revolution.

Many economists think that the global economy is better placed to avoid the soaring inflation, unemployment and recessions seen in many industrialized nations after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks. The ‘oil intensity’ of the global economy, that is, how much oil is needed to generate a unit of gross domestic product (GDP) in the form of goods and services, has fallen by more than 50% since the 1970s. And the IEA, established after the 1973 oil crisis, also requires its 32 member countries to keep reserves of at least 90 days’ worth of crude oil to guard against supply shocks. “For most of the developed world, it’s a big inconvenience, and, for some, a substantial budget squeeze, but it’s not the complete disruption of the economy seen in the 1970s,” says Borenstein.

But economic and energy-security challenges are also expected to grow owing to climate change. Droughts are becoming more frequent and severe, resulting in big reductions in hydropower generation in nations such as China, Brazil, the United States, Spain and Zambia. Low water levels in rivers, including the Rhine and Danube in Europe, the Amazon in South America and the Yangtze in China, have caused freight delivery problems. The other effects of climate change include reduced wind-energy generation and increased demand for power to run air-conditioning units.

Governments, policymakers and others who are working to tackle energy-security challenges have various options. Reducing energy demand, especially for oil and gas, by electrifying industrial processes and home heating, for example, helps with these issues, especially in nations that are heavily reliant on imported fossil fuels. Managing demand volatility through improved energy storage and ensuring that power grids can transition towards greater energy generation from renewables are also part of the picture, Marks says.

Generating security

Although governments and business leaders have parts to play in energy-demand management, electrification and infrastructure investments, researchers are driving scientific and technical innovations that support energy security. Tapping underground heat to produce geothermal energy, for example, emits only small amounts of greenhouse gases and can be used to generate electricity or to heat buildings. However, at present, geothermal energy produces less than 1% of electricity globally because few locations have the right combination of accessible underground heat, water and permeable rock.

That could change thanks to advances in enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), in which underground fractures are expanded or created in hot areas, and then fluids are pumped down, heated up and transferred back to the surface, usually to drive turbines and generate electricity.

There have been small-scale EGS research operations since the 1970s, but drilling times and costs have fallen substantially in the decades since thanks to techniques adapted from the oil and gas industries. These include the fracturing of rock with pressurized fluids, known as fracking, horizontal drilling to increase the exposure of fluid to heat reservoirs and the use of tougher, faster polycrystalline diamond compact drill bits. “It’s hard to overestimate how much of a game changer the new techniques have been,” says Roland Horne, a geothermal-energy engineer at Stanford University in California.

These innovations are driving investments in large commercial plants. One of the biggest of these is the Cape Station project operated by Fervo Energy near Milford in Utah, which began delivering power in September and plans to build the capacity to generate 500 megawatts (MW) by 2028 — enough electricity to power around 500,000 US homes.

However, there are obstacles to overcome. A number of EGS projects have been halted owing to earthquakes that geologists linked to increased underground forces generated by the EGS process. A magnitude-5.5 earthquake that injured 90 people was probably triggered by hydraulic fracturing at an EGS plant in Pohang, South Korea, in 2017. Lessons have been learnt from this and other incidents. For example, EGS developers are deploying networks of sensors to better predict seismic risks and using multistage stimulation. This involves the use of pressurised fluids or chemical agents to fracture rock sequentially and more gently at several points rather than at fewer locations.

Horne says that he expects the levelized cost of electricity — the average cost of generating a unit of electricity across a power plant’s lifetime — for EGS to drop to a commercially competitive $80 per megawatt hour (MWh) by 2027. The IEA says that this could drop to $50 by 2035 and that geothermal energy could generate 8% of global electricity supplies by 2050.

Efforts to develop more efficient solar cells could also help countries to improve their energy security by increasing sustainable domestic electricity supplies. In 2025, 9% of the world’s electricity came from solar, up from 3% in 2020. Today’s solar cells are mostly silicon-based and can typically convert light into electricity with efficiencies of around 20–24%.

When sunlight hits a solar, or photovoltaic, cell, electrons inside the semiconductor material that it is made from are knocked loose, creating an electrical imbalance that produces a voltage and generates electricity. Researchers are now developing next-generation solar cells that use metal halide perovskites, a family of crystalline compounds with high light absorption and charge-transport capabilities.

name: Clean Energy
title: AI's energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?
description:
Artificial intelligence is exploding in popularity, and many people have concerns about the sustainability of its energy consumption.
However, AI might also hold the key to improving energy efficiency: offsetting some of the demand it creates.
We want AI to reduce energy consumption overall, rather than adding strain to systems.
The Net-Positive AI Energy Framework is our North Star for clean, efficient and equitable AI.
We’re now working on an AI Energy Readiness Compass: a methodology to support responsible AI energy developments and identify the causes of upcoming bottlenecks in the power grid that could be problematic for AI energy use.
text:
Artificial intelligence is exploding in popularity, and many people have concerns about the sustainability of its energy consumption. AI models need vast amounts of electricity: according to the International Energy Agency, a typical AI data centre can consume as much energy as 100,000 households each year. Energy use by US data-centre servers more than tripled between 2014 and 2023 — reaching 4.4% of the nation’s total electricity consumption. This figure is expected to at least double by 20281.

However, AI might also hold the key to improving energy efficiency: offsetting some of the demand it creates. An article published by the World Economic Forum suggests that the use of AI tools across industries — in automating tasks or monitoring real-time energy use, for example — can reduce energy consumption by up to 60%. Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes, a sustainable-development specialist and an author of the article, has been working to lower AI’s energy demands while finding ways to use the tools to reduce wider emissions.

Nature Spotlight: Energy

Originally from Trinidad, Greene-Dewasmes became interested in solving energy-security issues for island states with few resources. In 2021, she completed a PhD on the green-energy transition across small island developing states at the University of York, UK, before joining the World Economic Forum in 2022. Now based in Geneva, Switzerland, Greene-Dewasmes has been the Forum’s AI and Energy Lead since 2024. Her work involves bringing together AI and energy leaders from around the world to identify shared challenges, align priorities and develop practical actions that can improve AI’s energy impact.

As well as looking at improving AI’s energy efficiency, Greene-Dewasmes and partners are exploring how models can find innovations that improve existing energy infrastructure, such as that in buildings that are already in use. Nature spoke to her about navigating the increasing energy needs of the technology and whether its benefits could outweigh this demand.

Why are AI models so heavy on energy consumption?

AI needs cloud networks, chips, graphics-processing units and cooling systems, all of which consume large amounts of energy. Developing and training models requires high levels of processing power to crunch the data, but AI use is much more energy intensive overall because of the scale. ChatGPT, the chatbot from technology firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, has more than 800 million users each month and receives more than 2.5 billion queries daily. As AI becomes mainstream, we need to build more energy infrastructure to keep up with the surge in demand.

But, when it comes to scaling up AI, I think the conversation is too skewed towards the energy needed to power centralized infrastructure, when there are lots of other things that will contribute to AI’s energy requirements. Large data centres will exist in only the few countries that have the money, space and resources to host them. For most of the world, AI infrastructure will be disaggregated and decentralized. For example, if one million people are using their phones more intensively because of AI, that affects the energy infrastructure.

Although more complex LLM queries are currently directed to remote data centres, some smaller tasks can be completed directly on new devices that have AI chips. As this becomes more common, what will that mean for infrastructure planning for energy? It’s much harder to measure this than the outputs from one data centre.

How can AI improve energy efficiency in other areas?

AI’s electricity impact is currently about 0.49% of total global electricity use — so it’s still fairly small, although it’s growing. The World Economic Forum, in collaboration with other specialists, has created a Net-Positive AI Energy Framework. It looks at how we can design AI models and infrastructure for efficiency — by optimizing chips, data-centre locations and liquid cooling, in which fluids are used for cooling owing to their high heat capacity — while using AI to bring down energy usage in high-impact sectors, such as transportation and urbanization, both by improving the efficiency of systems and coming up with solutions to global challenges.

For example, in Azerbaijan, operations that keep buildings running, including lighting, heating and cooling, account for a large proportion of the country’s carbon emissions. The Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution Azerbaijan (a public legal entity) is using AI-powered solutions to improve efficiencies as part of its nationally determined contribution commitments — the country’s pledge to reduce emissions. This includes AI solutions that adjust heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) on the basis of building occupancy and use trends, and that predict the need for maintenance before faults arise. In some cases, this use of AI to hone efficiency has brought down HVAC energy use by 25% and emissions by up to 40%.

We’re also encouraging people to use AI wisely. We want AI to reduce energy consumption overall, rather than adding strain to systems.

What’s involved in your community of AI and energy specialists?

The aim is to gather insights from leading voices in the AI ecosystem to generate thought leadership and encourage cross-discipline learning so people aren’t working in silos. It started off as one-on-one conversations with professionals working with AI, centred on the technology’s biggest challenges and opportunities. We convened a community of about 40 people, which has increased to around 70 in nine industries around the world and is still growing. We try to hear from lots of voices: university academics, public-sector entities and technology, AI and energy companies (including renewables and nuclear) are all involved. Together with our partners, we turn these insights into guidance and frameworks that can support the wider industry.

We’ve published two reports based on the learnings gleaned from these thought leaders. Artificial Intelligence Energy Paradox explores how to balance the challenges and opportunities of AI and energy. The Net-Positive AI Energy Framework is our North Star for clean, efficient and equitable AI. We’re now working on an AI Energy Readiness Compass: a methodology to support responsible AI energy developments and identify the causes of upcoming bottlenecks in the power grid that could be problematic for AI energy use.

One particular success from these collaborations is the willingness of hyperscalers — large organizations that operate cloud computing services and data centres — to embrace grid flexibility. At first, they were reluctant to adjust when they draw power because they wanted continuous access to reliable electricity, but they have come to see the benefits of balancing demand on the grid. As a result, they have embraced power flexibility, and 18 partners supported the launch of the AI Energy Management Alliance: a coalition of companies that promotes dynamic load-shifting (changing when energy is used to align with grid loads, the availability of green energy and the best pricing).

title: No SUV, no problem. Edmunds picks the five best cars with all-wheel drive - Greenfield Indiana
description:
All-wheel drive can help with acceleration on snowy or icy roads, and most people assume they’ll need an SUV to get it.
2027 Impreza starting price: $25,890 Toyota Camry The Camry is Edmunds’ top-rated midsize sedan.

The Sienna delivers an EPA-estimated 35 mpg combined with all-wheel drive, making it the most fuel-efficient minivan you can buy.
2026 330i xDrive starting price: $51,350 Edmunds says Buck the SUV and truck trend and get an all-wheel-drive car or minivan instead.
text:
Are you thinking about wanting a vehicle with all-wheel drive for this upcoming winter? All-wheel drive can help with acceleration on snowy or icy roads, and most people assume they’ll need an SUV to get it. However, there are alternatives. Plenty of sedans, hatchbacks and minivans offer all-wheel drive, allowing you to save money at the dealership and at the pump if you opt for one of them over an SUV. To help you narrow your search, Edmunds’ auto experts rounded up five of their favorites. They’re ordered by starting price with all-wheel drive, including destination and ordering fees.

Subaru Impreza

An article about all-wheel drive wouldn’t be complete without a Subaru listed. With the recent axing of the Legacy, the Impreza is Subaru’s last car that’s not a sports car. It’s also the brand’s most affordable model. Like most Subarus, the Impreza, which is only available as a hatchback, comes standard with all-wheel drive.

X-Mode, Subaru’s advanced traction control system, isn’t offered on the Impreza. But the Impreza’s all-wheel-drive system always delivers power to all four wheels, unlike most all-wheel-drive systems that are front-wheel-drive-based and only send power to the rear wheels when needed. The Impreza is one of the roomiest and most comfortable cars in its class and offers plenty of cargo space. Downsides are few but include slow acceleration and a bland interior.

2027 Impreza starting price: $25,890

Toyota Camry

The Camry is Edmunds’ top-rated midsize sedan. The current generation, introduced for 2025, is the only sedan in its class that offers all-wheel drive on every trim level. Even better, every Camry comes with a hybrid powertrain. Depending on the trim level, an all-wheel-drive Camry will offer an EPA-estimated 43 mpg to 50 mpg combined. That’s significantly better than most hybrid SUVs. To maximize fuel economy, aim for the base LE trim.

Beyond efficiency, the Camry stands out with excellent tech, including standard advanced driver assist features that operate well, and it’s surprisingly enjoyable to drive for a midsize sedan. A quiet, comfortable and roomy cabin complements this well-rounded Toyota. A coarse-sounding engine during hard acceleration is the Camry’s main drawback.

2027 Camry with all-wheel drive starting price: $32,520

Toyota Sienna

We get it: Minivans aren’t cool, but they’re great for families because of the vast space they provide. The Sienna is the only hybrid minivan with all-wheel drive, and it’s available on every trim level. The Woodland Edition is particularly noteworthy. It has a raised ride height, giving it a bit more ground clearance, and it can tow up to 3,500 pounds with its standard tow hitch, making it the most capable vehicle here.

The Sienna delivers an EPA-estimated 35 mpg combined with all-wheel drive, making it the most fuel-efficient minivan you can buy. It also comes with a generous list of standard features and is very comfortable. On the downside, acceleration is slow, and its second-row seats can’t be removed.

2026 Sienna with all-wheel drive starting price: $44,915

Tesla Model 3

For electric vehicle shoppers, the Model 3 is our top pick. It’s one of our favorite EVs thanks to its long range, strong performance, and long list of tech features. It’s also roomy and comfortable, with a large trunk and easy access to Tesla’s vast fast-charging network. The lack of Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, however, is disappointing.

Getting all-wheel drive isn’t cheap because it’s not available on the base model. You’ll have to step up to the midlevel Premium All-Wheel Drive or the top Performance model. In return, you’ll get an all-wheel-drive system enhanced by a Slippery Surface mode that provides additional traction during slippery conditions and Stuck Assist, which can dislodge the Model 3 when stuck on a loose surface.

Model 3 Premium All-Wheel Drive starting price: $49,130

BMW 3 Series

Our luxury choice is the 330i xDrive, the most affordable 3 Series with all-wheel drive. xDrive means all-wheel drive in BMW speak. The M340i xDrive is also available if you want more power and excitement and have a larger budget. xDrive works with a traction control setting called Dynamic Traction Control that allows the wheels to spin more than the default setting. It helps the car dig through snow and slush better but should only be used when needed.

The 3 Series’ stable handling, impressive tech, and powerful and efficient engines make it our favorite small luxury sedan. We just wish more advanced safety features were standard rather than costing extra. A redesigned 2027 model arrives next year and should be even better.

description:
Under its Maharashtra Electric Vehicle Policy 2025, the state government has set an overall EV adoption target of 30% with higher targets for two-wheelers and three-wheelers.
The Targets The Policy sets different adoption targets for individual vehicle categories, based on the proportion of new registrations by 2030.
Incentives to Buyers The Maharashtra government has earmarked approximately Rs 1,993 crore over five years for EV adoption incentives.
Electric passenger vehicles are also exempt from toll charges on the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, Mumbai-Nagpur Samruddhi Maharmarg and Atal Setu.
The two wheeler EV adoption has had the bigger piece of the "adoption percentage pie" this entire time.
text:
If you live in Maharashtra, there is a 30% chance your next car or 2-wheeler will be an EV. Or, at least, that is what the State government is aiming for. As per Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis. Under its Maharashtra Electric Vehicle Policy 2025, the state government has set an overall EV adoption target of 30% with higher targets for two-wheelers and three-wheelers. The plan involves a combination of incentives and subsidies for buyers, along with tax cuts and improvements in charging infrastructure and electrification of public transport and commercial fleets.

This target has been reiterated by the CM on November 4, during the launch of the Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric at the manufacturer's Chakan facility in Pune. The policy, which came into effect on April 1, 2025, is going to be valid till March 31, 2030.

The Targets

The Policy sets different adoption targets for individual vehicle categories, based on the proportion of new registrations by 2030. Public transport has been given more importance here. Maharashtra aims to electrify 40% of the public bus fleet operated by the State transport in major urban regions like Mumbai, Pune, Nagpur, Nashik, Chhatrapati Shambhajinagar and Amravati. For non-govt bus operators, the target is 15% of new bus registrations. The policy also targets 50% EV adoption in commercial aggregator fleets.

Incentives to Buyers

The Maharashtra government has earmarked approximately Rs 1,993 crore over five years for EV adoption incentives. Eligible electric two-wheelers receive a 10% purchase subsidy, capped at Rs 10,000. Electric passenger three-wheelers are eligible for up to Rs 30,000. Commercial electric passenger cars can receive up to Rs 2 lakh, subject to eligibility.

Eligible EVs sold and registered in Maharashtra also receive a 100 per cent exemption from motor vehicle tax and registration fees. Electric passenger vehicles are also exempt from toll charges on the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, Mumbai-Nagpur Samruddhi Maharmarg and Atal Setu. The key incentives include:

Electric two-wheelers: 10 per cent subsidy, capped at Rs 10,000.

Electric passenger three-wheelers: 10 per cent subsidy, capped at Rs 30,000.

Electric three-wheeler goods carriers: 15 per cent subsidy, capped at Rs 30,000.

Electric passenger cars used for commercial transport: 15 per cent subsidy, capped at Rs 2 lakh.

Electric light goods carriers: 15 per cent subsidy, capped at Rs 1 lakh.

Electric buses: 10 per cent subsidy, capped at Rs 20 lakh.

Better Charging Infrastructure?

The policy aims to develop charging infrastructure across cities, rural areas and highways with charging facilities planned at intervals of every 25 km along state and national highways. It also includes provisions for charging points in new residential buildings, commercial parking facilities and government offices.

Battery recycling and reuse facilities are another important part of the plan. With the number of EVs on the road expected to increase considerably over the next few years, establishing a recycling ecosystem will be crucial for used battery management. The policy also aims to encourage battery manufacturing, component production and research and development within the state.

Can Maharashtra Achieve this Target?

Maharashtra has a sizeable EV market but achieving 30% penetration across all new vehicle registrations will require a much more sustained increase in adoption across segments. The two wheeler EV adoption has had the bigger piece of the "adoption percentage pie" this entire time. Now the increased adoption of passenger cars, commercial vehicles, buses and goods carriers will need to contribute more substantially to the entire share. Currently the EV four-wheeler sales percentage is 9 to 10 percent of total volume, whereas the two-wheeler sales are at a whopping 80 percent plus. The remaining 8 to 10 percent is distributed among the three-wheelers, light goods and passenger vehicles and heavy passenger vehicles. Yes it isn;t necessary that everything has to be or will be perfect on the statistical front but the numbers do need to show rapid growth in order to balance the entire automobile ecosystem.

Charging accessibility, electricity supply interoperability between different charging networks and uncertainty around the resale value of used EVs remain some of the key challenges. The availability of charging infrastructure, in particular, will be crucial in convincing private vehicle buyers and commercial fleet operators to make the switch.

The state estimates that this policy could help reduce vehicular PM2.5 emissions by approximately over 300 tonnes and greenhouse gas emissions from the transport sector by around one million tonnes by 2030. This marks a bold statement and it will only be possible if developing a supporting ecosystem circling around battery manufacturing, better charging infrastructure and research and development are given equal importance as increasing the number of EVs on the road.

title: Centre bans battery black mass exports to boost domestic recycling - The Financial Express
description:
It comes amid a broader policy push to establish a domestic critical minerals ecosystem, spanning mining, processing, recycling and battery manufacturing.
Black mass is the powder obtained after used lithium-ion batteries or manufacturing scrap are shredded and separated from larger metal and plastic components.
Depending on the battery chemistry, it contains recoverable lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite, materials that can be processed and reused in battery manufacturing.
The domestic recycling industry has more capacity to process black mass than the material currently generated, leaving refiners short of feedstock, according to industry analysis.
The export ban could help bridge the gap between recycling capacity and feedstock availability, particularly as domestic battery manufacturing and EV adoption expand.
text:
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), through a notification issued on November 10, changed the export policy for specified battery waste and scrap from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’, with immediate effect. The restriction covers unsorted waste and scrap, including spent batteries that do not contain lead, cadmium or mercury, classified as lithium-ion battery black mass.

The move marks a shift in the country’s approach to battery recycling, from encouraging investment in domestic mineral recovery to ensuring that recyclable material remains available to local processors. It comes amid a broader policy push to establish a domestic critical minerals ecosystem, spanning mining, processing, recycling and battery manufacturing.

Black mass is the powder obtained after used lithium-ion batteries or manufacturing scrap are shredded and separated from larger metal and plastic components. Depending on the battery chemistry, it contains recoverable lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite, materials that can be processed and reused in battery manufacturing.

The domestic recycling industry has more capacity to process black mass than the material currently generated, leaving refiners short of feedstock, according to industry analysis. Retaining the material within the country could improve utilisation of existing facilities and reduce the need for battery makers to source recovered minerals from overseas.

The export restriction comes against the backdrop of the government’s National Critical Mineral Mission, approved in January 2025 with government expenditure of ₹16,300 crore and expected investments of ₹18,000 crore over seven years. The mission seeks to strengthen domestic supply chains for critical minerals through exploration, processing and recycling. In September 2025, the Cabinet separately approved a ₹1,500-crore incentive scheme to promote the recovery of critical minerals from battery waste and other secondary sources.

India recorded zero exports worldwide under this code in FY2026. The government acted to prevent future shipments and keep the material available to domestic refiners, according to Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).

The export ban could help bridge the gap between recycling capacity and feedstock availability, particularly as domestic battery manufacturing and EV adoption expand. It may also encourage recyclers to invest in technologies that extract battery-grade materials instead of stopping at intermediate products.

However, the sector experts say that the policy’s effectiveness will depend on enforcement. Battery waste can potentially be misdeclared as cobalt powder, nickel intermediates or other industrial products to circumvent export restrictions.

“Effective enforcement will depend on Customs checking how the material was produced as well as how it was declared since a different name or tariff code can conceal the same waste,” Ajay Srivastava, founder, GTRI said.

text:
In Short : West Bengal has announced an attractive investment assistance framework offering incentives of up to 120% for eligible semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery manufacturing projects. The initiative aims to attract large-scale industrial investments, strengthen advanced manufacturing capabilities and position the state as an emerging destination for strategic technology industries. The policy support is expected to encourage domestic and international investors, promote employment generation, develop local supply chains and accelerate the state’s participation in India’s expanding semiconductor, electric mobility and energy storage ecosystems.

In Detail : West Bengal is stepping up efforts to attract investments in advanced manufacturing by offering investment assistance of up to 120% for eligible projects in the semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery sectors. The incentive framework reflects the state’s ambition to establish itself as a competitive industrial destination and participate more actively in India’s rapidly expanding electronics, clean mobility and energy storage markets. The initiative is also expected to strengthen investor confidence and encourage the establishment of technology-intensive manufacturing facilities.

The proposed investment assistance is designed to improve the financial attractiveness of setting up industrial projects in the state. By providing substantial policy support, West Bengal aims to reduce the initial investment burden on companies entering capital-intensive sectors. Semiconductor fabrication, electronics manufacturing, battery production and electric vehicle facilities generally require significant upfront expenditure, advanced machinery, specialised infrastructure and long-term technology commitments. Targeted incentives could therefore play an important role in encouraging companies to consider the state for their manufacturing expansion plans.

The semiconductor sector represents a particularly strategic opportunity for West Bengal. Global demand for semiconductor chips is increasing across automobiles, consumer electronics, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, industrial automation and defence applications. India is making significant efforts to establish domestic semiconductor manufacturing capabilities and reduce dependence on international supply chains. West Bengal’s proposed incentives could help attract investments in semiconductor-related manufacturing, assembly, testing, packaging and supporting electronics industries.

Electric vehicle manufacturing is another important focus of the investment initiative. India’s transition towards electric mobility is creating opportunities across automobile manufacturing, electric motors, power electronics, charging infrastructure and associated components. West Bengal could seek to attract investments in electric two-wheelers, passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles and their supporting supply chains. Developing a local EV manufacturing ecosystem would also help create employment opportunities, encourage technological innovation and support the country’s broader clean transportation objectives.

Battery manufacturing and energy storage represent another critical area of potential investment. Rising demand for electric vehicles and renewable energy integration is increasing the need for advanced battery technologies and large-scale energy storage systems. Establishing battery manufacturing facilities within West Bengal could support domestic production of battery cells, modules, packs and associated components. Such investments could also strengthen the supply chain for stationary storage applications, which are becoming increasingly important for ensuring reliable electricity supply from solar and wind power projects.

The investment assistance framework could generate wider economic benefits through the development of industrial clusters and supporting infrastructure. Semiconductor, EV and battery manufacturing projects require specialised industrial land, reliable electricity, water supply, logistics facilities, skilled manpower and technology partnerships. Coordinated infrastructure development and a supportive regulatory environment will therefore be important for translating investment proposals into operational manufacturing facilities. Strong linkages with universities, technical institutions and research organisations could further strengthen the state’s industrial capabilities.

The initiative also reflects increasing competition among Indian states to attract strategic manufacturing investments. Several states are introducing sector-specific policies, capital subsidies, tax incentives and infrastructure support to secure projects in semiconductors, electronics, electric mobility and advanced materials. West Bengal’s offer of up to 120% investment assistance could provide a distinctive advantage in attracting investors, although the actual benefits will depend on eligibility conditions, project size, investment categories and the detailed implementation guidelines.

Successful implementation will require more than financial incentives. Investors will also evaluate policy stability, ease of doing business, infrastructure readiness, access to skilled workers, supply-chain availability and the speed of regulatory approvals. Establishing strong industrial ecosystems and ensuring effective coordination between government agencies and private companies will be essential for attracting long-term investments. The state will also need to build specialised training and research capabilities to meet the technical requirements of advanced manufacturing industries.

Overall, West Bengal’s proposed 120% investment assistance for semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery projects represents an ambitious attempt to strengthen its position in India’s next-generation manufacturing landscape. By targeting strategically important sectors linked to digital technology, clean mobility and energy storage, the state aims to attract capital, generate skilled employment and develop competitive industrial supply chains. If supported by effective implementation, infrastructure development and sustained investor engagement, the initiative could help West Bengal emerge as an important contributor to India’s advanced manufacturing and clean energy ambitions.

text:
Electric cars and energy storage setups are changing quickly, and battery makers are adapting just as fast. South Korean suppliers POSCO Future M and LG Energy Solution are partnering to ensure that shift has an ample supply of materials.

POSCO Future M signed a Future Cooperation MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) with LG Energy Solution. Under the deal, POSCO Future M expects to supply 720,000 tons of cathode and anode materials to LG Energy Solution over seven years, running from 2027 through 2033. Both sides plan to settle product roadmaps and sign a formal contract before the end of the year.

Shifting Gears to Meet Demand

A large part of the plan centers on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials. Demand for LFP is climbing fast, thanks to cheaper electric cars and power-hungry AI data centers.

To keep up, POSCO Future M plans to convert high-nickel production lines at its Pohang plant into LFP lines, aiming to start full-scale supply to LG Energy Solution early next year. Later on, they want to cut costs even further by tapping into POSCO Group’s lithium resources from salt lakes in Argentina.

The deal also covers synthetic graphite anode materials, produced in Korea and Vietnam. These help batteries charge faster and hold up better over time, making them a great fit for modern electric vehicles. For existing nickel-cobalt-manganese materials, the teams plan to recycle metals from spent batteries to keep production costs down.

Building for the Long Haul

Both teams agreed to collaborate on advanced tech, including materials for sodium-ion batteries, ultra-high-nickel cathodes, and silicon anode materials.

The two companies also plan to navigate shifting global trade rules as a team. That includes keeping an eye on prohibited foreign entity requirements in the U.S. and Europe’s Industrial Accelerator Act.

This move matches POSCO Group’s broader plan to become a national supplier of critical resources. With its own lithium reserves and graphite mines, POSCO Future M is setting up a steady, practical supply chain to keep electric cars and hardware moving forward.

text:
NEW YORK, Nov 10 (Reuters) – will rise to record highs in 2026 and 2027 due to power-hungry and electrification, the US said in its Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) on Tuesday.

The projected that will rise from a record 4,216 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2025 to 4,306 billion kWh in 2026 and 4,370 billion kWh in 2027. If correct, 2026 would be the third year in a row of record demand.

Demand is surging largely due to data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence. Homes and businesses have also been relying more on electricity and less on fossil fuels for heat and transportation.

The EIA forecast that power sales in 2026 will rise to 1,546 billion kWh for residential consumers, 1,557 billion kWh for commercial customers and 1,061 billion kWh for industrial customers.

The all-time highs stand at 1,519 billion kWh for residential consumers and 1,503 billion kWh for commercial customers in 2025 and 1,064 billion kWh for industrial customers in 2000.

As renewable output rises, the EIA said the share of power generation from coal will slide from 17% in 2025 to 15% in 2026 and 2027, while the share of in 2026 will hold steady from 2025 at 40%, then ease to 39% in 2027.

The percentage of will rise from around 24% in 2025 to 25% in 2026 and 28% in 2027, while nuclear power’s share will hold at 18% in 2026 and 2027, the same as in 2025, according to the outlook.

The EIA projected that gas sales in 2026 would slide to 12.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) for residential consumers and 9.4 bcfd for commercial customers, but rise to 23.8 bcfd for industrial customers and 37.4 bcfd for power generation.

Those figures compare with all-time highs of 14.3 bcfd in 1996 for residential consumers, 9.9 bcfd in 2025 for commercial customers, 23.8 bcfd in 1973 for industrial customers, and 36.8 bcfd in 2024 for power generation.

text:
China exported about 927,000 passenger vehicles last month, up 62.3% from a year earlier, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said Wednesday. Demand for electric vehicles and hybrids drove the growth.

However, domestic demand continued to be weak, with passenger vehicle sales declining 27.4%, to about 1.7 million units, compared with October 2025.

From January to October, China exported more than 8 million passenger vehicles, compared with 4.8 million in the same period in 2025, according to the association. Domestic passenger car sales fell to 14.5 million from 19.4 million in the same period last year.

Domestic car sales have fallen for months as cuts to some government subsidies for buyers and growing economic uncertainty have dampened demand. A fierce price war, intense competition and excess supply have also prompted automakers to step up their overseas push.

China’s domestic retail car sales could total about 18.5 million vehicles in 2026, the lowest level in years, according to Cui Dongshu, of the China Passenger Car Association.

But car exports could exceed 10 million, according to Cui and other auto analysts. Markets including Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and Southeast Asia are among those where Chinese carmakers are expanding.

“Exports are becoming a central growth driver for some Chinese automakers as domestic demand remains weak,” said Chris Liu, a Shanghai-based senior analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia.

Chinese automakers, however, face growing export challenges, including protectionist measures. The European Union, under mounting pressure to reduce its huge trade deficit with China, recently reached a deal with Beijing to curb Chinese hybrid vehicle exports over the next few years.

China’s planned reduction in export tax rebates starting next April is also likely to raise some export costs and squeeze automakers’ profits.

text:
Archrock, an energy infrastructure company listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), has agreed to acquire HiVolt Energy in an all-cash transaction valued at up to $450m.

Based in Texas, HiVolt Energy is a provider of electrical infrastructure solutions.

Archrock, which is also a Texas-based company, provides natural gas compression services to the energy industry.

The agreement includes an upfront payment of $415m at closing, along with earn-out incentives of up to $35m linked to the achievement of certain commercial milestones.

The transaction aims to expand Archrock’s range of energy infrastructure services by combining its existing natural gas compression capabilities with HiVolt’s prime power microgrid platform.

Archrock president and CEO Brad Childers said: “Combining HiVolt’s proven prime power microgrid platform with Archrock’s natural gas compression offerings will transform our company into a broader provider of energy infrastructure.

“HiVolt has built a proven, differentiated platform in the energy microgrid market that complements our core compression business and will enable us to provide additional essential services to customers across the energy value chain, particularly in power-constrained geographies.

“The transaction also offers upside from future industrial markets. We are confident that this transaction will advance our strategic priorities and drive long-term growth and value creation for Archrock shareholders.”

HiVolt currently has over 80MW of contracted prime power capacity supported by long-term power purchase agreements, typically lasting five to eight years.

The company has also secured access to more than 500MW of near-term generation equipment.

Archrock stated that the acquisition is expected to be immediately accretive to its earnings per share and cash available for dividend per share.

The company expects to fund the $415m cash portion of the purchase price using its available credit facility.

The transaction, including the earn-out component, reflects a multiple of approximately 6.1 times the midpoint of HiVolt’s projected 2028 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA) range of $70m to $75m. Around 70% of this EBITDA is supported by contracted and awarded opportunities.

The board of directors of Archrock has approved the deal, which is anticipated to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and standard closing conditions.

Following completion, HiVolt will operate as a separate business segment within Archrock and will continue to be led by its current CEO, Josh Evans.

Archrock plans to maintain HiVolt’s operations and personnel, including its presence in Midland, Texas, while working to extend its reach across the US.

text:
On-site gas contracts can run 15 to 20 years with fixed charges or minimum purchases, so a slower plant can cut output faster than it cuts the gas bill.

Air Products' fiscal fourth-quarter volume growth in the Americas came partly from an asset sale tied to a customer contract that ended early. In its Nov. 5 earnings release, the company said Americas sales rose 27% on 26% higher volumes, "including a significant asset sale associated with an early contract termination in the Americas." It did not name the customer, the plant or the terms that ended the agreement.

The release does not say whether the customer's production fell short or whether a minimum-purchase clause played a part. It does put a recent, concrete case behind a question manufacturers face whenever output slips. Industrial gas contracts for on-site supply can commit a plant to fixed monthly charges or minimum purchases for well over a decade, while production forecasts change every quarter. How much of the gas bill falls when a line slows depends on how the contract was written.

What an On-Site Gas Contract Commits a Plant To

Air Products' on-site and pipeline supply, which generates about half of the company's sales, is generally governed by contracts of 15 to 20 years, or 10 to 15 years for smaller on-site plants. Those contracts commonly include "fixed monthly charges and/or minimum purchase requirements," along with price escalation tied to external indexes. Electricity and natural gas costs are passed through by formula, surcharge or tolling arrangement.

Linde's 2025 annual report describes similar terms. Its on-site agreements are generally total requirement contracts running 10 to 20 years, with minimum purchase requirements and price escalation. Linde estimated about $62 billion in future revenue from minimum purchase requirements and engineering plant sales as of Dec. 31, 2025. That figure excludes on-site sales above the contractual minimums, and Linde expects about half of the minimum-purchase revenue within six years.

Bulk deliveries work differently. Air Products says its liquid bulk and packaged gas sales do not include minimum purchase requirements, and those contracts generally run five years or less. Linde's merchant agreements usually run three to seven years. The storage containers at the customer's site are usually owned and maintained by Linde and leased to the customer, so a change of supplier can also mean a change of tanks.

How Much of the Gas Bill Moves When Output Falls

Consider an on-site agreement with a fixed facility charge of $30,000 a month, a gas price of $0.50 per unit and a monthly minimum of 80,000 units. At a planned 100,000 units, the plant pays $80,000, or $0.80 per unit. If production drops and the plant takes 65,000 units, it still pays the fixed charge plus the 80,000-unit minimum, for $70,000. Volume fell 35%. The bill fell 12.5%, and the effective cost rose to about $1.08 per unit consumed.

Nothing in that example touched the quoted price of $0.50. The higher cost per unit came from the part of the bill that does not track consumption. A procurement team comparing two offers on price alone would miss that difference. So would a finance team that budgets gas as a variable cost per ton of output. Energy pass-through adds another layer, since a formula tied to contracted volume behaves differently from one tied to metered flow when the plant runs slow.

Suppliers are committing capital on the other side of these deals. Air Products expects $3.0 billion to $3.5 billion in capital spending for fiscal 2027. Some of that capacity is built for specific customers. Air Liquide's three new U.S. gas plants include an Indiana facility built to supply SK hynix's first U.S. semiconductor fab. A buyer asking for a volume band or a scheduled review is asking the supplier to carry part of the demand uncertainty on equipment built for one site.

Electronics Gains Diverge From Weaker Industrial Demand

One contract template may not suit every plant, and the suppliers' own outlooks show why. Air Products expect "limited growth globally" in manufacturing and "continued pressure in Europe due to higher costs and weak macroeconomic environment." The same slides cite pressure from imports on European metals and continued weakness in European chemicals. Electronics points the other way. Air Products booked more than $2.0 billion in new electronics wins, has a new asset ramping in Taiwan and is assessing a pipeline of more than $4.0 billion, largely in electronics and space.

Linde's results on Oct. 29 also leaned on electronics. In its third-quarter release, sales rose 9% to $9.4 billion, with volume growth led by electronics, chemicals and energy, and manufacturing.
