title: National Wealth Fund accelerates offshore wind rollout with £1 billion backing for 2.8GW of ...
description:
National Wealth Fund’s involvement widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7.
The National Wealth Fund has today announced two £500 million commitments for each of RWE and KKR’s Vanguard West and Vanguard East windfarms off the coast of Norfolk, for a total commitment of £1 billion.
With financial close reached for both projects, approximately £13 billion of project-backed financing has been secured from a consortium of 35 international banks including the National Wealth Fund.
Offshore wind is part of that mix, but it needs very significant investment, at pace.
In its recent Strategic Plan, the National Wealth Fund outlined how it would support the delivery of core infrastructure projects through the deployment of debt and guarantee financing in fixed offshore wind.
text:
The Fund’s lending forms part of £12.8 billion financing package from a consortium of lenders to support the construction of RWE and KKR’s Norfolk Vanguard East & West projects - the largest ever project financing in UK offshore wind.

The projects’ combined 2.8 GW of capacity – enough to supply the equivalent of around three million UK homes - will accelerate the deployment of clean, affordable, homegrown energy to millions of UK households and businesses.

National Wealth Fund’s involvement widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7.

The National Wealth Fund has today announced two £500 million commitments for each of RWE and KKR’s Vanguard West and Vanguard East windfarms off the coast of Norfolk, for a total commitment of £1 billion.

With financial close reached for both projects, approximately £13 billion of project-backed financing has been secured from a consortium of 35 international banks including the National Wealth Fund. KKR has also acquired a 50% equity stake in each of Vanguard West and Vanguard East, formally establishing the 50:50 joint venture with RWE.

The success of the Government’s Allocation Round 7 (AR7) in January earlier this year saw 8.4GW of potential new capacity awarded Contracts for Difference (CfD), making it the largest offshore wind auction in Europe to date. The scale of this roll-out will require those successful projects to raise tens of billions of pounds to finance construction, with the National Wealth Fund’s support for Vanguard East & West ensuring that developers can access a wider pool of capital that ensures the deployment of these critical projects.

The projects’ combined 2.8 GW of capacity is enough to supply the equivalent of around three million UK homes and marks another important step towards a more resilient and affordable home-grown energy system. Importantly, Vanguard’s Norfolk location materially enhances the cost‑effective delivery of offshore wind due to its proximity to areas of high energy demand in the south of England, reducing transmission distances, lowering grid‑constraints, and decreasing the system‑integration costs relative to more remote sites.

In addition, the National Wealth Fund estimates that, during construction, the projects will create and support around 2,3001 jobs each year, both directly and indirectly through the supply chain, plus over 100 long-term permanent jobs during the operational phase. Preparatory works are already well advanced for offshore construction, which is set to begin in early 2027.

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey said:

“Britain’s clean energy industry is essential to drive good growth, bring down energy bills, strengthen our energy security and create well paid jobs across the country.

“This investment from the National Wealth Fund will help unlock around £13 billion of financing for new offshore wind – a huge uptick in capability that could power the equivalent of around three million UK homes and supporting over 2,400 jobs.”

Oliver Holbourn, National Wealth Fund CEO, said:

“With recent volatility in global energy markets, the need for a reliable source of affordable homegrown renewable energy has never been stronger. Offshore wind is part of that mix, but it needs very significant investment, at pace. That's where the National Wealth Fund comes in, widening the pools of capital available and reinforcing momentum in the sector.”

Fixed bottom offshore wind is a central pillar of the UK Government’s clean energy strategy and is expected to form the backbone of the nation’s clean power system by 2050. In its recent Strategic Plan, the National Wealth Fund outlined how it would support the delivery of core infrastructure projects through the deployment of debt and guarantee financing in fixed offshore wind.

name: Texas and Evs
title: IBTTA ANNUAL MEETING: Federal funding, AI and V2X on the agenda
description:
The Council of Platinum Sponsors debates how AI will change toll agencies, in an invitation-only session moderated by Saida Williams of Indra Group.
8.30am to 9.30am, Monument A-E, Level 1.
Moderated by Amanda Boulden of the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority, winners from the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, Oklahoma Turnpike Authority, Central Florida Expressway Authority, Illinois Tollway, Riverside County Transportation Commission and 407 ETR accept their awards.
2.00pm to 3.00pm, Monument A-E, Level 1.
7.00pm to 10.00pm, Monument A-E, Level 1.
text:
We take a look at some of the biggest issues to be discussed and list every session taking place at tolling’s biggest annual gathering, which opens at the Loews Arlington, Texas, on Thursday, with more than 80 exhibitors in the hall and a conference hotel that sold out ahead of the meeting.

The 94th Annual Meeting & Exhibition of the International Bridge, Tunnel and Turnpike Association (IBTTA) is hosted by the North Texas Tollway Authority (NTTA), runs until Sunday 15 November and takes as its theme ‘Driving what’s next: Investment. Impact. Influence.’

It is the first annual meeting since Mark Chung took over as IBTTA’s chief executive, and he sees it as the place where the industry works out its direction. “The annual meeting is where leaders come together to talk about what’s next, and, more importantly, how we get there,” he says. “It truly brings together people who are building the future, and I think they’re all going to be represented at this meeting this year.”

Three subjects stand out from the programme: a federal funding debate with a deadline attached, the arrival of the connected car as a toll tag, and the question of how much of the back office artificial intelligence should be trusted with. TTi’s separate report covers the product launches on the show floor.

Washington comes to Texas

The headline slot belongs to Sean McMaster. The administrator of the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) joins IBTTA president Joi Taylor Dean, chief executive of the Richmond Metropolitan Transportation Authority, for a fireside chat on Saturday morning about federal priorities, infrastructure investment and what they mean for tolling.

The timing is pointed. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act expired on 30 September, and Congress has since extended surface transportation programmes only as far as 11 December. The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee’s answer is the BUILD America 250 Act, which it approved in May. IBTTA welcomes the bill’s hunt for new revenue, including annual registration fees for electric vehicles, but objects to the scrapping of the Congestion Relief Program, which lets up to ten urbanised areas introduce tolling and road pricing on interstates and other federal-aid roads.

McMaster has talked up public-private partnerships as a way of cutting congestion, and congestion is a stated federal target. “Gridlock and congestion have no place in the Golden Age of Transportation,” he says in the April release launching a federal bottleneck initiative. Road pricing itself has been a harder sell. USDOT moved in 2025 to withdraw federal approval for New York’s congestion relief zone, but a federal court blocked that move in May 2025 and overturned it in March this year, according to the Congressional Research Service, and the charges have continued throughout. IBTTA gave last year’s President’s Award for Excellence to MTA Bridges and Tunnels for the programme.

Chung is looking for a seat at the table. Before joining IBTTA he served on USDOT’s Transforming Transportation Advisory Committee, which the current administration has put on hold. “I hope that they will revive it, because I think having the industry voice included in the federal policy thinking is an important and a very integral part,” he says. “It should be an integral part to how the federal government operates, and I hope someday that we will do that again.”

Underneath it all is the question of how roads are paid for as fuel tax receipts fall. “The gas tax revenues are continuing to drop while costs are continuing to go up, and we’re going to be hundreds of billions of dollars in the red in terms of how we can actually fund our highways,” says Brad Stertz, director of Audi government affairs and a speaker at Friday’s OEM session. Ola Grieg of Q-Free makes the same point from the supplier side. “More and more governments around the world are concerned about the loss of fuel tax income with electrical cars,” he says. “This is a trend that will continue and continue to zero.”

The car as the toll tag

If Washington sets the money agenda, the vehicle makers may set the technology agenda. On Friday, a session billed as OEMs: what you always wanted to know but were afraid to ask puts carmakers and toll operators on the same stage. Sarah Puro of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation moderates, with Stertz joined by Manish Chourey, chief technology officer at the North Carolina Turnpike Authority (NCTA), Drew Van Duren of Qualcomm and Brock Aun of HAAS Alert. Connected-vehicle payments, interoperability, privacy and cybersecurity are all on the list, and Chung sees the last of those as inseparable from the rest. “With connected infrastructure we have to talk about cyber security, and they go hand in hand,” he says.

The session follows IBTTA’s May memorandum of understanding with the 5G Automotive Association (5GAA) on V2X-enabled tolling, and a year in which North Carolina has become the proving ground, with equipment on four gantries, two near Raleigh and two near Charlotte. For Stertz, tolling is the business case the connected car has been waiting for. “But now, after a lot of stops and starts and a lot of development, tolling offers perhaps the best opportunity to really unlock what connected vehicles and connected transportation can be all about,” he says.

The industry is not yet fully aligned on who does what. “We don’t necessarily want to be the tax collector, because we don’t really control how our customers use the car, and that would add a pretty significant burden to us,” Stertz says of road user charging. For agencies, the attraction is cleaner revenue. “Using this technology, we don’t have to do licence plate recognition, so all the leakage related to licence plate goes away,” says Chourey. “That’s huge, the one to two percent of toll revenue which we cannot collect today becomes possible.”

The worry for agencies is timing. “I think the biggest challenge for us is knowing when to pull the trigger,” says Tracie Brown, director of operations at the Central Texas Regional Mobility Authority (CTRMA) and one of the meeting’s chief organisers. CTRMA already has five V2X units on its roads, but Brown says she does not yet know when there will be enough equipped cars to justify deploying more.

AI, the back office and the customer

Artificial intelligence is on the agenda from the first day. Thursday’s invitation-only Council of Platinum Sponsors roundtable asks ‘The AI-powered toll agency: what changes and what stays human?’, and Friday’s innovation track covers AI-powered operations, digital twins and payments, moderated by NTTA’s Deepa Medooru. “Of course everyone’s talking about AI, so we also talk about AI and applications of AI in our industry,” says Chung.

The human half of that question may matter most on Sunday afternoon, when a panel led by Greg Slater of the Tampa Hillsborough Expressway Authority tackles Beyond the transaction: closing the customer experience gap. It is a theme that runs through the weekend. A Friday communications workshop begins from the premise that “Tolls have an image problem,” and Alan Williamson, construction engineering manager at the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, is clear that the disappearance of the booth has changed how drivers experience a toll road.

“Even for E-ZPass customers, the toll plaza was our customer touchpoint, our front office,” he says. “Now that’s more ephemeral, less prominent. So we’re still working on making sure people understand they’re entering or leaving our roadway, that they drove a toll-road system, and that they were a customer of ours.”

Investment on the Texas doorstep

Saturday afternoon’s investment track turns to P3s, unsolicited proposals and managed-lane procurements, with Bill Halkias of New Attica Tollway in Greece among the speakers. Friday’s technical tours include the LBJ Express managed lanes on I-635, which are already sold out. The host agency has a good story to tell: NTTA reported record toll revenue of about $1.3bn last year, according to the Dallas Morning News.

Awards, elections and the global view

Sunday is the formal business. IBTTA elects its 2027 officers and directors at 8am, and a session moderated by María Moreno of Spanish concessionaires’ association SEOPAN, IBTTA’s international vice president, takes a tour of tolling around the world with speakers from France, India, Chile and beyond. At 9.30am the Toll Excellence Awards are presented, and one of the public sector winners will be named recipient of the President’s Award for Excellence.

IBTTA named seven winners across six organisations. The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission wins administration and finance for its workforce development programme, Oklahoma Turnpike Authority wins customer service and marketing, and Central Florida Expressway Authority takes safety. Illinois Tollway wins social responsibility and also the separate Outreach, Opportunity and Engagement award. Riverside County Transportation Commission wins both technology and toll operations, engineering and maintenance, and Toronto’s 407 ETR takes private sector innovation.

The keynote

Saturday’s general session brings a speaker from well outside tolling. Leland Melvin, a former NFL player, NASA astronaut, engineer, author and executive producer, delivers the keynote at 9.30am, drawing on a career that spans sport, space exploration and education. He is billed to speak on leadership, resilience, overcoming barriers and reaching beyond what seems possible, themes that suit an industry in the middle of rethinking how roads are funded and used.

For Chung, the biggest surprise of his first year was not the technology but the people. “The tolling industry is extremely tight. They’re like family,” he says. In Arlington, that family finds out how much it agrees on the road ahead.

text:
Pennsylvania is already experiencing the effects of a changing climate, including increased flooding, more extreme heat days, harmful algal blooms, and shifting seasonal patterns.

These changes can threaten public safety, harm natural resources, and affect the places Pennsylvanians and visitors enjoy for outdoor recreation.

The plan builds on work already underway and sets goals for making DCNR’s operations and public lands more sustainable and resilient for future generations.

Governor Josh Shapiro and his Administration are committed to protecting Pennsylvania’s environment and ensuring that future generations can enjoy the Commonwealth’s natural resources and outdoor spaces, including upholding Pennsylvanians’ constitutional right to clean air, pure water, and the preservation of the environment.

“Pennsylvania’s state parks and forests are among our greatest natural resources, and we have a responsibility to protect them for generations to come,” said DCNR Secretary Cindy Adams Dunn. “This plan builds on the work DCNR is already doing to prepare our public lands for the impacts of climate change, protect the natural resources Pennsylvanians depend on, and reduce our own emissions. We’re setting clear goals and taking practical steps to ensure these special places remain safe, healthy, and accessible for everyone.”

The 182-page plan outlines steps DCNR will take to prepare its lands and facilities for climate impacts, protect visitors, and help communities address climate-related risks.

Drawing on findings from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection’s Climate Change Impact Assessment, the plan identifies how changing weather patterns and more extreme conditions could affect DCNR’s lands, operations, and mission.

The plan includes:

-- Updated climate projections for Pennsylvania.

-- A department-wide climate risk assessment.

-- DCNR’s first greenhouse gas inventory.

-- Agency-wide and bureau-specific climate actions and performance indicators.

-- Guidance on climate-resilient land management, carbon sequestration, and emerging technologies.

“As the effects of a changing climate continue to expand, DCNR’s work on their Climate Action Plan is another way that Pennsylvania is focused on the future,” said DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley. “DCNR’s tremendous work will help to preserve the natural and scenic beauty at state parks, forests, and public and private lands as guaranteed in Pennsylvania’s Constitution. As DCNR uses the plan to guide future actions, it will allow them to mitigate and adapt our public lands to continue to be an amazing resource for future generations.”

What’s in This Plan

The plan establishes specific goals and accountability measures, prioritizes support for vulnerable communities, and includes:

-- Reducing greenhouse gas emissions directly resulting from DCNR operations by 80 percent by 2050.

-- Generating or offsetting all electricity used by DCNR from carbon-free sources by 2035.

-- Providing both general and specialized climate change training to all DCNR staff by 2030.

-- Establishing 60 measurable climate action goals across the agency.

-- Implementing 49 bureau-led actions to strengthen climate resilience in infrastructure, grant programs, operations, natural resources, recreational spaces, and other agency functions.

-- Reporting progress each year to ensure transparency and accountability.

Helping Communities Prepare for Climate Impacts

DCNR designed the Climate Action Plan to serve as a resource for local governments, school districts, universities, and conservation organizations working to address climate change.

It includes regional climate projections, a statewide climate risk assessment, and guidance on forest management, carbon sequestration, and climate-resilient recreation design.

These tools can help communities identify and prepare for risks such as flooding, landslides, and extreme heat.

Building on Climate Action Already Underway

DCNR has already made significant progress in climate mitigation and adaptation. The agency has installed 40 small-scale solar arrays, added more than 50 public electric vehicle charging stations across state parks and forests, built 18 high-performance LEED-certified buildings, and converted about 10 percent of its vehicle fleet to electric or hybrid models.

DCNR’s Bureau of Facility Design and Construction consistently incorporates climate-resilient and sustainable design into its projects, including the rebuilt aqueduct at Delaware Canal State Park, which was engineered to withstand future storm events.

Adaptation efforts include upgrading trails and recreation infrastructure to withstand more severe storms, enhancing emergency response training, and expanding forest management practices that reduce wildfire risk, control invasive species, and strengthen ecological resilience.

DCNR serves as the lead agency for all wildfires in Pennsylvania and provides grants to volunteer fire departments to help equip and train crews across the state.

Investing in Communities and Local Resilience

DCNR invests millions of dollars each year through the Community Conservation Partnership Program to help local governments and nonprofits build climate-resilient parks, trails, and recreation areas, including a recent $81 million investment in community projects statewide.

Since taking office, the Shapiro Administration has invested approximately $315 million in more than 1,100 park and recreation projects.

More than 70 percent of Pennsylvania's forests are privately owned, meaning the long-term resilience of the state’s forests depends on the stewardship of private landowners.

Through its network of county-based service foresters, DCNR provides technical assistance and guidance to landowners, communities, and forest managers on sustainable forestry practices that strengthen forest health, protect water resources, enhance wildlife habitat, and prepare forests for future climate challenges.

Click Here to read the Climate Action Plan.

Here’s what Pennsylvania’s environmental and climate leaders are saying about the Climate Action Plan:

-- Lori Brennan, Executive Director, The Nature Conservancy in Pennsylvania and Delaware: “DCNR’s new Climate Action Plan establishes a science-based and measurable roadmap to conserve Pennsylvania’s natural resources against the most urgent threat facing people and nature.

“The actions outlined in the plan address the dual crises of climate change and biodiversity loss, emphasizing conservation, stewardship, and increased connectivity for wildlife across the Commonwealth’s wild lands.

“DCNR also leads by example in our great Commonwealth, demonstrating clean energy and other sustainable solutions at scale in its park facilities. TNC applauds DCNR for its proactive approach to climate change adaptation and mitigation across Pennsylvania.”

-- Prepare PA, joint statement: "The 2026 DCNR Climate Action Plan responds to the pressing challenges of climate change by charting a course to protect Pennsylvania's natural resources, communities, and infrastructure from increasing threats such as extreme heat, wildfire, and flooding.

“Through a set of practical, actionable strategies, DCNR is demonstrating leadership in building resilience across the Commonwealth. We look forward to leveraging Penn State's research, educational, and outreach capabilities, together with our broad network of partners, to help advance these important efforts."

-- Andy Loza, Executive Director, WeConservePA: “Climate change threatens wildlife habitat, biodiversity, and the economic productivity of our forests. It jeopardizes human health and safety with increased extreme weather events and flooding. WeConservePA greatly appreciates that DCNR is doing its part to proactively to address the problem.”

-- Belle Sherwood, Clean Energy and Climate Advocate, PennEnvironment: “DCNR's new climate plan serves as a role model for ways that agencies can help reduce climate pollution and protect our planet. From the new solar panel installations to more electric vehicle chargers, it’s clear that DCNR has already been a leader in making Pennsylvania cleaner and greener. PennEnvironment applauds DCNR’s ‘Forever Green' program and is looking forward to supporting the ambitious goals set out in this plan.”

The Mira Lloyd Dock Resource Conservation Center began as a small forest nursery in 1908 and has evolved into a statewide hub for reforestation and conservation support.

DCNR staff collect native seeds to preserve genetic diversity, grow trees and shrubs for restoration projects, and collaborate with researchers to improve forest health — work that directly supports the climate adaptation and mitigation goals outlined in DCNR’s Climate Action Plan.

The center also houses DCNR’s woodshop and sign shop, producing durable wood products and infrastructure used throughout state parks and forests.

text:
Thousands of jobs across the UK are set to be supported following a landmark £12 billion investment in two major offshore wind developments, as the government accelerates efforts to strengthen energy security and deliver cleaner, homegrown power.

Energy company RWE, alongside global investment firm KKR, has confirmed the final investment decision for the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind projects. The investment is believed to be the largest of its kind in UK history and will see the wind farms become operational by 2030.

Together, the schemes are expected to generate enough renewable electricity to power the equivalent of around three million UK homes, reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels and helping shield consumers from global energy market volatility.

The projects are expected to support more than 2,400 jobs throughout construction and operation, delivering significant economic benefits to coastal and industrial communities.

Construction activity onshore is already progressing, with offshore works scheduled to begin in early 2027.

The financing package includes a £1 billion commitment from the National Wealth Fund, representing the Fund’s largest investment in offshore wind to date.

The government says the investment demonstrates how public funding can be used to crowd in private sector capital while generating returns for taxpayers and supporting the transition to a cleaner energy system.

The announcement also follows the launch of the government's new Energy Wealth Fund, which will receive an initial £2 billion investment and use future revenues from the North Sea to support renewable and low-carbon energy projects across the UK.

Alongside the Vanguard developments, Scottish energy company SSE has announced that the next phase of its Berwick Bank B offshore wind project will support a further 2,677 skilled jobs across Scotland and northern England.

The company has awarded contracts to Siemens Energy for the manufacture of wind turbines and offshore substation platforms. The investment will also create 130 new project delivery roles in Glasgow and Montrose.

Located off Scotland’s east coast, Berwick Bank could become the world’s largest offshore wind farm once fully operational, with the potential to supply more than 6% of current UK electricity demand.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

“This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain. And it is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.

“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.

“Our National Wealth Fund means that public investment is working alongside private capital to build homegrown energy and bring a return for the taxpayer. Because for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.”

The investment forms part of the government's wider programme to create a cleaner, more affordable and resilient energy system.

Recent measures include the introduction of the Energy Independence Bill, designed to strengthen consumer protections, increase oversight of energy operators and remove barriers to delivering new clean energy infrastructure.

The government says reforms will give communities a greater stake in renewable energy developments, while efforts to remove standing charges and provide households with £100 towards energy bills this winter aim to help consumers manage rising costs during the transition to a low-carbon economy.

With billions now being committed to offshore wind, the UK continues to position itself as a global leader in renewable energy while seeking to combine economic growth, energy security and progress towards net zero.

text:
Nov. 10, 2026

By Gillian Pomplun

On Nov. 9, the U.S. Senate voted 73-25 to invoke cloture on S. 5363, the Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. Cloture is a legislative procedure that ends debate and allows a bill to proceed to a vote.

No 765 Line volunteer Tennille Osthoff of rural Genoa warned local residents about the legislation during the “Nature on the Line” event on Oct. 25, saying the bill could weaken state oversight of transmission projects, including the proposed MariBell and BECI 765-kilovolt transmission lines.

“Now you wouldn’t think that has to do with energy, but it does,” Osthoff said. “What it would do if it was law right now, the transmission line developer wouldn’t even file with the Wisconsin PSC. The developer would just file with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and then there would be a 30-day input period, and you would have to travel. That would not only take it completely out of the landowner’s hands, but also out of the state’s hands.”

Wisconsin Sen. Tammy Baldwin voted against invoking cloture, while Sen. Ron Johnson voted in favor.

The senators can be reached at:

Sen. Ron Johnson: Washington, D.C., office, 202-224-5323; Wisconsin office, 608-240-9629.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin: Washington, D.C., office, 202-224-5653; Wisconsin office, 608-264-5338.

Official summary

According to the bill’s official summary, the legislation would modify federal permitting processes, including environmental review requirements, to expedite a broad range of projects.

Among other provisions, the bill would:

Further limit the types of federal actions that trigger environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act.

Narrow the range of alternatives considered during environmental reviews.

Exempt additional types of projects from environmental review.

Establish deadlines for issuing permits once environmental reviews are complete.

The bill would also limit permit obligations under the Clean Water Act by narrowing water-quality certification reviews, extending permit terms under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System and limiting review periods for dredge-and-fill discharge permits.

In addition, the legislation would modify requirements related to threatened and endangered species by shortening timelines for certain federal consultations.

The bill also addresses multiple aspects of energy infrastructure permitting, including:

Expanding Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority to issue construction permits for certain interstate electricity transmission projects.

Directing FERC to establish ratepayer projections related to large computational loads, such as data centers.

Removing permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land.

Accelerating renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower and offshore energy projects.

The legislation would also limit the scope of the National Historic Preservation Act by reducing the types of projects that trigger review.

Support and opposition

According to congressional records, supporters and opponents of the bill cite sharply different reasons for their positions.

Supporters, including Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., along with organizations such as Club for Growth, argue the measure would reduce federal regulatory burdens, accelerate energy infrastructure projects and lower costs.

Opponents include No 765 Line, the National Congress of American Indians, Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation, Waterkeeper Alliance, the Center for Biological Diversity and the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers.

Before the cloture vote, the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers held a rally outside Congress.

“Chairman Leonard Forsman of the Suquamish Tribe was exactly right when he said federal agencies need to ‘work with Tribal Nations, not around us and certainly not against us,’” the organization stated. “And Pueblo of Laguna Gov. Harry Antonio Jr. provided us with a powerful reminder that ‘our sacred places are living places of prayer’ and that ‘a court ruling cannot restore a sacred place after it has been bulldozed.’”

The Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation also urged members to contact their senators.

“Later today, the U.S. Senate is considering S. 5363, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would expand federal authority to approve major interstate transmission projects even when state regulators reject them,” the organization stated. “Under this legislation, even if the Wisconsin Public Service Commission determines that a project like MariBell or BECI is not in Wisconsin’s best interest, federal regulators could potentially override that decision and allow the project to move forward.

“Wisconsin should have the right to say no to transmission projects that aren’t in our state’s best interest. Washington shouldn’t have the power to undermine those decisions.”

Waterkeeper Alliance Advocacy Director Jacqueline Esposito criticized the measure.

“This isn’t progress,” Esposito said. “Our environmental laws are intended to protect human health and our natural resources. Weakening these bedrock laws in the name of ‘clean energy’ is a significant step backward. Real progress means protecting our health, our communities and our environment, not making it easier for corporations to fast-track projects at the public’s expense.”

The Center for Biological Diversity also opposed the legislation.

“If this bill isn’t stopped, it could hinder future administrations from restoring protections and undoing the damage,” the organization stated. “The consequences could last for decades. Keep calling your senators and urge them to vote no on S. 5363, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.”

The National Congress of American Indians likewise voiced opposition.

“Tribal nations are standing together to oppose S. 5363 BAAJA, which threatens Tribal sovereignty and puts our sacred sites at risk,” the organization stated. “BAAJA was written without tribal consultation, leaves federal agencies alone to decide what’s sacred, penalizes and bypasses Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, and leaves no real remedy in court.”

title: States are counting on battery farms. Some towns don't want them.
description:
As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.
‘Meteoric growth’ Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS.
At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022.
But while data centers increase pressure on the grid, battery farms reduce it, they wrote, making the “conflation” an expensive mistake.
Some local activists have asked for battery farms to be sited in remote areas, where they would pose fewer risks.
text:
SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.

The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities.

The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power.

But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.

Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future.

‘Meteoric growth’

Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles.

At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants.

“The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.”

Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances.

With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand.

Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably.

Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects.

“As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said.

State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates.

In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage.

“It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.”

Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit.

Community concerns

For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke.

Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands.

Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities.

States OK solar panels for balconies. Safety guidelines haven’t caught up.

“They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.”

The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials.

Industry leaders say the Moss Landing facility was built using an older design, prior to the issuance of safety standards from the National Fire Protection Association that cover most systems on the grid today. Newer projects use an updated battery chemistry that burns at lower temperatures, and store the batteries in isolated, modular containers so that fires don’t spread to nearby units.

As a result, battery fires have become much more rare and far less devastating. Earlier this month, the Electric Power Research Institute, an independent nonprofit, published an analysis of battery system failures dating back to 2011.

The report found that failures (defined as large thermal events such as arc flashes, fires or explosions) have declined 97% in the U.S. since 2018, when adjusted for the amount of battery power on the grid. The incidents that have happened in new systems have largely remained small and contained, said Lakshmi Srinivasan, who authored the analysis.

“Specific design choices have really reduced not only the likelihood of a failure, but the impact of a failure if it happens,” she told Stateline.

Srinivasan said the risk profile of battery farms is similar to that of electrical transformers, components of the electrical grid that already exist in many communities.

But some communities feel a slim chance of disaster is still too high. Residents in Snoqualmie, Washington, have voiced opposition to a proposed battery project just outside city limits, prompting the city and several neighboring communities to enact moratoriums on such facilities.

“We need to think more carefully about what the worst-case scenario is, not just what’s typical,” said Dan Murphy, a council member in the city of Snoqualmie. “The science says (battery farms) are getting safer, but we’re still early.”

Amid the local backlash, the developer, Jupiter Power, has indicated that it will pursue approval from state-level energy siting regulators, removing the project from King County jurisdiction.

Murphy said his community supports clean energy, but objected to the site location near homes, a playground, a waterway and a critical evacuation route. He said Jupiter Power kept locals in the dark until they thought the project was a done deal.

“We are a very reserved and polite community,” he said. “To see the outcry and the animation and the mobilization, it’s really struck a nerve with our residents.”

In a document responding to community concerns, Jupiter Power noted that battery farms must be built near substations, which are located in close proximity to the communities they serve. That reality, the company said, makes it unrealistic for local officials to demand that battery systems keep their distance from populated areas. In King County, the company found, all 157 substations that are suitable for a battery project are located within a quarter-mile of schools, daycares, hospitals, natural areas or other sensitive sites.

Jupiter Power did not grant an interview request, but referred questions to Clean and Prosperous, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on reducing emissions.

“For any battery storage project there will inherently already be energy infrastructure nearby,” said Kelsey Nyland, communications director with Clean and Prosperous. “It often feels like we expect clean energy projects to be perfect in a way that we don’t expect from fossil fuel projects.”

Nyland noted that Washington state ranks dead last in the nation for clean energy growth, despite its ambitious climate goals. Battery storage, she said, can help population centers in western Washington harness surplus wind and solar power from rural eastern Washington.

She added that Washington has only one operational battery storage facility, making it difficult to alleviate local’s concerns by touring a nearby site.

Similar disputes have played out in dozens of communities across the country, and many have passed temporary measures banning the construction of battery storage facilities.

Earlier this month, a pair of former economic officials from the Biden administration wrote in The Washington Post that battery farms had been caught in a case of “mistaken identity” amid the nationwide backlash to data centers, which have stirred up similar feelings about industrial siting and environmental risks. But while data centers increase pressure on the grid, battery farms reduce it, they wrote, making the “conflation” an expensive mistake.

Some local activists have asked for battery farms to be sited in remote areas, where they would pose fewer risks. But industry leaders say they’re simply following the incentives set forth by utilities, which prioritize projects that can connect to the grid near population centers.

“If you have a source of power right where the power’s being consumed, the more efficient your system’s going to be,” Malaquias Encarnacion, managing director with Carina Energy, a development services firm that works on battery storage projects.

Carina Energy has tracked 175 battery farm moratoriums enacted or proposed by communities across the country. In some cases, Encarnacion said, those actions have been temporary measures enacted by local governments to give themselves time to learn about the issue.

“If I didn’t know anything about it, I would be nervous as well,” he said, encouraging developers to engage with communities early to alleviate those concerns.

text:
China exported about 927,000 passenger vehicles last month, up 62.3% from a year earlier, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said Wednesday. Demand for electric vehicles and hybrids drove the growth.

However, domestic demand continued to be weak, with passenger vehicle sales declining 27.4%, to about 1.7 million units, compared with October 2025.

From January to October, China exported more than 8 million passenger vehicles, compared with 4.8 million in the same period in 2025, according to the association. Domestic passenger car sales fell to 14.5 million from 19.4 million in the same period last year.

Domestic car sales have fallen for months as cuts to some government subsidies for buyers and growing economic uncertainty have dampened demand. A fierce price war, intense competition and excess supply have also prompted automakers to step up their overseas push.

China’s domestic retail car sales could total about 18.5 million vehicles in 2026, the lowest level in years, according to Cui Dongshu, of the China Passenger Car Association.

But car exports could exceed 10 million, according to Cui and other auto analysts. Markets including Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and Southeast Asia are among those where Chinese carmakers are expanding.

“Exports are becoming a central growth driver for some Chinese automakers as domestic demand remains weak,” said Chris Liu, a Shanghai-based senior analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia.

Chinese automakers, however, face growing export challenges, including protectionist measures. The European Union, under mounting pressure to reduce its huge trade deficit with China, recently reached a deal with Beijing to curb Chinese hybrid vehicle exports over the next few years.

China’s planned reduction in export tax rebates starting next April is also likely to raise some export costs and squeeze automakers’ profits.

To reduce risks, Chinese automakers have been expanding production overseas to replace some direct exports, including by setting up plants in Brazil and Hungary. S&P analysts say that shift could also weigh on China’s auto export figures in the months ahead.

text:
The advanced U.S. geothermal industry is heating up for many reasons: skyrocketing electricity demand, looming 2030 renewable energy targets, technical advances and a country abundant with promising geology.

But geothermal energy is still an expensive proposition — an average of $100 per megawatt-hour — for corporations mulling how to reduce emissions from purchased electricity (Scope 2). As one audience member at Trellis Impact 26 observed: “We hold four [virtual power purchase agreements] – two wind, two solar-plus-storage – and frankly $100/MWh is way too high. Our second pair of deals priced 25 percent to 50 percent below the first two years later. If I wait four to five years, will geothermal prices decline the same way?”

I put this question to Mike O’Connor, director at the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium (MWGC). “The binding constraint isn’t technology or even capital for scaling, it’s appraisal risk, the one risk no other generation industry carries,” O’Connor said. “Geothermal developers must develop the fuel as well as the large power infrastructure at the same time.”

The cost of exploration

Appraisal risk refers to the cost of digging to find viable geothermal resources, which can be located several kilometers below the subsurface.

Permitting, exploration and test-well drilling represent 10 percent to 15 percent of a geothermal project’s investment costs (roughly $27 million to $41 million), and a developer must spend this money before knowing if the site’s economics make sense. Only risk-tolerant investors are willing to get involved, so a geothermal developer’s cost of capital can be very high. Reducing those costs can, in turn, help lower the power purchase agreement (PPA) price.

One way to absorb some appraisal risk is to bring in public-private partnerships. For example, MWGC is working with its member states — currently Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Arizona — on policies that would support revolving funds for appraisal drilling that are similar to the proposed federal Appraisal Risk Program laid out in May by nonprofits Clean Economy Project and C3 Solutions, and planning firm Waypoint Strategy Group.

The program suggested in their proposal would support appraisal drilling for enhanced geothermal projects across a range of U.S. regions. Participating developers would be required to share their subsurface data publicly, so the whole industry benefits. The Department of Energy (DOE) ran a similar program from 1982 to 2012, which led to development of many conventional geothermal projects in the U.S. Germany, Japan and Turkey have also used public programs to share early drilling risk with developers.

The proposed state and federal programs would build on the $99 million allocated by the DOE Office of Geothermal in September to fund 21 projects across eight states. Five of those initiatives will conduct enhanced geothermal tests; the other 16 will focus on exploration drilling to gather subsurface data needed to identify promising next-generation and conventional hydrothermal geothermal resources.

Other signals to watch

Corporations interested in adding geothermal resources to their renewable energy portfolios should also watch for these developments.

Permitting reform: Supporters say the permitting reforms proposed in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 could shorten interconnection timelines that now exceed five years. But the changes would depend on Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rulemakings that could take years, and the bill’s geothermal provisions mainly speed up exploration permitting rather than grid connections.

Drilling speeds: Faster, cheaper drilling is one of the clearest signs enhanced geothermal is maturing. Fervo, the most active U.S. developer, publishes its drilling results through Securities and Exchange Commission filings, press releases and technical papers. Conventional geothermal wells can take up to 272 days to drill. In contrast, Fervo now takes 21 days to reach depths of 15,000 to 19,000 feet.

Delivery costs: Fervo frames its targets in dollars per kilowatt. The company estimates that phase two of its Cape Station project is on track to deliver at $5,500 per kilowatt, and it remains committed to cutting the expense to $3,000 per kilowatt. Mazama Energy, another developer, projects development costs of $4,500 to $4,950 per kilowatt initially, with a pathway to $3,200 per kilowatt at scale.

Utility adoption: Some utilities offer green tariffs that let customers choose a specific resource. Companies should tell their utility account manager that they want clean firm power, specifically geothermal. Deals can be structured in the form of special agreements under which the utility contracts with a geothermal developer and passes the costs and environmental attributes to the corporate buyer.

Operating performance from commercial plants and tests: Watch whether Fervo’s Cape Station hits its output targets and holds reservoir temperatures over its first years. There are other demonstration projects to watch. If they are successful in finding viable resources, it might be time to make an early agreement with a developer.

Price trends across successive deals, with the caution that prices are disclosed inconsistently.

The tax credit window: Projects that start construction by 2033 get tax credits worth up to 50 percent of upfront project costs. That’s because geothermal, nuclear, hydroelectricity and energy storage projects were spared the cuts that other renewable energy types endured under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Corporate support in the form of demand for clean firm power, policy advocacy, offtake agreements and buyer coalitions will also be paramount to reducing geothermal prices. For example, if a coalition of buyers wanted to invest in an appraisal fund —a portfolio of five to 10 projects — that would provide a guaranteed output and lower the risk across the board, O’Connor said.

text:
A bipartisan federal permitting reform package championed by U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito cleared a key procedural hurdle in the Senate Monday, advancing debate on legislation supporters say could accelerate energy and infrastructure projects and reduce costs for American consumers.

The Senate voted 73-25 to invoke cloture on a motion to proceed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a measure Capito helped develop as chairwoman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

The vote does not represent final passage of the legislation. It allows the Senate to move forward with consideration of the bill.

Capito spoke on the Senate floor ahead of Monday's vote, arguing that lengthy federal permitting and environmental review processes have delayed investments, prevented job creation and increased costs for businesses and consumers.

"Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions," Capito said.

She cited National Association of Manufacturers data estimating permitting delays cost manufacturers $12.1 billion annually, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia. She also referenced McKinsey data estimating $1.8 trillion in investments are tied up in the federal permitting system, including $22.3 billion in West Virginia.

The legislation was developed by Capito and Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, along with Democratic Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico.

The proposal would revise federal environmental review and permitting requirements under several laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. It also includes changes involving the National Historic Preservation Act and Federal Power Act.

Among its provisions is the Ratepayer Protection Act, which Capito said would require potential data center developers to pay their own infrastructure costs rather than shifting increased electricity expenses to other utility customers.

The bill has drawn support from the Electric Power Supply Association, which represents competitive power suppliers and formally endorsed the legislation Oct. 7.

"BAAJA will bolster electric grid reliability, lead to more affordable power, and continue to ensure critical environmental protections," said Todd Snitchler, EPSA president and CEO, following Monday's vote.

The organization said faster permitting for energy infrastructure would help competitive power generators deliver electricity to the grid. In competitive power markets, private investors, rather than utility ratepayers, assume the financial risk of building new generation capacity, according to EPSA.

Capito said the legislation is intended to benefit a broad range of projects, including coal mines, wind energy developments, natural gas pipelines, solar farms and steel mills. She also emphasized provisions intended to provide greater certainty for projects that have received permits and reduce delays associated with litigation.

Capito said her office had received letters of support from more than 1,000 stakeholder organizations, including energy producers, renewable energy groups, labor unions and business associations.

She also cited a White House Council of Economic Advisers analysis estimating the legislation could generate between $82 billion and $164 billion in additional economic output annually.

Capito said the proposed reforms could increase real wages, reduce electricity bills and lower everyday expenses for American households.

"The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can't be made," Capito said.

The legislation still must clear additional Senate consideration and receive approval from the House before it can reach President Donald Trump.

text:
(CBS NEWS) — With data centers cropping up around the United States, the cost of the energy infrastructure on which they rely, and who pays for it, are among the country’s most debated economic and political questions.

A new study finds that in 2025, the rising energy costs associated with AI data centers landed hardest on lower-income, rural households, which bore disproportionate shares of the financial burdens compared with the data centers themselves.

Authored by Cornell University researchers and published this week in the journal Nature Energy, the study analyzed growth in both energy demand and infrastructure projects along four major U.S. power grids between 2020 and 2025.

It also looked at data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers across the U.S. Its results showed that the AI boom, and the buildout of data centers used to support it, hike up energy costs in ways that place the greatest economic strain on people who benefit least from the technology.

The study found that data centers unevenly raised wholesale power prices.

Those costs are determined through an open marketplace where electricity is bought and sold in bulk between power generators and utilities before reaching transmission lines, and, eventually, consumers. Power grids that were already stretched saw the greatest price increases, researchers said.

In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to raise wholesale energy prices by almost 20% last year.

In Texas’ Dallas-Fort Worth area, the increase in 2025 approached 17%, according to their estimates.

Both regions have seen influxes of data centers in recent years.

Places like New York, where data centers are less prevalent, didn’t experience significant changes in wholesale energy prices, according to the study.

Higher wholesale prices had a downstream effect on energy consumers, the researchers said, as residential customers paid huge fractions of the spending on transmission built for data centers.

The study found that spending across the four power grids jumped from $2 billion in 2020 to $34.2 billion in 2025, with data centers responsible for $8.25 billion of energy infrastructure costs last year.

Residential users were responsible for just under $3.5 billion, but they were billed more than $16 billion while data centers were billed about $3 billion.

Researchers said that antiquated formulas used to allocate energy costs along a power grid have historically divided those costs based on previous energy consumption, rather than new growth. That means households take on much of the costs for developing new power infrastructure.

Residents of rural and lower-income areas saw their bills skyrocket, and in some cases faced increases in energy costs that were 76% larger than residents of urban communities, according to the study.

The researchers said that despite the concentration of data centers near metropolitan hubs, the financial loads they trigger often seep into surrounding suburban and rural areas because of policies that govern how energy costs are shared across regions.

They argued that such policies warrant review.

Researchers also pointed to what they called a “paradoxical mismatch”: According to the study, states that faced the largest cost increases, like West Virginia and Ohio, also reported the lowest uses of generative AI compared with other states around the country.

The study also found instances where states saw price increases linked to AI data centers located geographically far from them, essentially paying for infrastructure “they neither contribute to nor benefit from,” researchers said.

Residents in New Jersey and Pennsylvania helped pay for power grid updates tied to data center growth in Virginia, for example.

Disannexation became a critical issue following Brownsville commissioners' unanimous vote last week in favor of a 90-day moratorium on permits for data center construction.

McCorkle also touted the move as an opportunity to boost growth and help the water supply in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, a semi-arid region suffering a severe water crisis.

That crisis is largely due to overconsumption of water—a resource data centers require in massive quantities. SpaceX has projected that its Starbase operations will eventually require approximately 2 million gallons of water per day.

Many local residents oppose both the proposed tax break and the data center/power plant project.

"Please pass a full 180-day data center moratorium. And please remember that this is supposed to be a community-led environmental task force," South Texas Environmental Justice Center co-founder Bekah Hinojosa told commissioners during a November 4 Brownsville City Commission meeting.

"You need to make sure that you're taking every possible step to ensure meaningful public input throughout this data center moratorium," she continued. "We don't know what SpaceX is building on the 444 acres. It's frankly terrifying."

Attorney Jacqueline Morales told the commissioners: "The moratorium will not make us forget that you de-annexed 444 acres of land to SpaceX, which is now building a data center. "You either work to protect residents of Brownsville or you don't," Morales added. "There is no middle ground here."

The Brownsville dispute is part of the nationwide backlash against data centers, which consume enormous quantities of electricity and water while frequently seeking taxpayer-funded incentives.

Musk has met similar resistance in Louisiana, where Republican Gov. The proposed deal has outraged many local residents, more than 1,000 of whom submitted comments to the Federal Aviation Administration expressing concerns about the project's environmental consequences, including damage to fragile wetlands, wildlife habitats, and the rapidly eroding Louisiana coastline.

"I'm not anti-SpaceX," small farmer Karol Bourque told The Current in September. "It's all the secrecy, the NDAs, the laws protecting all these powerful people and companies."

She also pledged to end the enormous tax giveaways offered to the artificial intelligence industry.

EnviPath’s AI models predict whether new chemicals will degrade into substances which pose risks to human health or ecosystems and how long they will persist in the environment.

That’s important information for makers of fertilisers, pesticides, cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, and for environmental regulators, especially in the European Union where rules are strict.

As chemicals enter the environment, bacteria munch away on them. A harmless chemical can degrade into something toxic, while the opposite can also occur, with toxic chemicals becoming harmless.

EnviPath addresses a critical and well recognised gap in environmental risk assessment: while the hazards of parent chemicals are often well characterised, their transformation products are frequently unknown, despite often being more persistent, mobile, or toxic.

“These models can come up with answers in seconds or minutes,” says Jörg, who’s a senior lecturer in the School of Computer Science. “A company planning a new product can identify problems right at the start instead of years into the development process.”

UniServices, the University of Auckland company which supports the commercialisation of University research, funded Jörg to get the company off the ground in late 2024. Jörg is CEO and his former student Tim Lorsbach is co founder and chief technology officer, based in Germany. The company is likely to seek capital for expansion in 2027.

“I’ve worked on this project and its antecedents for my whole academic life, so you can imagine how keen I am for it to succeed,” says Jörg. “It’s not just the commercial opportunity, it’s doing something for the environment.”

EnviPath licenses companies to use its technology and access the data. It’s free for academic users, who number in their thousands. “There’s only one other commercial company in this area and we believe we’re providing a superior service,” says Jörg.

The company’s openly disclosed methods and scientific papers published by Jörg and his colleagues in peer-reviewed journals have established enviPath’s credibility with manufacturers and regulators.

The latter include the European Food Safety Authority, the Helsinki-based European Chemicals Agency (a regulatory arm of the European Union), and the Environmental Protection Agency in the US.

In the European Union, a strict regulation called REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) has applied to chemical substances since 2006.

EnviPath is promoted at scientific conferences and via a regular booth at SETAC Europe, one of the largest international conferences in environmental toxicology and chemistry. Regulators are kept informed via direct discussions, technical exchanges, and formal presentations.

Andy Shenk, former CEO of UniServices, is an adviser to enviPath. “From the perspective of university commercialisation and technology translation, enviPath represents a strong example of research with genuine market relevance,” he says.

“The platform combines scientific credibility with a clear value proposition for regulators and industry, which is essential for successful commercial development.”

NRC clears Long Mott

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued a construction permit on Nov. 9 for the Long Mott Generating Station, a four-reactor Xe-100 project planned for Dow's Seadrift Operations in Calhoun County, Texas.

Long Mott Energy, a wholly owned Dow subsidiary, will build four Xe-100 units that together would deliver 320 megawatts of electricity and 800 megawatts of thermal output, with each module designed for roughly 80 megawatts of electric capacity and 200 megawatts of heat.

X-energy said the project is configured around the energy needs of a chemical plant, with high-temperature steam for manufacturing processes and surplus electricity exported to the grid.

NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said, "Today, the new NRC is issuing America's first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century," as the agency described the approval as a series of firsts.

The NRC’s review moved on an 18-month schedule set when the application was formally accepted in June 2025, after Dow filed in March of that year, and the agency completed its environmental assessment and a finding of no significant impact in May and wrapped up its safety evaluation on Oct. 30.

Reporting for this sectionBigGo FinanceInteresting Engineering

Safety dispute and timeline

The Union of Concerned Scientists questioned both the safety claims and the pace of the review, and Edwin Lyman said, "The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should've fully resolved before green lighting construction." X-energy said the Xe-100 uses helium to carry heat away from graphite pebbles containing tri-structural isotropic, or TRISO, fuel particles, and the design avoids the shutdowns conventional plants need for refueling. The NRC permit does not allow fuel loading or operation, and a separate operating license is required before the plant can begin generating power.

Dow said the approval is not a final investment decision, and the company expects to weigh a preliminary investment decision in 2027 with full construction starting only after a final decision. TechCrunch said X-energy’s approval gave the company a "small jolt" while its shares were trading at less than half their initial offering price.

Reporting for this sectionTechCrunchBigGo Finance

Industrial heat and next steps

The Long Mott project is being developed with support from the Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, and X-energy said the department has signaled it intends to raise its support to a total of $2.15 billion. X-energy said the architecture supports siting close to industrial facilities and envisions an emergency planning zone of 400 meters, while the figure reflects the company's design assumptions rather than a blanket rule for future advanced reactors. The project’s four Xe-100 units are expected to start supply in the early 2030s, and X-energy said first supply is targeted for the early 2030s.

Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led a $500 million Series C-1 round for X-energy, and Amazon committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the startup. Erik Funkhouser, executive director of the nonprofit Good Energy Collective, said, "It is significant that there is an industrial customer involved who, specifically, plans to procure large-scale industrial heat," linking the project to validation of cogeneration of heat and electricity using advanced nuclear technology.

text:
The U.S. Senate voted this week to move ahead with debate of the permitting reform Act promoted by Oklahoma U.S. Sen. Alan Armstrong who hailed the vote as a “major step forward.”

In a statement following the Monday night vote of 73-25 to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), the Senator said, “I applaud my colleagues on both sides of the aisle for coming together to advance meaningful permitting reforms that will make it easier to build the critical infrastructure our economy needs and help keep energy affordable in America.”

He went on to state that the vote shows Congress can still tackle long-term, complex challenges.

“This is an incredibly important moment for our country. Now it’s time to finish the job and pass this bill.”

Armstrong emphasized permitting reform almost from day one when he was appointed by Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt last spring to succeed Markwayne Mullin following his appointment as Homeland Security Secretary.

Sen. Armstrong was joined by Oklahoma Sen. James Lankford in supporting the sweeping bipartisan energy and infrastructure permitting reform package. Of the 25 Nay votes, some came from oil and natural gas producing states.

They included Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colorado who explained why he voted against it.

“Our electric grid is under significant strain and faces growing demand. We need to build new transmission, bring more energy, especially clean energy, onto the grid, and keep electricity affordable. We should make it easier to build new infrastructure, and I strongly support efforts to make this a reality. However, permitting reform is complex, and the details matter. I am concerned that not all perspectives were sufficiently heard during the drafting of this far-reaching piece of legislation.”

He contended the bill does not do enough to ensure sovereign Tribal governments can protect their cultural resources and ancestral homelands.

Democrat Ben Ray Lujan, a U.S. Senator from New Mexico where the Permian Basin oil production is a strong economic factor, voted against the act and cited similar reasons.

“I share the serious concerns raised by New Mexicans across the state, particularly our Pueblo and environmental leaders, and believe they must be addressed. After spending the last month listening to these concerns, I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form.”

Another Republican who voted ‘no’ was South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. His office did not include a statement following the vote. He was the only Republican who voted against advancing the act.

However, he previously had stated on X and via his Official Facebook Page the legislation transfers contested transmission line cases to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) if they are not resolved within 12 months, which he argues gives a weighted advantage to developers over local input.

Montana U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy did not vote.
