text:
WeaveGrid has launched EVConnectNC, a managed charging program for North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives. The program is already operating at Roanoke Electric Cooperative and South River EMC.

Why it matters

The program is designed to help cooperatives monitor charging patterns and shift electricity use to lower-cost periods as electric vehicle demand grows. It also reflects an effort to align consumption with available grid capacity.

The program offers up to $120 per year to enrolled members who charge at least 90% of the time during off-peak hours and use a minimum of 200 kilowatt-hours per month. North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives supports 26 community-based cooperatives, though the source does not report how many have enrolled.

The players

WeaveGrid

WeaveGrid is a grid orchestration software provider for electric utilities that offers its DISCO platform for asset-level visibility and device-level control of EVs, batteries and flexible loads.

North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives

North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives is an organization that supports the state's 26 community-based electric cooperatives and their member utilities in operating the program.

The details

EVConnectNC allows members of participating cooperatives to earn incentives by charging electric vehicles during off-peak hours. WeaveGrid's software uses connected vehicle and charger data to monitor charging patterns, and the program works with certain EV models from Dodge, Jeep, Lexus, Tesla and Toyota, as well as home chargers from ChargePoint, Emporia and Wallbox.

Timeline

November 10, 2026: EVConnectNC program launch announced

WeaveGrid's DISCO platform, which provides device-level control of EVs, batteries and flexible loads, is now being applied to managed charging across North Carolina's cooperative network. The deployment extends that platform from vendor-level grid orchestration into a statewide cooperative incentive program already running at two utilities.

Electric vehicle owners who are members of participating North Carolina cooperatives can earn up to $120 a year by charging during off-peak hours. Qualifying requires charging at least 90% of the time off-peak and using at least 200 kilowatt-hours per month.

Electric vehicle owners in participating cooperative territories may be able to lower charging costs by shifting when they charge. Checking whether a local cooperative participates is a practical first step.

text:
Ford has hired former General Motors executive Marissa West as its new vice president of vehicle programs.

West will lead vehicle program and program operations teams as Ford plans to refresh most of its global vehicle portfolio.

Ford Motor Co. has hired a new executive to lead its vehicle development — an executive who spent years with General Motors.

The Dearborn-based automaker said on Nov. 10 that Marissa West will join the company as vice president of vehicle programs, effective Nov. 16.

That means West will lead vehicle program and program operations teams across Ford's portfolio. She will support vehicle development and integration, program execution and global product programs, the automaker said in a statement.

The role is critical as the automaker looks to refresh three-fourths of its global vehicle portfolio by volume by 2029, including launching a new electric vehicle midsize pickup, Fathom, as well as a new midsize pickup for the global market which Ford has not provided details or a name for it yet. Also, CEO Jim Farley has promised there will be no more "boring" cars out of Ford.

As the Detroit Free Press reported earlier this year, Ford's new vehicle plans could include bringing a few all-new vehicles and several redesigned vehicles to market in its Ford lineup and its luxury brand, Lincoln — and the automaker has told dealers it is committed to hybrid powertrains as hybrid sales have taken off due to high gasoline prices. Some of those possible vehicles could include a four-door Mustang to be priced less than $40,000, a Ford small SUV (to replace the Ford Escape) priced at about $25,000, a Lincoln all-new SUV based on the Bronco design, priced at about $70,000 or slightly more and, of course, the new family of EVs from Ford's new Universal Electric Vehicle platform that will follow the launch of the Fathom at the end of next year.

But Ford said hiring West to oversee vehicle development strengthens the company’s leadership and delivery of its next generation of vehicles.

“Marissa brings deep experience leading vehicle programs, integrating complex products and delivering successful launches,” said Sam Basile, Ford vice president of Advanced Product Development, Cycle Planning & Programs. “Her leadership and product-development background will be valuable as we work across teams to bring great vehicles and experiences to customers.”

On her LinkedIn page, West said she is excited to be joining Ford and going back to her "production roots, my true passion."

"I'm deeply energized by what lies ahead," West wrote on LinkedIn. "I look forward to learning from exceptional people, contributing with purpose, and helping shape the next generation of vehicles and experiences at Ford Motor Company!"

In a statement, West called it an "honor" to join Ford, calling it a "company with a proud legacy and an exciting future. I’m eager to get close to the product, collaborate with talented teams around the world and help deliver vehicles and experiences that matter to customers.”

In her most recent role, West was executive vice president and chairperson for OP Mobility's North American operations. OP Mobility is a French-based auto supplier that makes such things as bumpers, front lighting and tailgates.

But if her name and face seem familiar, they should. She spent 21 years at General Motors starting off as an engineer and progressing through several leadership positions in vehicle sales, service and marketing, as well as product development. West was president of GM Canada from 2022 to 2024 before being moved to senior vice president and president for North America where she remained until she left GM later that year in 2024.

Ford's release said West was chosen because "she brings more than 20 years of automotive and vehicle engineering experience, with much of her career focused on vehicle programs, integration and launches."

West earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from Michigan State University and a master of science in engineering from the University of Michigan. She also attended Stanford University's Transformational Leadership and Design Thinking Executive Education, according to her LinkedIn page.

text:
The automaker is building a new U.S. car factory built mainly around hybrid and conventional gas vehicles. At an estimated $3 billion, it will be Honda's fourth auto plant in the state and its ninth car-related production site in the country. It sits right next to three of Honda's existing Ohio operations. Per the company, the plant is scheduled to go operational in 2029.

This is Honda's first big move away from an electric-car push that didn't go well. The Acura RSX, Honda 0 Series Saloon, and Honda 0 Series SUV were all supposed to be built at a new EV hub in Ohio. Instead, the whole project was shelved as the financial losses mounted. Three EVs and a brand-new vehicle platform were retired before a single production unit rolled off the line. The fallout helped produce Honda's first loss in roughly seven decades, with $9 billion written off.

Having gone back to the drawing board, Honda settled on ultra-efficient hybrids as its next big U.S. play. The $3 billion spend supports a global plan for at least 15 new hybrid models, most of them bound for the American market. Honda expects the first of those cars to arrive in 2028.

According to Honda, the new Ohio plant will add over 2,000 jobs and build 240,000 vehicles a year, pushing the automaker's total U.S. annual production capacity to 1.3 million cars. The company also says it will boost hybrid powertrain system capacity in the state by 250 percent. True to form after the EV misadventure, Honda says the plant was built with flexibility in mind, and can add EVs to the mix later if needed.

Beyond the new build, Honda is retooling the Alabama Auto/Engine Plant, the Anna Engine Plant in Ohio, the Transmission Plant in Ohio, and the Transmission Plant in Georgia, adding equipment and new lines.

Earlier this year, Honda rolled out two vehicles on stage: one wearing a Honda sedan badge, the other an Acura crossover. Neither is confirmed. The company says the next-generation hybrid powertrain will offer electric all-wheel drive, that crossovers will dominate the lineup, and that the new system targets 10% better efficiency than the current setup that arrived in 2023.

text:
(MARYSVILLE, Ohio)— Ohio Governor Mike DeWine joined leaders from Honda, JobsOhio, One Columbus, and Union County yesterday to announce that Honda will build a new auto plant in Central Ohio, investing approximately $3 billion and creating more than 2,000 new jobs.

“Honda’s leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here,” said Governor DeWine. “For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda’s manufacturing lines. Today’s announcement isn’t just an investment in a new facility – it’s an investment in Ohio’s people and Ohio’s future.” The new plant will be Honda’s fourth auto plant in Ohio, building on nearly 50 years of manufacturing in the state. With a planned capacity of 240,000 vehicles a year, it will have the flexibility to produce multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid, gasoline-powered, and battery-electric vehicles.

In addition to the new plant, Honda is also investing in Honda’s Anna Engine Plant and Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio to expand production of engines and hybrid systems. In total, Honda’s new commitment in Ohio is 2,390 new jobs and a new investment of $3.38 billion.

“Ohio and its workforce have laid the groundwork that has written some of the most impactful chapters in Honda’s story of growth and innovation,” said Bob Nelson, executive vice president, American Honda Motor Co., Inc. “This investment reflects our commitment to building products close to our customers, and our confidence in the people, partners and communities of Ohio.”

The plant will be located between Honda’s Marysville and East Liberty auto plants, and production is expected to begin in 2029, pending final government approvals. When it comes online, the plant will be one of the most advanced in the world, with leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems.

Honda selected Ohio based on a number of factors, including its highly skilled workforce; close proximity to a large concentration of Honda’s U.S. supply base; nearby vehicle development operations, including Honda Development & Manufacturing of America, the North American Automotive Development Center and the Transportation Research Center; existing Honda manufacturing operations for vehicles, engines and hybrid systems; and the L-H Battery Company joint venture, which will have the flexibility to produce battery cells for both hybrid and all-electric vehicles.

Honda also announced the retooling of its Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio in Russells Point, Ohio, to support production of two next-generation Honda Hybrid systems, which will increase Ohio’s hybrid system production capacity by 250 percent in the coming years. Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio will also serve as the lead plant for a new Honda hybrid system for larger models. Honda will also retool a production line at the Anna Engine Plant to build a next-generation four-cylinder engine and expand an on-site parts consolidation center.

“This latest investment reinforces the state’s position at the forefront of the automotive industry’s future. With the nation’s second-largest auto manufacturing workforce and a robust supplier network at the heart of the North American auto market, Ohio is the ideal destination for Honda’s first greenfield auto assembly facility of this scale in Ohio in more than 35 years,” said JobsOhio President and CEO J.P. Nauseef. “Honda isn’t just investing in a new facility. It’s doubling down on our people, our manufacturing strength, and the next generation of workers who will build the future of the automotive industry”

“Honda’s long history in Union County got us to the starting line,” said Jonas Peterson, chief economic development officer and president of One Columbus. “The Region won this investment by demonstrating the skilled workforce, manufacturing know-how, and regional collaboration Honda needs to build its future. The message is unmistakable: the next generation of Honda has a home in the Columbus Region.”

The project was approved for a tax credit this morning by the Ohio Tax Credit Authority. Honda also plans to pursue assistance from JobsOhio, which will be made public after a final agreement is executed. Start of construction is pending government approvals.

Honda announced its first Ohio plant in 1977 and began building motorcycles in Marysville with 64 associates in 1979. In 1982, it built the first Japanese-brand car made in the United States at the Marysville Auto Plant. Since then, Honda’s Ohio operations have grown to more than 15,000 associates and more than $15 billion in investment.

Today, Ohio is home to the Marysville and East Liberty auto plants and the Performance Manufacturing Center; the Anna Engine Plant, Honda’s largest engine plant in the world; Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio, which builds two-motor hybrid systems for U.S.-made Honda vehicles, including the CR-V, Accord and Civic; Honda’s largest research and development center outside of Japan; and the L-H Battery joint venture with LG Energy Solution in Fayette County.

Honda’s growth has helped make Ohio a leader in American auto manufacturing. Ohio ranks No. 1 in the nation in engine production and No. 2 in transmissions, and about 100,000 Ohioans work in the auto industry. Honda works with more than 750 original equipment suppliers in North America, and many of the suppliers that support Honda’s Ohio operations are based in communities across the state.

Ohio was named America’s No. 1 Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC. Since 2013, JobsOhio has helped win more than 130 economic development projects with Japanese-owned companies, and more than 65,000 Ohioans work at Japanese-owned facilities across the state.

“This Bill is a BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE”, Trump posted on social media Monday as he encouraged lawmakers to support it.

The legislation would overhaul the permitting process for major energy projects – both clean energy and fossil fuel-run – across the US, reduce deadlines for environmental reviews and impose restrictions on when projects can be challenged in the country’s courts. It would also force owners of energy-hungry data centres to pay for the infrastructure that is needed to power them.

Growing anger in the US over those facilities’ use in powering artificial intelligence (AI), which has resulted in rising electricity bills for customers across the country, helped fuel last week’s takeover of the US Congress by Democrats.

“The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives,” Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, the ranking member on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said on Monday. “We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs. We can do that today.”

Authors of the bill claim it will provide $19bn in savings on residential electricity bills through 2040. The number of solar and wind projects connecting to the US electric grid would be doubled, with data centres paying $55bn over the next 10 years to cover their power usage.

But despite the bill’s claims of increasing clean energy projects, environmental organisations are opposed to the legislation. They argue it would also lock in development of fossil fuels, weaken environmental laws and make it harder for US residents to challenge projects in their communities.

Earlier this year, a coalition of national groups – including the Climate Justice Alliance, Indigenous Environmental Network and Western Environmental Law Center – issued a joint statement opposing the bill.

“We cannot allow the lies to continue, as the facts are clear: If this backroom permitting reform deal is pushed through, it will enable a no-guardrails buildout of dangerous projects that will harm our health and environment, drive up energy costs, and violate our rights,” they said in September.

“This will be especially harmful for communities of color and lower income neighborhoods already overburdened by pollution and climate impacts.”

While the legislation received rare overwhelming support from both major political parties, the Democrats’ midterm win could complicate its final passage.

Some in the party argue that the legislation should be shelved until new Democratic majorities in the US House and Senate are sworn in early next year.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to become the body’s new speaker in January, criticised the bill last week, warning it “falls short” in several areas.

“We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now,” a Jeffries spokesperson said in a statement released to the Associated Press.

Jeffries’s office added: “Leader Jeffries will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our Caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people.”

Four Business Priorities at COP31 1.

text:
When delegates gather in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20 for this year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference of the Parties, known as “COP31,” they will find themselves at the “COP of Implementation.” While the concept of implementation sounds comparatively simple, we expect this year’s COP to reflect a full range of complexities on the formal United Nations negotiations side and continuing widespread interest from the private sector and civil society.

For the COP’s Presidency – hosted this year by Turkey’s Environment Minister and responsible for shaping much of the conference’s agenda – implementation means meeting the goals for addressing climate change by setting measurable targets and working out how to operationalize the emissions reduction and financing commitments countries have long since made, including climate finance, adaptation, a new mechanism for a just transition, the future of the mitigation work programme, and the launch of the second Global Stocktake. But much of the momentum in Antalya will be outside the formal text, in voluntary pledges, investment platforms, and business-led initiatives, giving companies a direct hand in shaping what implementation looks like, particularly as issues such as surging energy demand posed by the expansion of Artificial Intelligence gain greater prominence on the international stage. What comes out of COP31 will shape the energy markets, trade rules, capital flows, and disclosure expectations those same companies operate within.

The Expanded Role of Business at COP31

Two forces increase the critical role that business will play at COP31. The first is the absence of the United States. COP31 is the first summit since the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement took effect in January 2026, and the United States will leave the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change itself, the first country ever to do so, on February 27, 2027. While a congressional delegation organized by the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition Institute plans to meet with policymakers, civil society groups, and business leaders, and state and local leaders will attend under the America Is All In coalition, the U.S. will not have a formal delegation.

For U.S. companies, the absence of their government from the negotiating table does not mean absence from the consequences. U.S. exporters face carbon border measures regardless of Washington’s posture, multinationals face transition-planning and disclosure expectations from other jurisdictions, customers, and investors, and many of the investment opportunities discussed in Antalya are open to U.S. developers, equipment suppliers, and financial institutions. Companies that engage through business forums, coalitions, and subnational partnerships will have a voice in Antalya even without an official governmental delegation.

The second force is the need for capital. The climate finance goal adopted at COP29 calls on all actors to scale up finance for developing countries to $1.3 trillion a year by 2035. Roughly half of that, about $650 billion, is expected to come from cross-border private finance. The opportunity is large: global energy investment is expected to reach $3.4 trillion in 2026, with about $2.2 trillion going to clean energy, grids, storage and electrification, nearly twice the $1.2 trillion directed to fossil fuels. The Presidency has made the point structurally, scheduling the COP31 Business and Investment Summit alongside the Leaders’ Summit and tasking its Private Sector Envoy with presenting a business roadmap prepared by more than 700 business leaders.

Four Business Priorities at COP31

1. Clean Energy Transition and Electrification

The Presidency’s flagship 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge would raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption from about 23% today to 35% by 2035. Australia’s Chris Bowen, the COP31 President of Negotiations, calls electrification “a practical way to lower energy bills, reduce emissions, and strengthen energy security,” a framing with broad appeal amid volatile oil and gas prices. If countries sign on, most of the build-out will fall to the private sector: utilities and transmission developers, grid equipment and storage manufacturers, EV and heat pump supply chains, and data center developers. For companies that buy power, the same push affects how quickly projects connect to the grid, how power is procured, and what industrial electricity costs.

Still, grids and storage have not kept pace with renewables, and the cost of capital remains a major barrier in emerging economies. Artificial intelligence makes these challenges more acute. The IEA estimates that data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024 and expects that figure to more than double by 2030; in the United States, data centers’ share of electricity use reached 4.7% in 2024 and could reach about 11.8% by 2030. The voluntary Antalya AI Pledge responds by inviting business commitments such as disclosing energy data and powering data centers with clean energy. A companion AI for Clean Technologies Initiative provides opportunities to develop AI-enabled pilots in areas such as smart energy and connect them with industry partners and investors, reflecting AI’s potential to forecast renewable output, balance grids, and reduce curtailment.

In the formal UN negotiations, the questions are whether the 35-by-35 goal makes it into the negotiated outcome or remains a voluntary pledge; whether France’s push for a binding COP decision tying electrification to cleaner power gains support, given that the pledge does not specify how the additional power is generated; and whether parties agree to continue the mitigation work programme, the main formal venue for emissions-reduction discussions, beyond 2026.

2. Industrial Competitiveness and Decarbonization

Green industrialization is one of the Presidency’s ten Action Agenda priorities. The Antalya Green Industrialization Compact will launch alongside the talks, building on Turkey’s Industrial Decarbonization Investment Platform, launched with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) in 2024, which aims to deploy €5 billion of investment by 2030 to decarbonize the steel, aluminum, cement and fertilizer sectors.

The more contentious industrial issue is trade, and in particular the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM. Under it, European producers pay for their emissions under the EU Emissions Trading System, and CBAM charges EU importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity a matching price for the carbon embedded in those goods. CBAM is important at COP31 because many developing countries see it as a unilateral trade measure that shifts the cost of Europe’s climate policy onto their exporters. China wants COP31 to address green-technology “protectionism” and the African Group has asked for a formal agenda item on trade.

Formally, trade is not on the COP31 agenda; it is confined to a dialogue held at the June Bonn sessions through 2028. Still, this year’s mitigation work programme topic is industry, and the June Bonn talks ended without agreed text, so negotiators will arrive in Antalya without a consensus draft. The other question is whether CBAM and similar measures resurface in the just transition mechanism negotiations affecting developing measures, under the response measures agenda item that covers cross-border impacts of climate policies, or in the final negotiated text, since developing countries have pushed for a standing trade agenda item.

3. Climate Finance and Carbon Markets

The COP29 goal, developed at the Conference in Baku, commits developed countries to take the lead in delivering at least $300 billion a year in climate financing by 2035. Since then, there has been some momentum: in 2024, developed countries provided and mobilized $136.7 billion, up from $61.8 billion just ten years prior, and multilateral development banks have estimated that they will provide $120 billion a year by 2030. The harder task is mobilizing the private capital behind the broader $1.3 trillion goal. The tools for doing so include guarantees and other risk-sharing instruments, blended finance, local currency lending and “country platforms” that bring public and private finance together behind national transition plans. Turkey’s Renewable Energy Acceleration and Clean Transition Platform (REACT), which aims to facilitate up to $100 billion of clean energy investment, is one such example. For developers, lenders, insurers and equipment suppliers, these structures are the entry point to MDB-backed projects in emerging markets.

Additionally, carbon markets are now operational and looking to scale. The Paris Agreement’s crediting mechanism issued its first credits in February 2026, and country-to-country trades under Article 6.2 have been under way since the first transfer, from Thailand to Switzerland, in December 2023, so integrity and authorization rules will increasingly determine which credits hold their value. Financial institutions will also be asked to lower the cost of capital in emerging markets, price climate risk, and show how their own transition plans hold up.

In the negotiations, watch who is expected to pay. Developing countries want the new climate finance work programme to focus on developed countries’ legal obligation to provide finance, while developed countries want it to cover the broader finance provisions, which also encourage contributions from other countries and the mobilization of private capital. Keep an eye on whether parties make progress on the Paris Agreement’s goal of making all financial flows consistent with low-emissions, climate-resilient development. And notice whether parties agree on how to fund the registries and reporting systems that countries need to trade carbon credits with one another, a decision parties at the last COP in Belém slated for adoption in Antalya.

4. Fossil Fuel Transition

In Dubai in 2023, nearly 200 countries agreed for the first time to the goal of “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.” In Belém, more than 80 countries backed a roadmap to implement that commitment, yet the final agreement failed to explicitly mention fossil fuels after opposition from major oil producers. Exporters argue the target should be emissions, rather than fuels. Large emerging economies resist prescriptive language, the poorest countries want finance and flexibility, and small island states and the EU want firm timelines.

With consensus out of reach, UN leadership moved the discussions outside the formal negotiations in order to attempt to make some progress on this contentious issue. Brazil’s COP30 Presidency released a voluntary roadmap on November 3 that urges every country to “start now,” using a common framework to assess its exposure to fossil fuels and its readiness to transition across energy demand, energy supply and the broader economy, and proposes a collective agenda to accelerate coordinated action through 2033. In April, 57 countries met in Santa Marta, Colombia, for the first conference dedicated to transitioning away from fossil fuels, with a second planned in Tuvalu, co-hosted with Ireland, in early 2027.

That work will also feed into the second Global Stocktake, the Paris Agreement’s five-year review of collective progress, which begins in Antalya. The stocktake assesses whether countries’ combined emissions reduction commitments, measured against actual global emissions trends, put the world on track to meet the Paris Agreement’s collective temperature goals, and it also reviews progress on adaptation and finance. A technical assessment starts in June 2027, and the process concludes in November 2028, in time to inform the next round of national climate plans due in 2030. The first stocktake, completed in Dubai in 2023, found that collective efforts were not on track to meet the Paris emissions target goals and produced the general commitment to transition away from fossil fuels; the second will measure what has been delivered since then.

For business, the absence of specific negotiated international language does not mean an absence of expectations. These processes give investors, lenders, regulators and customers benchmarks for judging the transition plans of oil and gas producers, utilities, heavy industry, and the financial institutions that fund them. In the negotiations, watch whether any fossil fuel language reaches the final negotiated text; how the stocktake’s launch frames the gap between current commitments and the Paris goals, including progress on the Dubai commitment; and how parties settle the functions of the new just transition mechanism.

Looking Ahead

COP31 is unlikely to produce a breakthrough agreement. Its significance will lie in whether implementation is made to be measurable: signatures on the electrification pledge and a clearer link to clean power, a credible start to the second Global Stocktake, finance that moves capital rather than restating goals, and a sense of whether the fossil fuel debate can be bridged between the formal process and the coalitions forming around it. It is increasingly clear that the climate agenda now runs through markets, supply chains, and investment decisions in the United States and globally, with or without full government participation.

The UN Climate Conference organizes its activities around daily themes – illustrating the breadth of climate effects and opportunities. Of COP31’s thematic days, those likely to be most relevant for business are Energy and Transport (November 10), Finance and Trade (November 13), Science, Industry and Technology (November 16), and “İmece”: Enhancing Implementation through collective actions (November 19).

For businesses that will be on the ground in Antalya, the following pavilions and events are particularly worth a look:

COP31 Business and Investment Summit (November 12–13, Blue Zone). Organized by the COP31 Private Sector Envoy, the Union of Chambers and Commodity Exchanges of Turkey.

World Climate Foundation Impact Weeks (November 9–20). An Implementation Hub in the Blue Zone, an Investment COP with the Milken Institute, and the 17th World Climate Summit on November 15.

IETA BusinessHub (Blue Zone, November 9–20). The International Emissions Trading Association’s programming on carbon markets, technology and climate finance.

Sustainable Innovation Forum (November 10–11). Climate Action’s flagship forum, aligned with the 35-by-35 target, held at the Climate Action Innovation Zone, an independent venue with its own registration that does not grant access to the Blue or Green Zones.

Global Sustainable Insurance Summit (November 13–14). Convened by UNEP and the Insurance Association of Türkiye, focused on climate resilience.

America Is All In Pavilion (opening November 9; main programming November 12–16). Hub for U.S. state, local and business engagement in the absence of a federal delegation.

Covington will have representation on the ground in Antalya and will publish a post at the close of COP31 with on-the-ground insights and what the outcomes mean for business.

Gabriela Nalvio Melillo, Associate, contributed to this blog post.

text:
New York, November 11, 2026 – Data center power demand is set to surge as developers seek to bring new computing capacity online quickly. BloombergNEF (BNEF) expects data center electricity demand to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 7% of global electricity consumption, according to a new report commissioned by Bloomberg Philanthropies.

Powering the Data Center Boom: How Grid Policy Can Deliver Clean Power Faster finds that grid constraints in the US and Europe are delaying new connections for large loads, while the financial rewards for energizing quickly are driving some developers to build on-site gas-fired power as they await a grid connection. BNEF has tracked 181GW of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of which is in the US. The announced pipeline varies widely in maturity and timing and should be viewed as an indication of potential scale rather than a forecast of what will ultimately be built.

If all announced on-site gas plants proposed for US data centers were built and operated at the assumptions used by BNEF, they would emit about 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent a year. That would be 152MtCO2e more than if the associated data center capacity were supplied by average US grid electricity, an amount equivalent to 10% of US power-sector emissions in 2025. Although many of these projects are intended to supply power while data centers await a grid connection, BNEF finds that once they are online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk beyond the annual emissions.

In developed markets such as the US and Europe, ensuring new data centers are grid-connected is the more sustainable option, making faster grid connections important to limiting near-term emissions impacts and fossil-fuel lock-in risk. Continuing to decarbonize the power system in parallel also remains vital.The report reviews policies across 17 markets that aim to accelerate the grid connection process. The policy landscape is still emerging and while many efforts should reduce waiting times for connections, there is currently limited empirical evidence to demonstrate which will be most effective.

Mark Daly, Head of Data Centers and Emerging Tech at BloombergNEF said, “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on data center developers. The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.”

In emerging markets, the challenges of mitigating the climate impact of data centers differs. BNEF finds that, where power systems remain heavily reliant on coal, grid-connected data centers can be even worse than those powered by on-site gas. This highlights how much more central it is in these markets to enable more clean generation alongside sources of new power demand.

The four emerging markets examined in the report are:

Brazil: BNEF expects almost all incremental generation needed to meet data center demand through 2035 to come from renewables. Large consumers buy directly with renewable generators, and new data center demand could absorb some renewable generation that is currently curtailed, although transmission remains a constraint.

India: Data center electricity demand is expected to rise from 11TWh in 2025 to 91TWh in 2035. Existing coal plants supply much of the additional electricity in the near term under BNEF’s Economic Transition Scenario, but data centers can procure clean power through bilateral and captive projects, and companies are already backing new solar and wind capacity.

Indonesia: Coal and gas supplied 82% of state utility PLN’s on-grid power in 2025. Current rules do not allow data centers to contract directly with independent renewable generators, limiting their ability to link corporate demand clearly to new clean-power capacity.

Malaysia: Data center electricity demand is set to rise from 7TWh in 2025 to 45TWh by 2035. Additional demand is expected to increase the use of existing coal and gas plants in the near term, while continued demand growth is likely to result in new gas capacity and coal life extensions over the longer term. Data centers can contract with third-party renewable generators and are already supporting new solar projects, although network charges can affect the economics of these contracts.

The report finds that policies to accelerate grid connections can help limit the near-term emissions impact and fossil-fuel lock-in risk in developed markets, but the challenge differs across markets. Continued power-system decarbonization and frameworks that allow data centers to support additional clean power will also be important as data center electricity demand grows.

text:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.

McALLEN — SpaceX is planning to build a $24 billion data center and power plant just outside of Brownsville on property that the city had just de-annexed earlier this year at the company’s request, circumventing Brownsville’s data center moratorium that went into effect last week.

On Monday, the city of Starbase, which later annexed land where the project will be built into their city limits, notified the public that SpaceX is building a $24 billion “gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility.”

The $24 billion investment is expected to cover the initial phases of the project which could include future expansions, according to the Monday notice which stated that the Starbase city commissioners are scheduled to hold a public hearing in December in which they will consider tax breaks for the project.

The 444.45 acres of land where the project will be located was the subject of local scrutiny over the summer, when SpaceX asked the city of Brownsville to de-annex that land. In exchange, the company offered to fund $220 million for city water and wastewater projects.

A SpaceX representative didn’t provide details as to why the company wanted the land, located near the Port of Brownsville out of Brownsville’s city limits, but the company pressured the city to approve the de-annexation quickly or else the $220 million would be off the table. The city agreed, but the move drew widespread condemnation from residents and environmental activists who believed the city was allowing SpaceX to further take over land in the area.

Soon after the city approved the deal, speculation circulated online that SpaceX planned to build a data center on the property and wished to circumvent a data center moratorium that was advancing within Brownsville.

That speculation appears to have been correct all along.

In response to the news, the South Texas Environmental Justice Network, announced a protest against the project, arguing that the new facilities would pollute the air, use up water and increase energy bills for residents.

Other residents responded positively, seeing the project as a source for more jobs.

“There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” said Janie Melendez, a Brownsville resident and school teacher.

She previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee but said her politics don’t influence her view on data centers and SpaceX.

“Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. “But I’m one of those [people] that tries to find a balance in everything.”

SpaceX did not respond to questions regarding the project.

What the future holds for data centers in Texas

However, a majority of Texans oppose data center construction, which has received a wave of pushback across the state due to concerns over how much power and water they require to operate at a time when utility bills remain high and water scarcity fears mount. In response to public backlash, several communities have issued temporary moratoriums on data centers.

As criticisms of these facilities grew, Gov. Greg Abbott directed operators of the electric grid in August to pause requests for data center connections to the grid until the data centers could be audited. However, not all data centers rely on the state’s power grid and therefore could still move forward by supplying their own electricity.

The gas-fired power plant that SpaceX plans to build could provide power to its data center to avoid connecting to the state’s power grid.

Abbott also ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing permits for data centers, though critics say that some permits have continued to advance through the permitting process.

Data center developers could face stronger headwinds under Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who said she would issue a ban on all data center approvals until state legislators can pass laws “to protect Texans,” she said in a video posted on X.

Brownsville approved its own 90-day moratorium which went into effect last week, temporarily hitting pause on data center applications within the city and its extraterritorial jurisdiction. Had the 444.45-acre tract of land remained within Brownsville’s city limits, the SpaceX project likely would have had to find a different location.

The city of Brownsville said it stood by its decision to de-annex the property, which was based on “information and circumstances presented at the time,” the city said in a statement. That included the property’s location, municipal service considerations and potential long-term benefits to Brownsville.

The city further noted that the land was privately owned and its sale to SpaceX was a transaction between private parties.

The $220 million that the city received for the de-annexation will fund critical water infrastructure which the city said would help ensure their water supply keeps up with their future growth.

“The City recognizes the concerns raised about data center development and takes those concerns seriously,” the city said. “It remains committed to evaluating those concerns and protecting water resources, evaluating infrastructure impacts and ensuring responsible growth that serves Brownsville’s long-term interests.”

Further, the city assured that any future de-annexation requests will be evaluated independently under state law and the city commission will take the circumstances and legal requirements into consideration before taking action.

“Residents should have confidence that their concerns about data center development, water resources, energy consumption and responsible growth are being taken seriously,” the city said. “Our responsibility is to ensure that Brownsville’s growth is intentional, that residents’ interests remain a priority, and that decisions involving our community’s future are made with transparency, accountability and careful consideration.”

text:
The incoming Democratic majority on the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology is preparing to wield its new power to conduct oversight of President Donald Trump’s cuts and reshuffling within the federal science and research enterprise.

“We’re going to do oversight, and we’re going to take a look at how we can structure legislation in ways that make it more difficult for the Trump administration to continue to do this damage,” said Rep. Zoe Lofgren, who is now poised to lead the committee.

In an interview this summer and recent emailed responses following the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, Lofgren told FedScoop the panel is preparing to dive deeper into controversial Trump administration policies such as to grant cuts at the Department of Energy that targeted blue states, apparent impoundment of funds at the National Science Foundation, an Environmental Protection Agency reorganization that replaced its research office, and political appointees making grant award decisions.

The administration’s actions give the committee — which has oversight of almost the entire federal research enterprise — “a lot to cover,” Lofgren said.

While the list of oversight priorities for Democrats may be long, Lofgren and colleagues also have some optimism about legislation in areas that have traditionally had more bipartisan buy-in. Specifically, Lofgren said her priorities will be quantum, fusion, and artificial intelligence.

The House science panel has broad oversight of federal research and science agencies, making it an unavoidable venue for major science and technology legislation. Over the past decade, that’s included bills such as the National Quantum Initiative Act, the CHIPS and Science Act, and the Weather Act Reauthorization.

Politicization within AI might make legislation in that space “tricker,” but the 31-year House veteran said “all three — and certainly fusion and quantum — have always had a bipartisan effort in the House and in the committee.”

While Lofgren has previously chaired other House panels, including committees on administration and ethics, the coming Congress would be the first time taking the gavel on the chamber’s science panel. The California congresswoman, whose district includes part of Silicon Valley, has led the Democrats on the committee as the ranking member since 2023.

When asked about what the committee might start with, Lofgren said everything she’d pointed to was on the table.

“I will stop at nothing to earn back the trust of our allies across the globe, end the brain drain, restore scientific integrity across our agencies, and reaffirm our leadership in science,” Lofgren said.

‘More prescriptive’

Notably, committee Democrats identified legislation as a possible mechanism for holding the current administration in check.

As the second Trump administration has sought to alter what the federal government spends its money on, science funding has been among the targets. Science grants and programs were subject to termination as the administration sought to purge activities related to diversity, equity and inclusion and climate research from the federal government.

Despite Congress mostly rejecting Trump’s deep proposed cuts to science agencies during the last appropriations cycle, the administration has continued to push for significant reductions and, according to analysis by advocates like Grant Witness, appears to be withholding science funds at multiple agencies.

As a result, Lofgren said the committee will be closely looking into legislative levers to prevent the Trump administration’s actions, such as language that’s “more prescriptive on how money is spent,” she said.

“When you have agencies withholding money that Congress instructed them to spend so that they can move it around for their own pet projects, we have to come up with ways to get in front of that sort of blatant corruption so it cannot happen again,” Lofgren said.

In an interview speculating about a Democratic-led committee this summer, Rep. Deborah Ross, D-N.C., similarly told FedScoop that a priority would be taking back Congress’s funding authority for science and research by directing how things are done at agencies.

“We are going to have to be much more prescriptive with this administration and give them much less discretion about what to do,” Ross said.

A spokesperson for the current committee chair, Rep. Brian Babin, R-Texas, didn’t respond to FedScoop’s requests for comment on strategy or priorities under a Democratic-led panel.

‘Hatchet’ to science

In terms of oversight, Lofgren pointed broadly to the impact Trump has had on the science and research ecosystem as a focus.

“The Trump administration has taken a real hatchet to the science enterprise in this country,” Lofgren said. “They have illegally defunded research that has been directed by law … in doing so, they have done huge damage to science research and all endeavors. Not only the product of the research, but the pipeline of scientists.”

Lofgren said she’s spoken to multiple university leaders about their inability to admit doctoral students and postdoctoral students because they lack the resources to pay for the research. Moreover, she said, policies targeting international students threaten the pipeline of innovators who are Americans by choice.

When asked about priorities for a Democratic-controlled panel this summer, committee member Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., similarly pointed to the need to show the impact of the administration’s choices.

“I think it’s important that the American people understand the grievous harm that is being done to the American research establishment during this administration, and that harm will be felt for decades,” said Whitesides, former NASA chief of staff who was the first CEO of Virgin Galactic.

People won’t immediately see the impact of the discoveries that would have been made as a result of that funding, but Whitesides said the United States will be lacking, particularly in comparison to international competitors. The administration’s policies, for example, have caused researchers to leave the U.S. for Europe and China, he noted.

In September, Grant Witness and States United Democracy Center launched a tool that estimated $177 billion in federal dollars has been disrupted under the second Trump administration. Those organizations, which used public records to analyze impacted federal funding, concluded that Texas had lost the most federal funding of any state and Vermont lost the most per resident.

Also on Lofgren’s radar for oversight: The Trump administration’s push to gain equity stakes in private industry. That includes equity in quantum business and, more recently, stakes in semiconductor supply chain companies. Per a Cato Institute tracker, the Trump administration has made roughly 40 such investments.

“I have deep concerns about the government’s growing ownership interest in industry, and it is only compounded by the fact that these seem to be concentrated in certain industries,” Lofgren said.

Such a mechanism has only been used in emergency situations in the past and shouldn’t be part of regular business with the government, she said. Lofgren likened the activity of seizing “control of the means of production” to communism and noted that there’s irony given Trump’s frequent comments calling political opponents communists.

“We’re going to have some oversight over that and the impact on the science enterprise,” she said.

Some of the possible focuses for Democrats were previewed at a hearing just before the August recess featuring Trump’s top science and tech advisor, Michael Kratsios.

The committee members pressed the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy director on various research and science policies, including White House activity in grants decisions at NSF and the agency’s apparent withholding of funds.

Since then, public records obtained by Democracy Forward and shared with FedScoop provided new insight into activities at the agency and, for some, called into question the veracity of Kratsios’ testimony denying White House involvement.

Legislative priorities

Lofgren’s legislative priorities align with work the committee has already been conducting over the past couple of Congresses, and there’s still a chance legislation that’s already approved by the panel could win passage before the end of the current session. That includes key quantum legislation and multiple AI-related bills.

“We’re still working to get them finished this year, but if not, we would hope to move them next year,” Lofgren said of the legislation.

With respect to AI, the committee has advanced a number of bills in the current Congress — including the CREATE AI Act (H.R. 2385), which would formally establish an AI research resource at NSF, and the AI Security and Innovation Act (H.R. 9363), which would codify the AI standards body within the National Institute of Standards and Technology.

On quantum, the committee has approved the National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization (H.R. 8462), which would re-up legislation that established the national strategy for quantum research and development.

Fusion, meanwhile, is beginning to get more attention from the panel, with Lofgren and committee member Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., recently introducing the American Leadership in Fusion Act (H.R. 10574) to advance the energy technology as a source of power that’s free of greenhouse gasses. That bill includes millions in funding for NSF and DOE for fusion work. Lofgren said she intends “to move on that quickly.”

The bill’s Republican co-sponsor is also looking for movement and questioned the Trump administration about its support.

In July, Obernolte asked Kratsios about the absence of funding for fusion in Trump’s fiscal 2027 budget request when AI and quantum each received ample support. The OSTP leader said fusion was a priority, citing a goal to be able to demonstrate commercial fusion power by the mid-2030s. Obernolte pointed to the need to work with Congress.

“It’s going to require a partnership between Congress and the administration to get that funded, and commercialization is an important part of that strategy,” Obernolte said.

AI variables

Of her three focus areas, Lofgren identified AI as potentially the more difficult to reach agreement on given the divide between Democrats, who are generally pro-regulation, and Republicans, who worry that regulation stifles innovation.

But she said the committee “can regulate and innovate at the same time, just as we always have.”

At the same time, there’s also interest in centralizing the chamber’s AI work under a single committee, which could change each panel’s share of issues involving the technology.

According to reporting from Politico in September, Democratic leaders in the House are weighing an AI select committee. That effort is reportedly being led by Reps. Bill Foster of Illinois and Ted Lieu of California, and if advanced, may require some committee leaders to give up jurisdiction of AI issues.

Foster spoke to FedScoop about why the House should create a committee to deal with AI this summer.

The particle physicist-turned-congressman noted that Obernolte, who co-chaired the temporary House Task Force on AI in 2024, had tried to make the case for turning that group into a select committee but ran into seven committee chairs who all wanted their panel to be doing AI. A full standing committee, he noted, is what most other countries have.

“We got to get past this,” Foster said. “And frankly, if you’re interested in whether the Democrats are going to be doing something serious about AI, look to see if they’re willing to put in place in Congress an organization capable of dealing with it.”

text:
Vistra Energy, a Texas-based power company, long had plans to build and operate a 600-megawatt battery storage facility on about 24 acres of a 107-acre waterfront property in the city of Morro Bay. The site is a retired oil-and-gas fired power plant owned by Vistra. The company withdrew its application in April 2025, which turned out to be a smart move. The Morro Bay City Council last week unanimously passed a permanent ban on battery plants within the city limits, months after enacting a temporary moratorium.

While state law says that local approval for the project can be bypassed, the city has an ally in Sacramento. The project would require approval from both the California Energy Commission and the California Coastal Commission, the latter expressing significant environmental and land-use concerns about the project in an August 2024 letter to the city.

It’s hard to be critical of the city’s decision. The community is troubled by last year’s battery fire a couple of hours up the road in Monterey County’s Moss Landing. That fire burned for several days. It was dangerous enough for county officials to declare a state of emergency and evacuate 1,200 residents. It was not the first fire at the facility, nor the last. The burned remains of the January 2025 fire reignited in September 2026, causing officials to order nearby residents to shelter in place. Moss Landing has the distinction of being both one of the largest — if not the largest — battery farms in the world, and also the site of one of the world’s largest battery facility fires in history.

Sometimes NIMBYism is a reasonable position.

Morro Bay’s decision is in direct conflict with the state’s green ambitions and will impact more than the local community. If California is to meet its target to have a zero-emissions power supply by 2045, it will require a massive expansion of industrial-scale battery facilities to store energy when the wind doesn’t blow and the sun isn’t shining. With a precedent on the board, which locality will next say no to a proposed battery farm and further hamper the state’s ambitions?

The governor’s office tells us that 52,000 megawatts of battery storage needs to be available in less than 20 years. The total now is less than half that — 23,000 megawatts. It took a little more than seven years to reach that point, starting at 700 megawatts in early 2019, says the California Energy Commission.

Even if that goal is reached, the batteries need wind and solar farms to generate energy to be stored, and it’s not a sure thing that those sources will be built out enough to provide an adequate supply. NIMBYs have been stonewalling renewable projects all over the world, even in we’re-so-green California, where local governments have blocked projects in unincorporated areas.

Battery performance itself is also in question. Their job is to resolve the intermittency challenges of wind and solar. There are, however, physical and economic realities that can’t be ignored. While utility-scale batteries have value in providing “valuable short-term support to the grid,” says the National Center for Energy Analytics, they “are not long-duration, dispatchable power sources.” In addition to being “energy sinks that carry significant economic and environmental costs,” their storage capabilities are short, from one to four hours.

Unless these limits are clearly understood, the NCEA says investments and regulatory regimes “could undermine energy reliability and security while misallocating and depleting raw materials, energy, finances, and other resources.” This would intensify the environmental concerns that batteries are supposed to solve while misdirecting “much-needed investment in peak-power-capable, dispatchable energy generation infrastructure toward short-term, energy-consuming storage infrastructure.”

Maybe the shortcomings will be overcome by 2045. But what about before then? Are Californians expected to live with a system that is already vulnerable and could easily grow worse as reliable sources of power are taken down?

Like the perpetually stalled high-speed rail, a carbon-free power supply is a “big hairy audacious” project separated by a yawning gap between expectation and reality. Granted, the energy transition has moved more smoothly than the train, but Morro Bay is telling us that things are only going to get harder.

Kerry Jackson is the William Clement Fellow in California Reform at the Pacific Research Institute and co-author of The California Left Coast Survivor’s Guide.

text:
GE Vernova announced a new $34.5 million investment to expand its transformer manufacturing operations in Shreveport, Louisiana, "strengthening the company’s ability to support growing demand for electrical infrastructure needed to power industry, energy systems and digital technologies," it said on Nov. 10.

The expansion is expected to create 175 direct new jobs, adding to the more than 630 existing positions at the facility. In addition to the 175 new jobs being created, Louisiana Economic Development estimates the project will support an additional 185 indirect jobs, bringing the total potential employment impact to 360 new job opportunities across the Northwest Louisiana region.

To support the expansion, the state of Louisiana offered GE Vernova Transformers Shreveport LLC a competitive incentives package that includes a $300,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements. The company is also expected to participate in the state’s Quality Jobs and Industrial Tax Exemption programs.

The expansion will take place at GE Vernova Transformers Shreveport LLC existing facility in Shreveport.

Planned improvements include new manufacturing equipment, process enhancements and supporting infrastructure across key production areas. The upgrades are expected to increase production of industrial and renewable energy transformers. Production is expected to reach full capacity in 2028.

The expansion is part of GE Vernova's broader plan to invest nearly $1.3 billion across its U.S. manufacturing facilities and research centers between 2025 and 2028 to strengthen domestic manufacturing capacity, accelerate innovation, and help meet growing electricity demand.

name: EPA
title: Podcast - How the Midterm Elections Could Reshape Environmental Policy | Insights
authors: Matthew Z. Leopold, Michal I. Freedhoff, Jennifer L. Hernandez
description:
I'm a partner with Holland & Knight here in Washington, D.C., in their environmental practice and formerly with EPA (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency), where I served as the general counsel of the agency.
And before that, I spent about 20 years on Capitol Hill, both the House and the Senate side, committee and personal office, working primarily in the environmental policy space.
Environmental and land use siting and permitting is what we do, and it's very challenging.
As we look at environmental issues, could you talk a little bit about how you see things unfolding in Congress in January?
That will mean that Democrats control the committees of jurisdiction that do work on environmental and energy issues.
text:
Matthew Leopold: Hello, my name is Matt Leopold, and I'm here today to discuss the results of the midterm elections as part of Holland & Knight's midterm post-election podcast series, where we're going to explore the impacts of the election on different industries, companies and policy areas as we head into 2027 and the new Congress. I'm a partner with Holland & Knight here in Washington, D.C., in their environmental practice and formerly with EPA (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency), where I served as the general counsel of the agency. And with me, I have Michal Freedhoff and Jennifer Hernandez, who will introduce themselves.

Michal Freedhoff: Hi there. My name is Michal Freedhoff. I am a senior policy advisor here at Holland & Knight. I came to Holland & Knight pretty much directly from the EPA, where I served as the Senate-confirmed head of the chemicals office for the entirety of the Biden Administration. And before that, I spent about 20 years on Capitol Hill, both the House and the Senate side, committee and personal office, working primarily in the environmental policy space.

Jennifer Hernandez: I'm Jennifer Hernandez. I'm the California representative on this call. I lead the West Coast Environmental and Land Use Group. Environmental and land use siting and permitting is what we do, and it's very challenging. And I'm here to sort of represent both a state perspective, and a blue state at that, in this election debrief.

Matthew Leopold: Thank you both. So, Michal, I would like to start with you, and as you pointed out, you spent time on Capitol Hill before going into EPA and then joining the firm. As we look at environmental issues, could you talk a little bit about how you see things unfolding in Congress in January?

Michal Freedhoff: Sure, Matt. So, first off, I should mention that we're recording this on the afternoon of Wednesday, November 4, before all races have been called, but it's safe to say that there is a commanding majority in both the House and the Senate for the Democrats. That will mean that Democrats control the committees of jurisdiction that do work on environmental and energy issues. On the House side, there will be probably less change than on the Senate side in terms of the specific people involved because Congressman Frank Pallone from New Jersey, was the ranking member on the Energy and Commerce Committee in the last Congress, and he will become the chairman in January.

Similarly, Congressman Jared Huffman was the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee in the last Congress, and he will become the chairman. On the Senate side, we'll be looking at Senator Heinrich from New Mexico, who will likely take the reins of the Senate Environment and Natural Resources Committee. And he led that committee for the Democrats in the last Congress, but we will see a change in the Environment and Public Works Committee on the Senate side because Senator Whitehouse is expected to become the head of the Senate Judiciary Committee. So we'll expect Senator Jeff Merkley from Oregon to become the new leader and chairman of the Senate Environment Public Works Committee.

Matthew Leopold: Great. So, in light of that and the new leadership, obviously, the priorities are going to be very different. And we know there's going to be a lot of oversight, in particular, of executive agencies. Have you been thinking about what kind of investigations the environmental committees might take up?

Michal Freedhoff: Yeah, you know, if you look at the oversight letters requesting information and documents both from the executive branch in the Trump Administration, as well as from a wide range of private sector companies, you know, you'll see a lot of these letters have already been written. And I think we'll be looking at everything from probing the connections between the past occupations of current administration officials and policy decisions that they may have made. I think we'll see a lot of looking at the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda and how those goals are described by the MAHA-adjacent groups to have not really been realized in the way that they might have hoped. And, you know, some investigating by congressional Democrats as to why particular decisions made by EPA might not have really advanced the MAHA agenda objectives.

I also think some of the various Trump Administration projects related to the golf courses, the arch, the ballroom connections and contributions that companies might have made to those efforts will be an area of focus. And I also think some of the efforts to claw back the funding in the Inflation Reduction Act that were enacted during the Biden Administration and a lot of the grant programs and loan guarantees and contracts and permits that have been rescinded or pulled back by this administration will be another strong area of focus.

Matthew Leopold: That certainly makes sense that a lot of those are coming, and we'll talk in a second about how the administration might react to a lot of those inquiries because I know they've been getting ready for it with the expected change in the House, at a minimum. And now the Senate as well will elevate that, for sure. But before we go on to the executive branch, you know, obviously, everyone's been talking about the permitting bill, also known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Any idea on the chances of passage of that in a lame-duck session? I'm thinking that might be one piece of legislation that could potentially move.

Michal Freedhoff: Yeah, I think it's sort of too soon to tell, given the results from yesterday and the fact that, you know, all the seats haven't been called yet. But I think the pointer to what to expect in the lame duck, which is those last bunch of weeks before the end of this Congress, is a really important one to consider because it's not just the permitting bill, which I agree, before the election, stood a very strong chance of enactment in this Congress. There's also a wide range of other things that touch the energy and environment space. And those include, you know, funding the government and at what levels. It includes the Farm Bill. It includes the reauthorization of the Toxic Substances Control Act fees. It includes the pesticide fees provisions as well.

And I think the question for incoming Democratic chairmen of committees of jurisdiction will be, do I want to clear the decks now and then have two years to work on advancing my own priorities and the priorities of my party, or do I want to carry some of those things over into a new Congress and potentially make some changes to what might have been a good deal before the election, might not look like as good a deal now? So, I think the jury's still out on that, but I think it's going to be a very action-packed and very busy lame-duck session.

Jennifer Hernandez: So, with respect to the view from California and the states more generally, I think it's also going to be noteworthy what isn't on the congressional agenda. There were a number of hearings, for example, around forest management, wildfire response, climate programs of various types, water management, that were fairly pointed in criticizing various California undertakings. And I just don't, obviously, see those kinds of proceedings continuing in the new Congress. And with respect to the permit reform bill, that was a compromise bill. And so, before that compromise was struck, I think the sides were pretty locked down on permit reform for me, but not thee. And the compromise is just that, a compromise. There was widespread opposition in the environmental advocacy community against permit reform, notwithstanding that compromise. And so, for me, one of the telling indications of this election outcome will be the lame-duck session's treatment of permit reform because, more than special interests of any kind, including environmental, I think the electorate spoke around affordability and wanting a more effective form of government. And so, if we devolve and take a pass on this permit reform bill and go to respective corners again, I would view that as an early loss for what the voters are hoping to achieve with a different slate.

Matthew Leopold: I agree that, you know, there seems to be broad agreement we need more infrastructure built in this country, and environmental aspects of permitting, in particular, are a huge impediment to that, whether you're building renewable energy or fossil fuel projects. But kind of turning to the administration's current agenda and focusing, particularly, on EPA and what it's been doing in regulatory reform and deregulation, frankly, my view is, one, as I mentioned, this was anticipated to some degree, and I don't know that the change in Congress is going to dramatically change the trajectory of the agency, particularly with the high-profile deregulatory efforts, like on climate regulation, particularly under the Clean Air Act. The die has been cast, and they've made their major significant proposed rules and completed a number of them already. For example, the endangerment finding has been completed and already in litigation. And the administration did that early so it could focus on defending that and, hopefully, from their perspective, getting it up to the Supreme Court. So, there will certainly be congressional oversight of EPA on climate, the endangerment finding, among other things, but I think the administration is well-prepared to defend that.

And more broadly, you now, I served in the first Trump Administration when the House of Representatives changed hands in the midterm elections and in receiving some of the incoming oversight, the agency can walk and chew gum at the same time, in my view, right? There's a function in which they're going to be responding to congressional oversight, and that does take up a lot of time and effort, but at the same time, the people who are writing the rules at the agency are generally a different group and are somewhat insulated from the back-and-forth between Congress and the agency, with certain exceptions. But I think on the priorities, you know, Administrator Zeldin's list of 50-some-odd deregulatory actions, many of them are well underway or already completed. And I think those will continue forward and, you know, it says to the extent businesses affected are listening. You know, I think you could count on those priorities being completed. As far as beyond those priorities, that's a question because there's certainly limited resources at the agency, but interested to hear what others think.

Michal Freedhoff: I generally agree with what you said, Matt, but I think that it really does absorb a great deal of agency time whenever a principal needs to go and testify before Congress. And it does divert a lot of the energy from the political team away from whatever it is that they're trying to accomplish and towards, you know, whatever defensive measures they feel they have to take based on whatever Congress is doing. But I do fully agree with you. I don't think their agenda is going to change in any way. Jennifer?

Jennifer Hernandez: Yeah, so I think that the longtime sort of catchphrase in California is the last step in the permit process is litigation. And I feel like the rulemaking process has devolved into the last step in that rulemaking is litigation, not just on the EPA side, but also on the DOI side with respect to things like endangered species or some of the habitat-related issues, public lands issues, all heading to litigation. And all of that litigation, I think, is going to consume some time and, depending on its posture, may or may not be ready for review or accepted for review by the Supreme Court. If a huge generalization about this court is permissible, I would say that this court seems disinclined to make big policy decisions that it believes Congress should be making.

And so, however that litigation tsunami continues, I suspect that Congress is going to end up having to make a new law to the extent it wants to advance new legislative priorities that aren't already solidly grounded in existing regs and precedent as it's been shaped, which includes precedent that's new around major questions around climate change and GHG (greenhouse gas). So, I think litigation is going to continue to be a very dominant feature of our rulemaking landscape at the federal level and keep uncertainty alive at the implementation level and at the state level. And that's a syndrome California has already been experiencing now for multiple years with hangover litigation, even from Trump one. So, I think continued uncertainty is an unfortunate byproduct. And frankly, the permit reform bill would help address some of that.

Matthew Leopold: Yeah, I agree totally [with you], Jennifer, on that, and I know the administration's planning to be able to, you know, file the major briefs on defense of their actions in this administration. And so, eyes will be more focused on DOJ over the last couple of years as some of the initiative shifts from the rule makers to the rule defenders. But, I mean, you kind of raised the point about litigation. Much of the litigation is really driven now by state attorneys general. And with the deepening of the Democrat control of state capitals and attorneys general offices, I think we'll see more of that. What's your thinking on how states are going to rise to fill some of the void that they've seen left by the federal government?

Jennifer Hernandez: So, I think that's a very, very interesting question because, while running against Trump and running around the broad theme of affordability were, I think, the dominant themes from yesterday, I don't think the Democratic Party has really grappled with a synthesis between affordability, adequate supply and some of the environmental priorities, especially in the climate arena. And so, I don't think that newly elected governors are simply going to, in what are now blue states, are simply going to sign on to some of the high-cost regulatory priorities that their blue colleagues have undertaken and had to either walk back or qualify or live with to some detriment.

So, I think states have, in many cases, sort of taken some of the lead in how to legislate around climate, especially. And I think that it's going to be a challenge for the newly elected crew to just do what California and New York has done and hope for better affordability outcomes. That seems unlikely. So, I think we're going to see continued uncertainty, Matt, in the litigation arena rather than a straight partisan split.

Matthew Leopold: And I think the one big case, of course, I'm watching, and you're watching, Jennifer, is the Suncor case pending at the Supreme Court, which could have major impacts on the scope of state and local authority with respect to climate regulation or allowance of these so-called climate nuisance suits. So, that's going to be a major decision coming down before June this year.

Thanks, everyone, for tuning in to our podcast series. And stay tuned for more content coming from Holland & Knight on other areas. Thank you.
