text:
President Donald Trump said he was “100 percent” behind a bipartisan energy permitting bill advancing in the Senate on Monday but balked at its inclusion of wind turbines.

“The permitting bill is a great bill that's supposed to be bipartisan. We are behind it 100 percent,” Trump told reporters.

Asked whether he would help whip votes for the legislation in the House, Trump said, “Well, we may see, but the Democrats want that—I mean, maybe they've changed—but they wanted it as much as the Republicans."

Read More on News

After a reporter said that wind provisions were part of the bill, Trump added: “I know, but I won't approve it. Well, the bill hasn't been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Trump’s comments came as the Senate moved ahead with consideration of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a sweeping package intended to speed the approval of energy and infrastructure projects.

The exchange highlights an unresolved issue in the bipartisan permitting negotiations, which have unfolded as Trump has aggressively targeted wind power.

A White House official told Newsweek that Trump “stands 100% behind the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act” and had reiterated his support Monday.

“The White House has been working in good faith with Senate Democrats for months to get this bill passed which will unleash American energy and lower costs,” the official said Monday. “The time for permitting reform is now.”

Newsweek contacted the offices of Democratic Senators Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, two of the bill’s four lead negotiators, about Trump’s remarks.

What Is the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act?

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act was introduced in September by Whitehouse, Heinrich, and Republican Senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah. The bill would overhaul federal permitting and environmental-review processes for energy and infrastructure projects.

Its provisions cover areas including transmission, natural gas, oil, geothermal, hydropower and renewable-energy projects. An analysis by the Environmental Policy Innovation Center identifies provisions affecting both onshore and offshore wind, as well as solar energy.

The legislation has also emerged as one of Congress' first attempts since the midterm elections to address growing concerns about data centers and electricity costs. It would require large data center operators to shoulder more of the costs of transmission and grid upgrades needed to serve them, while including protections intended to prevent other utility customers from being left with those costs if projects fail.

The legislation is designed in part to make federal permits more durable, accelerate environmental reviews and make it easier to construct energy and other major infrastructure. Republican supporters have emphasized regulatory reform, while Democratic backers have highlighted its potential to speed clean-energy development.

The four lead senators released a substitute amendment on Saturday following feedback from lawmakers, environmental and labor groups and Tribal leaders. In statements announcing the revised measure, Whitehouse said it could “juice the clean energy economy,” while Capito said it preserved the foundation of the bipartisan agreement.

Whitehouse told Reuters that the legislation would allow Democrats to immediately begin delivering on campaign promises involving affordability and data center accountability. “We'd be silly not to take this win,” he said.

But its passage is far from assured. Some Democrats and environmental groups argue that the legislation weakens environmental protections or makes it easier to build data centers and fossil-fuel infrastructure. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said the bill needs greater input from House Democrats, while Democratic Senator Ron Wyden has called for a different permitting agreement after his party's midterm victories.

The Senate voted 73-25 on Monday to advance the legislation. The bill will now undergo an amendment process before a vote on final passage.

Following the vote, Whitehouse said the bill's “ultimate success” depended on the Trump administration allowing wind projects to move forward.

“As I have said all along, the ultimate success of this bill depends on the Trump administration getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid, and we still need to make progress on that front before final passage,” Whitehouse said in a statement shared with Newsweek.

Trump’s Opposition to Wind Energy

Trump’s objection to provisions affecting wind energy in the permitting package comes after months of efforts by his administration to restrict or reconsider wind-energy development.

In October, Trump issued a proclamation declaring that imports of wind turbines and their components threatened U.S. national security, citing a Commerce Department investigation that raised concerns including cybersecurity vulnerabilities, radar interference and U.S. reliance on foreign-made components.

The proclamation did not immediately impose new wind-specific tariffs. Instead, Trump directed the Commerce Department and U.S. trade representative to negotiate with foreign trading partners and report on their progress within 180 days, while leaving open the possibility of additional measures, including tariffs.

The proclamation also repeated Trump’s broader criticism of wind as an intermittent source of electricity, arguing that wind energy burdens the power grid.

That action came amid an administration campaign against offshore wind projects. In October, the administration asked a federal judge to allow it to reconsider a major permit for the New England Wind project off Massachusetts, one of several offshore wind developments targeted by the administration.

Trump’s opposition to wind had already complicated negotiations over the permitting legislation. When the deal was announced in September, Whitehouse said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how it would prevent the Trump administration from blocking wind and solar projects. Whitehouse and Heinrich had accused the administration of a “reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy.”

Trump had also offered to ease his administration's holdup of renewable-energy projects as Democrats and Republicans negotiated the permitting agreement, but Whitehouse said in September that the issue remained “unresolved.”

Those concerns intensified in October. Whitehouse said at the time that the administration's actions risked undermining the deal, telling the Associated Press: “This is how you blow up a permitting deal.”

Trump has attacked wind turbines for years, criticizing their reliability, cost and appearance. That rhetoric has increasingly translated into federal policy since Trump returned to office, including moves to slow or reconsider offshore wind development.

Environmental Group Warns Democrats Over Trump, Wind Energy

Trump’s latest remarks immediately drew criticism from opponents of the permitting legislation.

“The Democrats supporting this bill are sleepwalking into catastrophe by handing Trump virtually unlimited power to further entrench fossil fuels and enrich data center tech oligarchs in the last two years of his presidency,” Brett Hartl, government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, told Newsweek on Monday.

“A week after voters overwhelmingly rejected Trump, it’s madness and political malpractice to turn around and give Trump a win that cements the decades-long Republican deregulatory agenda with sweeping giveaways to the richest corporations on Earth,” Hartl said.

“As Trump just admitted, he won’t stop his attacks on renewable energy and this bill won’t set the foundation for future climate success,” he added.

Hartl singled out Whitehouse and Heinrich, accusing the two Democrats of advancing an approach based on “a ludicrous belief that only free markets unencumbered by environmental safeguards will solve our problems.”

The Center for Biological Diversity has opposed the bipartisan legislation, while its Senate sponsors have argued that changes to the permitting system could make it easier to build clean-energy projects as well as more traditional energy infrastructure.

The divide underscores the political balancing act underpinning the legislation: securing enough Republican support for a broad permitting overhaul while convincing Democrats and environmental interests that the changes will accelerate, rather than undermine, the transition to cleaner sources of electricity.

Trump’s comments Monday may sharpen that debate as the Senate moves forward with consideration of the bill.

text:
LEILA FADEL, HOST:

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to keep building a wall along the southern border in Texas, including within a national park. As Carlos Morales reports, the decision comes despite an ongoing legal battle in a lower court over the project's legality.

CARLOS MORALES, BYLINE: The Supreme Court's order reverses a decision from a federal judge in El Paso that had halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers and patrol roads through desert shrubland and sweeping canyons carved by the Rio Grande.

LAIKEN JORDAHL: This decision greenlights the contractors. It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert.

MORALES: Laiken Jordahl is with the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that brought forward a lawsuit, along with a landowner who fears losing his property through eminent-domain proceedings. In the justices' five-page ruling, the court wrote that federal law allows the Trump administration to waive environmental protections. And as a result, there's a, quote, "clear preference for expeditious border construction" over the harms of the plaintiffs.

STEVE VLADECK: The ruling, I think, is unfortunately all too typical.

MORALES: Steve Vladeck is a law professor at Georgetown University and studies the Supreme Court.

VLADECK: The court has taken the position over the last 21 months that the executive branch suffers irreparable harm anytime a lower court stops it from doing something it wants to do, whether or not the thing it wants to do is illegal.

MORALES: In a statement to NPR, U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott said the agency will now be moving forward with critical border-security construction. Scott said the agency has met with local residents and has readjusted their plans for Big Bend National Park to preserve its unique landscape. The Trump administration has maintained barriers are needed in the Big Bend region to stop illegal crossings. Hillary Pierce is with the group Conserve Big Bend.

HILLARY PIERCE: The truth is, we do not have an immigration emergency in the Big Bend sector.

MORALES: The Big Bend sector is a nearly 500-mile stretch patrolled by CBP. Historically, it sees the fewest numbers of encounters along the Texas border, according to CBP data. The lawsuit at the center of the Supreme Court's intervention still needs to be ruled on in full. Meanwhile, landowners have lodged a separate lawsuit to stop the federal government from taking their properties.

For NPR News, I'm Carlos Morales in Marfa, Texas.

title: This environmental advocate says new Maricopa County rule is not a path to faster clean air
description:
MARK BRODIE: The federal Environmental Protection Agency late last week officially approved a rule for Maricopa County known as Rule 205.
MARK BRODIE: But some environmental advocates are less enthusiastic and worry the rule could make the Valley’s air quality worse.
Sandy Bahr is director of the Grand Canyon Chapter of the Sierra Club, and she joins me.
SANDY BAHR: It would have to not emit that, but the concern is where these are located, right?
MARK BRODIE: All right, that is Sandy Bahr, director of the Grand Canyon Chapter of the Sierra Club.
text:
MARK BRODIE: The federal Environmental Protection Agency late last week officially approved a rule for Maricopa County known as Rule 205. It allows for emissions reduction credits to the owners of vehicle fleets who replace or upgrade high-emitting on-road vehicles.

The EPA earlier this fall also announced its proposed approval of Rule 204, which offers the same kind of credits to owners and operators of non-road vehicles, like construction equipment and locomotives.

In announcing that last move, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the county had come up with multiple ways to allow it to grow and come back into attainment with federal ozone rules.

LEE ZELDIN: They aren’t increasing emissions. They aren’t increasing emissions. And they aren’t breaking federal requirements. They’re not breaking federal requirements. They are finding new, innovative ways to work within their circumstances.

MARK BRODIE: At the same announcement, the chair of the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, Kate Brophy McGee, said she’s excited that a regulatory agency decided to govern through incentivizing and listening.

KATE BROPHY MCGEE: It is possible to do what is being proposed with Rule 204 and maintain the quality of life, maintain what we value here in Maricopa County, and support and drive the robust economic development that we are undergoing.

MARK BRODIE: But some environmental advocates are less enthusiastic and worry the rule could make the Valley’s air quality worse. Sandy Bahr is director of the Grand Canyon Chapter of the Sierra Club, and she joins me. Sandy, what would this new rule do, exactly?

SANDY BAHR: Yeah, so this is a voluntary program to allow for non-road engines emissions credits, and it can deal with locomotives or really any non-road vehicles.

MARK BRODIE: Like construction equipment, things like that.

SANDY BAHR: Yeah, or non-road engines — I said vehicles, sorry. So, yeah, it’s really to address, but it’s a voluntary program to provide for that. And the thing that it does is allow for emissions credits for stationary sources, which is the part that is concerning.

So a voluntary program to reduce emissions from construction equipment and other engines that aren’t part of vehicles that go on the road. That’s fine, although, of course, we like to see requirements because they’re more enforceable. But the concern is about it being used to offset emissions from these stationary sources, like power plants, or chip manufacturers, or data centers, or those types of things.

MARK BRODIE: So is it not a one-to-one offset? In other words, if a power plant emits X amount of emissions, the non-road engine would not have to not emit that same amount of emissions?

SANDY BAHR: It would have to not emit that, but the concern is where these are located, right? And I should put this in context, too: This would not even be the direction we’re going if the Environmental Protection Agency did what it should have done and bumped Maricopa County to serious for ozone, because our pollution is serious. But they didn’t; they kept it at moderate.

And so what that did is kept more stringent requirements from being enacted. Why are we now citing big gas plants right in the non-attainment area? There’s a 700-megawatt gas plant that is being proposed out in Glendale. If we were serious for ozone, you wouldn’t even be seeing that. And then a program like this can help facilitate more siting of that.

I know there has been discussion related to chip manufacturing relative to this program as well. And from our perspective, we think it’s important that we be reducing pollution from these stationary sources and not siting these heavily polluting industries in the non-attainment area, as well as reducing pollution from these non-road engines.

MARK BRODIE: Is your concern, then, that this rule will actually make air quality worse or just that it won’t actually improve it?

SANDY BAHR: Well, the main concern is that it won’t improve it, and there is potential it could worsen, although the Clean Air Act has a no-backsliding provision and Congress hasn’t changed that. So if indeed it was demonstrated that it did, then it would not be able to be implemented.

MARK BRODIE: How do you see this rule meshing with Rule 205, dealing with credits basically to owners of vehicle fleets who upgrade or replace on-road vehicles, those engines, and reduce emissions there?

SANDY BAHR: Again, we would like to see them do more to require that these are not voluntary programs, that there are requirements for people to upgrade, reduce, phase out vehicles or engines that are heavily polluting, and also reduce emissions from the stationary sources.

And so, I think that one of the concerns that we have, it’s not like we want to see programs that are punitive, but we’ve been suffering with poor air quality in the Phoenix area for a long time. And this is not a path to clean air faster. I see this as more of status quo or potential for backsliding.

I don’t think it should be an either/or; it should be a both/and. What we’re saying is you shouldn’t be able to just offset the pollution at the power plants, or the chip manufacturer, or the data center, and allow for more pollution in a particular area because you did the construction equipment. Let’s find a way to do the construction equipment and require more of these stationary sources.

MARK BRODIE: All right, that is Sandy Bahr, director of the Grand Canyon Chapter of the Sierra Club. Sandy, thank you.

text:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Duke Energy Florida filed plans with the Florida Public Service Commission to build four new solar energy sites by mid-2028. Together, these sites will add 300 megawatts (MW) of clean energy to the electric grid while delivering an estimated $1 billion in customer savings over their operational lifetimes.

Why it matters:

Duke Energy Florida currently owns, operates and maintains 25 solar energy sites that contribute 1,850 MW to the grid. Each site can power about 15,000 homes, helping meet the rising demand for electricity across the third-fastest-growing state in the nation.

Because solar energy sites run off the sun – rather than natural gas, oil or another source – each one can save customers $250 million in displaced fuel costs during the roughly 30 years that it operates.

Through the Inflation Reduction Act, Duke Energy Florida also transfers approximately $75 million in production tax credits to customers per year, which reduces their monthly bill by at least $2.50 per 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity used – and that amount will only increase as more solar energy sites come on line.

From an environmental perspective, the emission-free energy produced at each solar energy site saves about 1.1 million cubic feet of natural gas, 12,000 barrels of fuel oil and 9,000 tons of coal annually.

More details:

The four new solar energy sites will be located in Orange and Sumter counties and will tentatively be in service by June 2028:

Nova Renewable Energy Center (Orange County)

Expected construction start: January 2027

Expected completion: February 2028

Bull Creek Renewable Energy Center (Orange County)

Expected construction start: March 2027

Expected completion: April 2028

Hogeye Renewable Energy Center (Sumter County)

Expected construction start: May 2027

Expected completion: May 2028

Wewahootee Renewable Energy Center (Orange County)

Expected construction start: May 2027

Expected completion: June 2028

Our view:

"At Duke Energy Florida, our job is to make smart, disciplined investments today that will benefit our customers tomorrow," said Melissa Seixas, Duke Energy Florida state president. "These solar energy sites are just one example of how we're planning for the future and strengthening our system to continue providing safe, reliable power, at the lowest possible price, for years to come."

Expanded impact:

Duke Energy Florida is enhancing its solar sites through the use of utility-scale batteries that can store energy when demand is low and make it available when customers need it most. That means customers can benefit from solar energy even when the sun is not shining.

Over the next 10 years, Duke Energy Florida plans to build over 1 gigawatt of battery storage, which will also allow the company to pass on significant additional savings from investment tax credits directly to customers.

Additionally, through an innovative tax strategy, Duke Energy Florida is accelerating the delivery of investment tax credits associated with its seventh battery site – Powerline Battery Energy Storage System in Citrus County – to avoid a scheduled base rate increase and help lower customers' bills in 2027.

Duke Energy FloridaDuke Energy Florida, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 12,500 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 2 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 13,000-square-mile service area in Florida.

Duke EnergyDuke Energy (DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America's largest energy holding companies. The company's electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, and collectively own 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.

Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.

title: Aliya Haq and Rich Powell on Energy Affordability and the New Congress
description:
As part of that, energy affordability has become the most politically consequential issue in US energy policy, but energy affordability is wrapped up in many other issues from the war in Iran to surging energy demand and an aging electric grid.
This is Columbia Energy Exchange, a weekly podcast from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University.
And so how the next Congress figures out how to deal with energy, energy affordability is not separate from several other issues that need to be dealt with.
The show is brought to you by the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs.
You’ll find more information about the show or the Center on Global Energy Policy online at energypolicy.columbia.edu or follow us on social media at Columbia U Energy.
text:
Aliya Haq:

For just kitchen table folks, for businesses who need to make decisions, for all kinds of things, we need to be moving away from let’s just undo what the last guy did. That can’t be it. I do think a lot of these grid investments are places where you can find really, really important bipartisan support that will really help everyday people.

Rich Powell:

Our next Congress could make significant forward strides on, let’s call them the clean firm technologies. And so they can do that through the appropriations process by giving the Energy Dominance Financing Program at the Department of Energy a larger budget to go out and do even more. A very important part of this is just making sure that the projects that are nearly about to come out and start to add new generating resources into our system across the finish line.

Bill Loveless:

The affordability crisis drove US voters to the polls last week, and the resulting message for the newly elected Congress is clear. Driving down costs is job number one. As part of that, energy affordability has become the most politically consequential issue in US energy policy, but energy affordability is wrapped up in many other issues from the war in Iran to surging energy demand and an aging electric grid. So what can lawmakers do to address today’s energy affordability crisis while also making durable improvements to the resilience and security of the US power supply?

This is Columbia Energy Exchange, a weekly podcast from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University. I’m Bill Loveless. Today on the show, Aliya Haq and Rich Powell. Aliya Haq is president of the Clean Economy Project, a nonprofit focused on accelerating clean energy. She previously led US policy and advocacy at Breakthrough Energy and served as federal climate policy director at the Natural Resources Defense Council. Rich Powell is CEO of the Corporate Energy Buyers Association. Previously, he led ClearPath, a conservative organization advocating clean energy policies. We talked about how lawmakers might approach energy policy decisions in the coming months and years. We looked at areas of near term opportunity, but we also considered some possible road bumps to progress. Here’s our conversation. Aliya Haq, Rich Powell, welcome back to Columbia Energy Exchange.

Aliya Haq:

Thanks for having us.

Rich Powell:

Thanks so much for having us. Great to be back.

Bill Loveless:

Yeah, I agree. It’s great to have you both back. And before we start, let me congratulate you on your new podcast, Energy Frenemies. Welcome to the world of podcasting.

Aliya Haq:

It’s quite a time.

Bill Loveless:

It is quite a time and so much to talk about.

Aliya Haq:

It’s hard to walk down the street and have to sign all the autographs. It’s been a real adjustment, but we’re making due.

Rich Powell:

We’re going to try to make fun of each other less here on The Exchange than we do on Energy Frenemies. It’s a little bit different tone over here.

Bill Loveless:

Okay.

Aliya Haq:

Rich is going to try to make less fun of me. I’m not committing to that.

Bill Loveless:

Okay. Don’t hold back.

Rich Powell:

Unilateral disarmament here. Unilateral disarmament.

Bill Loveless:

Well, we last spoke in November 2022. I don’t know if you recall that, but that’s when Republicans had taken control of the House and Democrats had retained the Senate. Today we’re looking at sweeping wins by Democrats in the Senate and the House in an election in which prices, especially for gasoline, diesel fuel, and electricity figured prominently in voters’ decisions. Aliya, what do the results tell us about the political environment for energy policy over the next two years?

Aliya Haq:

Affordability was absolutely at the center of this election. Energy affordability was a big piece of that as well as other kinds of affordability. What’s so funny about what it means moving forward is I think it’s extremely unclear what the next Congress will actually do about energy specifically because it’s really wrapped up in so many other pieces, whether that’s the Iran war, whether that’s data centers, whether that’s the fear of AI. And so how the next Congress figures out how to deal with energy, energy affordability is not separate from several other issues that need to be dealt with. And I don’t know that there is a clear agenda in this moment on what they do in the next two years to fix prices for people or to bring down the costs, I should say.

Bill Loveless:

Right. Rich?

Rich Powell:

Well, I’ll say one of the very few things we know that they could do, and the Corporate Energy Buyers Association has published multiple studies on this topic as have many others. The thing we know they could do is reform the federal permitting and transmission system. And indeed there’s an opportunity in the weeks ahead during the lame duck to do that, to pass the BAAJA as it’s called in DC, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This is a moment in time podcast, but I think we’re actually going to have a vote on that maybe on Monday before this podcast airs on Tuesday. But I think a big part of the congressional agenda next year will be determined by whether the BAAJA was passed right now. So if it does pass, that sort of clears the decks and will allow people to move on and start thinking more expansively about other policy measures that you could take on.

If it’s not cleared, that will remain the top priority in the next Congress, getting more generation built, more transmission built, more grid upgrades built, faster interconnect, faster projects.

Bill Loveless:

Right. And that certainly is the issue of the moment here in Washington and one we’ll look at, and we can talk a little bit more about it in our discussion today. But I wonder, I get your point, Aliya, and it’s difficult to say how they would address an issue like affordability on Capitol Hill given the extent to which it’s tied to so many other issues. It’s so complex. It raises the question of how much influence can the election have on energy policy given that the president retains considerable authority over federal agencies and can veto any bill passed by the Democratic Congress.

Aliya Haq:

Well, one thing I’m trying to adjust still, it’s now been several days since the election results came in. I know a lot of folks in energy policy have been thinking about if we really want to advance clean energy, let’s get our plans together for 2029. Let’s figure out what we do in that timeframe. And then given the margins that we’re seeing in the House and the Senate that Democrats have 54 senators, maybe 56, I don’t know, depending on when this podcast airs, what results will be in by then. But there’s a universe where you could imagine getting to 60 votes, getting a few Republican senators to vote with Democrats on things over the next couple years. And the majorities in the house, the margins are so wide that I’m sure we will unfortunately see some level of more progressive Democrats and more moderate Democrats having a lot of in-party fights.

But you could see still getting to the vote count that you could get something done, which is super interesting and then changes the entire frame of what can we actually do in two years? What can the country collectively do in the next two years that would help energy policy? I think there’s this assumption that well Trump will veto anything that happens. I don’t know that we should have that assumption. I actually think that there’s a universe where we could do something significant. I’m hopeful to see something on, to Rich’s point, we need to build transmissions so much faster in this country. It will absolutely lower the costs of the entire system. We need to be able to see AI companies, data centers paying. A lot of people say their fair share. I would say potentially investing more than their fair share to bring down the cost for everybody.

I think there’s a lot of really interesting things that could happen in the next year or two that need to happen. And I’m a little nervous there’s not a clear plan for what those things need to be and that we all need to get our act together and think about 2027 rather than 2029 for a major shift in policy. So I’m hopeful that hopefully within the next couple of weeks we start seeing some really strong agenda emerging around what do you do around transmission and data centers. To Rich’s point, I think I would love to see the bipartisan permitting reform bill pass before the end of this year because if you are a Democrat right now, if you were Speaker-elect Jeffries or if you were Leader Schumer, you might be thinking, I really want to unify this very diverse Democratic caucus that’s about to be inaugurated.

If you want to unify your caucus, I don’t know that permitting reform is actually the easiest way to do that. And clearing the decks, as Rich said now, would be a much easier way to get started, make that down payment on transmission that we need to move forward, be able to enable the clean energy rush that would happen with that. So that would be step one. And then step two is what can we do around AI data centers and electricity that would be going even further than that?

Bill Loveless:

Well, Rich, I mean, do you think that’s what we’re likely to face when this new Congress comes in or even before as they prepare their agendas on the Democratic side that are they looking for things they can act on rather quickly or are they acting to establish an agenda for the long term, perhaps with an eye to the presidential election in a couple of years?

Rich Powell:

Well, I definitely agree with Aliya that the right thing to do is to not wait two years. I don’t think the country can wait two years for significant relief on a lot of these issues and whether they pass the BAAJA now or not. I think there will still be significant opportunity to improve policy and many potential windows and vehicles. I mean, I think a lot of folks are counting out federal action right now in the federal legislative action in the next two years because of how far apart the perception is that the administration will be and congressional leadership will be in both houses. And yet there’s a bunch of things on the agenda that typically, even in really partisan situations, folks have found ways to come forward on some kind of bipartisan approach. We’re due up for a highway bill, National Defense Authorization Acts, just our standard appropriations process.

There should be at least several significant moving vehicles through which significant policy could be done in the next Congress, and I sure hope that people will find a way to come forward and find some path to get to some kind of bipartisan approach and all that. I won’t lie, I might be a little less sanguine on it than Aliya is. There’s also been a lot of signaling that a significant priority for Democrats coming in will be very significant oversight of the administration. And obviously the more oversight you do, typically the more capital you burn with your counterparties in the administration and their willingness to work with you on legislation might be lower. And so I hope that folks try to strike a balance on that and find ways to actually move things forward on a faster pathway than holding all their ammunition for a perceived window in 29.

The one thing we know about the American pendulum right now is it seems to be swinging back and forth faster and harder than ever. And so I hope that folks don’t lose the opportunity they have right now to potentially get some things done.

Bill Loveless:

Yeah, that’s interesting Aliya, because I’m thinking, as Rich mentions, congressional oversight, there will be congressional oversight. It’s an obligation of Congress typically, and you can certainly expect it with a large Democratic majority coming into the House and to the Senate next year. On the other hand, you have executive branch policymaking. The president has been very willing to use his executive authority to implement policies as well. And with each, I guess, there’s the potential for overreach, right?

Aliya Haq:

Executive overreach? Absolutely. I think one of the reasons that achieving permitting reform in this Congress has been so difficult has been the fighting over whether or not the permits that are issued will have the stability and certainty that they can actually move forward. And the shenanigans of the Trump administration to pull back several clean energy projects that were already underway has really made it more difficult to find that deal space, to find the place where we can move forward together. I think the lessons that are being learned from this election are, it was all about affordability and corruption. And so I do think the Democrats are getting ready for a very serious amount of oversight.You’re seeing members saying lawyer up and get ready for the hearings that are coming. I’m of two minds of this, which is one, really we can’t let any public official from any party cannot look at what’s been happening over the last few years and think, oh, we are allowed to do that now.

This is fine. So there needs to be some kind of accountability and some kind of drawing a line in the sand of what is appropriate behavior for an elected official to do and administrations to do. And also, I don’t think that as punitive oversight is what the American public was voting for. I think to the extent that the corruption is all about everyone’s getting rich except for you, to the extent that the corruption was about potentially increasing costs on other people while the people at the top are getting rich, that is something people are looking. They’re probably looking for that, but I don’t think that’s not an agenda and that’s not the vision that I think the American people are looking for. And I really hope the Democrats don’t over-index to oversight hearings when they could be passing really, really important policy and legislation that can actually make people’s lives better.

So finding that balance is really important and it remains to be seen how it’ll play out.

Bill Loveless:

I just wonder, Rich, balance is important, finding it is important. We’ve seen a sharp reversal in energy policy from the Biden administration to the Trump administration from when we last spoke four years ago to now. I mean, just given the political dynamics in Washington right now, do you think it’s unlikely where we’ll see any sharp reversal in energy policy beginning next year?

Rich Powell:

So I think to go back to where we started, to go back to where Aliya started us, the message from the last two election cycles has been abundantly crystal clear that affordability is a top of mind priority for Americans. And so I strongly suspect, and all of my conversations with legislators from both parties and the run up to this election has been that they have heard that loud and clear, hence the word affordability being worked into the title of this permitting bill before us right now. So I strongly suspect that the H.R.1, which is typically the bill in the House, which sort of sets the House legislative agenda, will say something like the American Affordability Act, and it will be a laundry list of ideas that attempt to control prices across a range of things, probably including energy prices. To Aliya’s earlier point, it is a little difficult to know what Congress can do on some of those measures.

So things that are linked to global commodities like oil or even national commodities where we just have fundamental constraints now, like the number of refineries we have. Diesel prices are really hard to get back under control, for example, despite the best efforts of the current administration. There are things though that could be done above and beyond even what’s currently being contemplated on electricity prices, for example. We know that there’s low-hanging fruit before us, for example, in reconductoring the electricity grids that we have today that could happen relatively quickly, but because we haven’t set up an incentive structure for utilities around the country to make those particular kinds of investments, we see relatively little of that kind of thing. We could do a massive push on that that might actually start delivering benefits very, very quickly in the next couple of years. And so I think that folks are going to be looking at opportunities like that, and I actually think that that’s a place.

I mean, the current administration’s been very excited about advanced conductoring technologies and things of that nature as a potential near-term solution. I think those might be places where Congress and the administration could see eye to eye and move quickly.

Bill Loveless:

But is there much that Congress can do on those issues? I just had a conversation on the energy exchange with Katie Dykes, a longtime energy policymaker and regulator in Connecticut who reminded us that many of the decisions on the cost and availability of energy are made at the state and local level, not the federal level, and there’s no silver bullet.

Aliya Haq:

Yeah, Rich and I are both big fans of Katie Dykes, so plus one of what Katie said. I was actually just at a dinner with a bunch of energy people and affordability came up and the question posed to the group was, “Is affordability a trap or is affordability an opportunity for Congress?” And the group was very split. And I think in part, the folks who think it’s a trap are the ones who fully understand what Katie’s point is, which is the federal government, it’s not like they can just flip a switch and then everybody’s electricity bills are cut in half. It’s not easy for… Federal government levers are not going to create the immediate relief that I think people might want. That said, I think the folks who felt like it is an opportunity are also correct in that most people never think about energy.

And so you only think about energy when either it’s shut off and you don’t have it or you’re paying more for it and it’s annoying. And so that does create a political opportunity to do some of these more systemic reforms that are the responsibility of the federal government to do. And so there’s part where we have to be clear about what do those federal levers, if we start building more transmission, if we start doing some of the reconducting Rich just mentioned, if we start doing the things that would make a much more efficient high-tech system that makes it easier to deliver cheap and clean electricity to all the parts of the country that need it, that is something the federal government can and should do. And the reality is that relief isn’t felt for quite some time. But I will say the other thing, when I think about affordability, I think that there’s a little bit, it’s like a canary in the coal mine to me where the issue is not going to be if people see lower bills that they will suddenly feel trust in their government and happy with what’s going on.

I think actually the affordability focus is more a sense of the rules are written in a way that people feel like they cannot get ahead. So there’s this concept of fairness or a sense, like I said, everyone’s getting rich except for you. There’s something about there’s a lack of shared prosperity that as the economy grows, there’s just a cabal of a few people who see the benefit of that and most people don’t. I think the federal government has a lot of things they can do to address that, and energy is one of those pieces and figuring out how to tap into the incredible wealth that is going to be created from AI that is coming from new technologies and otherwise, and figuring out how to reinvest that into things that make people’s lives better, I think is a huge piece of what we need to see moving forward.

Rich, you may have said this to me earlier, that the Republicans were big losers in the midterm elections this cycle, and data centers were the bigger losers. If anything, I’m quoting someone else to say, “All candidates are tripping over their pitchforks. They hate data centers more.” And it’s very clear to me that you can’t really separate the energy questions that we’re talking about from the data center questions and the AI questions because so much of the load growth that we’re seeing, so much of the needs for changes on the system are coming from that new technology that’s coming on board. It’s not all of it. There’s much more, there’s also advanced manufacturing, there’s also electric vehicles, there’s many other reasons that we need to invest in the electric grid. That said, it is now completely intertwined in people’s minds that more electricity might be helping AI, and we really need to figure out this entire morass, AI safety, what does it mean for these job transitions to be happening quickly?

What does it mean to have these loud, noisy, ugly boxes in your neighborhood? Are those benefiting the community or not? There’s all these larger questions. When we talk about energy affordability, it’s very reductive to just think that it’s about people’s monthly electricity bill. It is much broader than that one question, and I do think the federal government has so much to do to fix that.

Rich Powell:

I’ll just add on the data center front. I think if you look at, for example, all of the referenda that were up across the country, either specifically on local moratoria or local restrictions or recalls of policymakers who’d supported data centers, they did do worse than Republicans overall, which was pretty bad. I think the industry understands deeply, deeply that they’ve got an issue on social license around this with communities around the country, and they’re working like crazy to regain that license. And so all of the CEBA members, for example, that are either hyperscalers causing a lot of this demand for compute or actually building the compute out have signed onto the ratepayer protection pledge with the White House and this administration and pledged to pay more than their fair share of the grid upgrades required to serve them, pay for all the costs of the power required to serve them, and go above and beyond actually and help communities and help affordability.

How that actually gets translated, to Katie Dykes’ really good point, into the very, very specific state by state or regional transmission organization or independent system operator by ISO process around the country, that’s now the big question ahead. So how are you actually going to memorialize those kinds of commitments into policy, whether those are large load tariffs or incentives for flexibility in the order in which we allow these new large loads to come into systems around the country. Now the devil’s going to be in the details of crafting all those in a way that actually maximizes the benefits for rate payers around the country. We know that there’s a lot of resources potentially at the table here and a lot of willingness to use those resources to help aid everybody’s affordability situation. So now how do we get that right and how do we maximize the benefits of large loads?

I mean, we know that in many parts of the country where we’ve got huge clusters of data centers like Northern Virginia, for example, they also have been able to maintain some of the best affordability in the whole country. So we know that done well done right, this can be a terrific thing for local community benefit and local electricity price increases, but how do we export the best of those policies out to the rest of the country and capture the upsides of this without, to use the example, without killing the golden goose, because there aren’t a lot of other big pools of resources rapidly coming into communities around the country on the horizon other than these large data center developments. So if we calibrate the policy wrong such that those folks don’t have an opportunity to come into those grids, I don’t see many other groups of cavalry on the horizon, and then the rate payers are going to be left to cover the costs of upgrades due to all the other things, extreme weather, wildfire prevention in the West, simply the reality of aging grids around the country.

Right now, we got a long list of expensive bills just to maintain the energy affordability and reliability we have today, and so we do need to figure out a system that gets that balance right.

Bill Loveless:

I mean, just given the preponderance of concern among voters in this election, across the country, there were votes against data centers. I think the only vote in favor of them was in North Dakota. Aliya, will the next Congress seek to impose greater federal oversight on data center electricity consumption? Will they simply feel under some inordinate pressure to do something? And if so, I mean, what could they possibly do?

Aliya Haq:

Yeah. Well, I think it will be a failure of the next Congress to not address AI safety, a new social contract for what AI means more broadly. And then also as part of that, what does it mean to have a secure and safe electricity grid to enable AI growth that isn’t put on the backs of household rate payers? So that is absolutely something the next Congress should be addressing, working on, advancing. We’ve talked enough about the current bipartisan permitting reform bill, which should be a really important step in that direction. And then there’s also a need for –

Rich Powell:

And does include, sorry, I should just add, does include provisions that make data centers pay their own way. That is in the BAAJA. So if you’re concerned about this issue, you should pass the BAAJA. I’m obligated, contractually obligated to mention it 10 or 20 times on this podcast.

Aliya Haq:

Yeah, you’re well below your quota, Rich, so you’ve got at least 12 more BAAJA mentions before we have to cut it off. But I will say a comprehensive plan would be how does… So much of what’s wrong with the electricity grid is a total lack of accountability or who is supposed to be in charge of what. So because there’s the state PUCs, there’s the RTOs, there’s the federal government, there’s FERC, there’s all these pieces where it’s like, well, who’s in charge of the inter-regional transmission actually? Or who’s in charge of this piece actually? It’s not really clear who’s supposed to be making sure these things are happening. So number one, the federal government needs to figure out who is in charge of the planning for what the grid needs to look like and how do you actually then pay for that and how do you make sure the supply chains and the ability to build that grid out is there?

That is something that the Congress can absolutely do and should do potentially in the next two years advancing that. Whether or not Trump signs it is another question, but work needs to be done actively right now on that. I mean, the grid that we have currently is a hundred years old and that technology is not impressing anybody. We need to get to a place where we have a grid that’s ready for the next 100 years of economic growth, that is ready for the next 100 years of technology innovation. We don’t have that grid. Congress needs to figure that out. And BAAJA is an important first step at that. It is not the complete process. We can go further. And at the same time, if you’re advancing a grid that will enable that AI growth, you also have a responsibility to make sure that your kids are safe, that people who will be in transitions of jobs won’t be left out on the street, and that there’s some level of security that our P doom level can be very low, that we’re not literally going to destroy humanity.

Those are all super valid concerns that all need to get addressed kind of at the same time. We’re behind.

Bill Loveless:

Aliya, it almost seems like you’re suggesting there needs to be a lesson presented. I mean, we don’t have a grid in the United States. We have a grid that has multiple parts across the country run by different operators as well as utilities and independent power operators. It’s regulated by 50 states. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has some say in this, but not complete say in where things are built. And so it’s very complicated, right? There’s no easy answer for it that say a Congress could come in and offer a piece of legislation that would offer a sweeping change. It could affect the entire country in some way.

And Congress in the past has tried to deal with this right back in 20 years ago with Energy Policy Acts, trying to give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission more authority to do some things. Anyway, we’re probably getting more into the permitting reform discussion there and how all of this is regulated, but it seems as though it’s going to be a tough one for this affordability issue with electricity is going to be a tough one. And I might add to that too. I mean, there’s a lot of confusion over what the impact of data centers is Is on electricity rates, right? I mean, I read in the Washington Post today a new study by Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania saying data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices. Here at the Center on Global Energy Policy, we had a research that said concerns about affordability of electricity in the US have been rising with prices.

And while the headlines have pointed to AI and data centers as the underlying factors, the exact causes are much more complex. They get into things, Aliya, that you mentioned, aging infrastructure and all of that sort of thing. So it’s not an easy… Affordability when it comes to electricity is not going to be an easy one for this next Congress or any Congress to deal with.

Aliya Haq:

Well said. Yeah. Again, it goes back to the, is affordability a trap for Congress or is affordability an opportunity? And the answer’s both probably, but if anything, the answer is don’t sit around for two years planning for what you’ll do in 2029. The answer is do something right now and get moving.

Bill Loveless:

I take it you don’t anticipate any sharp reversals on this overall energy policy. I mentioned it before, but in the Trump administration, fossil fuels have been the prerogative. It’s been what the administration has focused on so heavily. During the Biden administration, it was the clean energy issues, the Inflation Reduction Act that was the commanding feature of energy policy in the United States. Despite the big wins by Democrats in Congress, Rich, I mean, do you necessarily see any sort of shop reversal in this approach to energy policy in this country?

Rich Powell:

It’s interesting, many of us, this is actually one of the themes of Energy Frenemies. Many of us talk about energy as a sort of a trifecta challenge where you obviously need a system that is highly reliable and secure and just runs all the time, ideally insulated against geopolitical shocks and whatnot. You need that system to be highly affordable so that you can have robust economic growth because energy is just a means to an end. And ideally that system is increasingly low emissions, environmentally friendly, carbon emissions free over time. That’s the trifecta. And I think it’s fair to say that the Biden administration was heavily indexed toward the carbon emissions free clean energy portion of that. And the Trump administration was heavily indexed toward the reliability portion of that, with a big part of that being a focus on national security and trying to rebalance resources toward domestically produced resources they felt they were better under control on.

And on the reliability front, they were very alarmed by the decline of firm power capacity production around the country. And so they’ve done things like keep aging fossil assets online that are firm capacity because they’re really worried about wide scale blackouts as we saw in events that some folks attributed at least partially to the over reliance on intermittent resources. My strong bet is that in the next two years, and maybe for a while going ahead, we’re actually going to see a pivot yet again to the third stool of that, which is that the affordability part of this, which probably was ignored to the detriment of both the Biden and the Trump administrations who were over indexed on the other two. And I think we’ve seen that the public is just as concerned about affordability as they are about the reliability and security of the system and as they are about the carbon emissions in the system.

I think that’s the lesson. So my guess is you’re going to see, I would hope, a better balance amongst those three, but certainly if there’s a hard pivot in any direction, it’s going to be toward that affordability measure as we go into policymaking. And I bet that’s going to be just as much from the administration as it’s going to be from Congress.

Aliya Haq:

Just to add to that, I think a number of Democrats that I’ve heard from who are interested in reinstating the tax credits that were repealed in the Big Beautiful Bill Act. Yeah, it’s definitely possible that the Democrats try to put something like that back in place. And I could imagine if they’re tying it to this affordability piece that Rich is saying, that these kinds of wind and solar accelerants mean that we will get cheaper electricity on the system for you and rate payers will pay less. There may be ways that they could do that. The only thing I would caution is people, if you are trying to dress up an old agenda with a new message, it is really disingenuous and people will see through that. And so if there’s a return to the old policies, that needs to be done with a real eye toward this question that Rich mentioned, which is are we actually making a system that is cheaper?

I do think that there’s a way that that happens, but it has to be done thoughtfully.

Bill Loveless:

Yeah. Aliya, do you think there are clean energy technologies that both parties could agree deserve continued federal support?

Aliya Haq:

I mean, I think there’s a lot. Yeah. Well, I mean, I think you saw that in the Big Beautiful Bill Act where they did not repeal a bunch of the tax credits for innovative new early stage technologies. So a lot of really good tech can move forward. I think geothermal’s having a real moment, Fervo Energy that many of us are fans of, had a really successful IPO recently. I think that there’s an interesting moment for advanced nuclear that folks on all sides are starting to be like, oh yeah, we could move this forward. There’s a lot of pieces on some of these clean firm technologies that I think people understand we do need them and we need to invest more in them. So I can imagine both parties getting behind a number of different technologies that are important to do.

Rich Powell:

I’ll say from our perspective in the energy buyers space, we’re increasingly looking at the firm carbon emissions-free technologies as a bigger and bigger part of the mix. It’s everything that Aliya just mentioned. I’ll just kind of add to that list. It’s expansions of the existing nuclear reactors. And so a number of our members have done these big up rates for existing nuclear plants. We’re bringing plants that were shut down back online, like Palisades in Michigan and Duayne Arnold in Iowa and now the Crane Clean Energy Center, the old Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania back online. I think people are looking more and more too about how do you offer those same capacity benefits from large scale renewables installations? That does mean you have to think a little bit differently about those installations. So you’ve got to put more energy storage on site for them or you’ve got to strategically pair wind and solar that generate at different times of the day and different times of the year together to get higher and higher capacity factor resources.

We’re being asked whenever we’re connecting new large loads around the country to bring our own capacity with us in the system. And when those grid operators say capacity, they mean twenty four seven, 365 capacity or at least very high capacity factor. So everyone is thinking a lot more about capacity as part of that system, but that’s appropriate as we’re back into a growth mode in the overall system when we have shut down a lot of the high capacity generators before. And so we need to add more capacity into the system, more of that dispatchable capacity in the background. So I think increasingly that’s going to be part of the narrative conversation. Couldn’t agree with Lee more that I think that there is actually broad bipartisan consensus on the importance of capacity. And so that ended up showing up in a lot of those OB3 tax credits.

I also think it’s a place that our next Congress could make significant forward strides on, let’s call them the clean firm technologies. And so they can do that through the appropriations process by giving the energy dominance financing program at the Department of Energy a larger budget to go out and do even more on those technologies that it’s already done. That’s a part of the Trump administration that’s been really active in trying to put out large scale low cost financing to get grids upgraded and to get a lot of these generating units going on grids around the country. The last thing I’ll say, because this is my last part of the quota, a very important part of this is just making sure that the projects that are nearly done, nearly about to come out and start to add new generating resources into our system across the finish line and the vast majority of the projects that are in the interconnect queues around the country but are often held up by some kind of permanent constraint, whether that’s just the natural sort of sand in the gears of the system or more recent actions that slowed down a particular project, the BAAJA addresses a lot of those issues and should help get as many of those projects that are just nearly in the queue onto grids around the country as quickly as they can.

And that’s going to be essential if we’re going to preserve the affordability of the generating side of our energy grid. That’s before we have to pay for all the upgrades on transmission and distribution and all that. But if we don’t keep pace with all the new demand with new generating assets coming in, we are going to see significant affordability problems from that side of the power bills as well. And so we need to pass that legislation and get all the things out of those queues.

Bill Loveless:

Again, I’m getting the impression you don’t think there’s going to be, I mean, given the wide differences between the Biden and the Trump administrations on energy policy, you don’t necessarily see any actions that would directly focus on reversing things. Rather, it seems to be more a matter of finding where there’s an opportunity to find some agreement and address these very specific issues that voters have brought up in these recent elections.

Aliya Haq:

I mean, I would say my hope, I don’t know that this is how it turns out, my hope is that this is an election where the Democrats feel like they’ve got a large enough margin. A lot of folks have already said this in the last week, the Democrats don’t have a mandate, they have an opportunity. I think the electorate has just been in a throw the bums out strategy for the last every two years. We’re just seeing a throw the bums out situation. So my hope is that where we are going in this Congress is less about partisan reversals, fighting back and forth, back and forth. And it’s more about a moving forward agenda where we can actually see real results for people and that there’s some sense of progress moving forward that is my desire of my hope for this entire country and the way we move forward.

We can’t just keep going back and forth for just kitchen table folks, for businesses who need to make decisions, for all kinds of things, we need to be moving away from let’s just undo what the last guy did. That can’t be it. I do think a lot of these great investments are places where you can find really, really important bipartisan support that will really help everyday people. It is very clear no matter where the electron comes from, we need to be able to move it faster and move it further and get more of them. I think that there’s a really huge opportunity to move that forward in the next couple of years. And I think there’s a lot of agreement on different types of technologies that we should be increasing and bringing down the costs for.

Bill Loveless:

Right. And Rich, Aliya, I was going to ask, looking ahead to the 2028 presidential elections, what would you most like to see the next Congress accomplish to put US energy policy on a more durable footing? Aliya, I think you more or less just addressed that. Rich, what do you think about that?

Rich Powell:

Well, I would love to see folks just more broadly embrace the three-legged stool approach to this and just say for better or for worse, I mean you might personally care more or less about one of these issues, but it is obvious that all three of them need to be solved for the reliability of our grids and energy system, the affordability and the increasingly clean carbon emissions production, all that. So these are co-equal challenges and that as we pursue an energy policy going forward, we should really embrace those three things and we shouldn’t do things that are heavily overweighted in one of those directions because then we end up with electorates and interest groups and folks pulling us just radically in other directions. If we could just get into a more steady pathway, certainly for the benefit of my buyers and the many energy providers that are also part of our association, having more steady certainty so we could do some better clearer long-term planning would be greatly appreciated.

And frankly, that would be a heck of a lot cheaper and more straightforward going forward over the next decade than the really intense swings we’ve seen over the last couple of years.

Bill Loveless:

Well, finding that steady path forward is always a challenging one for lawmakers and members of an administration. It will certainly continue to be so, but with a new Congress and two more years of the Trump administration, it certainly is going to be an interesting time to see what the effects will be on energy policy going forward. So Aliya, Rich Powell, thanks for joining us today on Columbia Energy Exchange to talk about this.

Aliya Haq:

Bill, did we agree too much? Should we have been fighting more on the podcast? I mean, we could have brought more of that in, so I apologize if we let you down.

Rich Powell:

I disagree with everything Lia said there toward the end.

Bill Loveless:

That was good guys. I enjoyed it. I hope you guys did as well.

Rich Powell:

Huge, huge. Thanks for having us, Bill.

Aliya Haq:

Thank you so much for having us.

Bill Loveless:

That’s it for this week’s episode of Columbia Energy Exchange. Thank you again, Aliya Haq and Rich Powell. And thank you for listening. The show is brought to you by the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs. The show is hosted by Jason Bordoff and me, Bill Loveless. Mary Catherine O’Connor, Dara Diamond, and Kyu Lee produced the show. Gregory Vilfranc engineered it. You’ll find more information about the show or the Center on Global Energy Policy online at energypolicy.columbia.edu or follow us on social media at Columbia U Energy. If you like this episode, leave us a rating on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. You can also share it with a friend or a colleague to help us reach more listeners. Either way, we appreciate your support. Thanks again for listening. We’ll see you next week.

text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta joined a coalition of 18 attorneys general in sending a letter to Congress opposing a U.S. House of Representatives bill, H.R. 7866, which would eliminate states' ability to opt out of the interest-rate preemption provisions of the Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act (DIDMCA). H.R. 7866 would disempower states from protecting borrowers by eliminating states' power to enforce state usury laws, which set maximum legal limits on the interest rates that lenders can charge consumers as to certain loans.

“States play a crucial role in consumer financial protection. California has laws protecting consumers from predatory lending, including when it comes to how much interest banks can charge consumers,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Through H.R. 7866, Congress is attempting to preempt these important laws, slashing states’ rights to protect consumers, and leaving Californians paying more. Alongside a coalition of attorneys general, I’m asking Congress to reject H.R. 7866. Especially amid a crisis of affordability, we must remain laser focused on championing policies that protect consumers from high-cost lending.”

BACKGROUND

Banking and consumer protection are core areas of states’ historic enforcement ability. States have a strong interest in sound financial institutions and honest financial practices because they are essential to the health of states’ economies and their resident’s financial wellbeing. Under Section 521 of DIDMCA, state-chartered banks can charge the interest rate allowed by the state where the bank is located, regardless of where a borrower lives, thereby preempting state interest-rate caps by charging more than the state where the borrower lives would typically allow. However, Section 525 of DIDMCA provides an opt-out right for states: a state can enact legislation to opt out of the federal interest-rate preemption for loans made in its state.

TODAY’S LETTER

In the letter, the attorneys general argue that in passing DIDMCA, Congress acknowledged the importance of states’ role in regulating interest rates by creating the Section 525 opt-out. This opt-out right has only become more important as nonbank lenders have increasingly exploited interest-rate preemption by entering into sham partnerships with state banks in order to evade otherwise-applicable interest rate caps. For example, in 2023 the Colorado Attorney General found that one “rent-a-bank” operator was making thousands of loans in the state with annual interest rates in excess of 100%, resulting in significant default rates that harmed consumers’ credit scores and access to more affordable future credit. Section 525 opt-out is an important tool for states to protect consumers, and H.R. 7866 would rob state legislatures of this important right, facilitate the actions of predatory lenders, and limit states’ ability to protect their citizens from high-cost lending.

In July 2026, Attorney General Bonta joined a multistate amicus brief in National Association of Industrial Bankers v. Weiser, supporting Colorado's argument that DIDMCA opt-out from preemption allows a state to apply its usury laws to loans made in that state by out-of-state lenders.

In sending the letter, Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Oregon, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Virginia, Washington.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

November 10, 2026

Contact: Chyna Fields, cfields@naacpnet.org

WASHINGTON – Yesterday, members of the Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) Bill which is aimed at expediting permitting reviews to power big energy projects like data centers. The NAACP raised concerns about the bill earlier this month, emphasizing the potential implications that the legislation could have on Black communities and others already facing disproportionate exposure to pollution.

Abre' Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice, shared the following statement:

"Let's be clear–naming a piece of proposed legislation 'Bipartisan' doesn't actually make it good for the American people. Senate leaders should be prioritizing what's best for their constituents, not what appeases their colleagues across the aisle."

"The NAACP strongly opposes BAAJA because we should not rush through a decision that directly threatens the health, safety, and future of Black and frontline communities. This bill puts our community and our planet's health in the hands of billionaires and their interests. We refuse to let our future be determined by corporate polluters and people who seem more aligned with them than people who live in sacrifice zones."

"A more just approach to permitting requires building from the ground up with community protection at its core, a foundation that BAAJA fundamentally lacks in any form. The NAACP calls for legislation that protects our neighborhoods and preserves our power to hold polluters accountable, not legislation that shields them."

The NAACP will continue to fight against any harm to our environment and our communities. For more information about our stance against BAAJA, visit our website.

###

About NAACP

The NAACP advocates, agitates, and litigates for the civil rights due to Black America. Our legacy is built on the foundation of grassroots activism by the biggest civil rights pioneers of the 20th century and is sustained by 21st century activists. From classrooms and courtrooms to city halls and Congress, our network of members across the country works to secure the social and political power that will end race-based discrimination. That work is rooted in racial equity, civic engagement, and supportive policies and institutions for all marginalized people. We are committed to a world without racism where Black people enjoy equitable opportunities in thriving communities.

NOTE: The Legal Defense Fund – also referred to as the NAACP-LDF – was founded in 1940 as a part of the NAACP, but now operates as a completely separate entity.

text:
Many households have embraced sustainability. Families install solar panels, buy electric vehicles, compost, and coordinate shared resources to reduce waste and costs.

Those choices often involve shared investments and long-term commitments. When relationships change through separation or divorce, the green decisions a family made together can become complicated financial and legal questions. Clear agreements help prevent confusion before it starts.

Shared Investments Create Shared Questions

Sustainable upgrades are frequently large purchases:

Rooftop solar systems with loans or leases

Electric vehicles with financing tied to both partners

Home energy improvements that increase property value

Shared memberships in community gardens or car-sharing programs

When a couple separates, someone must decide who keeps these assets, who pays remaining balances, and how any tax benefits are handled.

Solar Leases and Home Sales

Solar leases and power purchase agreements can complicate a home sale or transfer. The lease may need to be assumed by a buyer or by one spouse, and some contracts carry transfer requirements.

Couples should review solar agreements carefully during a divorce so the system’s obligations are not overlooked. A system that was financed rather than leased may also carry a lien or a fixture filing that has to be cleared before the house can be refinanced or sold.

Getting Legal Guidance Early

Dividing property during a divorce involves more than splitting bank accounts. In Arizona, which treats most property acquired during marriage as community property, couples often consult the legal team at Gillespie, Shields & Taylor or other family law attorneys to understand how shared assets, debts, and support obligations are likely to be handled.

Arizona courts generally aim for an equitable division of community property, which does not require an equal split. Sustainable investments are included in that analysis like any other asset. An electric vehicle bought during the marriage, for example, is usually treated as community property even if only one spouse drives it. Questions about what counts as separate property, such as an inheritance used to pay for solar panels, often require careful tracing of funds.

Tax Considerations

Tax credits for solar installations and electric vehicles can raise questions during divorce. The IRS publication on divorced or separated individuals explains filing status, dependents, and how property transfers between spouses are treated for tax purposes.

Credits already claimed may affect basis or future tax obligations, and understanding those effects helps couples negotiate fairly. Filing status in the year of separation can also change which spouse is able to claim certain credits, so timing deserves attention.

Parenting and Shared Values

Families who prioritize sustainability often want to keep those values consistent for children after separation. Parenting plans can address practical issues such as transportation, school routines, and activities.

Some parents include shared commitments, such as limiting screen time or supporting outdoor activities, though courts focus primarily on the child’s best interests. Agreements that are specific and realistic tend to work better than broad statements of values, which are hard to apply consistently between two homes.

Practical Agreements Before Problems Arise

Couples who are not separating can still benefit from clarity:

Keep records showing who paid for major upgrades

Note whether purchases used joint or separate funds

Store solar contracts, warranties, and loan documents together

Discuss how shared investments would be handled if circumstances change

Prenuptial or postnuptial agreements can address these issues directly. Even an informal written summary of who paid for what can help if questions arise years later.

Reducing Waste in Everyday Life

Sustainability goals remain important through life changes. Intelligent Living’s guide with tips to minimize your carbon footprint covers energy, transportation, and consumption choices that apply whether a household is one person or five.

After separation, each new household can still continue habits such as energy efficiency, recycling, and thoughtful purchasing.

Communication Makes the Difference

Sustainable living depends on cooperation, and so does a smooth separation. Calm communication, organized records, and early advice reduce conflict and cost. Mediation is often a practical option for couples who want to divide shared investments without lengthy litigation.

When families plan ahead, the investments they made for the planet do not have to become sources of lasting dispute.

This article provides general information about family law and sustainable households and is not legal advice for any individual situation.
