description:
WASHINGTON, D.C.–People’s Action today urged senators to vote “no” on S. 5653, legislation that would accelerate the construction of data centers powered by fossil fuels.
Meanwhile, 80 percent of independents and 83 percent of Democrats oppose local data center construction.
As drafted, S. 5653 would make it faster and easier to build hyperscale data centers on federal public lands, brownfields, and Superfund sites.
The bill would fast-track federal permits for interstate gas pipelines, transmission lines, and other data center infrastructure.
“The new majority can draft and pass better legislation,” People’s Action Director of Federal Affairs Megan Essaheb said.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.–People’s Action today urged senators to vote “no” on S. 5653, legislation that would accelerate the construction of data centers powered by fossil fuels. While the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 would boost clean energy production and lower energy bills, it goes too far in rolling back environmental protections and ultimately increasing the buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure and data centers. By making it easier to rapidly build out the massive fossil fuel energy infrastructure necessary to feed hyperscale data centers, the bill would ultimately facilitate their construction. The Senate voted on Monday, Nov. 9, to open debate on the bill but a final vote on the legislation is still pending.

“After last Tuesday, what senator in their right mind would vote to speed up data center construction and enrich Big Tech and fossil fuel CEOs?” People’s Action Climate Justice Campaign Director Victoria Kaplan said. “We don’t need to compromise with Elon or Exxon to build clean energy projects.”

Prior to Election Day, polls showed that three-quarters of Americans opposed data centers in their communities, and Republicans were warned that support for data center projects would be catastrophic for their Senate campaigns. Meanwhile, 80 percent of independents and 83 percent of Democrats oppose local data center construction.

The legislation, in an effort to compromise between those who want to make it easier to permit clean energy and those in Big Oil’s pocket, is overbroad and unnecessary. As drafted, S. 5653 would make it faster and easier to build hyperscale data centers on federal public lands, brownfields, and Superfund sites. The bill would fast-track federal permits for interstate gas pipelines, transmission lines, and other data center infrastructure. And, the bill’s provisions would gut Clean Water Act protections, shore up fracked gas profits, and limit the incoming Congress’ ability to slow down the buildout of hyperscale data centers on federal lands.

“The new majority can draft and pass better legislation,” People’s Action Director of Federal Affairs Megan Essaheb said. “We need to build out our clean energy grid, stop utility company price gouging for fossil fuel infrastructure, and stop Big Tech’s data center buildout. Passing a bill that would hinder the new Congress from doing these things is contrary to the mandate that the American people just gave Democrats.”

Over the past year, People’s Action state-based affiliates mobilized to stop the development of new AI data centers in Pennsylvania, Indiana, New York, and West Virginia, citing massive energy consumption, environmental harm, and higher utility bills.

title: Texas's Energy Reset: The Supply Chain Consequences for Houston - Logistics Viewpoints
description:
However, the immediate supply chain risk is not necessarily reduced energy production or even total capital spending.
It is a change in the timing, location, and composition of industrial investment, a distinction that deserves considerably more attention than the political headlines.
Capital Investment Is Where Political Change Reaches the Supply Chain Large energy projects operate on multiyear investment cycles.
CenterPoint Energy illustrates the scale of infrastructure investment already required in the Houston region.
A dramatic monthly increase does not necessarily indicate a sustained acceleration in industrial investment.
text:
An election can change the direction of government overnight. Changing the direction of an industrial economy takes considerably longer. That distinction matters in Houston, where oil and gas production, refining, petrochemicals, engineering, and international trade form one of the world’s most interconnected industrial ecosystems.

Texas voters delivered a historic political realignment on November 3, 2026. According to the Texas Secretary of State’s official election results, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott. At the same time, Democrats captured the lieutenant governorship, attorney general’s office, control of the Texas House, and a seat on the Railroad Commission. James Talarico also won election to the U.S. Senate.

For Houston’s energy industry, the election introduces a different regulatory and investment environment. However, the immediate supply chain risk is not necessarily reduced energy production or even total capital spending. It is a change in the timing, location, and composition of industrial investment, a distinction that deserves considerably more attention than the political headlines.

The Election Changes the Policy Environment, Not the Industrial Foundation

Houston’s energy economy extends far beyond drilling. Refineries, chemical plants, pipelines, export terminals, power infrastructure, and manufacturing facilities depend on an extensive network of suppliers and transportation providers. These operations represent decades of investment in physical assets that cannot simply be relocated in response to an election. Nevertheless, political decisions influence the economics of maintaining, expanding, and modernizing those assets.

One important change involves the Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates oil and gas production. Democrat Jon Rosenthal, an oilfield engineer with more than two decades of experience, won the election after advocating stronger enforcement, restrictions on routine flaring, improved well-plugging programs, and additional oversight of wastewater disposal.

The commission will retain a Republican majority, limiting Rosenthal’s ability to implement significant changes without support from his colleagues. Republicans also retained control of the Texas Senate, with a 19–12 majority, despite Democratic gains elsewhere.

Incoming Lieutenant Governor Vikki Goodwin will preside over that Republican-controlled chamber, creating an additional institutional complication. Although the lieutenant governor traditionally exercises substantial authority over committee assignments, legislative scheduling, and the movement of bills, much of that power derives from Senate rules rather than the state constitution. Republican senators could revise those rules when the Legislature convenes in January, potentially reducing Goodwin’s influence over the legislative agenda. As The Texas Tribune explains, this creates uncertainty over how the incoming administration’s priorities will advance through the Legislature.

These institutional realities mean regulatory change may occur unevenly rather than through an immediate industry-wide restructuring. For Houston’s industrial suppliers, however, even incremental changes can matter, particularly when they affect the timing and composition of capital investment.

Consider ExxonMobil’s Baytown refinery, which the U.S. Energy Information Administration lists at approximately 564,500 barrels per calendar day of refining capacity as of January 2026. Together with neighboring chemical operations, the complex represents a substantial concentration of equipment, maintenance, and industrial service requirements.

A change in environmental standards could shift investment toward emissions controls, instrumentation, monitoring systems, or process modifications. A decision to defer expansion, by contrast, could postpone orders for large equipment packages and associated construction services. Regulatory changes do not necessarily eliminate industrial spending; they can redirect it toward different technologies, suppliers, and project schedules.

Capital Investment Is Where Political Change Reaches the Supply Chain

Large energy projects operate on multiyear investment cycles. Engineering, permitting, equipment procurement, construction, commissioning, and operations are closely coordinated, meaning decisions affecting one stage can create consequences throughout the project.

An LNG terminal, refinery expansion, or gas-processing facility may require compressors, turbines, pumps, transformers, pressure vessels, steel pipe, specialized valves, and industrial control systems. Much of this equipment involves long manufacturing lead times and complex transportation arrangements, making investment predictability a key concern for suppliers and logistics providers.

Enterprise Products Partners provides a useful illustration. In its third-quarter 2026 earnings announcement, the Houston-based company reported approximately $6.3 billion in growth capital projects under construction, with commercial operations scheduled through 2028.

Among these investments is an expansion of its LPG export terminal on the Houston Ship Channel. The project is expected to increase loading capacity by approximately 300,000 barrels per day, bringing the terminal’s total loading rate to roughly 1.1 million barrels per day.

These projects were underway before the election, and there is no basis to conclude that Enterprise has changed its plans because of the results. Their significance is the scale of procurement and construction activity that depends on predictable project execution.

The same principle applies to Houston-headquartered Cheniere Energy. In a September 2, 2026 announcement, Cheniere confirmed that its Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage 3 project had achieved substantial completion on August 28, with Bechtel Energy serving as the engineering, procurement, and construction contractor.

Although Corpus Christi is outside the Houston metropolitan area, the project demonstrates the importance of Gulf Coast energy development to Houston-based engineering, management, and industrial supply networks. LNG facilities depend on global equipment sourcing, specialized marine transportation, and carefully sequenced construction activities.

Federal authorities retain primary responsibility for LNG export authorization and terminal siting, limiting the direct influence of Texas elections over those decisions. State environmental permitting and infrastructure policies nevertheless remain relevant. For suppliers, a delayed project does not merely shift revenue from one quarter to another; it can disrupt manufacturing capacity, engineering schedules, transportation reservations, and contractor availability across multiple businesses.

Electricity Policy Is Becoming Industrial Supply Chain Policy

The election’s potentially more immediate consequences involve electricity infrastructure and the growing competition for grid capacity. Governor-elect Hinojosa has supported a moratorium on new data center approvals until Texas establishes stronger protections addressing electricity costs, water consumption, and local communities. As The Texas Tribune reported on November 4, her proposal could extend restrictions until the Legislature adopts additional protections.

Importantly, the data center debate did not begin with the election. On September 21, Governor Abbott had already directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt data center permits pending completion of an ERCOT audit of proposed developments and their infrastructure requirements.

The incoming administration therefore inherits an existing regulatory intervention rather than beginning entirely from scratch. The unresolved question is how future policy will balance large new electricity loads against industrial competitiveness, grid reliability, and consumer costs.

This matters because electricity is not simply an operating expense for manufacturers. Reliable power is a prerequisite for refining, petrochemical production, refrigerated storage, processing facilities, and automated industrial operations. Power availability and interconnection schedules can materially influence industrial investment decisions.

CenterPoint Energy illustrates the scale of infrastructure investment already required in the Houston region. In its October 2026 Greater Houston Resiliency Initiative update, the utility reported installing more than 83,500 storm-resilient poles and 850 automation devices, alongside extensive undergrounding and vegetation-management work.

Those projects preceded the election, but they demonstrate how utility investment translates into demand for transformers, conductors, switchgear, construction materials, field services, and specialized transportation. Changes in electricity policy could affect the pace of additional infrastructure spending and how costs are allocated among residential, commercial, and industrial customers.

For manufacturers considering new facilities, those decisions may prove as consequential as changes to traditional oil and gas regulation. Power availability, interconnection schedules, and long-term electricity costs increasingly influence industrial site selection and capital planning.

The Houston Ship Channel Will Reveal the Economic Consequences

The Houston Ship Channel offers a useful lens for assessing the eventual effects of these policy changes. According to Port Houston’s October 2026 report, September steel imports increased 181% compared with the same month in 2025, reaching approximately 540,000 tons. Yet year-to-date steel imports were only 1% higher.

That contrast is instructive. A dramatic monthly increase does not necessarily indicate a sustained acceleration in industrial investment. Supply chain executives must distinguish temporary fluctuations in cargo movements from changes in the underlying capital expenditure cycle, and the same discipline should govern assessments of the election.

If regulatory changes delay major construction projects, the effects may eventually appear in equipment orders, project cargo shipments, engineering backlogs, and specialized freight demand. Conversely, increased investment in electrical infrastructure, environmental controls, pipeline modernization, or well remediation could support additional industrial logistics activity.

The composition of that demand is important. Transporting heavy process equipment for a refinery expansion requires different capabilities than supplying electrical infrastructure or environmental monitoring systems. Changes in investment priorities can therefore redistribute business among manufacturers, distributors, carriers, and engineering contractors without producing a comparable change in total industrial activity.

For Houston’s logistics providers, the indicators worth monitoring are not political announcements alone, but capital expenditure revisions, construction contract awards, procurement commitments, permitting timelines, and sustained changes in cargo volumes. Those measures will reveal whether policy changes are delaying investment, redirecting spending, or creating new industrial opportunities.

Houston’s energy industry has navigated commodity cycles, technological transitions, regulatory changes, and shifts in global demand before. Its infrastructure, skilled workforce, and industrial concentration provide substantial continuity, even as the political environment changes. The 2026 election may alter how companies evaluate future investments, but its ultimate consequences will be measured in projects approved, equipment ordered, facilities constructed, and materials transported.

description:

text:
US President Donald Trump may not be a big fan of solar, but it’s the country’s fastest-growing source of power generation. Standing up an independent domestic solar supply chain is critical to the country’s energy security and AI ambitions, and to lowering power prices, especially as Beijing moves to restrict the export of some key solar technologies.

But, although it may be wise to raise trade barriers that push more China-affiliated solar components out of the US market, China’s role in global solar supply chains is so pervasive that instantly severing all ties could kill many US solar manufacturing efforts in the crib. Future growth for this industry depends on a more nuanced trade policy that gives US companies the space to benefit from China’s world-leading solar expertise while the next phase of home-grown plants gets built.

At this point, the US imports almost no solar cells or other core components from China, and imports of panels from anywhere recently hit a seven-year low now that more US module assembly factories are cropping up. But even T1, like many of its peers, still needs China for some vital aspects of its operations. And when I visited the company’s factory, it was clear that achieving a full divorce between the American and Chinese solar industries could be more complex than many in Washington appreciate.

T1 operates a sprawling, cutting-edge solar module factory on the outskirts of Dallas, and is a few months away from finishing a second factory to manufacture its own cells based on technology that was first developed for the Chinese firms it’s looking to supplant. Last month, the company was granted special permission from Commerce to continue importing cells from Asian suppliers without being penalized for stockpiling ahead of the 232 deadline. It is also awaiting a verdict on a second Commerce waiver that would allow it to dodge the 232 tariffs altogether while it completes its onshoring investments.

The company was born from the clean tech trade wars that have engulfed the US, Europe, and China in recent years. In the early 2020s Barcelo, whose background is in global oil and gas finance, was working to set up an EV battery factory in Norway. But that company, Freyr, got pushed by intense competition from Chinese rivals — and simultaneously pulled westward by inducements in Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act. The company’s first plan was to build a $2.5 billion battery factory in Georgia. But that was scrapped after Barcelo spotted a better deal in solar, where there were only a few domestic manufacturers at a moment when demand was exploding and Chinese firms, who could see a US crackdown coming, were looking to pull up stakes. He pivoted, and agreed in December 2024 to a $621 million deal to buy the Dallas factory, along with supply contracts and other assets, from Changzhou-based Trina Solar, one of the world’s biggest producers, which had just completed building it.

A wave of similar US takeovers swept the industry around that time, including some in which Chinese firms retained a minority stake. Indeed, more than 40% of the 66 GW of operational US module manufacturing capacity today originated as facilities owned by Chinese manufacturers or joint ventures involving Chinese firms, according to Wood Mackenzie analyst Elissa Pierce. In T1’s case, Trina dropped its stake entirely. But T1’s relationships with Trina and other Chinese firms remained essential: A Trina executive briefly came over to serve as the new venture’s chief strategy officer. The factory’s anchor customer became Trina itself, which committed to buy 1 GW of panels per year, one-fifth of the factory’s capacity; on the day I visited, robotic arms were gingerly packaging panels into Trina-branded boxes. The first thing I saw on the factory floor was a stack of specialized glass from a company in Zhejiang.

Other Asian countries are essential, too: T1 imports cells and other components from a range of suppliers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. T1 inherited Trina’s polysilicon supply contract from a Michigan company called Hemlock, which is minority owned by a Japanese chemical firm. In July, it paid $135 million to a Singaporean solar firm for intellectual property behind the cell and module technology that Trina and others use.

Russell Gold, a veteran Wall Street Journal energy journalist who is now T1’s spokesperson, said that although the company now feels “pretty comfortable running this factory by ourselves,” it still works closely with outside contractors, including some from China, to maintain equipment and train its workers on what is essentially a Chinese factory floor plopped in East Texas. Chinese solar manufacturing equipment, Gold said, is still “the best in the world.” Inside a gleaming warehouse the width of a few Manhattan avenues, a succession of machine arms, conveyor belts, and ovens press cells onto dinner-table-sized panels, more than 17,000 every day. Several hundred humans are needed to keep things moving and ensure quality control. A few autonomous robots roll around moving heavy stuff while playing Darth Vader’s Imperial March to signal their approach.

The staff reflects the diversity of the strong immigrant communities in Dallas: I met workers, at least half of whom seemed to be women, from Equatorial Guinea, Mexico, Peru, and Venezuela. One group was clustered around a machine that seemed to be malfunctioning. It turned out they were receiving an impromptu lesson from a contractor from the Chinese equipment manufacturer Wuxi Autowell — “technology transfer in action!” Gold observed. The contractor was born in China but had lived in Texas for a decade, helping to stand up the state’s surging clean tech industry. The member of his student cohort with the strongest English translated some of his instructions into Spanish for the rest of the group.

“We need to do more of this in the US,” Gold said. “Or we can kiss energy security goodbye.”

text:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – Today, Duke Energy Florida filed plans with the Florida Public Service Commission to build four new solar energy sites by mid-2028. Together, these sites will add 300 megawatts (MW) of clean energy to the electric grid while delivering an estimated $1 billion in customer savings over their operational lifetimes.

Why it matters:

Duke Energy Florida currently owns, operates and maintains 25 solar energy sites that contribute 1,850 MW to the grid. Each site can power about 15,000 homes, helping meet the rising demand for electricity across the third-fastest-growing state in the nation.

Because solar energy sites run off the sun – rather than natural gas, oil or another source – each one can save customers $250 million in displaced fuel costs during the roughly 30 years that it operates.

Through the Inflation Reduction Act, Duke Energy Florida also transfers approximately $75 million in production tax credits to customers per year, which reduces their monthly bill by at least $2.50 per 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity used – and that amount will only increase as more solar energy sites come on line.

From an environmental perspective, the emission-free energy produced at each solar energy site saves about 1.1 million cubic feet of natural gas, 12,000 barrels of fuel oil and 9,000 tons of coal annually.

More details:

The four new solar energy sites will be located in Orange and Sumter counties and will tentatively be in service by June 2028:

Nova Renewable Energy Center (Orange County)

Expected construction start: January 2027

Expected completion: February 2028

Bull Creek Renewable Energy Center (Orange County)

Expected construction start: March 2027

Expected completion: April 2028

Hogeye Renewable Energy Center (Sumter County)

Expected construction start: May 2027

Expected completion: May 2028

Wewahootee Renewable Energy Center (Orange County)

Expected construction start: May 2027

Expected completion: June 2028

Our view:

“At Duke Energy Florida, our job is to make smart, disciplined investments today that will benefit our customers tomorrow,” said Melissa Seixas, Duke Energy Florida state president. “These solar energy sites are just one example of how we’re planning for the future and strengthening our system to continue providing safe, reliable power, at the lowest possible price, for years to come.”

Expanded impact:

Duke Energy Florida is enhancing its solar sites through the use of utility-scale batteries that can store energy when demand is low and make it available when customers need it most. That means customers can benefit from solar energy even when the sun is not shining.

Over the next 10 years, Duke Energy Florida plans to build over 1 gigawatt of battery storage, which will also allow the company to pass on significant additional savings from investment tax credits directly to customers.

Additionally, through an innovative tax strategy, Duke Energy Florida is accelerating the delivery of investment tax credits associated with its seventh battery site – Powerline Battery Energy Storage System in Citrus County – to avoid a scheduled base rate increase and help lower customers’ bills in 2027.

Duke Energy Florida

Duke Energy Florida, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 12,500 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 2 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 13,000-square-mile service area in Florida.

Duke Energy

Duke Energy (NYSE: DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America’s largest energy holding companies. The company’s electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, and collectively own 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.

Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.

text:
(HARTFORD, CT | November 10, 2026) – Governor Ned Lamont and representatives from several Connecticut state agencies met at the State Capitol in Hartford today for the annual GreenerGov Awards ceremony, an annual celebration recognizing projects and initiatives within Connecticut state government that are reducing environmental impacts, lowering operating costs, and helping the state meet its climate goals.

The GreenerGov initiative, established by Executive Order No. 1 in 2019 and expanded by Executive Order No. 21-3 in 2021, challenges state agencies to lead by example by reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing energy efficiency, conserving water, diverting waste, expanding renewable energy, and deploying electric vehicles throughout state government operations.

“Since we launched GreenerGov in 2019, Connecticut state agencies have demonstrated that government can lead by example in reducing emissions, conserving resources, and lowering costs,” Governor Lamont said. “Reaching our greenhouse gas reduction target for state agencies ahead of schedule is an extraordinary achievement and a testament to the dedication of our agency staff, senior sustainability officers, facility managers, and sustainability champions across state government. Together, we are building a greener, healthier, and more affordable Connecticut for future generations.”

The ceremony highlighted significant progress achieved by state agencies over the past several years. According to the latest GreenerGov data, state agency greenhouse gas emissions have fallen an additional 10% from fiscal year 2024 levels, bringing the total reduction to 36.3% below fiscal year 2019 levels. This achievement exceeds the state’s 2030 greenhouse gas reduction target for state agencies several years ahead of schedule.

The reductions have been driven by increased use of clean electricity, reduced consumption of fossil fuels, expanded renewable energy generation, and improvements to building operations and energy management practices across state government facilities.

The GreenerGov initiative is led by the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP), the Connecticut Department of Administrative Services (DAS), and the Connecticut Office of Policy and Management (OPM).

“As we review the latest GreenerGov data, it is clear that the outstanding efforts of our state agencies are producing meaningful results,” Emma Cimino, DEEP acting commissioner and GreenerGov co-chair, said. “State agency greenhouse gas emissions reductions have now exceeded our 2030 reduction target. These achievements reflect years of collaboration, innovation, and commitment from agencies across Connecticut, and they demonstrate that environmental stewardship and operational excellence go hand in hand.”

State leaders also highlighted ongoing work to accelerate sustainability efforts. During the past year, the GreenerGov program partnered with the Connecticut Green Bank to identify new solar development opportunities at state facilities and worked with agencies statewide to improve the quality and completeness of sustainability data used to track progress toward GreenerGov goals.

“DAS is proud to support GreenerGov through initiatives that help agencies reduce emissions, lower operating costs, and plan for the future,” Michelle Gilman, DAS commissioner and GreenerGov co-chair, said. “The agencies recognized today are demonstrating how strategic investments and collaboration can create lasting environmental and fiscal benefits for Connecticut.”

“The success of GreenerGov is rooted in collaboration,” Joshua Wojcik, OPM secretary and GreenerGov co-chair, said. “By bringing agencies together around shared sustainability and cost-saving goals, Connecticut has been able to achieve significant emissions reductions while generating millions of dollars in utility savings. Programs such as GreenerGov show how coordinated planning, data-driven decision making, and strong partnerships can help state government deliver meaningful results for residents today while preparing for the challenges of tomorrow.”

The annual GreenerGov Awards recognize agencies and individuals whose efforts support the governor’s sustainability and cost-saving goals while serving as examples for other organizations throughout Connecticut. Award selections are based on utility bill data collected through EnergyCAP, information submitted by agency senior sustainability officers, and documented sustainability achievements.

As Connecticut celebrates reaching its state agency greenhouse gas reduction target years ahead of schedule, GreenerGov partners are now focused on achieving the initiative’s next milestone: reducing state agency greenhouse gas emissions 70% below 2016 levels by 2040. Continued investments in clean energy, building decarbonization, resiliency planning, and agency collaboration will help drive progress toward that goal.

The GreenerGov Awards demonstrate how Connecticut state agencies are successfully balancing environmental stewardship, operational efficiency, and fiscal responsibility while building a cleaner, healthier, and more resilient future for all residents.

2026 GreenerGov Award Recipients

Sustainability Achievement Awards

Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions

Winner: Connecticut Department of Labor (CTDOL)

CTDOL achieved a 21% reduction in emissions between fiscal year 2025 and fiscal year 2026 through mechanical system improvements and building automation system optimization at its headquarters in Wethersfield.

Waste Reduction

Winner: University of Connecticut (UConn)

UConn launched a pilot program utilizing 23 Food Cycler tabletop composting appliances in student residences, helping divert food waste and promote sustainable behavior among students.

Electric Vehicles

Winner: Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV)

DMV installed 11 electric vehicle charging stations during fiscal year 2025 and fiscal year 2026, expanding access to charging infrastructure at agency facilities.

Expanding Solar Capacity

Winner: Connecticut Department of Correction (DOC)

DOC installed ground-mounted solar projects at three facilities, adding more than two megawatts of solar capacity and generating an estimated $11 million in lifetime savings.

Water Consumption Reduction

Winner: Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA)

CHFA was recognized for implementing landscaping improvements featuring native drought-resistant plants that reduce irrigation needs, improve water infiltration, support pollinators, and reduce stormwater runoff.

Environmental and Fiscal Steward Award

Winner: Connecticut State Colleges and Universities (CSCU)

CSCU earned this award for installing three fuel cell systems in New Britain, Manchester, and Waterbury. Implemented through power purchase agreements with no upfront capital costs, the projects are expected to generate approximately $2 million in annual utility savings.

Eco Champion Award

Winner: Shelly Mondo, Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA)

Shelly Mondo is being recognized for creating an employee engagement program that encourages sustainable workplace practices through a Green Team Member recognition initiative, helping foster a culture of sustainability within her organization.

Data Quality Recognition Awards

Special recognition was also given to agencies that maintained complete and highly accurate utility data in EnergyCAP, supporting the state’s ability to measure sustainability progress and identify opportunities for improvement. Award recipients included the Connecticut State Library, the Connecticut Department of Labor, the Connecticut Department of Social Services, the Connecticut Department of Economic and Community Development, and the Connecticut Office of Legislative Management.

text:
The Energy Bad Boys recently released a very handy report on how the 2026 midterms will impact state energy policy in 2027 and beyond. The report is called “State of the States” (SOTS) and is edited by American Experiment alumni Isaac Orr and Mitch Rolling.

[Last week] Tuesday’s midterm elections delivered massive victories for Democratic candidates across the country. To give readers a resource to understand how this will affect state energy policy, we reached out to our network of contacts across the country and asked them to contribute a short, 250-word summary of how energy policy will change as a result of the midterms.

Yours truly contributed a 250-word summary regarding Minnesota, which I reposted here as “Post election blues: Energy policy overview.” Energy policy highlights from SOTS, along with my comments and charts, follow next. The focus below is on the four other Midwest SOTS entries besides mine for Minnesota (MN) i.e.:

Indiana (IN)

North Dakota (ND)

Ohio (OH)

Wisconsin (WI)

Indiana (IN)

Republicans still control both legislative chambers, but losing the House supermajority gives Democrats greater leverage. Electricity affordability and data center development emerged as significant campaign issues. More than half of Indiana counties have adopted some form of data center restriction. The 2027 session will likely bring increased scrutiny of data center tax incentives, large-load customer protections, utility rates, and electricity costs.

Two opportunities should dominate [ND’s] energy policy discussions in 2027. First, accelerating carbon capture for enhanced oil recovery could unlock additional oil production while extending the productive life of [ND’s] coal-fired power plants. Second, [ND’s] abundant, reliable electricity and existing energy infrastructure provide significant competitive advantages, [including] strategically locating data centers near existing power plants and coal-producing communities, while protecting existing electricity customers from additional costs.

Dr. Amy Acton [is] Ohio’s next governor [Democrat]. Republicans retained both chambers of the General Assembly. [They all] should ensure that the reforms enacted under House Bill 15 in 2025 are preserved and implemented. The law ended subsidies for inebcient power plants, eased the permitting process for new generation, and made progress toward adopting grid-enhancing technologies. Governor-elect Acton has proposed a conditional moratorium on new data centers tied to electricity costs, labor, and environmental requirements.

Governor-elect David Crowley has already put coercion at the core of his energy platform. text:
The United States Senate has voted to move forward on a bipartisan bill that would speed up the process to build new data centres and energy infrastructure in the country.

Nearly all of the chamber’s Republicans, as well as more than a dozen Democrats, voted 73-25 on Monday to take up the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which supporters, including US President Donald Trump, have said is necessary to meet the nation’s growing demand for electricity.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centres

list 2 of 3AI stocks plunge after US election, driving down markets

list 3 of 3Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China spy scandal?

end of list

“This Bill is a BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE”, Trump posted on social media Monday as he encouraged lawmakers to support it.

The legislation would overhaul the permitting process for major energy projects – both clean energy and fossil fuel-run – across the US, reduce deadlines for environmental reviews and impose restrictions on when projects can be challenged in the country’s courts. It would also force owners of energy-hungry data centres to pay for the infrastructure that is needed to power them.

Growing anger in the US over those facilities’ use in powering artificial intelligence (AI), which has resulted in rising electricity bills for customers across the country, helped fuel last week’s takeover of the US Congress by Democrats.

“The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives,” Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, the ranking member on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said on Monday. “We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs. We can do that today.”

Authors of the bill claim it will provide $19bn in savings on residential electricity bills through 2040. The number of solar and wind projects connecting to the US electric grid would be doubled, with data centres paying $55bn over the next 10 years to cover their power usage.

But despite the bill’s claims of increasing clean energy projects, environmental organisations are opposed to the legislation. They argue it would also lock in development of fossil fuels, weaken environmental laws and make it harder for US residents to challenge projects in their communities.

Earlier this year, a coalition of national groups – including the Climate Justice Alliance, Indigenous Environmental Network and Western Environmental Law Center – issued a joint statement opposing the bill.

“We cannot allow the lies to continue, as the facts are clear: If this backroom permitting reform deal is pushed through, it will enable a no-guardrails buildout of dangerous projects that will harm our health and environment, drive up energy costs, and violate our rights,” they said in September.

“This will be especially harmful for communities of color and lower income neighborhoods already overburdened by pollution and climate impacts.”

While the legislation received rare overwhelming support from both major political parties, the Democrats’ midterm win could complicate its final passage.

Some in the party argue that the legislation should be shelved until new Democratic majorities in the US House and Senate are sworn in early next year.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to become the body’s new speaker in January, criticised the bill last week, warning it “falls short” in several areas.

“We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now,” a Jeffries spokesperson said in a statement released to the Associated Press.

Jeffries’s office added: “Leader Jeffries will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our Caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people.”

text:
The dominant narrative about the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections has focused on President Donald Trump’s brash ineptitude and voters fed up with the costs of living amid reports of corruption emanating from the White House. The climate crisis appeared to take a backseat to concerns about rising energy prices driven by data center build-out and inflation linked to the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, but experts say an emerging class of Democrats successfully fused momentum behind economic populism with the need for climate action to win over voters.

“Voters rewarded economic populists who tied that message to climate, and I think there is a lot of appetite and movement in that direction,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at the Climate and Community Institute (CCI), in an interview with Truthout.

In surveys, potential voters ranked climate change behind most other concerns, with the economy, health care, and the war on Iran consistently topping the list. However, Bigger said victories for Democrats such as Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine suggest that voters are making connections between an economy rigged by elites and environmental concerns such as fossil fuel extraction and noise pollution from data centers.

“We had Troy Jackson in Maine talking about heat pumps and cost of fuel oil, and Abdul El-Sayed talking about reining in Michigan’s utility companies and data centers,” Bigger told Truthout. “How our economy is being organized and its link to the natural world, that is very much front of mind even if people don’t say they’re voting on climate specifically.”

Bigger is the co-author of a new report tracking the success of midterm candidates that embedded messages about climate action within a broader populist economic agenda, reflecting what CCI calls “Green Economic Populism.” The report finds that the 2026 candidates aligned most strongly with Green Economic Populism — virtually all of them Democrats — won 39 out of 56 races for Congress, including six of the seven Senate seats that were up for grabs.

Multiple green populist-aligned candidates also won state and local races or defeated moderates in primary races, most notably Angie Nixon of south Florida, a progressive who won a Democratic congressional primary by tying climate to broken housing insurance markets, according to the report. Nixon narrowly lost to Republican Ashley Moody, and the progressive’s supporters complained that she received little support from the Democratic Party.

According to the CCI report, these candidates offered policy platforms that drew connections between the climate crisis and the rising cost of living by identifying many of the same culprits driving both, including energy utilities, fossil fuel companies, corporate landlords, AI companies, and data center developers. Candidates such Democrat Claire Valdez, the first Native American woman to win a U.S. House seat from New York, and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, argued that one way to lower costs is to “take back power from the elite” and invest in cheap clean power and green infrastructure built by union labor.

”Our polling shows that people link these costs of living crisis to the climate crisis,” Bigger said.

Other incoming House members who ran on a green economic populist platform include Democrats Angela Gonzales-Torres of California, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Patty Garcia of Illinois, Will Lawrence of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, according to the report. Incumbent green populist Democrats returning to Congress after fending off GOP challengers include Rep. Ro Khanna of California, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Rep. Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, among others.

Climate and energy policy remains a challenge for Democrats. On November 9, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance a permitting “reform” bill that split the Democratic caucus, with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) arguing Democrats should negotiate a new deal once they take the majority.

“I cannot support a bill that relies on a handshake promise from the same administration that’s spent the last two years waging a war on new clean energy projects to hold up its end of the bargain, and continues to do so even after negotiating the reform proposal,” Wyden said in a statement.

The bill would speed up permitting for transmission lines needed for clean energy infrastructure but also defang bedrock environmental laws that communities rely on to challenge polluters and fossil fuel projects.

While CCI does not comment on pending legislation, Bigger suggested policy makers could speed up permitting for clean energy projects by properly funding the federal agencies responsible, which have suffered from deep staffing and budget cuts under Trump.

“If you are wanting to get more renewables on the grid, get more transmission on the grid, accelerate the clean energy build-out in any shape or form — you have to staff the requisite agencies to do that permitting,” Bigger said. “Gutting the Endangered Species Act instead of rebuilding staff at the Bureau of Land Management seems like a stupid way to do it.”

Support for green economic populism — and frustration with industrial and Silicon Valley elites — was also visible in the results of state-level ballot initiatives. Of the 56 ballot measures related to climate and energy tracked by CCI, including proposals for prohibiting electric utilities from using profits to influence politicians, 21 initiatives restricting the industry passed while 10 pro-industry initiatives failed.

The backlash to the AI industry and data center build-out is profound: According to Bigger, 45 out of 46 local data center measures in the midterms went against developers, and 30 of 31 ballot measures that seek to impose restrictions passed while all 15 pro-development measures failed.

Green economic populism has been brewing at the nexus of the climate action and labor movements for the past two decades, with environmental justice activists and union members finding common cause in a “just transition” away from reliance on climate-warming oil and gas. This coalition shaped federal policy under the Biden administration, which pushed to expand clean energy infrastructure and pledged to address environmental racism.

However, much of the limited progress made under President Joe Biden was quickly reversed by Trump and the current GOP majority in Congress. Frustrated with Trump and Republicans, voters handed Democrats a solid majority for 2027.

Founded in 2006 by the Sierra Club and United Steelworkers, the BlueGreen Alliance promotes job-creating policies that fuse worker power with environmental justice. As midterm election results revealed a “blue tsunami” last week, BlueGreen Alliance Executive Director Jason Walsh said that creating opportunity for workers while addressing environmental challenges is not just good policy, it’s good politics.

“Across our coalition, we’re seeing those concerns come together around good-paying union jobs, affordable energy, and healthier communities,” said Walsh in an email. “In this election, union households demonstrated strong support for Democrats who won majorities in the House and Senate.”

Beyond Congress, Bigger is encouraged by Democrats winning state and local elections, including races for governor in Ohio, Texas, and Pennsylvania — three states where fracking has exploded over the past two decades, providing the oil and gas industry with serious political leverage. The midterm results are a signal that the industry’s political and economic dominance in these states may be fading as the ruling class faces a backlash from voters.

“There is cool stuff happening not just at the federal level, but across the country,” Bigger said.

description: The proverbial dust is now mostly settled on the 2026 midterm election in which Democrats swept statewide executive offices, gained a majority in the Texas House, and flipped a special
text:
Greetings,

October greetings, Texas!





Holly Hansen is a Senior Reporter
for The
Texan where she has written extensively on criminal
justice, public corruption,
politics, and property rights, and is one
of the state’s most recognized journalists covering Houston and
Harris County. She is a frequent guest on radio and television
shows, discussing local, state, and federal public affairs. She
graduated from the University of Central Florida with a degree in
History, has called Texas home for three decades, and now lives in
the Austin area where she enjoys the outdoors and reading historic
literature.







The proverbial dust is now mostly settled on the 2026 midterm election in which Democrats swept statewide executive offices, gained a majority in the Texas House, and flipped a special state appeals court.

Despite the Blue Tsunami, however, Republicans will maintain control of the Senate and keep narrow majorities on the Railroad Commission and the state’s top two courts, and Texas now enters a rare period of divided government.

According to exit polling, the top issue on voters' minds this year was the economy and the cost of living — a topic Democratic Party candidates hammered in a way that clearly resonated with the electorate.

The question now is how Texas’ new leadership will address these issues and what impact new policies will have not only on the state’s economy, but on what has been a business-friendly environment that has drawn new industry and strong job growth for more than a decade.

Executive Branch

Gov.-elect and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D-Austin) will have the power to reshape state agencies through appointments, though some will require the Senate’s approval.

Although Texas leads the nation in new data center construction and capacity, Hinojosa leveraged public opposition to the centers during her campaign and has vowed to require them to cover infrastructure costs and pay a larger share of grid and water costs. She also wants to impose a moratorium on new data centers until the Legislature adopts guidelines and ends certain long-term tax breaks.

While the Texas governor has limited authority, questions for the industry surround how gubernatorial appointments to the Public Utility Commission, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, and other permitting bodies might alter timelines, standards, and costs for data centers, other industrial facilities, and related energy and transmission projects.

While Railroad Commissioner-elect Jon Rosenthal will join Republican Commissioners Christi Craddick and Wayne Christian in regulating the energy industry, it is unclear how the agency might change oil and gas permitting in Texas.

As attorney general, state Sen. Nathan Johnson (D-Dallas) will have discretion over enforcement of existing laws, including anti-Environmental, Social, and Governance measures that affect contracts and underwriters, consumer protection laws, and litigation involving businesses and state agencies.

While the state’s newly elected Democrats in the executive branch have indicated a policy shift, it will take time to see the net effect on residential electricity rates, property tax burdens, and housing costs.

Legislative Branch

With Democrats controlling the House and Republicans the Senate, the 90th Legislative Session will likely produce some stalemates, but perhaps a few bipartisan compromises as lawmakers grapple with the budget and consider policies related to property taxes, energy and infrastructure, economic-development incentives, and regulation of industry.

Another issue relevant to the business environment is whether lawmakers will preserve tort reforms or roll back policies that have contributed to the state’s pro-business environment.

Even with state Rep. Vikki Goodwin (D-Austin) replacing Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick as the president of the Senate, the GOP majority is expected to rewrite chamber rules to give a yet-to-be-determined Republican majority leader control over committee assignments, bill referral, which bills are scheduled for consideration on the floor, and conference committee appointments.

While the presumptive House speaker, state Rep. Senfronia Thompson (D-Houston), signaled on Friday that she planned to work with both Democrats and Republicans to enact legislation, the Senate could serve as a check on any overly aggressive House attempts to transform the state’s business landscape.

Judicial Branch

How newly elected members of the state’s judiciary could affect the business environment is harder to predict, but the now fully Democratic 15th Court of Appeals (COA) is bound to have an impact.

Created by the Texas Legislature in the 2023 legislative session, the 15th COA has statewide jurisdiction over civil matters that involve the state government. It also hears appeals from the Business Court , which the Legislature established in 2023.

For the next two years, the court will adjudicate constitutional challenges to state laws, regulatory challenges, tort issues, and commercial disputes.

The Supreme Court of Texas , however, remains 5-to-4 Republican and can overturn 15th COA opinions, although the process is often slow and litigants may have to wait years for a final decision.

For the past decade, Texas has been a top destination for businesses and residents fleeing blue states like California and Illinois, but any dramatic policy changes could shift migration trends to sunnier business prospects in Florida, still governed by presumptively business-friendly Republicans.

Ultimately, any push to radically reform Texas policies affecting the business climate is likely to be slowed by the state’s structural constraints, but some changes are to be expected in the coming year and could be either expanded or curtailed depending on the 2028 elections.

If the Democratic Party agenda does not result in greater affordability and prosperity, the state could see another electoral swing, but only time will tell.

Felon Elected to Texas House

In the aftermath of the 2026 election, some national pundits have suggested that perceived candidate quality led to GOP losses in states like South Carolina and Texas. They may have a point when talking about top-of-the-ticket races, but voters anxious to elect state Rep. James Talarico (D-Austin) to the U.S. Senate probably did not closely scrutinize down-ballot candidates.

Although Democratic candidate Ericka Lommick suspended her campaign for Texas House District 93 in Tarrant County earlier this year, voters elected her over Republican Alan Blaylock with 50.5 percent of the vote. The problem is that Lomick has three felony convictions in North Carolina for mortgage fraud, bank fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. According to CBS , records show she was sentenced to 63 months in prison.

Under Texas law , candidates convicted of a felony “from which the person has not been pardoned or otherwise released from the resulting disabilities” are not eligible.

Lomick’s ineligibility could result in a new special election to fill the seat vacated by former state Rep. Nate Schatzline (R-Fort Worth) earlier this year.

Voters Keep a Harris County Treasure

Speaking of candidate quality, voters also seemed untroubled by the trials and tribulations of down-ballot incumbent Harris County Treasurer Carla Wyatt. Since winning her first term in 2022, Wyatt has been arrested three times: once for vehicle burglary and twice for Driving Under the Influence.

Two of her pending charges have been dismissed, although she did not fully comply with the terms of a pretrial diversion program. In September, Wyatt was cited for failing to control her speed related to an accident in which she allegedly hit three other cars, and victims say she did not have auto insurance at the time of the crashes.

During an interview with the Houston Chronicle editorial board, Wyatt dismissed concerns about her behavior and said that “ there were no babies thrown through the windshield or anything of that nature .” She was re-elected last week with nearly 60 percent of the vote.

text:
ANTALYA – In a tale of America at a crossroads, former US Secretary of State John Kerry declared at COP31 on Tuesday that the country would soon return to a leadership role in the global response to the climate crisis, as a new report found President Donald Trump’s war on Iran had inadvertently tipped global fossil fuel emissions into decline.

“After two years of pulling back from international cooperation, after attacking clean energy and weakening our climate [protections], especially the [Environmental Protection Agency], after mocking renewables and showing scorn for science,” Kerry said.

“The US election offers powerful proof that, given a choice between denial and delay on the one side and innovation and common sense on the other, Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Soaring oil prices and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz are set to push global emissions from coal, oil and gas down 0.4% this year, to 38.2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2), according to the annual Global Carbon Budget report, compiled by more than 140 scientists and presented at COP31. It is the first drop since the COVID-19 pandemic, led by a 1.9% fall in emissions from oil.

“The price of petrol and supply chain disruptions are clearly a cause of the decrease in global fossil CO2 emissions in 2026,” said Corinne Le Quéré of the University of East Anglia, who led a companion study published in Nature Climate Change.

Adding to the irony, the war waged by the president who took the US out of the Paris Agreement is also speeding the world’s turn away from fossil fuels. With the world in its second war-driven oil shock in under five years, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, energy security has overtaken environmental concern as the main driver of renewables growth, the International Energy Agency (IEA) found last week.

“No country can block the sun from shining. No one can block any wind from blowing,” Kerry said. “Clean energy is not just a climate strategy; it is a national security strategy, an economic strategy, and a way to give countries much greater control over their own futures.”

The blue wave reaches Antalya

New optimism around the future political direction of the United States follows a sweeping Democratic victory in last week’s midterm elections, in which the party took both chambers of Congress and won races in long-time Republican strongholds including Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Ohio.

That same victory has inspired hope for renewed focus on health and environmental regulation gutted under the Trump administration. Democrats have pledged to restore withheld research funding, repeal deep Medicaid cuts and call in Environmental Protection Agency chief Lee Zeldin for questioning over the rollback of pollution rules, Health Policy Watch reported on Monday.

For now, the US is not in the room in Antalya. Washington formally left the Paris Agreement in January, has sent no official delegation to a COP for the second year running, and in February will become the first country ever to quit the UN climate convention itself. In 2025, Trump’s first year back in office, the US posted the largest emissions increase of any country, the UN Environment Programme found last month.

Anyone who still calls climate change a hoax, Kerry said, “should not be serving in public office.”

A dip, not a peak

Yet the Iran war was not the only factor in dropping fossil fuel emissions, and the dip may not last, scientists behind the report warned.

Solar, wind and electric vehicles met about two-thirds of this year’s rise in energy demand, Le Quéré said, with the oil shock accounting for the rest. Total CO2 emissions still rose, from 42.8 billion to 43.3 billion tonnes, as peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia drove up emissions from land use.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging,” said Pierre Friedlingstein of the University of Exeter, who led the study. “But a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution.”

The world can emit just 150 billion more tonnes of CO2 before warming passes 1.5°C, less than four years of emissions at current rates. Holding the 1.5C line would mean taking emissions to zero within a decade, Friedlingstein told reporters, “which is extremely unlikely to happen.”

Kerry, who signed the Paris Agreement as secretary of state and later served as President Joe Biden’s special envoy for climate, conceded that the world had agreed “1.5 degrees was the target, and we have not delivered.”

“This is what makes it so damn frustrating,” Kerry said. “Solving this challenge is not a mystery. We know what to do.”

‘A second round of suffering’

The people paying for that failure live in the 44 least developed countries (LDCs), which have done the least to cause the crisis.

“For the LDCs, 1.5 is not just a number,” Ambassador Adão Soares Barbosa of Timor-Leste, who chairs the group, told reporters in Antalya. “Every fraction increase imposes a greater threat to our people’s homes, livelihoods, food and water security, and ability to recover from disasters.”

At a press conference setting out the bloc’s demands for COP31, Barbosa said the LDCs back Türkiye’s flagship 35% electrification target by 2035 but cannot reach it without money, technology and training from developed countries.

“That target is clear,” he said. “But then, how can we move together?” The biggest emitters must move off fossil fuels first, Barbosa said, and any support for LDCs must come as grants.

Repayments on climate loans to developing countries nearly tripled between 2020 and 2024 and could overtake new lending by 2036 if lending stays at current levels, a CARE analysis found. Some 3 billion people already live in countries whose governments spend more on debt interest than on health and education combined, according to the UN.

“It’s not loans,” he told reporters. “If we have loans… we will lose something. We don’t want to have a second round of suffering.”

Fossil fuels off the COP agenda

Three years after nearly 200 countries agreed in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels, the issue is not formally on the agenda in Antalya.

Co-hosts Türkiye and Australia deliberately left it off after the fight over a fossil fuel roadmap torpedoed last year’s talks in Belém, Brazil, instead staking the summit instead on voluntary targets for electrification, waste and building efficiency.

On Tuesday, Brazil’s COP30 presidency tried to put the issue back before governments, presenting a voluntary roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels that it drafted after Belém ended without one.

The document is a toolkit rather than a plan, setting no deadlines or targets, leaving each country to assess its own dependence on coal, oil and gas and choose from a menu of measures. Those include scrapping fossil fuel subsidies and halting new fossil fuel power plants to cutting the flaring and venting of gas at oil and gas sites.

The transition away from fossil fuels, the roadmap concludes, is “urgent, inevitable and yet possible.”

No new backers were announced, and some fossil fuel producers are expected to resist any mention of the roadmap in the summit’s final decision.

“We have to make sure that we really do a roadmap,” Kerry said, “and we’ll find all kinds of ways to pressure and pull those CEOs to the table who are slow to move their companies.”

Host Türkiye charts path to more fossil fuels

The host, meanwhile, is heading the other way. On opening day, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced two new oil fields in Türkiye’s southeastern Gabar region holding an estimated 135 million barrels. State oil company TPAO is projected to nearly triple its gas output by 2035, according to a Global Witness analysis.

“The message from Türkiye could not be more contradictory,” said Jeni Miller, executive director of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, a network of more than 300 health organisations. “How can a country host the world’s most important climate conference… and on the same day announce plans to expand production of the fossil fuels driving that crisis?”

Türkiye’s flagship electrification pledge, championed by the presidency at Tuesday’s Electrification Forum, calls for lifting electricity’s share of final energy use from about 23% to 35% by 2035, but sets no requirement that the extra power be clean. Coal supplied 34% of Türkiye’s own electricity last year, according to the energy think tank Ember. Electrification “only limits overshoot if the electricity is cleanly generated,” said Samuel Guéret of Climate Analytics, a Berlin-based climate science and policy institute.

The EU, which co-hosted the first Electrification Forum on Tuesday, wants the target at the heart of the summit’s outcome but frames its own push as “clean electrification.”

“Expectations are low,” EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra told reporters on Tuesday, pointing to a string of “underwhelming” COPs. “That’s just a reflection of reality.”

No list of backers has been published, and none is expected this week, Climate Home News reported. India has said it will not sign.

“We think this is not yet [the peak],” Le Quéré said of this year’s dip, “but the further acceleration of renewable energy and electric vehicle deployment is needed to really secure… a peak and decline afterwards.”

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Five countries have backed a plan to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels worldwide by 2030, as U.N. climate talks in Turkey focus on expanding access to electricity and transitioning away from fossil fuels.

The new Global Rooftop Solar Declaration launched Tuesday on the second day of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31. The aim is to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels from about 150 million today to at least 300 million by 2030.

“This is the future of affordable energy," said Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council. "This is the way we can help average working people insure themselves from future price rises to come.”

COP31 comes after a year of deadly climate-related disasters and as concern grows that governments are not doing enough to curb global warming. Recent energy shocks from the Russia-Ukraine war and Iran war have also increased interest in renewables.

The U.N. climate talks have been criticized in the past for making promises that later fall flat. For rooftop solar goals to actually make a dent in the emissions contributing to climate change, experts said policies to upgrade power grids and subsidize solar panels and batteries must quickly follow.

“The pledge is a pledge," said Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance. “We now need to see national policies and frameworks in place.”

More rooftop solar may help regular people

Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu joined Australia by endorsing the rooftop solar declaration in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, where COP31 is being co-hosted by Turkey and Australia.

Lawmakers from 21 other countries — including the United Kingdom, South Africa and Sri Lanka — have also endorsed it. So has Indonesia’s state-owned electric power company Perusahaan Listrik Negara.

The declaration is voluntary and non-binding, like many of the agreements made at U.N. climate talks.

“We know the world is currently facing the greatest energy cost of living crisis the world has ever seen," Dunlop said. “We know that families all over the world are struggling to pay their bills and what we are saying with the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration is that we have a solution that will bring down your bills."

Electrification is a cornerstone of this year's talks, with Turkey pushing for electricity — preferably from renewables like solar and wind — to make up 35% of global energy consumption by 2035.

“Electrification by itself is incredibly beneficial because of the efficiency gains. Renewables by themselves, again, very beneficial. Put the two together and it is really a killer combination,” Douglas said.

Nations lean on fossil fuels, despite solar gains

Turkey's electrification pledge and Australia's rooftop solar declaration put a spotlight on the energy mix of both nations, which still rely heavily on fossil fuels.

In Turkey, home to one of Europe's largest solar farms, solar and wind make up nearly 23% of energy generation. But coal was still the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation, according to Turkey’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources.

In Australia, one in three homes has rooftop solar and more than 700,000 homes have batteries to store excess energy. But coal still makes up more than 40% of electricity generation in Australia, which is also one of the world's largest coal exporters.

“Setting ambitious renewable targets without addressing grid capacity, storage and the continued role of coal risks undermining energy security, reliability and affordability," said Michelle Manook of FutureCoal, an industry-backed group formerly known as the World Coal Association.

The tension between renewable rollouts and continued coal use is mirrored in the world's most populous countries, China and India. They have both installed record-breaking amounts of renewables, but sometimes lose the energy because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity.

“Energy storage deployment must catch up with the speed of renewables deployment," said Nikit Abhyankar, with the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley.

"Otherwise, it creates massive operational challenges for the grid, resulting in significant curtailment," he said, referring to the practice of limiting electricity output because the grid cannot handle it.

Solar spreads, but barriers remain

Rooftop solar panels are often decentralized from power grids, meaning that electricity is generated, stored and managed near where it is consumed, rather than coming from distant power plants.

This makes solar ideal for remote communities and hard-hit areas, like refugee camps and disaster zones.

Renewables, largely driven by solar from China and India, generated more than a third of the world's electricity last year, overtaking coal for the first time.

The Iran war's energy shock has also spurred solar interest in energy-hungry regions, like Southeast Asia, which was hit hard by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent into a state of energy triage.

Indonesia pledged to install 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2029. Thailand and Vietnam are offering subsidies for rooftop solar installations, and the Philippines became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026.

National policies must swiftly follow the COP31 promises to address issues like the funding of subsidies for consumers, clearer policies for solar companies and the availability of qualified installers, according to Sheryl Estella, with the nonprofit New Energy Nexus in the Philippines.

“This is an opportunity that we should not waste,” she said. “This is the biggest wave of interest in rooftop solar that we have seen so far.”

___

Delgado reported from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The Senate voted Monday to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a major piece of permitting reform legislation, but some experts and lawmakers have voiced skepticism about its future in the lame duck session following midterm elections in which Democrats handily won control of both chambers of Congress.

Immediately following the election results, analysts at TD Cowen cut their outlook for the bill’s success from about 40% to around 25%. Democrats’ large victory “likely emboldens voices” arguing the BAAJA gives too many concessions to the oil and gas sector, and that the party should delay reform until 2027 when it can pursue a “party-line, renewable-focused bill,” the analysts said.

The version of the bill that advanced this week included a manager’s amendment, added over the weekend, that sought to address some concerns, including tribal consultation and Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority. But Democrats in both chambers, including at least one senator who voted to advance the bill, have said they want to see more changes.

Dive Insight:

The cloture vote to advance the bill received 73 yesses, 25 nos and two abstentions. Among the nos were Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.; Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont; and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore.

According to Politico, Schiff said he was voting no following President Donald Trump’s comment Monday that he supports the bill but “will not approve wind turbines,” adding, “The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated.”

“He has not changed course in any way when it comes to renewable energy, and any wiggle room left in the bill to prioritize oil and gas over renewables he’ll make full use of,” Schiff told Politico.

In a Monday release, Merkley said he “strongly supports” the parts of the bill that seek to increase transmission and clean energy, and ensure fair cost allocation for data centers, but said the legislation has “features that merit careful analysis” and “robust consideration of the bill should be a priority in the new Congress.”

“At the demand of the fossil fuel titans, this bill also accelerates the extraction and burning of fossil fuels,” Merkley said. “This bill could make it easier to build more data centers powered by ‘behind the meter’ natural gas plants. And it impacts the sovereignty and rights of Tribes.”

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., voted to advance the bill but warned in a Monday release that tribes in Nevada still have concerns regarding the legislation’s changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, and if those aren’t struck from the bill, she will not vote for final passage.

“The manager’s amendment to BAAJA does not adequately address the serious concerns raised by Tribal Nations across the country,” a coalition of tribal organizations said in a Sunday release.

In a research note sent Monday following the vote, Jefferies analysts said the manager’s amendment “largely preserves” the bill’s original framework “but is incrementally better for transmission, offshore-wind projects, nuclear, and non-RTO utilities, and worse for large BTM gas configurations, incumbent RTO utilities and projects relying on strong permit certainty.”

“Senate passage is possible, but enactment remains unlikely without a clear House strategy,” the note said. “The irony is that the bipartisan Senate coalition has made meaningful progress just as the opportunity to convert that progress into law is narrowing. House Democratic leaders argue that the Senate bill falls short, while Republican support for accepting the Senate product also appears uncertain.”

The analysts said the bill could see more revisions to reflect House concerns.

Some of those concerns were voiced by Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz, who was reelected last week.

“Just one week after voters resoundingly rejected the Trump agenda, Congress should not be rushing to pass a bill that gives him even more unilateral authority to bypass our laws,” she said in a Monday statement. “I am a hard NO on BAAJA.”

On Sunday, the Sierra Club said in a release that the manager’s amendment was released amid a “continued rush to hold a vote during the lame duck session,” adding that while the amendment “partially addressed” the group’s previously outlined concerns, “major substantive issues remain.”

Former FERC Chairman Mark Christie said in a Monday LinkedIn post that the manager’s amendment had not “at all” addressed two of his three major concerns with the legislation.

“The ‘public interest’ standard in the bill remains a blank check for FERC to override the states and order trillions of dollars in new transmission built to fit the policies of a President or more likely, special interest lobbying of RTOs,” Christie said.

He added that the legislation doesn’t give states authority over cost allocation for large transmission projects “that will cost their consumers tons of money.”

“The transmission provisions are a DC lobbyists’ dream list,” Christie said. “Massive expansion of federal power that will cost consumers literally trillions of dollars.”

Paul Cicio, CEO of the trade association Industrial Energy Consumers of America and chair of the Electricity Transmission Competition Coalition, criticized the bill in a Monday LinkedIn post, saying it “fails to unleash transmission competition and deliver cost savings to ratepayers.”

“Without competition, a monopoly utility has zero incentive to reduce costs,” he said. “Section 2105 codifies existing exceptions to competition that are used by the monopoly utilities to evade competition.”

Cicio also objected to a change the manager’s amendment made to Section 2104 of the bill, saying it “now gives FERC the ability to dismiss a state’s request to investigate actions by a utility to evade competition and actions that would harm consumers.”
