The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) today announced the financial close of a $480 million loan for Arena Energy's Project Elkhorn to increase oil and natural gas production across the Gulf of America shelf. The project will modernize 22 offshore platforms off the coast of Louisiana and, at peak production, is expected to add up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day and up to 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day to U.S. energy production.

Today’s announcement is made possible by President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut and marks the Energy Department's first closed loan supporting domestic oil and natural gas production, underscoring DOE’s commitment to advancing American energy dominance and delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy for American families and businesses.

“The United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs. By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come.”

Arena Energy currently produces approximately 30,000 barrels of oil per day offshore in the Gulf of America. Project Elkhorn will modernize existing offshore infrastructure and expand production capacity—adding approximately 125 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to U.S. energy production over the life of the project. The project will create 2,400 construction-related jobs and 400 operations jobs in one of the nation's most important offshore energy corridors.

“Thanks to President Trump and Secretary Wright’s leadership, EDF is putting existing energy infrastructure back to work for the American people,” said EDF Director Gregory A. Beard. “Project Elkhorn will expand domestic oil and natural gas production, create good-paying American jobs, and strengthen our energy security while generating substantial returns for American taxpayers.”

Under President Trump’s leadership, EDF is financing American energy infrastructure projects that increase domestic production, strengthen U.S. energy security, and lower costs for all Americans while responsibly managing taxpayer dollars.

text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet released the following statement after voting against advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026:

“Our electric grid is under significant strain and faces growing demand. We need to build new transmission, bring more energy, especially clean energy, onto the grid, and keep electricity affordable. We should make it easier to build new infrastructure, and I strongly support efforts to make this a reality.

“However, permitting reform is complex, and the details matter. I am concerned that not all perspectives were sufficiently heard during the drafting of this far-reaching piece of legislation.

“As drafted, the bill does not do enough to ensure sovereign Tribal governments can protect their cultural resources and ancestral homelands, which they have stewarded since time immemorial. The bill also fundamentally overhauls how the federal government engages with the public and local communities as projects move through the permitting process. These changes must be vetted more thoroughly before passing into law. Given these concerns, I cannot support advancing this bill at this time.

“There is no doubt that we must act on these issues. That means working toward meaningful, bipartisan permitting reforms that provide certainty and reduce unnecessary delays – while also protecting our environment, respecting Tribal sovereignty and self-determination, and preserving meaningful public input. I stand ready to work with my colleagues on a path forward that achieves these goals and supports Colorado’s communities, workers, and energy priorities.”

text:
The U.S. Senate voted 73-25 Monday to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) just minutes after President Donald Trump vowed from the White House press room to keep blocking wind energy.

Politico reported in September that President Trump told his aides he would direct the Pentagon to clear its queue of onshore wind projects to strike a deal on permitting legislation. The White House released a formal statement endorsing the bill just before the Monday procedural vote, only to be contradicted shortly after when President Trump told reporters at a White House media briefing that he won’t approve wind turbines even if the bill becomes law.

Despite some positive changes to the legislation over the weekend, BAAJA would still largely lock in the Trump administration’s attacks on our public lands. Center for Western Priorities Communications Director Kate Groetzinger said in a statement, “Last week’s election showed that Americans want Congress to stand up to the Trump administration. The next Congress can pass a permitting package that builds a better grid without selling out our environment and public lands.”

The Center for Western Priorities, in partnership with Earthworks, released an interactive map last week illustrating how the bill would negatively impact specific national public lands. The map, now updated to reflect the November 7 manager’s amendment, shows that landscapes from Bears Ears to the Tongass to the Boundary Waters to California’s Mojave Desert remain at risk of permanent destruction under BAAJA.

Supreme Court will allow border wall construction in Big Bend

The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration to continue construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwest Texas, including within Big Bend National Park. In October, a federal judge had blocked construction in order to consider a legal challenge brought by a church preservation group, a river guide, and an environmental organization. The high court’s decision on Monday will allow the administration to resume its efforts to erect barriers and put up surveillance equipment along a 500-mile stretch of the U.S. border with Mexico as the battle over the project’s legality continues in a lower court. Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity, swiftly condemned the court’s decision. “I’m completely devastated. This decision clears the way to bulldoze the most pristine parts of the park,” Jordahl said. “They’ve effectively signed off on the destruction of the wildest place left in Texas.”

South Africa’s slow pace of transitioning local manufacturing to new energy vehicles, battery propulsion and renewable energy storage technologies can be played to our advantage – if we shift from thinking about how to catch up, to how to meet the next disruption.

Delays in adapting and implementing industrial policy to global market shifts and technology advances have left local manufacturers hamstrung against more agile and faster-moving competitors, heightening the threat of local de-industrialisation in an environment of factory closures, downscaling and rising unemployment.

Yet this has also given us the luxury of watching and learning from the mistakes and new technologies being developed in early-adopter countries.

While SA’s grid-connected renewable energy generation is growing and there has been progress on policy to support areas such as new energy vehicle (NEV) and battery manufacturing, we are still effectively playing catch-up while the early stages of NEV technology development are already closed and the world is moving on.

This is a key issue for Nelson Mandela Bay, as the hub of SA vehicle and components manufacturing and exports, with employment concentrated in the auto sector and the surrounding ecosystem of value chains that it supports.

Methods of achieving low carbon emissions, initially and still predominantly focused on lithium-ion batteries in fully electric vehicles, are now being re-thought as new evidence emerges of the environmental impacts of mining and manufacturing, and concerns move to the full life-cycle costs of an electric vehicle rather than tailpipe emissions alone.

A further dilemma

From a cost point of view for consumers, it is becoming more affordable to replace the entire vehicle and gain more up-to-date technology and features, rather than just replacing the battery. Thus, creating a further dilemma of how to sensibly dispose of the old vehicle, since the high costs of battery replacement limit the second-hand market for electric vehicles.

It remains questionable whether the carbon emissions involved in manufacturing an electric vehicle are lower than those in manufacturing a vehicle powered by an internal combustion engine, be it powered by petrol, diesel, hydrogen or new carbon-neutral fuels from renewable sources.

It is still cheaper to mine lithium than to recycle and repurpose it, creating concerns around the environmental impact of mining and the associated low-income employment in the lower-income countries where it is mined, and what to do with spent batteries in the higher-income countries where they are used.

Alternative methods for achieving low-carbon manufacturing and mobility are reaching proof stages, such as hyperefficient internal combustion engines using traditional or biofuels, on their own or providing propulsion assistance to hybrid vehicles powered by sodium, hydrogen or ammonia batteries or fuel cells, as alternatives to lithium-ion batteries.

At the same time, economic pressures on the traditional auto manufacturing giants, amid tariff wars and erosion of their market share by the rise of more affordable Chinese-made electric vehicles, threatening the sustainability of manufacturing and its high employment, have led to a softening of targets for the removal of all internal combustion engine vehicles within the next decade in significant territories such as the European Union.

South Africans have no shortage of innovative thinking, but we often lack support for implementation. We now need to be looking at the unsolved problems, no matter how small, and how to support them from idea to commercialisation so they don’t drown in the “valley of death of good ideas”.

As a country and consumer market, we are too small to bet on one big idea as players such as China can. We now need to avoid trying to follow one big player or one big idea and to look at multiple possible futures, to look at the gaps and the problems no one else has yet tried or bothered to solve.

This is where real innovation lies – not in coming up with solutions for problems that we don’t have, but in solving in the gaps where there is a need but no current practical solution. In a sense, creating demand for a market that will exist tomorrow.

Leap-frogging

This is what we mean by leap-frogging.

Finding small-scale problems and proposing solutions also means the opportunity to fail small, pick yourself up and start again.

There is no doubt South African consumers will continue adopting electric and hybrid vehicles – the sales figures are there to prove it – and there is still a need for policy to support the transition of local manufacturing, protect local jobs, and to incentivise consumers to buy local.

However, when it comes to manufacturing, there is a strong case to forget trying to achieve full local manufacturing of EVs and rather look at how we can fill gaps that aren’t already plugged by more advanced and faster-moving competitors, with local innovations to solve local problems, using local and renewable resources, that can be scaled globally.

While it is highly unlikely that South African manufacturers could ever find a business case to compete with China on the manufacture of plug-in and full EVs, and the lithium-ion battery market that they own, we have a proven ability to make electric motors and internal combustion engines to global standards.

This opens a door to thinking about adapting our internal combustion engine manufacturing capacity to be powered by fuels other than petrol or diesel, such as hydrogen, ammonia, green methane or, as Brazil does, with carbon neutral, sugarcane-derived fuel.

We have the capacity in existing vehicle manufacturing plants to shift to the new mode of “propulsion-assisted hybrids” – a smaller battery, with a smaller hyper-efficient fuel-burning engine – that uses existing infrastructure and reduces issues of range anxiety and limited charging infrastructure for vehicle owners.

There is further opportunity for local auto component manufacturers to think about building range-extenders, a small petrol or ammonia engine as an aftermarket add-on to an electric vehicle, that charges the battery while driving. (Given that, even in countries with far better charging networks than SA, drivers spend more time planning their trips around charging stations than on the actual trip, this would offer a great peace-of-mind selling point.)

There is also opportunity for local entrepreneurs to get involved in areas from battery pack assembly to charging infrastructure, provided that policy support is there for them to do so.

A key opportunity

Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau’s comment in his address at the recent SA Auto Week, that the government recognises that the automotive industry is a key opportunity to connect a minerals beneficiation strategy with industrial development, is a welcome recognition of the interconnectedness of the country’s primary and secondary industrial sectors that is often unacknowledged and unleveraged.

Equally welcome is his statement that government has begun work on an end-of-life vehicle policy to position SA at the starting point of the new industry of recycling and repurposing new energy vehicle batteries.

If we can get this right, we can leverage a slow-mover advantage of learning from the mistakes of others, and not only build an industry around repurposing spent lithium-ion vehicle batteries into static renewable energy storage for homes and schools, for example, but also leapfrog to a future of manufacturing fuel cells with alternative and renewable energy sources.

South Africa needs to be looking at new battery contents such as sodium, or iron-air batteries for energy generation and long-duration storage, and the possibility of reviving older nickel-zinc batteries with new technology – all of which would support greater local minerals beneficiation.

Our strength in catalytic converter production is another opportunity. While global demand for catalytic converters is declining, we already have advanced technology in place for platinum-based hydrolisation to convert hydrogen for vehicle or battery storage use, and refuelling hydrogen-powered vehicles in a conventional filling station setting.

This in turn supports the overall goal of beneficiating South Africa’s mineral wealth rather than exporting raw materials.

Further, South Africa needs to look at market realities.

If we focus on Europe, we are competing with China. In the US, we are competing with the US itself and it has made it clear it doesn’t want to play. Opportunities in Asia are limited, due to the tech dominance of China and India, and our lack of free-trade agreements with BRICS partners.

However, as the dominant and most industrialised economy in Africa, we have an opportunity to develop technological and manufacturing solutions for the continent we inhabit.

Across the Global South, the transition from internal combustion engine to new energy vehicles is likely to be slower, and there are opportunities to expand South African-made solutions such as micro-mobility and battery-powered last mile delivery.

It is possible for South Africa to manufacture the small 10kwh battery packs needed for micro-mobility, powered by rooftop solar which could also be locally manufactured and rolled out, together with locally manufactured capacitive battery technology.

These components are possible by drawing on the capabilities of local auto component manufacturers, needing no reliance on imported components.

It is also vital that these initiatives around innovation and localisation incorporate development of regional value chains – building on particular national strengths in raw materials, manufacturing capability and logistics, so that the SADC region, or Africa as a whole, becomes an interconnected hub of markets and output that can compete globally.

At the same time, we need to develop the skills that South Africa will need in the next 10 to 20 years – flexible and adaptable rather than just focusing on labour absorption.

This will take a leapfrog in education similar to a leapfrog in manufacturing, developing learners who don’t necessarily know how to build or code artificial intelligence, but know how to use it.

Future needs

In addition to maths, basic science and engineering understanding, we need to develop problem-solving skills and people able to look into the blind spots – in other words, to solve for the gaps where future needs exist.

If we play our cards right, this could be a unique situation in which South Africa’s slow pace of industrial policy keeping up with global market developments works to our advantage.

This will take a shift in mindset by both the government and industry. Rather than planning for keeping up, or worse, for catching up, we need to be making greater use of futures thinking to identify and prioritise the most likely future scenarios, and translate this into policymaking geared to leap-frogging ahead.

text:
Medium- and heavy-duty electric vehicles are hitting the road in 2026, and we’ve collected last month’s most exciting news. In 2025, EDF delivered monthly deployment updates on the biggest zero-emission transportation stories. By the end of 2025, it was clear that momentum was sustained throughout a challenging year. This year will undoubtably see more big announcements, and we’ll be here to showcase the biggest orders and deployments of zero-emission trucks happening around the country.

October announcements highlight the accelerating adoption of zero-emission transportation, with autonomous electric freight trucks, expanded electric transit fleets, and increased investment in electric truck conversions supporting more sustainable and efficient transportation operations..

Einride and EASE Logistics partner on driverless electric trucks

EASE Logistics and vehicle manufacture Einride have launched a daily freight route using two L4 autonomous electric trucks in Marysville, Ohio. The vehicles will transport freight between EASE warehouses without drivers in the cab, while remote operators monitor the vehicles and intervene when necessary. The deployment, which began last month, is part of the $8.8 million Truck Automation Corridor Project, a partnership involving the Ohio Department of Transportation, DriveOhio and the Indiana Department of Transportation to advance autonomous freight transportation across Ohio and Indiana. Operational data on safety, reliability, efficiency, mileage, cargo volumes and vehicle uptime will help evaluate the technology and guide future expansion.

Sonoma County Transit expands electric fleet and opens new EV charging facility

Sonoma County Transit has added seven new 40-foot electric buses, bringing its total zero-emission fleet to 18 buses currently in service. The new buses are supported by a fully operational charging system with backup power generation, ensuring vehicles can remain charged and available during power outages, emergencies and wildfire evacuations. The fleet expansion is part of the county’s goal to electrify most of its heavy-duty transit fleet by 2030, reducing emissions while improving the reliability and sustainability of public transportation throughout the county.

Janus Electric receives repeat conversion order from King Fio Trucking

Janus Electric Holdings has received a repeat order from California-based King Fio Trucking for six additional Class 8 electric truck conversions, bringing King Fio’s total commitment to 12 converted electric trucks. The new trucks will use the company’s existing battery-swapping infrastructure and charging equipment, allowing King Fio to expand its electric fleet for container drayage and other freight operations across Southern California. The purchase reflects King Fio’s continued commitment to transitioning its approximately 30 truck fleet toward zero-emission operations.

Now is a critical time for fleets to invest in medium- and heavy-duty electric trucks. These vehicles improve public health and help combat the climate crisis by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution. Unlike traditional diesel-powered trucks, electric trucks produce no tailpipe emissions, which significantly cuts down on health-harming pollution. Adoption represents a key step toward a more sustainable and resilient transportation industry.

Check back here next month to see a collection of the most exciting zero-emission vehicle announcements from November. In the meantime, check out EDF’s Electric Fleet Deployment & Commitment List to track announcements as they happen in real time, and view all October announcements.

text:
Project Elkhorn will retool, refurbish, and repower offshore platforms in the Southern Eugene Island area off the coast of Louisiana

THE WOODLANDS, Texas, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Arena Energy, LLC ("Arena"), a leading independent oil and natural gas exploration company focused on the shallow waters of the Gulf of America, today announced that its wholly owned subsidiary, Elkhorn Offshore, LLC, has reached financial close on a $480 million loan from the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) supporting Project Elkhorn, an energy-infrastructure reinvestment project in the Gulf of America. The financing will be used to retool, refurbish, repower, and expand capacity across offshore platforms in the Southern Eugene Island area off the coast of Louisiana, extending their use and enabling critical infrastructure upgrades.

Project Elkhorn will return idled platforms to service and expand production and water-handling capacity at active facilities. The project also includes the development of new natural gas pipeline infrastructure to connect future wells into existing pipelines, improving midstream connectivity across the field. Together, these investments are expected to add approximately 125 million barrels of additional oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas production over the life of the project, helping ensure Americans have access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy while maintaining the highest standards of operational and environmental safety. This increase in domestic production will lead to an estimated $1.6 billion in additional royalties collected by the federal government, a total return of more than three times for American taxpayers.

The closing follows completion of the technical, legal, environmental, and financial due diligence required under DOE's loan program.

"The United States is the world's largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. "Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs. By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come."

"Arena was founded on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf Shelf still hold vast potential, and Project Elkhorn is a critical part of that strategy," said Mike Minarovic, CEO and Founder of Arena Energy, LLC. "The Southern Eugene Island area is one of the most prolific oil-producing regions in American history, and its infrastructure still has decades of productive life ahead. What it needed was long-term capital to match the opportunity. This financing from the Department of Energy delivers that capital and lets us put existing infrastructure back to work, develop proved reserves, and keep producing some of the most reliable barrels in the world right here at home – with American workers, on American leases, for American refineries."

"The Office of Energy Dominance Financing conducted a rigorous review of this project, and we are pleased to have earned its confidence," Minarovic continued. "Reinvesting in existing infrastructure is one of the most efficient ways to add American energy production, support skilled jobs, and generate value. Arena has paid more than $1.8 billion in royalties to the federal government since 1999, and Project Elkhorn will allow us to accelerate additional royalty income for American taxpayers for decades to come."

Project Elkhorn will support 2,800 jobs, including 400 operations roles and 2,400 construction jobs, helping strengthen regional workforce opportunities in one of the nation's most important offshore energy corridors.

Arena will execute the project with its long-standing affiliated partners White Fleet Drilling and Rosefield Pipeline.

About Arena Energy

Arena Energy, LLC was founded in 1999 on the belief that mature producing areas of the Gulf of America Shelf still held vast potential – and that with the right technology, talented oil and gas finders could unlock these drilling opportunities. Today, that vision has been realized many times over. Since its founding, Arena has grown into one of the largest private offshore oil and natural gas companies, having invested more than $5 billion of capital in the Gulf of America, paid more than $1.8 billion in royalties to the federal government, and decommissioned over 300 wells and 45 platforms and other structures. Arena takes pride in safely and responsibly producing the energy that powers the United States and the world.

Elkhorn Offshore, LLC is a wholly owned subsidiary of Arena Energy, LLC formed to own and reinvest in the offshore production infrastructure serving Arena's Southern Eugene Island fields in the federal waters of the Gulf of America.

text:
One year after its launch, the Pact for the Mediterranean is delivering concrete benefits and new opportunities for citizens, businesses and communities on all shores of our shared sea.

Today, the European Commission and the European External Action Service presented to representatives of EU Member States and Southern Mediterranean partners the updated Action Plan, which highlights the progress made under the Pact's first set of actions under the Action Plan, alongside nine new key initiatives.

These bring the total to 30 initiatives under the Pact, advancing the EU and its partners' shared ambition to build a connected, prosperous, resilient and secure Common Mediterranean Space.

Key achievements and new actions

First pillar – People. Driving Force for Change, Connections, and Innovation

Progress has been made across the eight actions under the first pillar, including important steps towards establishing the Mediterranean University, which will strengthen transnational education and research through closer cooperation between universities and academics. Work has also advanced on innovation and research centres to support scientific collaboration, skills development and competitiveness across the region. Other actions, including the MED Skills Tracker, are advancing to help young people develop skills and access employment opportunities. These efforts pave the way for the new Mediterranean Youth Skills and Jobs Initiative, announced by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her State of the Union address this year.

The updated Action Plan introduces two new actions. The first is the establishment of a Mediterranean Science Diplomacy Centre to serve as a regional hub for coordination, capacity-building and knowledge exchange. The second is an initiative raising awareness about the benefits of sport for physical and mental health across the region.

Second pillar – Stronger, more sustainable and integrated economies

Progress has been made across four actions under the second pillar, including the launch of the Trans-Mediterranean Renewable Energy and Clean Tech Cooperation Initiative (T-MED) on 9 June. The T-MED Investment Platform is already in place to build a pipeline of renewable energy, grid and clean-tech projects, combining EU financing and risk-sharing instruments to attract investment and industrial partnerships, with investment of €25 billion expected to be mobilised.

The StartUp4Med, to promote inclusive growth and decent job creation is also on track, along with the Surging Women's Employment Initiative (SWEI), launched on 23 September 2026 together with UN Women, to create 500,000 jobs for women in sectors with high growth potential. Around 900 companies across the MENA region and the Gulf have already committed to implementing the Women's Empowerment Principles underpinning the programme.

The updated Action Plan introduces six new actions, such as measures to modernise and strengthen trade and investment relations and promote sustainable transport for a better-connected region. Several climate-related actions for a clean transition, sustainable growth and resilience are also included, alongside the Blue Mediterranean Mission fostering a blue economy and water resilience.

Third pillar – Security, preparedness and migration management

Progress has been made across nine actions under the third pillar, including the European Firefighting Hub, a centre based in Cyprus, which extends disaster preparedness and response support to southern Mediterranean countries for the first time. Six aircraft were pre-positioned at the Paphos airbase to strengthen preparedness for the 2026 fire season, and partners also participated in a regional wildfire workshop in May 2026, identifying shared priorities and needs.

The MED-OP action, which will support operational efforts to combat serious and organised crime in cooperation with Justice and Home Affairs agencies, will be launched on 11 November at the first regional dialogue on internal security between the EU and partner countries. The Secure Borders action will be launched at the same time to strengthen operational and institutional border management capacities and security sector governance. The first EU-MED Peace and Security Forum will take place on 18 November in Brussels and provide an informal setting to foster joint regional situational awareness, share views and coordinate approaches on issues of common interest.

The Action Plan is also delivering in preventing illegal migration and fighting smuggling and trafficking in human beings. Actions under the Talent Partnerships were undertaken in Egypt, Morocco and Tunisia, to better align labour migration pathways with labour market and employer needs in sectors such as transport, tourism, hospitality and construction.

The updated Action Plan introduces one new action to strengthen protection for vulnerable migrants, asylum seekers and refugees in the southern Mediterranean through a regional, whole-of-route approach.

Next steps

Amid an increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape, the EU remains committed to strengthening partnerships across the Mediterranean. The Action Plan is a flexible and dynamic document that will be regularly updated and adapted to the changing context through continuous consultations with stakeholders and partners, ensuring its relevance and effectiveness.

Another update to the Action Plan is expected in Spring 2027.

An interactive webpage has also been launched to allow stakeholders to identify concrete projects and initiatives, explore them by country and sector, and follow their progress, ensuring transparency and engagement while showing the tangible impact of the Pact across the region.

Background

The Pact for the Mediterranean was adopted by the College in October 2025, ahead of its official launch by EU and Southern Mediterranean partners on 28 November 2025.

Rooted in the principles of co-creation, co-ownership and shared responsibility, it is the result of an unprecedented, and inclusive consultation process, ensuring alignment with the real needs and aspirations of the citizens on both shores of the Mediterranean.

The Pact is a joint effort between the EU, its Member States and the Southern Mediterranean partners to work together on shared priorities for a connected, integrated, prosperous, resilient and secure Common Mediterranean Space.

The initiatives proposed under the Pact were welcomed by Member States during the Foreign Affairs Council on 20 November 2025, as well as at the European Council meeting of 18 December 2025. Leaders called for a swift and efficient implementation, underpinned by principles of co-creation, co-ownership, mutual interest and joint responsibility.

title: COP31 climate summit begins after disastrous year of extreme weather | PBS News
authors: Suzan Fraser, Associated Press, Sibi Arasu
description:
"For too many people, climate change is deadly," U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell said on Monday.
Kurum, the COP31 president, has said that rather than establishing new targets, he wants the summit to focus on turning previous climate commitments into action.
Delegates are also expected to discuss at the Nov. 9-20 summit how to help poorer countries pay to adapt to rising temperatures and extreme weather events, both tied to climate change, and transition away from fossil fuels.
At the center of the disagreements are developing countries, which seek more discussions on financing for the goals agreed on at the 2015 Paris climate talks.
"No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight," said Stiell, the climate chief.
text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday kicked off talks in Turkey on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures and deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond, and played a role in disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal.

This U.N. climate summit — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, hiking global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and increased investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

"For too many people, climate change is deadly," U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell said on Monday. "At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock. Rewire the global economy for the electric age. Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms and governments."

"The climate crisis is now a global health crisis of pandemic proportions," he said.

Earlier, Stiell also said that agreeing on practical solutions, such as reducing methane emissions, can be "planetary icepacks" that can help reduce global heating. Methane stays in the atmosphere for a shorter time but warms the planet much faster than other planet-heating gases. Using renewable-powered electricity instead of oil, gas and coal can also help reduce global warming.

Delegates, meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, will come under pressure to develop new pledges for climate action while implementing previous promises. The stakes are high: Climate scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s.

Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it's been a focus of international climate negotiations.

The fact that the goal is no longer realistic underscores how difficult it's been for the world to cut greenhouse gas emissions, which are released into the atmosphere when fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned, leading to climate change.

"This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target," said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum. "We will not look away, and we will not lower our ambition."

Kurum, the COP31 president, has said that rather than establishing new targets, he wants the summit to focus on turning previous climate commitments into action.

He has announced an "Action Agenda" that includes reducing methane emissions and building climate-resilient cities. There is also the aim of increasing the use of electricity — preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind — from 21% to 35% by 2035, to reduce greenhouse emissions.

"Success begins when our decisions reach that last mile," said Kurum. "If we are to share a future, we must share the responsibility for it."

Climate talks kick off with a tense start

Long lines formed outside the registration center on the opening day of the summit, forcing organizers to urge attendees "without essential business" to postpone collecting their accreditation badges until Tuesday.

An estimated 68,500 people are registered to attend the two-week event and nearly 25,000 people will help ensure the conference goes smoothly.

Delegates are also expected to discuss at the Nov. 9-20 summit how to help poorer countries pay to adapt to rising temperatures and extreme weather events, both tied to climate change, and transition away from fossil fuels.

Even as leaders delivered speeches talking about ambition and implementation, negotiators from nearly 200 countries were already wrangling in the backrooms about disagreements over funds for climate adaptation and recovery from climate disasters and other long-pending bottlenecks.

READ MORE: Outdated power grids a major hurdle in renewable energy transition

"Countries that did the least to cause this crisis shouldn't have to borrow their way through it," said Meena Raman from the Malaysia-based climate advocacy group Third World Network.

At the center of the disagreements are developing countries, which seek more discussions on financing for the goals agreed on at the 2015 Paris climate talks.

"After years of disappointment, developing countries want to know clearly how rich countries plan to provide the funds needed to tackle climate change," said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, a veteran of many climate talks and adviser to African negotiators at this year's talks.

"Agenda proposals from the 54-country African Group were backed by many developing countries but contested by rich countries from the European Union and Canada," he said.

The last two summits, COP30 in Brazil and COP29 in Azerbaijan, came under criticism for ending with little agreement on how to reduce greenhouse emissions. The final texts of those conferences didn't even mention fuels. At COP28 in Dubai, delegates had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels.

The United States is missing in action again

The United States — the world's second-largest polluter after China — is again absent from the summit.

During his first term, and again when he took office for a second time in January 2025, President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.

"No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight," said Stiell, the climate chief. "But every recent COP has made essential progress. COP31 in Antalya will, too."

In a change from previous summits, Turkey and Australia are jointly holding this summit after the two jostled over which would be the host. As a compromise, Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations. Both countries have come under criticism for their strong reliance on coal.

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

title: Norway Halts New Grid Reservations for Server Facilities - Environment+Energy Leader
description:
Statnett, Norway's transmission system operator, stopped accepting new grid capacity reservations from data centers on Nov. 9.
The same day, the government moved to announce a licensing scheme that will decide which data centers the country wants.
Data centers use about 3 TWh a year.
If all allocated grid capacity is used, NVE estimates that figure could reach about 25 TWh by 2035.
Norway is going further by deciding which uses get power at all, as grid reliability concerns tied to AI load spread.
text:
Statnett, Norway's transmission system operator, stopped accepting new grid capacity reservations from data centers on Nov. 9. It also paused work on some of the technical approvals that projects need before they can energize. The same day, the government moved to announce a licensing scheme that will decide which data centers the country wants. Statnett's figures show 800 megawatts (MW) of data center load connected, 4,200 MW reserved, 9,100 MW in the queue and inquiries for another 18,000 MW. Norway's peak demand is just over 25,000 MW.

Reserved Capacity Is Not Clearance to Connect

The pause covers new reservations and new applications for approval of plant functionality under Norway's system responsibility regulation. Statnett also halted pending applications from facilities that would connect directly to the 420-kilovolt grid. Regional-grid applications for plants close to startup will continue, and some smaller facilities may still be considered. Plants with approved functional requirements can still connect, and existing connections are unaffected.

Statnett expects to lift the pause by Aug. 1, 2027, once it has set functional requirements for data centers and the Norwegian Energy Regulatory Authority (RME) has approved them. Those rules will address when a data center may drop off the grid during a disturbance, how fast its load can ramp and how to limit grid oscillations. Peer Olav Østli, Statnett's executive vice president for system operation and markets, said the pause is needed to put those tools in place. Statnett has not said how much of the 4,200 MW already holds approved functional requirements.

A National Surplus Does Not Settle Local Limits

The power market scenarios published in October by the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE) put the country's normal-year surplus at about 15 terawatt-hours (TWh). Data centers use about 3 TWh a year. If all allocated grid capacity is used, NVE estimates that figure could reach about 25 TWh by 2035. With strong demand and no new wind power, one scenario shows a 4 TWh deficit in 2035 and higher prices. An annual surplus says little about whether one substation can carry a new load, which is where Statnett's rules apply.

Licensing Will Cover New and Existing Sites

Digitalization Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said the licensing scheme should be ready in autumn 2027 and will apply to existing data centers as well as new ones, with transition terms to be worked out with industry. He cited health, defense, mobile networks and artificial intelligence as beneficial uses. Cryptocurrency mining will not qualify. Energy Minister Terje Aasland said Statnett has received applications for about 26,000 MW of new consumption this year. Data centers account for three-quarters of that total.

The government also wants large new consumers to pay more toward grid and system operating costs. It plans talks with industry on new generation such as offshore wind and gas power with carbon capture and storage.

Ireland Asked Data Centers to Bring Power

Ireland took another route. Its Commission for Regulation of Utilities now requires new data centers to supply generation or storage that matches their maximum draw, plus new Irish renewables covering at least 80% of annual demand on a six-year glide path. In the U.S., Florida regulators rejected Duke Energy Florida's large-load tariff on Nov. 3 over eligibility and cost recovery. Norway is going further by deciding which uses get power at all, as grid reliability concerns tied to AI load spread.

For cloud customers holding Norwegian capacity, the status that matters during the pause is approval of each phase's functional requirements. Later phases may fall under rules that RME has yet to approve.

text:
Honda plans to invest $3 billion in an Ohio assembly plant that would expand its U.S. manufacturing capacity for gasoline-powered, hybrid and electric vehicles. Honda said demand for its vehicles was a reason for adding capacity. The new plant is expected to focus on hybrids.

The proposed plant would be near Honda’s existing facilities in Marysville, Ohio, and Honda expects production to begin in 2029. The plant is designed to produce up to 240,000 vehicles a year and is expected to create more than 2,000 jobs. Honda has not named the models it plans to build there.

Honda expects the new plant to bring its annual U.S. light-duty vehicle capacity to about 1.3 million. The company operates 12 manufacturing plants in the country; eight produce engines or light-duty vehicles.

Honda has made vehicles in the United States since 1982. It has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the country, and employs more than 30,000 people in the U.S. The proposed Ohio site would be its first new U.S. mass-production vehicle assembly plant since its Indiana plant opened in 2008.

The company also has manufacturing operations elsewhere in Ohio. A $70 million performance vehicle facility opened in the state in 2016, and a multibillion-dollar joint-venture battery plant began operating there earlier this year.

Honda’s electric-vehicle plans have shifted this year. It canceled three electric models planned for the U.S. market. Honda indefinitely suspended its proposed Canadian electric vehicle and battery project.

text:
Toyota has officially resurrected the Scion nameplate, but not as the youth-focused compact car badge of the early 2000s. Instead, Toyota is positioning Scion as an incubator for specialized mobility, low-speed utility vehicles, and niche lifestyle concepts.

Automotive Analyst Lauren Fix attended Toyota’s global reveal event to break down three standout vehicles anchoring this next chapter: the BKE electric folding commuter, the 300-hp SXS side-by-side concept, and the U.S.-built Kei 01 micro-truck.

The BKE Concept

Taking direct aim at ultra-compact ride-on commuters like the Honda Motocompacto, the BKE concept represents Toyota’s take on foldable, last-mile electric transit.

Sign up for CBT News’ daily newsletter and get the latest industry stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Designed as a fully compacting, ride-on EV that collapses or sets up in roughly one minute, the BKE concept fits neatly into the trunk of a Corolla or GR86 when folded flat. It plugs directly into standard household wall outlets for routine charging and features an integrated mini display screen with hand controls. Notably, during field testing, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda experienced tire spray kicked up his back, prompting him to mandate an extended rear fender to redirect water and mud, a distinct design touch tailored for urban commuters, college campuses, industrial properties, and car enthusiasts looking for a versatile trunk companion.

The SXS Concept

From urban streets to rugged trails, Toyota introduced the SXS side-by-side concept, a purpose-built off-roader with serious hardware.

Rather than relying on a small-displacement powersports motor, the SXS features a high-output turbocharged 4-cylinder hybrid system producing over 300 horsepower. To complement this powerful drivetrain, it features heavy-duty suspension, genuine off-road knobby tires, integrated recovery hooks, and full trail-ready underbody protection. High-contrast performance cues highlight the interior, including an asymmetric seating design with a Porsche-inspired red driver’s bucket seat paired with black passenger seating. While currently presented as a concept, the vehicle is slated for near-future production as a premium outdoor recreational vehicle.

The Kei 01

The centerpiece of the Scion showcase is the Kei 01, a dedicated micro-truck that brings Japan’s iconic Kei-class commercial formula to North America, with domestic manufacturing.

Specification/feature Details Engine 660cc 3-cylinder gas engine Drivetrain All-Wheel Drive (AWD / 4×4) with CVT Top speed 25 mph (Compliant with U.S. Low-Speed Vehicle standards) Payload capacity 600 lbs (with drop-down fold-flat bed sides) Interior layout Right-hand drive (RHD), heated/cooled cabin, analog gauges Assembly location Toyota Manufacturing Facility in Indiana (~50 new jobs) Expected timeline Initial rollout targeting mid-2027

Why right-hand drive and analog controls?

The Kei 01 keeps its Japanese-market heritage with a factory right-hand-drive layout. Fix notes that for delivery routes, parking enforcement, and campus maintenance, RHD offers ergonomic curbside entry and exit. The dashboard deliberately eschews large touchscreens for mechanical switches and a physical analog speedometer, delivering the straightforward reliability and low repair costs commercial fleets prioritize.

Fleet-First Rollout & Consumer Potential

The initial rollout of the Kei 01 will target dedicated commercial, property, municipal, and campus fleets, including hotels, universities, logistics depots, and delivery hubs. After this fleet-first phase, consumer availability is planned for later stages, tapping into strong U.S. demand for imported vintage Kei trucks while bypassing 25-year import restrictions and high tariffs through domestic assembly in Indiana.

title: Gina Hinojosa wants to freeze electricity rates in Texas. New Jersey shows why that won't work.
authors: Tosin Akintola, C.J. Ciaramella, Jacob Sullum, Matthew Petti, Christian Britschgi
description:
In Texas' decentralized market, retail providers, not regulators, set electricity prices.
Abigail Spanberger called for a six-year freeze on residential electricity rates as a condition for approving the proposed $67 billion merger between utilities Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy.
Regardless of where it's proposed, a rate freeze is a superficial fix for a problem that requires less government thumb on the scale, not more.
Without the price signals they receive from electricity rates, utilities can't properly plan for upgrades, expansion, or future demand.
Freezing electricity rates clearly polls well as policy, but it works better on the campaign trail than in practice.
text:
When Democrat Gina Hinojosa is sworn in as Texas governor in January, one of her first acts, "within an hour of taking the oath of office," she recently told The Texas Tribune, will be to "declare a high-cost emergency in the state of Texas and issue an emergency executive order to: one, suspend the gas and diesel tax; and two, freeze electricity rates."

Hinojosa—who tied increases in property taxes and electricity bills to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's policies—promised during her campaign that if elected, she would "direct the Public Utility Commission to freeze the rates residential customers pay until we have laws to ensure that data centers and other high-load users pay for themselves."

With Texans seeing a 3.3 percent increase in the average electricity price for residential customers between August 2025 and August 2026—roughly in line with the national increase—the state's electorate clearly found Hinojosa's pledge compelling. However, it's unclear if Hinojosa actually has the power to follow through on her campaign promise.

In Texas' decentralized market, retail providers, not regulators, set electricity prices. This means Hinojosa has very little authority over residential prices, and her order would not lower costs. But as Click2Houston.com points out, Hinojosa could still impact prices; she could use her influence over the state budget "to push lawmakers toward her priorities," including forcing data centers to pay more. Of course, this would do little to address the primary cause of nationwide electricity spikes: transmission and distribution charges.

Instead of Texas imposing price controls on the free market, Hinojosa could learn from the mistakes of New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a fellow Democrat who has failed to meaningfully lower electricity prices in her state despite signing an executive order that declared a state of emergency and froze rate hikes by the state's utilities.

Sherrill realized that even if she froze rates, it wouldn't erase the factors driving higher electricity prices, such as the supply and transmission costs providers pay. In June, to offset the increases utilities typically pass on to customers, Sherrill signed off on a budget authorization that allocates $500 million to provide ratepayers short-term relief. Yet in October, a CBS News report found that even after the rate freeze, utility costs in the Garden State remained high, with one resident remarking her electricity bill had "nearly doubled."

In July, the consulting firm E3 released a report—commissioned by Sherrill for the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities—that found that changes to state policy mainly affect distribution, which is "roughly a quarter" of the charges on residents' electricity bills, and that "no single reform or modernization option" could be presented as a standalone fix.

It's not just New Jersey that has tried (and failed) to bring down utility costs by freezing electricity rates; last July Georgia's Public Service Commission unanimously approved an agreement to freeze base power rates for at least three years. A year after the freeze was implemented, the average electricity price for residential customers in Georgia rose by 2.3 percent. Meanwhile, in October, Virginia Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger called for a six-year freeze on residential electricity rates as a condition for approving the proposed $67 billion merger between utilities Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy.

Regardless of where it's proposed, a rate freeze is a superficial fix for a problem that requires less government thumb on the scale, not more.

At least one Democratic governor has declined to use rate freezes as a temporary panacea for rising energy costs. In a March appearance on CBS 2's "The Point," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul was asked if she thought a "two-year moratorium or freeze on utility rates statewide" was "doable." She quickly rejected the idea, favoring an "all-of-the-above approach to find more sources of energy to help drive down [costs]."

What rate freezes like Hinojosa's miss is that states have little direct impact on electric prices. As the E3 report notes, "Most of a typical bill…is set in federal and regional markets with limited ability at the state level to influence those costs."

Still, that doesn't make the idea behind these policies—that government should interfere in the market—any less harmful.

Without the price signals they receive from electricity rates, utilities can't properly plan for upgrades, expansion, or future demand. Freezing electricity rates clearly polls well as policy, but it works better on the campaign trail than in practice.

text:
Scion by Toyota Launches a "Freedom Lab" for Exploring New Possibilities for Mobility, Adventure and Personal Expression

KEI-01 will be Assembled at Toyota's Indiana Plant

660cc Three-Cylinder Engine, Continuously Variable Transmission and Four-Wheel Drive

Designed to Comply with Federal Safety Requirements Applicable to a Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV)

Initial Distribution will Focus on Fleet Customers Through a Small Network of Authorized Scion by Toyota Dealers to be Selected from the Existing Toyota Dealer Network

SxS and BKE Concepts Preview New Possibilities for Outdoor Adventure and Personal Mobility

PLANO, Texas, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Yesterday, at simultaneous events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas, Toyota Motor North America (TMNA) introduced Scion by Toyota, a new brand built around curiosity, possibility and the freedom to explore mobility in new ways. The company also unveiled the brand's first vehicle, the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck that will arrive in the U.S. in the second half of 2027.

The company also showcased two additional vehicles—the SxS Concept and the BKE Concept—which represent different expressions of the brand's vision for future mobility. Together, the three vehicles explore new ideas in utility, adventure, capability and personal expression.

Scion by Toyota is a "freedom lab" built around bold ideas, curiosity and possibility. It starts by asking what's next—and how far an idea can go. That curiosity is where beyond starts, and opens new possibilities to explore, experiment and make something entirely your own. Scion by Toyota will learn and evolve through new vehicle concepts, designs, capabilities, and experiences that could help shape the future of Toyota mobility.

The brand builds on the experimental spirit associated with the original Scion, reimagined for a new generation. This new endeavor gives Toyota a space to challenge conventions and provide drivers with more freedom to experiment, personalize and create something that is uniquely theirs.

At its heart is the simple idea that there is no single way forward—only the one you choose to make your own. Scion by Toyota explores what becomes possible when mobility supports personal expression, adventure and capability.

"The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology or one way of thinking," said Simon Humphries, Chief Branding Officer, Head of Design, Toyota Motor Corporation. "Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way."

The KEI-01: Where the Journey Begins

The KEI-01 is the first manifestation of the Scion by Toyota vision.

Providing the functionality, efficiency and versatility of Japan's legendary kei trucks, the KEI-01 brings a proven concept to American customers in a packaged way that only Toyota companies can deliver. Designed to meet applicable low-speed vehicle federal safety requirements, the KEI-01 comes standard with a 660cc three-cylinder engine, a continuously variable transmission, and four-wheel drive (4WD) making it an affordable, highly capable, and remarkably maneuverable package.

Toyota has long focused on bringing customers vehicles that fit the way they live and work. For decades, kei trucks have earned a strong reputation in Japan and some other Asian markets for their practicality and versatility. The KEI-01 brings that combination to a new audience while challenging the traditional blueprint, giving customers the freedom to make it their own.

That spirit of going beyond blueprints, combined with Toyota's commitment to "Fun to Drive," makes the KEI-01 a natural first expression of the Scion by Toyota brand.

Bringing the KEI-01 to Customers

As an intentionally low-volume, niche vehicle, the KEI-01 will initially be offered through a fleet-focused pilot program to help the company learn how it can best serve U.S. customers and use cases. Initial fleet sales are planned through Scion by Toyota dealers selected from current Toyota dealers, which will serve as the customer-facing sales channel. Based on market conditions, customer demand, and operational considerations, Toyota may consider expanding availability to limited retail sales at a later date.

Additional information and the broader sales strategy will be shared as plans are finalized.

Three Vehicles. Three Ways to go Beyond.

While the KEI-01 is designed to bring a unique form of utility to U.S. customers, the SxS and BKE concepts demonstrate the broader range of ideas Scion by Toyota is intended to explore.

SxS Concept – Beyond Limits

First shown at the 2025 SEMA Show, the SxS Concept is a purpose-built side-by-side concept that reimagines the all-terrain vehicle for a new generation of outdoor enthusiasts. Developed by the company's North American engineering team, the concept combines a high-output turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid powertrain producing more than 300 horsepower with a compact, purpose-built off-road package.

Designed for everything from spirited desert running to technical rock crawling, the SxS Concept features significant suspension articulation and a nimble footprint. It also features a Silent Mode that allows the vehicle to operate using electric power, offering a different way to experience the outdoors.

Representing Scion by Toyota's willingness to take Toyota technology and engineering into entirely new spaces, the SxS Concept pushes beyond the limits of terrain, performance and what this kind of vehicle can be. The SxS Concept is more than an exercise in imagination. Toyota will continue advancing the concept, exploring its potential, and evaluating how it could bring an entirely new kind of off-road experience to enthusiasts.

BKE Concept – Beyond Permission

The BKE Concept explores another dimension of personal mobility, bringing together compact packaging, utility and adventure in a concept designed to expand the possibilities of how people move through and experience the outdoors.

Where the KEI-01 emphasizes practical utility and the SxS Concept showcases off-road performance, the BKE Concept opens up the space in between—offering freedom to choose your own direction, to take the unexpected turn, and explore beyond permission. Its small, highly adaptable form creates new possibilities for different lifestyles, activities and experiences.

Together, these three distinct vehicles illustrate the breadth of the Scion by Toyota laboratory: from everyday utility, to high-performance adventure, to entirely new forms of personal mobility.

Assembled in America

The KEI-01 will be assembled at Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indiana (Toyota Indiana) starting in the second half of 2027, supported by a $34 million investment that will add approximately 50 new jobs.

Assembly at Toyota Indiana represents the company's continued commitment to investing in the U.S. and American jobs. The investment will establish new vehicle assembly operations and upgrade production and logistics infrastructure, bringing this unique utility vehicle closer to U.S. customers.

Small Footprint. Big Capability.

Despite its compact footprint, the KEI-01 delivers capability, versatility and operator comfort. Key highlights include:

Efficient Powertrain: Powered by a proven 660cc three-cylinder engine mated to a continuously variable transmission, delivering a balance of low-end torque and exceptional fuel efficiency for all-day operation.

Rugged Drivetrain: Standard selectable four-wheel drive (4WD) with auto mode and push-button lock up to help the KEI-01 tackle mud, snow and uneven terrain.

Versatile Cargo Access: An easily accessible three-way fold-down cargo bed allows operators to load and unload materials from a lower height.

Extended Cabin Comfort: An extended-cabin design with a raised roofline allows for reclining and sliding seats, plus secure interior storage behind the seats for tools and gear.

All-Weather Climate Control: An enclosed cabin with heat and air conditioning helps keep operators comfortable throughout the year.

Maneuverable Footprint: Measuring just over 11 feet in length and under 5 feet in width, the KEI-01 offers exceptional agility and maneuverability in tight spaces.

Impressive Payload and Towing: A payload capacity of up to 600 pounds in the bed and structural rigidity for towing small trailers and equipment make it a versatile utility performer.

Built for Work, Play and Everything in Between

The KEI-01 will provide customers with a practical, right-sized solution for buyers who need versatility and durability without the size or expense of a traditional pickup.

The KEI-01 is a right-hand-drive vehicle designed to comply with FMVSS No. 500 requirements for LSVs. Its maximum speed will be 25 miles per hour.

The KEI-01 is designed to meet a wide range of customer needs, including:

Small business owners looking for an affordable urban commercial vehicle.

Farmers and ranchers requiring a dependable daily workhorse.

Municipalities, universities and corporate campuses seeking efficient fleet vehicles.

Delivery and service providers operating in urban environments.

Outdoor enthusiasts and hobbyists wanting a versatile utility vehicle.

Although intentionally small in scale, the KEI-01 delivers impressive cargo capability and excellent maneuverability backed by the company's reputation for quality, durability and reliability.

Beyond Starts Here

Scion by Toyota is more than a return of a familiar name. It is a reinvention of Scion's experimental spirit around curiosity, possibility and freedom for a new era of mobility.

We're wired to wonder. What's next? What's more? What happens if we try another way? Scion by Toyota starts with those questions—challenging what's given, pushing past limits and exploring where mobility can take us.

The brand is a freedom lab—a place where ideas can be tested, challenged and evolved, and where something capable from day one can become uniquely yours.

The KEI-01 puts the Scion by Toyota vision into motion, representing it in tangible form: a small, unconventional vehicle that opens up new possibilities for affordable, capable and personal mobility. The SxS Concept goes beyond limits, demonstrating how Toyota can explore the intersection of performance, hybrid technology and off-road adventure. The BKE Concept goes beyond permission, expanding the exploration into new forms of personal mobility. Together, they demonstrate different modes, different ideas and different directions—showing that there is no single way forward. Scion by Toyota will continue exploring new possibilities in design, capability, versatility and personal expression—giving people more freedom to explore, experiment and make something their own.

There is no final version. Every build is a draft. Every direction is a test. Every idea can become something else. Scion by Toyota is not a finish line—it is an invitation to prototype your freedom.

The KEI-01 is where that exploration begins.

About Toyota

Toyota (NYSE:TM) has been a part of the cultural fabric in the U.S. for nearly 70 years, and is committed to advancing sustainable, next-generation mobility through our Toyota and Lexus brands, plus our nearly 1,500 dealerships.

Toyota directly employs approximately 48,000 people in the U.S. who have contributed to the design, engineering, and assembly of more than 36 million cars and trucks at our 11 manufacturing plants. In 2025, Toyota's plant in North Carolina began to assemble automotive batteries for electrified vehicles.

description:
Democrats will take over state attorney general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas.
Florida, where Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won a new term on Tuesday, would be the remaining plaintiff if Texas withdraws from the case.
Nathan Johnson, the Democrat elected Texas attorney general this week, told Reuters he will assess pending lawsuits that Paxton’s office brought to determine whether or not he will support them.

Several Texas families, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, have asked the justices to invalidate the 2025 state law.
text:
WASHINGTON – Republicans lost state attorney general races to Democrats in key states in the November 3 midterm elections, with potential consequences for lawsuits related to abortion, transgender rights and other issues that the outgoing Republicans championed.

Democrats will take over state attorney general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas.

Here are some of the pending lawsuits that could be affected by the election:

Abortion and transgender rights

Texas is among the states suing the Food and Drug Administration over its approval of the abortion drug mifepristone, arguing that the agency failed to thoroughly evaluate the drug’s safety and effectiveness. Florida, where Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won a new term on Tuesday, would be the remaining plaintiff if Texas withdraws from the case.

The Democratic Attorney General-elect in Kansas, Chris Mann, could withdraw the state from a separate challenge to regulations that expanded access to mifepristone, which would leave Missouri and Idaho as plaintiffs.

Texas has also filed numerous lawsuits against out-of-state providers for remotely prescribing mifepristone to Texas residents, and is involved in a $1.8 billion Medicaid fraud lawsuit against Planned Parenthood. Nathan Johnson, the Democrat elected Texas attorney general this week, told Reuters he will assess pending lawsuits that Paxton’s office brought to determine whether or not he will support them. “Everything will be examined,” Johnson ​said. The Department of Justice has signaled that it will step into the Planned Parenthood case as a plaintiff.

Johnson also could decline to defend the state’s near-total abortion ban in a lawsuit by the family of Tierra Walker, a Texas woman who died from a pregnancy-related condition after doctors refused to perform an abortion.

The state also could back away from at least three pending cases seeking to enforce a 2023 law banning gender-affirming treatments such as puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors.

In Georgia, Democrat Tanya Miller’s election could impact the state’s defense of HB 481, the 2019 law banning abortion after six weeks. Litigation over the ban is ongoing after the Georgia Supreme Court revived the law in 2024.

Pharmaceuticals

Another lawsuit that could draw scrutiny from Johnson, the Texas attorney general-elect, is his state’s case against Kenvue, which alleges the Tylenol maker concealed purported links between acetaminophen use during pregnancy and autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children. Kenvue has denied any wrongdoing.

Doctors and medical groups consider acetaminophen, the active ingredient in Tylenol, as the preferred treatment for pain and fever during pregnancy, and there is no firm scientific evidence of a link between its use and autism or ADHD.

Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, in 2023 in another lawsuit accused drugmaker Pfizer of misrepresenting the efficacy of its widely used COVID-19 vaccine. Pfizer in a prior statement said its representations about its vaccine have been “accurate and science-based,” and that Paxton’s lawsuit had no merit.

Republican Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, who narrowly lost a reelection bid to Mann, also has sued Pfizer over similar claims.

Environment

Texas and 12 other Republican-led states are suing top asset managers including BlackRock, accusing them of violating antitrust law through climate activism that reduced coal production and boosted energy prices.

The lawsuit in federal court is one of the most prominent legal challenges to environmental, social and governance initiatives. Kansas is among the plaintiffs in the lawsuit. BlackRock has denied any wrongdoing. Vanguard Group in February settled claims against it in the lawsuit for $29.5 million.

Immigration

The new attorney general in Texas could also drop the state’s defense of SB4, a Republican-backed Texas law that allows state authorities to arrest and prosecute people suspected of illegally crossing the US-Mexico border. The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in April allowed the law to take effect as a challenge proceeds.

In another matter, the Supreme Court is weighing whether to take up Iowa’s appeal of a ruling blocking a law that would allow state officials to arrest and prosecute people who are in the U.S. illegally. The state’s attorney general-elect, Democrat Nate Willems, could decline to defend the law if the Supreme Court takes the case.

Voting rights and elections

Paxton’s office is appealing a Boston federal judge’s order that stopped the Republican attorney general from continuing to pursue a lawsuit against Democratic ​fundraising platform ActBlue over its donation practices.

In June, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns granted ActBlue’s request for a preliminary injunction after the platform argued that Paxton’s lawsuit violated its free speech rights.

In Georgia, a federal judge is weighing a fight over the state’s congressional maps, which challengers said harmed Black voters. A federal appeals court in August vacated a 2023 ruling by the lower court that said the state’s Republican-backed plan illegally diluted Black votes in violation of the Voting Rights Act.

In a ruling on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Jones in Atlanta paused further action in the litigation, citing “impending changes” in the leadership of the state attorney general’s office.

Religious liberties

At the Supreme Court, the new Texas attorney general could revisit the state’s defense of a Texas law mandating the ​display of the Ten Commandments in public schools. Several Texas families, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, have asked the justices to invalidate the 2025 state law.

A ​divided appeals court in April ruled that Texas can require public schools to ‌display the Ten Commandments in every classroom. The Supreme Court has not decided whether to take up the case.

(Reporting for Reuters by Mike Scarcella and Daniel Wiessner, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Jonathan Spicer and Andrea Ricci).

American farmers are facing yet another year of financial challenges, and undermining RFS volumes now would make an already difficult economic situation even worse.

text:
However, final passage now hinges on a small group of Democrats seeking tribal protections and assurances that President Donald Trump will not block wind and solar projects.

Trump cast doubt on those assurances hours before the vote. At a White House briefing, he said he supported the bill, then rejected a question about approving wind turbines.

“No, I will not approve wind turbines,” Trump said. He had called the bill “a great bill” and said, “We are behind it 100 percent.”

The vote on a procedural measure advances the legislation to an amendment process; it does not make the bill law.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., said supporters expected a “very healthy amendment process.”

The bill would make it harder to challenge projects in court on environmental grounds and limit the ability of states and the Environmental Protection Agency to block them before construction. Its supporters also point to provisions intended to make it easier to build power lines and add electricity — including renewable power — to the grid.

Whitehouse argued before the vote that the bill would benefit consumers and cut emissions.

He said it could save consumers $60 to $80 a month and prevent 1.5 billion to 1.8 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions.

Whitehouse also said the measure would increase U.S. wind capacity by 25%, solar capacity by 28% and battery-storage capacity by 70%, though he did not mention the source of his numbers.

“This is a climate and clean energy bill,” Whitehouse said, adding that its effect on the power sector could exceed that of the Inflation Reduction Act, which he said had been weakened by Republicans.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., opposed advancing the bill.

He argued that its renewable-energy provisions would not offset measures he said could encourage more fossil-fuel use, including gas-fired power for data centers and expanded natural-gas pipelines and liquefied natural gas exports.

He said climate estimates that exclude gas burned overseas leave out emissions that still affect the global climate.

The bill’s project-certainty provisions are intended to prevent administrations from revoking existing permits and allow developers to sue over what the legislation calls “disparate treatment” of energy sources.

That could protect renewable projects from one administration and fossil-fuel projects from another.

The legislation also includes a provision requiring data centers to pay at least their fair share for the electricity and infrastructure they use, supporters say. The bill has support from industry groups in fossil fuels, renewable energy, chemicals, construction and manufacturing.

If the Senate passes the bill, it would move to the House, where it has support from Republicans and some Democrats but is expected to face opposition from progressive lawmakers. The schedule for amendments and a final Senate vote was not provided.

Whitehouse said the bill would be “the floor, not the ceiling” of Democrats’ climate and environmental ambitions.
